visits.text: A Coruña—its Galician name. A city of 245,000 inhabitants facing the Atlantic, with a more open and modern character than other Galician cities. Its nickname: the “city of glass”, for the glazed galleries on the façades along Avenida da Mariña—typical of the 19th century, designed to capture every ray of sunlight and provide shelter from sea winds. It's Galicia's most emblematic urban waterfront: follow the Mariña from the port to the Méndez Núñez gardens, a walk of about 1 km.

The Tower of Hercules, 2.5 km north of the center. UNESCO-listed in 2009—it's the only Roman lighthouse still in operation since antiquity. Built in the late 1st century CE, with 34 meters of Roman construction plus 21 meters from the neoclassical restoration of 1791 by Eustaquio Giannini, totaling 55 meters. The farum Brigantium guided ships on the Atlantic sea route linking the Mediterranean to northern Europe. Celtic legend has it that Hercules buried the giant Geryon's head there. 234 steps to the summit, a 360° view over the Atlantic, with the Cíes Islands to the south on clear days.

The sculpture park around the Tower of Hercules houses some emblematic works: Manolo Paz's Menhirs for Peace, Daniel Buren's Marine Snail, and especially the colossal statue of Breogán—a mythological Celtic hero who is said to have founded Brigantia (ancient A Coruña). The Monte dos Bicos petroglyphs, carved in the Iron Age, are a reminder that the site was sacred long before the Romans. Beside it, the 19th-century Muslim cemetery—surprising in A Coruña—where North African sailors who died in shipwrecks are buried. Moving.

Praza de María Pita, the heart of the modern city, is named after the local heroine who is said to have saved the city from Francis Drake's English attack in May 1589. According to the chronicle, after her husband died defending the city, María Pita seized a lance, killed the English standard-bearer and drove the attackers away, shouting “Quien tenga honra, que me siga”. 160 by 100 meters, surrounded by arcades, with city hall (1909) at the center. On the sunny terraces, Coruñans have their coffee as soon as the sun appears—a rare commodity in a Galician winter.

The Castelo de San Antón, at the entrance to the port, occupies a rocky islet connected by a footbridge. A fortress built in the 16th century to defend A Coruña from English attacks—Drake's in 1589, precisely, which inspired the heroine María Pita. Now the provincial archaeological museum: Iron Age petroglyphs, the Celtic torc of Burela in solid gold, Roman funerary stelae. A small museum, never crowded, with a magnificent view over the bay from the ramparts.

The Cidade Vella, the old town on the peninsula north of the port, preserves A Coruña's historic soul. Plaza de Santa Bárbara, with its convent founded in 1613, is one of the city's quietest corners—cobblestones, an enclosed monastery, cats in the sun. Beside it, the Church of Santiago, a 12th-century Romanesque building, the city's oldest. The 13th-century Gothic Colegiata de Santa María del Campo is worth visiting for its carved tympanum. A pedestrian district, perfect for strolling.

The Domus—Casa do Home—is one of A Coruña's three science museums, dedicated to human beings: genetics, anatomy, perception, the brain. A building on the cliff designed by Arata Isozaki in 1995, with a curved slate façade that follows the contours of the coast. Beside it, the house museum of Emilia Pardo Bazán, a pioneer of the Spanish naturalist novel (1851–1921), a feminist figure ahead of her time. A rare combination: contemporary science and 19th-century literature, 200 meters apart.

To breathe the sea air, head up to Monte de San Pedro at the western end of the Paseo Marítimo. A former military fort converted into a park with panoramic views, accessible by a glass elevator (€1.50 round trip) that climbs the cliff face. At the summit, two Vickers guns from 1929, a 360° view over the Atlantic and the Tower of Hercules to the east. A memorable sunset. A restaurant with panoramic views for lunch on site. Bus 14 or a car to the foot of the elevator.

activities.text: A walk along the Paseo Marítimo—13 kilometers of seafront, one of the longest in Europe. Coruñans come here for all their sports: running, cycling, roller skating and walking. Urban beaches: Riazor (sporty, with surfing in winter) and Orzán (wilder). Sunset from Monte de San Pedro (at the western end, with a panoramic view and a panoramic glass elevator) is a highlight.

Dinner in the Pescadería district or around Praza de María Pita—A Coruña's cuisine is entirely centered on fish and seafood. Reliable places: Mesón do Pulpo, Pablo Gallego, Casa Pardo, As Salinas (Bib Gourmand-starred). Specialties: centollo (spider crab), percebes (gooseneck barnacles, controversial but with a cult following), nécoras (velvet swimming crabs), pulpo a feira, lubina (sea bass). Bottles of Albariño or Godello to accompany the meal. Allow €50 per person for a full dinner of good quality.

A half-day excursion to the wild beaches northwest of A Coruña—toward Caión, Sabón, Razo. Immense beaches, turquoise waters, but strong currents and no lifeguards. Caión is also an unspoiled fishing village: a morning fish auction, restaurants serving very fresh fish. For surf enthusiasts, Razo is one of Galicia's surfing spots. 30–40 minutes from A Coruña.

If you prefer to stay in the city: a walk through the Os Mallos district, followed by dinner and a show at Centro Ágora or Caracolas, two concert venues featuring Galician folk music (bagpipes, tambourine, muiñeira). Galician traditional music survives as a living genre rather than folklore staged for tourists. Check the program the day before—concerts are mainly on Friday and Saturday evenings.

places.name: Aguilas

visits.text: An 18th-century castle built against pirates - and it's surprising that Águilas still feels like a real fishing town, not a beach resort. The castillo de San Juan overlooks the bay from a volcanic cliff. Inside: short exhibition on the harbor's history. From the battlements, view over the municipality's 35 beaches and calas.

Golden sand, volcanic formations, turquoise water - Calarreona and La Carolina are two of the protected beaches in the Cuatro Calas sector. La Carolina measures 500 meters, is Blue Flag certified, and remains less known than its Murcia neighbors. Access from the RM-D14, track the last few kilometers.

Cabo Cope, 10 km north of Águilas, is a rocky headland with a medieval watchtower and waters popular for diving. The Cabo Cope-Puntas de Calnegre regional park protects this stretch of coast. Access via the RM-332 towards Lorca; the turn-off is signposted. No facilities on site.

activities.text: Águilas eats well: fresh fish, no folklore. The marina lines up restaurants with no tourist menu. Caldero de pescado (fish rice) and grilled dorada are the standards. Dine early - kitchens close around 10pm, unlike the big Andalusian cities.

The seabed in the Cuatro Calas area is home to intact marine wildlife, dense Posidonia meadows and a few moray eels beneath the lava rocks. Snorkelling from Calarreona or La Carolina, with no special equipment required. Masks can be rented at Águilas harbour. Avoid weekends in July and August.

visits.text: Cliffs tower above Aigües Blanques, but the access road and car park are currently closed because of the risk of falling rocks. Obey the signs and do not enter prohibited areas.

activities.text: Do not ride down towards Aigües Blanques by scooter: the access road and car park are closed because of the risk of falling rocks. Respect the closure and avoid the mud baths until access has reopened.

days_plan.itin_title: Ibiza & Formentera by Scooter: Calas & Beaches in 7 Days

places.name: Alba De Tormes

visits.text: Alba de Tormes is inseparable from Saint Teresa of Ávila. She died here on October 4, 1582, exhausted from a final journey from Burgos, in the Carmelite convent she had founded in 1571. Her body—declared incorruptible at the three tomb openings in 1750, 1914, and 2024—rests in the Church of the Annunciation, in a carved marble urn above the main altar. You can see two reliquaries displaying her heart and left arm. John Paul II came on pilgrimage here November 1, 1982, for the fourth centenary of the saint's death.

The Theresian Basilica, built in 1896 on orders of the Bishop of Salamanca to accommodate the influx of pilgrims, is Alba de Tormes's most visible religious building from the road. Its tower measures 34.6 meters. It's the heart of Marian pilgrimage in Castile and León. The combined visit with the Carmelite Museum (CARMUS)—installed in the convent's renovated cloister—offers the most complete historical and spiritual context on Teresa and John of the Cross.

The Castle of Alba, whose watchtower has guarded the town since the 12th century, symbolizes the Duchy of Alba de Tormes—one of Spain's great noble houses. In 1472, García Álvarez de Toledo obtained the title of Duke of Alba and made Alba a major cultural center of the Golden Age, attracting poets and thinkers. The El Espolón park laid out around the old fortress offers fine views over the Tormes.

San Juan Church, built in the 12th and 13th centuries, is listed as a National Monument. Its Romanesque-Mudéjar style and combination of brick and stone make it an interesting monument. It retains the three apses of its original east end.

activities.text: Walk along the banks of the Tormes below the castle—this is where Teresa loved to pray, drawn by the view of the river from her convent. The medieval bridge and old ruined mills on the Tormes compose a calm, photogenic landscape.

At the table, look for rosquillas de Ledesma—sweet doughnuts—and bollo maimón, a soft egg cake found in bakeries throughout Salamanca province. Alba restaurants also serve cabrito (kid goat) and roast lamb.

visits.text: Provincial capital without appeal? False. The Pasaje de Lodares, shopping arcade built between 1925 and 1929 by Valencian architect Buenaventura Ferrando, unfolds 90 metres of columns, ironwork, and allegorical sculptures under a skylight that floods everything with white light. Free entry, open access from the street. In the morning, before the shops open, the atmosphere is strange and photogenic.

The Museo Municipal de la Cuchillería is really worth the hour it asks: it traces the tradition of Albacete's cutlers since the Bronze Age, with a reconstruction of an artisan workshop and remarkable pieces from European collections. Europe has only three museums dedicated to cutlery—this is among the best designed. Entry €3 (free Wednesday). Closed Monday.

Join Plaza del Altozano to admire the Baroque façade of the Catedral de San Juan Bautista (construction began in the 16th century, façade unfinished) and the modernist sculptures of the square—the Gran Dama Oferente and the Bicha de Balazote (reproduction). The plaza is the living heart of Albacete; café and tapas on the terrace to breathe.

days_plan.itin_title: Castilla-La Mancha: Windmills and Sierra in 11 days

visits.text: Albarracín comes into view around a bend of the Guadalaviar, clinging to a rose sandstone cliff at 1,100 meters. Declared a National Monument in 1961, this village of 1,000 inhabitants is considered one of Spain's most beautiful. Its houses, with their reddish rodeno sandstone facades and wooden balconies, create a medieval storybook atmosphere.

Albarracín's ramparts enclose an area far larger than the village itself. Three building phases can be read in the stone: the 10th-century bastion and Torre del Andador, the 11th-century walls of the Berber taifa of the Banu Razin, then the Christian fortifications built after the Reconquest. From the top of the Torre del Andador, the view takes in the whole valley.

The Cathedral of El Salvador, built in the 16th century on a medieval base, surprises with the austerity of its facade and the richness of its interior. The adjoining Diocesan Museum displays Flemish tapestries, a 14th-century processional cross, and a 16th-century rock crystal fish.

Get lost in the sloping alleys climbing toward the castle. The Casa de la Julianeta, crooked and lopsided near the Portal de Molina, has become the village's photographic symbol. The absence of vertical lines in its structure gives it an unreal air, as if lifted from an illustrated storybook.

The Plaza Mayor, ringed by arcaded galleries, is dominated by the 16th-century Town Hall and its fine wooden balconies. From the upper floor, the view looks straight down on the Guadalaviar meander that wraps around the village like a natural moat.

activities.text: Follow the riverside path along the Guadalaviar to admire the ramparts from the valley. The contrast between the red sandstone of the walls, the green of the pines, and the blue of the river makes one of Aragon's most photogenic landscapes.

A few kilometers from the village, the red rocks of Pinar del Rodeno shelter UNESCO-listed rock paintings dating from 6,000 to 1,000 BC. These white figures of animals and archers stand out against reddish rock and are unique throughout the Levantine rock art region.
The Sierra de Albarracín offers exceptional night skies for astrotourism. Far from any light pollution, starry nights reveal the Milky Way to the naked eye.

days_plan.itin_title: Aragon Tour: Zaragoza and Mudéjar Villages

visits.text: Alcossebre stretches along 10 kilometers of unspoiled coastline. Its beaches—Las Fuentes, Cargador, Tres Playas—and watchtowers dot the Blue Flag-certified shore.
The Sierra d'Irta plunges into the Mediterranean for 12 kilometers. The last undeveloped coastal range in the region, it shelters cliffs, wild coves, and undisturbed wildlife.
The castle of Xivert dominates the sierra at 500 meters. An 11th–12th-century Templar fortress of Muslim origin, recently restored, it still stands watch over the Alcalà plain.
The Torre Ebrí rises 8.5 meters on a clifftop. Built in the 16th century, this watchtower alerted the castle of Xivert in the event of a pirate attack.

The Church of San Juan Bautista boasts the tallest octagonal bell tower in the Valencia Region (58 meters). Its classical baroque interior preserves a painting by Traver Calzada depicting the martyrdom of Saint John.
The Hermitage of Santa Lucía y San Benito crowns Monte San Benito. This lookout offers one of the finest panoramas in Castellón province, sweeping across the coast and hinterland.
Cala Mundina and Cala Ribamar are tucked inside the Sierra d'Irta Natural Park. These wild coves ringed by Mediterranean vegetation invite contemplation.

activities.text: Coastal bike paths wind between sea and sierra. The gentle route lets you discover viewpoints and coves at your own pace.
Rent a kayak to explore the sheltered coves. The clear water reveals the rocky seabed and the marine life of the reserve.
The port of Alcossebre serves fish and seafood straight from the day's catch. Marina restaurants offer grilled sea bream, zarzuela, and black rice with cuttlefish.
Hiking trails cross the Sierra d'Irta. The waymarked network offers several levels of difficulty.

days_plan.itin_title: Castellón and Maestrazgo Route: Castles and Coves

visits.text: Begin your journey 30 km from Madrid. Alcalá de Henares, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998, was the world's first purpose-built university town. Cardinal Cisneros founded the university in 1499 with the ambition of creating the City of God (Civitas Dei)—a blueprint later exported to the Americas. Head to the Colegio Mayor de San Ildefonso, the founding building: its Plateresque façade, completed in 1553 by Rodrigo Gil de Hontañón, ranks among Spain's finest. Inside, the Paraninfo (ceremonial hall) hosts the annual Cervantes Prize ceremony every 23 April—the Nobel of Hispanic letters, presented by the King of Spain.

Walk down Calle Mayor, one of Europe's longest arcaded streets, to the Casa Natal de Cervantes. Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra was born here in 1547—his baptismal certificate (9 October 1547) is preserved in the town hall. The house, reconstructed as a 16th-century bourgeois residence, is now a free museum: period furniture, the father's medical office (he was a barber-surgeon), and early editions of Don Quixote. Right next door, don't miss the Corral de Comedias (1601), Spain's oldest documented theatre, restored and still in use.

The Catedral Magistral de los Santos Niños Justo y Pastor is the only cathedral apart from Leuven's to bear the title Magistral – meaning all its canons had to hold doctorates in theology from the university. Built in the 15th–16th centuries in Isabelline Gothic style, it houses Cardinal Cisneros' tomb. Climb the bell tower for views over the town's rooftops and the storks nesting on the bell towers – Alcalá has one of Spain's largest white stork populations.

activities.text: Spend the end of the day wandering around Plaza de Cervantes (the old Plaza Mayor), the heart of the town, lined with cafés and terraces. The central bandstand and colourful façades create a very pleasant atmosphere. The university quarter around the Colegio Mayor is lively thanks to the 25,000 students who attend the university. Sample the costrada (puff pastry cake filled with cream) and rosquillas (anise doughnuts), Alcalá's two typical sweet treats.

days_plan.itin_title: Alcarria and Guadalajara: Between Madrid and Aragon

visits.text: White houses suspended above the canyon: Castillo de Alcalá del Júcar crowns a rocky spur surrounded by a meander of the río Júcar whose vertical walls reach 150 metres. A Historic-Artistic Ensemble, castle entry costs €2.50 and includes a visit to a traditional cave-house carved into the rock. From the ramparts, you simultaneously see both sides of the canyon.

Alcalá del Júcar's natural caves are its real surprise: part of the village isn't built on the rock but in it. The Cueva del Diablo, carved into the cliff, is a visitable troglodyte house (paid entry). The extent of the natural underground network fitted out as dwellings over the centuries—Moorish, then Christian—has no equivalent in the province.

Cross the Puente Romano to reach the mirador on the opposite bank—that's where the classic silhouette of the village on the rock is photographed. The 'Roman bridge' is actually medieval, but the name stuck. The right bank also offers the Ermita de San Lorenzo (16th century) 3 km away on the CM-3201 road.

activities.text: The hoz del Júcar deserves to be walked: despite its name of 'gorge', the riverside senda at the canyon bottom remains easy and highly photogenic (shade, running water, cliffs). Start from the bridge, about 4 km round trip to the abandoned balnearios. Closed shoes recommended; the trail can be slippery after rain.

days_plan.itin_title: Castilla-La Mancha: Windmills and Sierra in 11 days

visits.text: Alcaraz's Plaza Mayor, built between 1518 and 1578, has been a Cultural Heritage Site since 1945: a rectangle of Renaissance loggias in golden stone, with arcades that nothing masks. Architect Andrés de Vandelvira left his mark here before building Jaén Cathedral—this is where he learned. Free and open visit at all hours.

Between the two towers facing each other—the Torre del Tardón (the clock) and the Torre de la Trinidad (the church)—there's an almost theatrical tension: they've been staring at each other for 500 years without touching. The Torre del Tardón has an irregular prismatic plan, like its neighbour, which makes the whole even more singular. A bench by the plaza fountain to appreciate them is the best seat in Castile.

Push open the door of the Iglesia de la Santísima Trinidad, a Gothic jewel of Albacete province with 16th-century Renaissance additions. Inside: a statue by Salzillo, two paintings by the Master of Albacete, and a Gothic star vault above the apse. Check opening hours at the neighbouring tourist office (same building as the Lonja).

activities.text: Spectacular after rain and ordinary in a dry summer, the Nacimiento del Río Mundo emerges from a karst gallery in the Calar del Mundo and cascades through a rocky breach. The reventón phenomenon—a sudden surge after heavy rain—can project the water several metres. A 2 km trail runs from the Riópar car park to the foot of the waterfall. Very busy at weekends. Plan a day trip from Alcaraz.

days_plan.itin_title: Murcia Coast and Hinterland: 13 days from La Manga to Cuenca
Castilla-La Mancha: Windmills and Sierra in 11 days

visits.text: Alcoy presents itself as an industrial city—and it doesn't lie. Nicknamed 'the city of bridges,' its complex terrain has spawned an architecture of viaducts and unusual footbridges. What few guides mention: a Llotja by Santiago Calatrava in the center, spare and geometric. The covered market merits a pause before climbing toward the Serra.

activities.text: The park air smells of thyme, rosemary, and warm clay. The Serra de Mariola, designated a natural park in 2002, covers 17,000 hectares between Alcoy and Banyeres. It harbors the southernmost yew forest in Europe and over 1,200 different plant species. The summit of Montcabrer (1,390 m) offers views all the way to the sea. Visitor center on the Alcoy-Banyeres road, km 18.

days_plan.itin_title: Costa Blanca & Alicante Hinterland: 12 days

visits.text: Alcúdia's ramparts date to the 14th century. Stretching 1.5 kilometers with 26 towers, they once guarded the town from pirates. Access begins at Porta de Vila Roja.
Porta de Xara—a monumental gateway—opens onto the old town. Its golden stones and semicircular arch exemplify Majorcan medieval architecture.
The Roman site of Pollentia was founded in 123 BC. Remains include a theater, forum, and patrician houses from the ancient Balearic Roman capital.
The Monographic Museum displays artifacts unearthed at Pollentia. Pottery, jewelry, coins, and sculptures trace 2,000 years of history.
Sant Jaume Church rises at the heart of the old town. Its Baroque interior contrasts with the medieval cobbled lanes surrounding it.
Alcúdia Beach stretches for 3.5 kilometers. Its fine sand, shallow waters, and Blue Flag status make it one of Majorca's most family-friendly.
Port d'Alcúdia is the modern resort area. Its seafront promenade, restaurants, and marina bring the waterfront to life.

activities.text: The bike path follows the north coast for 15 kilometers. It passes through beaches, pine forests, and the wetlands of S'Albufera Natural Park.
Kayaks set out toward Cap de Formentor. The rocky peninsula reveals wild coves and plunging cliffs.
Alcúdia Market is held on Tuesday and Sunday mornings. Fruit, vegetables, crafts, and local products are laid out in front of the ramparts.
S'Albufera Natural Park shelters over 200 bird species. Flamingos, herons, and ducks populate the marshes and reedbeds.

days_plan.itin_title: Majorca Road Trip: Serra de Tramuntana and Coves

places.name: Aldea Del Rey

visits.text: The Castillo de Calatrava la Nueva crowns the Cerro Alacranejo at an altitude of 936 m. The seat of the Order of Calatrava from 1217 to 1804, it is a fortified castle and convent that controlled the main passage between the Meseta and the Guadalquivir valley.

The Order of Calatrava, founded in the 12th century by Abbot Raimundo de Fitero, was the Iberian Peninsula's first military order. The stone-paved path climbing to the castle dates from Philip II's visit in 1560. Opposite, the Castillo de Salvatierra forms a spectacular defensive pair with it.

From the castle ramparts, views stretch across the Sierra Morena dehesas and the volcanic Campo de Calatrava. In the 16th century, the fortress was protected by a star-shaped bastioned enclosure to withstand new artillery. On clear days, you can make out the Castillo de Salvatierra on the far side of the pass.

activities.text: In October, the Jornadas Medievales recreate the castle's atmosphere with a market, combat, and food. The rest of the year, the site is tranquil and the walk up from the parking area takes about fifteen minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: Campo de Calatrava and Valle de Alcudia in 5 Days

map_keywords: Castillo de Calatrava la Nueva Aldea del Rey

visits.text: In 1086, García Jiménez held this rocky stronghold for six years against the Almoravids, harassing territories as far as Granada and Alicante from a handful of towers. The village perched at 800 m dominates the Totana plain with undiminished insolence. The Torre del Homenaje (13th-14th century, 19 m high) houses the tourist office—admission €1.50 on weekdays. From the terrace, you see Sierra Espuña behind and the coast on clear days.

days_plan.itin_title: Murcia Coast and Hinterland: 13 days from La Manga to Cuenca

visits.text: Twelve caves carved into the cliff at Alfafara, in the barranco del Pont Trencat. These artificial cavities from the Andalusian period look from below like windows cut into the rock—hence their name. Access via a wooden ladder, with several interconnected chambers inside. They likely served as granaries. Free entry, 30-45 min visit. Signage sometimes absent: take the track from the ermita de San Antonio.

days_plan.itin_title: Costa Blanca & Alicante Hinterland: 12 days

visits.text: In Alfaro, the bell towers of the 16th-century fortified church of San Miguel house the largest urban stork colony in Europe—more than 150 recorded nests, several hundred birds in spring. It's both absurd and fascinating: storks have been nesting 30 meters up on the Baroque gargoyles for centuries, and nobody disturbs them. Look up, it's noisy and spectacular.

Bodegas Palacios Remondo—family estate of Álvaro Palacios, the winemaker who revolutionized Priorat in the 1990s with L'Ermita. For several years now, he's been returning to the lands of Rioja Oriental to prove that Garnacha from this scorned area can be great. The Propiedad cuvée, from Garnacha vines aged 80 to 100 years, is the most convincing argument. Visits by appointment only, around €30.

activities.text: Lunch at Restaurante La Capellanía in Alfaro: market-driven cuisine, vegetables from the local market gardens. The piquillo peppers stuffed with cod are the house specialty—the piquillo peppers here have their own PGI, and are sweet and fleshy, bearing no resemblance to the industrial versions found in jars.

Drive through Rioja Oriental before reaching Alfaro: the landscape changes radically. Drier, hotter, almost desert-like in places, with red, iron-rich clay soils. Stop at a roadside vineyard to observe the old Garnacha vines—twisted, low-growing vines, sometimes 80 to 100 years old. Nobody trains them on trellises here; they are goblet-trained.

days_plan.itin_title: La Rioja in 7 Days - The Kingdom of Tempranillo

visits.text: Alhama de Granada—'al-hammam,' the bath—is one of the strongholds that fell before Granada during the Reconquest war. On February 28, 1482, the Catholic Monarchs seized it by night assault. The fall was so striking that a Castilian romance, '¡Ay de mi Alhama!,' was composed immediately after and sung for centuries as the announcement of the Nasrid kingdom's end. The village of 6,000 residents today clings to the edge of a vertiginous 50 m canyon, the Tajo de Alhama. Intact old quarter, white sloping alleys, houses with flowered balconies. Half a day suffices.

The Casa de la Inquisición, on the main square, is an early 16th-century Gothic-Renaissance palace that never served as a Holy Office tribunal—the local name is misleading. But the golden stone facade with its coats of arms and Gothic windows is one of western Andalusia's finest. Today private property, exterior visit only, free and open. The supposed presence of the Inquisition in Alhama more likely relates to the persecution of Moriscos after 1568 in the neighboring Alpujarras.
A viewpoint on the neighboring square offers a plunging view over the canyon - one of the village's signature photographs.

The Mazmorras of Alhama, underground dungeons carved in the Almohad period into two jar-shaped silos (12th century), served as a medieval prison, then as a grain store, then as a shelter during the Civil War, and today as a cultural space.

activities.text: Bath at the Alhama Thermal Baths, 2 km from the village. Natural springs at 47°C known since Roman times (1st-century BC bridge right next door), developed into free outdoor pools by the town hall. Open 365 days a year. Bring swimsuit, towel, non-slip sandals. Go early in the morning (before 9 AM) or on weekdays to avoid weekend crowds. Ideal in winter, the water steams in contact with the cold air.

days_plan.itin_title: Dark Andalusia: 10 Days from Seville to Málaga

visits.text: Reforested from 1889 after an almost total ecological disaster, Sierra Espuña is a lesson in forest resilience. Engineer Ricardo Codorníu planted thousands of Aleppo pines on bare slopes. The result is a 17,804 ha park rising to 1,585 m at Morrón de Totana. Declared a regional park in 1992 and listed as Natura 2000. The Ricardo Codorníu visitor centre, reached by a mountain road from Alhama de Murcia, is a good starting point - it explains the full history of the reforestation.

activities.text: Local people still call them the fridges, and for good reason: the Pozos de Nieve, 25 circular structures dug into the ground at an altitude of around 1,400 m, stored snow from the 16th century onwards to supply the villages in summer. The Pozos de Nieve are reached on foot from the Collado Mangueta car park along a short trail. Allow for a day return trip from Alhama de Murcia. Views of the coast in clear weather.

days_plan.itin_title: Murcia Coast and Hinterland: 13 days from La Manga to Cuenca

visits.text: Santa Bárbara Castle stands at 166 meters on Mount Benacantil—visible from everywhere in the city. Its origins date to the 9th century; it was reconquered by the Castilians in 1248 (on Saint Barbara's feast day, hence the name). It was converted into a prison during the civil war. Free access via the elevator carved through the rock from Postiguet beach (€2.70 for the elevator) or on foot from Santa Cruz.

The Explanada mosaic crunches underfoot with thousands of tri-colored tiles. This 500-meter seafront promenade runs along Alicante's port with its palms and terraces. A stone's throw away, the Basilica of Santa María—built in the 15th century on the former main mosque—conceals an interesting Baroque altarpiece. Entry is free.

A lively regional capital, yet its beaches are underestimated by those who merely pass through. San Juan Beach, 6 km from the centre, is the longest. The MARQ - Provincial Archaeological Museum - brings together collections from prehistory to the Islamic period with noteworthy modern displays. Allow 2h for a complete visit.

activities.text: Lose yourself in Santa Cruz, the old quarter that climbs the slopes of the castle. Cobbled lanes, geraniums on balconies, hidden little squares: here the city still breathes. In the evening, the terraces on Calle Labradores and around the central market come alive with locals. Arroz a banda or calamar a la romana are the must-try dishes.

If you have an appetite for markets, the Mercado Central (Monday-Saturday, mornings) brings together fresh fish and produce from the Vega Baixa. TRAM line L4 connects Luceros with the Playa de San Juan area - handy for ending the day at the beach without a car.

days_plan.itin_title: Costa Blanca & Alicante Hinterland: 12 days
Costa Blanca & Alicante Hinterland: 12 days

visits.text: The Parque Minero de Almadén takes visitors 50 meters underground in a mine cage, into the heart of 16th-century galleries. These mercury mines, worked from Roman antiquity until 2003, have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2012. The guided tour lasts between 2.5 and 4 hours.

The Real Hospital de Mineros de San Rafael, an 18th-century building, cared for miners suffering from mercurialism, or mercury poisoning. Prisoners sentenced to forced labor were also treated here. Three museum rooms trace Almadén's medical, metallurgical, and social history.
Almadén's hexagonal bullring, built from 1752 as miners' housing, is one of Spain's oldest. National Monument since 1979. It now houses the tourist office and a hotel.

activities.text: The Museo del Mercurio offers interactive experiments on mercury's physics and chemistry. Models show how cinnabar was shipped by galleon to America to extract silver. Advance booking required, adult admission around €17.

days_plan.itin_title: Campo de Calatrava and Valle de Alcudia in 5 Days

visits.text: Two hours' drive south from Madrid and you enter the heart of La Mancha—Don Quixote's plains. Almagro, declared a Historic-Artistic Ensemble, is a complete surprise in this landscape of windmills and fields. The Plaza Mayor is its jewel: a rectangular square bordered by two stone-arcaded galleries with 81 columns, and characteristic green-painted glazed balconies—a legacy of the German Fugger bankers (los Fúcares in Spanish) who settled here in the 16th century to manage the Almadén mercury mines on behalf of Charles V.

The Corral de Comedias is the reason for your visit to Almagro. Built in 1628 by Leonardo de Oviedo in the former Mesón del Toro, it's the only Spanish Golden Age theatre preserved intact and still active in the world. Its 300 m² rectangular courtyard, its two-storey wooden galleries, its cazuela (balcony reserved for women), and its tablado (stage) transport you directly to the era of Lope de Vega, Calderón de la Barca, and Tirso de Molina. Closed in the 18th century by royal decree, it was rediscovered by chance in 1954 beneath the partitions of a boarding house. Every summer, the International Festival of Classical Theatre revives Golden Age plays there.

The Museo Nacional del Teatro, housed in the 13th-century Maestral Palace of the Knights of Calatrava, is Spain's only national museum devoted to theatre. It traces the history of performing arts from the Middle Ages: set models, period costumes, manuscripts, puppets, and posters. An entire section is dedicated to the corrales de comedias and theatrical life during the Golden Age.

The Almacén de los Fúcares - the Fugger warehouse - is an imposing 16th-century building that served as a granary and mercury store for the Augsburg bankers. These financiers were so powerful that they lent money to Charles V in exchange for the monopoly on Almadén mercury. The building, sometimes called a palace because of the care taken in its construction, now hosts exhibitions. Right next door, the church of San Agustín, listed as a Site of Cultural Interest, is worth a look.

activities.text: The gastronomy of Almagro and the Campo de Calatrava belongs to the heart of La Mancha. Try the berenjenas de Almagro—small round aubergines pickled in vinegar with cumin and chilli, a local speciality with its own protected designation. Add to that migas manchegas (fried breadcrumbs with chorizo), pisto manchego (a local ratatouille), and a glass of Valdepeñas wine from the neighbouring appellation.

days_plan.itin_title: Madrid to Cazorla: La Mancha, the Sierras of Jaén, and the Forgotten Renaissance
La Mancha Road Trip: Don Quixote's Windmills and Cuenca
Castilla-La Mancha Route: In the Footsteps of Don Quixote

visits.text: On 25 April 1707, the plain of Almansa changed the course of the War of the Spanish Succession: Philip V’s victory over the troops of Archduke Charles shaped the monarchy that would govern Spain to the present day. The Castillo de Almansa, standing on the Cerro del Águila with a spiral staircase carved into the rock, overlooks this battlefield.

If you visit late April, the International Historical Re-enactment of the Battle of Almansa mobilises hundreds of participants and thousands of spectators—one of the region's most important historical re-enactments. For other months, the Museo de la Batalla (in the Ermita de San Blas) tells the tactics, uniforms, and political consequences of 1707 with models and audiovisuals. Free entry.

days_plan.itin_title: Castilla-La Mancha: Windmills and Sierra in 11 days

visits.text: The Alcazaba of Almería towers over the city from its hilltop perch. Built in 955 by Caliph Abd al-Rahman III, this citadel—Spain's largest after the Alhambra—unfolds across three walled enclosures: the gardens of the first, the five-nave caliphal cistern of the second, and the Christian castle erected by the Catholic Monarchs in 1489.

Step inside the Cathedral of the Incarnation, a unique fortress church built after the 1522 earthquake. Its thick walls, battlements, and arrow slits bear witness to attacks by Barbary pirates. Inside, the neoclassical cloister and ambulatory chapels are worth a visit.

The Civil War Shelters burrow 9 meters beneath Paseo de Almería. These 4.5-kilometer underground galleries, designed by architect Guillermo Langle Rubio in 1937, could shelter 40,000 residents. The reconstructed operating room is particularly striking.

The Cable Inglés, an ore-loading pier built in 1904 in the style of Eiffel, juts into the sea from Las Almadrabillas beach. Declared a Cultural Heritage Site in 1998, it offers a beautiful view of the port at sunset.

Make your way to Plaza Vieja, the city's administrative heart. The 19th-century neoclassical town hall borders this shaded square. The Monument to the Martyrs of Liberty at its center commemorates victims of absolutist repression in 1824.

Paseo de Almería connects Puerta de Purchena to the port. This shopping avenue, lined with century-old ficus trees, cuts through downtown and passes above the underground shelters. Café terraces come alive as evening falls.

activities.text: Walk along the waterfront promenade of Parque Nicolás Salmerón to the marina. Palm trees line the promenade, with the illuminated Alcazaba in the background.
Head to Mercado Central for a tapas crawl. Almería upholds the tradition of free tapas served with every drink—the bars around the market compete in generosity.
A swim at the end of the day at El Zapillo beach, Almería's urban beach, with views of the Cable Inglés and the Sierra de Gádor mountains.

days_plan.itin_title: Almería Road Trip: Volcanic Coves and Tabernas Desert
Wild Coast: Málaga to Cartagena in 9 Days
White Villages & Sierras: 9 Days Málaga-Almería

visits.text: Twenty minutes west of Córdoba, the castle of Almodóvar del Río appears from afar, perched on a 252-meter hill above the Guadalquivir. This fortress of Umayyad origin, built around 760, is one of the best-preserved in Spain. Its crenellated towers—the Cuadrada, the Redonda, and the Keep—stand out against the sky like an illustration from a medieval book. The interior can be visited: courtyards of arms, furnished halls, armor, dungeons, and oubliettes where Peter I the Cruel supposedly imprisoned his enemies in the 14th century. The building was restored between 1901 and 1936 by the Count of Torralva, which explains its remarkable condition. If the place seems familiar, that's normal—scenes from Game of Thrones (Season 7, Highgarden and Casterly Rock) were filmed here. Allow 1.5 hours for the visit.

In the afternoon, head for Sierra de Hornachuelos Natural Park, approximately 24 km from Almodóvar del Río, a 30-minute drive. The Mediterranean forest of holm and cork oaks is home to Iberian lynx, black vultures, Spanish imperial eagles and deer. The village of Hornachuelos overlooks a striking gorge carved by the río Bembézar. From the village viewpoint, the views over the gorge and the Sierra Morena are impressive.

The Monastery of San Jerónimo de Valparaíso stands near Medina Azahara, outside Córdoba, rather than beside Hornachuelos park. Founded in the 15th century, it retains a cloister and church with Gothic and Mudéjar features. The interior can only be seen on certain dates on tours organized through Medina Azahara, with advance registration: do not expect to drop in on the way past. From Almodóvar del Río, plan a separate round trip for this visit.

activities.text: Guides in Hornachuelos park offer wildlife walks. The paths passing through Fuente del Valle cross cork oak woods where you may see deer and birds of prey. During the rut, from September to October, deer calls echo through these forests. Kayaking trips on the Bembézar reservoir are also possible.

days_plan.itin_title: Córdoba and the Sierra Morena: From the Caliphate to the Dehesas of Los Pedroches

visits.text: Founded under the name Sexi, Almuñécar already existed when the Phoenicians set foot here nearly 3,000 years ago. The castle of San Miguel, perched on its hill, has witnessed every successive occupation. In the neighboring archaeological museum (Cueva Siete Palacios), the centerpiece is the Vase of Apophis I: an Egyptian alabaster vase dating from the 16th century BC, considered by the municipality to be the oldest written document found on the peninsula.
El Majuelo botanical park is home to around one hundred Mediterranean species. Free admission. Ideal for a break before the long drive to Almería.

activities.text: Before heading on, taste the tropical fruits grown in the local microclimate: avocados, mangoes, chirimoyas (custard apples) - the Thursday morning market stalls are best stocked. Almuñécar chirimoya has protected designation status. Prices well below French rates.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Coast: Málaga to Cartagena in 9 Days

visits.text: In the morning, stop at Aínsa, former capital of the kingdom of Sobrarbe and one of the Most Beautiful Villages in Spain. Perched at the confluence of the Ara and Cinca rivers, beneath the gaze of the Peña Montañesa, the medieval village seems frozen in the 12th century. The Plaza Mayor is trapezoidal and lined with Romanesque arcades. Climb the square bell tower of the church of Santa María (11th-12th century) for a full view of the Pyrenees. The restored castle houses an ecomuseum and hosts a music festival in its courtyard in July.

In the afternoon, drive to Alquézar (1h from Aínsa). The name comes from Arabic al-qasr (the fortress) - it was a 9th-century Muslim stronghold conquered by Sancho Ramírez in 1064. The village, clinging to a promontory above the Río Vero canyon, is classified as a Historic Site and ranks among Spain's Most Beautiful Villages. Climb up to the Collegiate Church of Santa María la Mayor, which preserves a Romanesque cloister with carved capitals and a major altarpiece. From the square, the view plunges into the limestone gorges - a dizzying spectacle.

activities.text: Don't miss the Pasarelas del Vero, Aragón's most popular aerial trail. This 3 km route (approximately 2h loop) descends into the Río Vero canyon via metal walkways attached to limestone walls above turquoise water. The trail is paid and well-secured - no technical difficulty, but spectacular views over the gorges and natural pools. In warm weather, bring a swimsuit for a dip.

Near Alquézar, the Río Vero Cultural Park has more than 70 shelters with rock paintings listed as UNESCO World Heritage (1998). Among them, the shelters of Quizans (schematic art, 5000-1500 BC) and Chimiachas (a deer in Levantine art of striking realism, 6000-3000 BC) can be reached on foot from Alquézar along a waymarked trail. Allow about 1 hour 30 minutes of walking to reach Quizans, then Chimiachas a little further on, making a good half-day there and back. Access is free, but a guide greatly enriches the visit.

days_plan.itin_title: Aragonese Pyrenees and Lower Aragón: From Ordesa to Teruel

places.name: Altea

visits.text: The cobbled streets climb toward a blue-and-white dome visible from across Altea bay. The Iglesia Nuestra Señora del Consuelo, built in the 19th century modeled on a 17th-century Baroque chapel, crowns the old town from its promontory. White façades, flower-draped stairways, wrought-iron balconies: Altea's old quarter stands in sharp contrast to the concrete of Benidorm 10 km away. Church entry free.

An artists' village, yes—but the bougainvillea cascades down the walls long before the galleries appear. The viewpoint at Plaza de la Iglesia offers an unobstructed view of the bay and the Sierra Bernia mountains. Heading back down, the alleyways between Portal Vell and Portal Nou preserve stretches of Renaissance-era walls. Caution in August: packed on weekends, restaurants fill up early.

days_plan.itin_title: Costa Blanca & Alicante Hinterland: 12 days

map_keywords: Iglesia Nuestra Señora del Consuelo Altea

visits.text: The valleys of Ansó and Hecho are the hidden jewels of the western Aragonese Pyrenees. Ansó, at 860 m altitude, is a museum-village of stone and slate, listed among Spain's Most Beautiful Villages. Its traditional ashlar stone houses, with their cylindrical chimneys typical of Pyrenean architecture, have remained virtually unchanged for centuries. The parish church of San Pedro (16th century), in late Gothic style, dominates the village. Wander through the sloping streets and don't miss the Museo del Traje Ansotano, which displays the valley's traditional costumes - worn until the mid-20th century.

Then head to the Hecho Valley (30 min drive), parallel to Ansó. The village of Hecho is another magnificent example of Pyrenean stone architecture, with narrow streets and a Romanesque church. Three kilometers north, the Monastery of San Pedro de Siresa (9th-11th centuries), one of Aragón's oldest, was founded in the Carolingian era and is said to have housed the Holy Grail before its transfer to San Juan de la Peña. The church, massive and austere, is a gem of Aragonese pre-Romanesque art.

activities.text: Drive up the Hecho Valley to the Selva de Oza, a beech and fir forest occupying the floor of an ancient glacial valley - one of the most pristine landscapes in the Pyrenees. The Camino de la Boca del Infierno (Mouth of Hell) follows a spectacular trail along limestone gorges. Allow 2 hours round trip for this easy walk that follows the Aragón Subordán river between 200-meter vertical walls.

days_plan.itin_title: Aragonese Pyrenees and Lower Aragón: From Ordesa to Teruel

visits.text: The Dolmens of Antequera open another dimension in the road trip: death on a grand scale, 5,700 years before us. The Dolmen de Menga, built around 3750-3650 BC, is one of Europe's largest megalithic tombs—27.5 m long, 32 stone blocks, the heaviest weighing 180 tonnes (slightly more than a Boeing 737). When it was opened in the 19th century, the skeletons of several hundred people were found inside. Atypical orientation: not toward the rising sun like most European dolmens, but toward the Peña de los Enamorados, a human face-shaped mountain 7 km away. Direct ritual link with the landscape. UNESCO 2016.

The Dolmen de Viera, 70 m from Menga, is later (2500-2000 BC) and more modest—long narrow corridor leading to a rectangular burial chamber. It's the only one of the three oriented toward the rising sun: at the spring and summer equinoxes, the sun's rays traverse the corridor and illuminate the chamber. Five minutes to visit, but see it to understand the diversity of funerary conceptions on a single site.

The Peña de los Enamorados, an 880 m limestone mountain toward which Menga points, owes its name to a local legend from Al-Andalus times: Tagzona, Moorish princess of Antequera, falls in love with Christian soldier Tello, taken prisoner. Pursued by the girl's father, they jump together from the top of the cliff. The rock's shape, seen from Antequera, indeed evokes a human face in profile looking toward the sky. Legend or not, the dolmen's prehistoric orientation predates this story by 5,000 years.

Standing stones become architecture at the Dólmenes de Antequera. Menga, Viera, and El Romeral display different forms; the UNESCO property also links the monuments to their natural landscape. Locate the entrances to the different sites and check opening hours, as they cannot all be visited through a single entrance.

activities.text: Lunch in Antequera before resuming the road to Málaga. Restaurante Arte de Cozina, calle Calzada 27, seasonal Andalusian cuisine at reasonable prices (25-35 euros menu). Local specialty: porra antequerana, Antequera's version of Cordoban salmorejo, thicker, garnished with hard-boiled egg and tuna.

Choose a marked loop in the Torcal de Antequera to walk among the limestone formations. Erosion has carved stacks that sometimes look like built structures, although the terrain is natural. Plan for the drive from Antequera; if the upper parking lot is full, the final stretch is covered by shuttle or on foot from the lower parking lot. Start at the Centro de Visitantes Torcal Alto, then choose a marked loop and turn back if fog obscures the landmarks.

days_plan.itin_title: Dark Andalusia: 10 Days from Seville to Málaga
White Villages & Sierras: 9 Days Málaga-Almería
Algarve, Andalusia, and Alentejo Road Trip in 20 Days

visits.text: Beneath downtown Aracena, through an unassuming door on Calle Pozo de la Nieve, lies another world: 2,130 meters of karst passages, 1,200 of them open to visitors, with 12 chambers and 6 underground lakes. Opened to the public in 1914, it's Spain's first tourist cave. The interior temperature stays between 16 and 19°C—bring a jacket even in August. Mandatory guided tour, 45 minutes.

Aracena rises toward its medieval castle through a maze of whitewashed lanes—the area is well preserved and sees few visitors outside weekends. The Plaza Alta and the viewpoint over the sierra of Huelva below: two hours are enough to see everything at a leisurely pace.

The Museo del Jamón in downtown Aracena explains the stages of Iberian ham production: the dehesa, the montanera, the curing facility. Small museum, modest entry fee. Not essential if you're already visiting a secadero, but useful for understanding the appellations and avoiding misleading labels when buying.

Beneath the castle hill, another Aracena awaits in the Gruta de las Maravillas. The pools and mineral formations completely transform the landscape, just a few steps from the village above. Book a guided tour, bring a light layer, and check the photography rules before descending.

The climb to the Castillo de Aracena helps place the cave in its landscape. Visiting the summit and the fortified ruins offers views of the houses and hills, rather than a fully furnished castle. Walk up to the summit after visiting the cave beneath the same hill.

The Museo del Jamón de Aracena places ham in the context of the surrounding landscape. The exhibits cover livestock farming, the dehesa, and ham production. Combine this museum and the castle with the Aracena tourist card, then save the tasting for the shops in the center.

activities.text: The smell of hanging ham hits you at the entrance to a secadero. In the Sierra de Aracena, black pigs (cerdo ibérico) roam freely in oak dehesas, feeding on acorns (bellotas) during the montanera. The final product—100% jamón ibérico de bellota—is cheaper and fresher here than in Madrid. Cinco Jotas or Eíriz offer tours with tastings.

If you buy a ham to take home, ask the seller for the date the curación began—a bellota ham is cured for at least 24 months, often 36. The skin (rind) should be supple, the fat white-yellow and soft enough to melt. Hams bearing the DOP Huelva or Jabugo appellation guarantee their origin.

days_plan.itin_title: Huelva, the Forgotten Land: Doñana to Faro in 7 Days
Algarve, Andalusia, and Alentejo Road Trip in 20 Days

visits.text: The Royal Palace of Aranjuez (16th–18th centuries) served as a summer residence for the Bourbons. Rococo salons, the Porcelain Room and the Throne Room follow one another.
The Jardín del Príncipe (18th century) covers 150 hectares along the Tagus. Shaded avenues, neoclassical fountains and the Casa del Labrador (a neoclassical pavilion).
The Jardín de la Isla follows the contours of an island in the Tagus. Geometric flowerbeds, canals, mythological statues and water jets make up this Renaissance-Baroque garden.
The Museo de Falúas Reales displays 18th-century royal boats. These ornate vessels were used for the monarchs' river outings.
The Plaza de San Antonio (1750) is lined with Baroque façades and a church. This regularly laid-out square forms the urban heart of Aranjuez.
The Casa del Labrador (1804) features neoclassical salons and Empire-style décor. This pavilion, with its marble and bronze, illustrates Bourbon refinement.

activities.text: Embark on a mini-cruise on the Tagus. A route with commentary takes you past royal gardens, historic bridges and tree-lined banks.
Picnic with Aranjuez strawberries. These renowned strawberries are harvested from April to June and sold at local markets.
Cycle along the Tagus. Bike paths run through royal gardens, orchards and vegetable gardens that made Aranjuez famous for its agriculture.
Board the Tren de la Fresa (Strawberry Train). This tourist train links Madrid to Aranjuez with strawberry tastings and period entertainment.

days_plan.itin_title: Madrid and Castile Tour: Palaces, City Walls and Museums

places.name: Arcos De La Frontera

visits.text: The void begins at your feet: the Plaza del Cabildo, perched at the cliff top above the Guadalete, is one of the most vertiginous viewpoints in Andalusia. Below, more than 100 meters of limestone wall, and the plain beyond. The medieval castle (an 11th-century Andalusí alcázar) and the national parador occupy the corner of the square. You can't go in, but the exterior can be freely admired.

Built on the ruins of a mosque and extensively transformed from the 1520s onwards under the direction of Alonso Rodríguez then Diego de Riaño, the Basílica de Santa María de la Asunción juxtaposes late Gothic, Plateresque and Baroque across six centuries of construction. Declared a National Monument in 1931. Its Baroque tower watches over the gorge. Paid entry, a few euros.

San Pedro is a church on the edge of the precipice: literally built at the extremity of the rocky promontory, it gives the impression of being poised over the void. The interior is more discreet than Santa María, but the location is unique - turn toward the valley from its forecourt.

The sheer drop suddenly comes into view at the edge of Plaza del Cabildo in Arcos de la Frontera. The overlook opens onto the Guadalete Valley, while the buildings around the square conceal its depth until the last moment. Walk into the center and avoid driving in without knowing the access routes.

An unfinished tower catches the eye at the Basílica de Santa María de la Asunción. Its side facade borders Plaza del Cabildo and already reveals several stages of construction. Take time to observe the exterior, then check opening hours if you would like to include the interior in this brief stop.

activities.text: If you arrive outside monument opening hours, it's the right time for the historic center. Arcos's labyrinthine layout - alleys a meter wide, passages under houses, dead ends - is inherited directly from the Arab medina. Two hours getting lost beats any guide.

The people of Arcos say that the view over the plain from the Mirador de la Peña Nueva is worth the journey alone. In late afternoon, when the low sun gilds the olive groves below, the light is unlike anything else you'll see in Andalusia. Ten minutes on the stone balcony, no effort required.

days_plan.itin_title: White Villages: Arcos, Grazalema, Ronda - 6 Days
Algarve, Andalusia, and Alentejo Road Trip in 20 Days

map_keywords: Plaza del Cabildo Arcos de la Frontera

visits.text: The castle of Aroche has occupied a hilltop since the 12th century—Almohad structure reworked after the Reconquista, then again during border conflicts with Portugal. The surprise: a bullring was built inside the ramparts in the early 19th century. The two still coexist. Panoramic view of the sierra from the battlements.

More than two thousand rosaries donated by personalities from around the world—popes, heads of state, actors, astronauts. The Aroche Rosary Museum was founded in the 1960s by a local resident, Paulino Díaz Alcaide, and appears in record books for the collection's scale. Entry via the tourist office. An unapologetic local curiosity, strangely fascinating.

activities.text: From the Cerro del Castillo, the first Portuguese hills are visible in clear weather—the border is less than 5 km away. This feeling of being at the edge of the world, before crossing into Portugal, is one of the strongest on the itinerary. The Sierra de Aracena y Picos de Aroche Natural Park covers 186,827 hectares of the surrounding area: no noise, no national roads.

days_plan.itin_title: Huelva, the Forgotten Land: Doñana to Faro in 7 Days

visits.text: The Charco de San Ginés defines Arrecife: a natural seawater lagoon in the heart of the capital, lined with whitewashed fishermen's houses. This natural harbor has existed for over six centuries—the city was born here after the Franco-Norman conquest in the 15th century. César Manrique redesigned it as a serene promenade. Walk its perimeter in early morning when the light is soft and the terraces still quiet.

The Castillo de San Gabriel deserves an hour of your time. Built in the 16th century on an islet to defend the town against Berber pirates—it was first burned by the corsair Morato in 1586 before being rebuilt in stone—it now houses the Arrecife History Museum with more than 3,000 items. To reach it, you cross the Puente de las Bolas, a drawbridge topped with two stone cannonballs: it is Arrecife's postcard image. The castle was declared a national historic monument in 1972.

The Castillo de San José, perched on the bay of Los Mármoles port, houses the International Museum of Contemporary Art, founded in 1975 on César Manrique's initiative. The building itself dates to the 18th century, and its construction traces back to a legend: in 1630, a French merchant named Francisco García Santaella supposedly founded a hermitage here. The interior blends Baroque, Mudéjar, and Neoclassical styles—a typical Canarian architectural fusion. The castle's panoramic restaurant offers harbor views worth the visit alone.

End with Calle Real—officially called León y Castillo—Arrecife's main artery for centuries. You'll find the Plazuela (Constitution Square) and San Ginés Church, whose white dome dominates the square where an artisan market sets up every Saturday. The church became a parish in 1798 and was dedicated to San Ginés, the city's patron saint. The complete walk takes 2 to 3 hours.

activities.text: Lunch around Charco de San Ginés: the area brims with restaurants serving Canarian classics—papas arrugadas with mojo verde or mojo rojo, fresh fish from the port, and malvasía wines from the island. It's also the best spot to watch fishing boats maneuver through the lagoon.
Swimming and relaxing on Playa del Reducto, Arrecife's main beach. It stretches for more than half a kilometre with golden sand and calm water, ideal for a mid-afternoon break.

Late afternoon, return to stroll around Charco de San Ginés at sunset. Locals gather here for terrace drinks. If you're there on a Wednesday or Thursday, a popular market sets up around the lagoon—a chance to pick up local crafts.

days_plan.itin_title: Lanzarote & La Palma: Volcanoes and the Art of César Manrique

places.name: Astorga

visits.text: The Episcopal Palace of Astorga is one of the few works by Gaudí built outside Catalonia. After the old palace burned in 1886, Bishop Joan Grau i Vallespinós—a Catalan and Gaudí's personal friend—commissioned him to rebuild. The project began in 1887: Gaudí designed a neo-Gothic building in white granite that blends castle, temple, and palace, with turrets, battlements, and multicolored stained glass inspired by León Cathedral. The bishop's death in 1893 caused a rupture between Gaudí and the curia—he walked off the job, leaving the top floor unfinished, which another architect completed more soberly. Today the palace houses the Museum of the Ways, dedicated to pilgrimage routes. Allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes.

Astorga's Cathedral of Santa María, built from the 15th to 18th centuries, is one of Spain's most eclectic monuments—Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque, and Plateresque styles appear in succession on its façades and inside. On one of its apsidal pinnacles, look for the statue of Pedro Mato, a Maragato about whom nothing is known for certain, though local legends abound. The cathedral museum houses a magnificently chased silver casket belonging to Alfonso III the Great.

Astorga was the Roman capital of Asturica Augusta, crossroads of several Roman roads. The Roman walls preserved in several sections throughout the city are among the best preserved on the peninsula. Don't miss the Roman Museum to understand the city's importance in imperial times—and the Chocolate Museum, since Astorga was historically one of the first European cities to import and process cacao from the Americas via Maragato muleteers.

Castrillo de los Polvazares is La Maragatería's most perfectly preserved village. Its cobbled streets, red-stone houses with large round-arched doorways and windows painted blue or green form a homogeneous 17th-century ensemble declared a Historic-Artistic Site in 1980. Those oversized doorways weren't architectural whimsy: they allowed carts and mules to enter interior courtyards. From the 16th to 19th centuries, Castrillo was the heart of the Maragato muleteer network—those semi-nomadic transporters who linked Galicia and Madrid with their mule caravans. English writer Richard Ford described them in 1846: “as nomadic as Bedouins, but with mules instead of camels; they charge a lot, but their honesty makes up for it”. The arrival of the railroad in Astorga in 1866 spelled their end. The village had 1,200 inhabitants in 1870; it has about a hundred today.

Santa Colomba de Somoza, around 17 km from Astorga, is another well-preserved Maragato village, inhabited since the 11th century and associated with mule transport since the 16th century. The Casa Maragata - an ethnographic museum housed in an authentic muleteer's home - recreates the domestic and working spaces of Maragato life: a kitchen with a large hearth, a cart shed, farming tools and traces of the chocolate trade. Every August, residents open their courtyards for a craft fair.

activities.text: Bar and restaurant tour around Plaza Mayor to dine on Maragatería specialties: cocido maragato (the Spanish stew eaten backwards—meat first, soup last), mantecadas de Astorga (small butter and cinnamon cakes), and artisanal chocolate that has earned the city its reputation since the 18th century. Book a restaurant for the cocido—it's a meal lasting several hours.

Lunch in Castrillo de los Polvazares with cocido maragato: the legend about the reversed eating order (meat before soup) is tied to the War of Independence—Spanish soldiers ate the most nourishing parts first before an imminent battle against the French. Book ahead, especially on weekends—the restaurant is often full.

Hiking the “Senda Maragata” from Santa Colomba de Somoza—several marked circuits let you discover remnants of Roman mines and the Maragatería landscapes between oak groves and heathland. The Mirador de la Laguna Cernea offers views over the eroded hills and Roman gold workings of the region.

visits.text: At an altitude of 1,131 meters, Ávila is one of Spain's highest cities—and you feel it in winter, when it often snows. The city reveals itself first through its ramparts: 2.5 kilometers of intact wall, 88 semicircular towers, 9 monumental gates. Built from 1080 on the orders of Raymond of Burgundy, son-in-law of Alfonso VI of Castile and León, completed in 1101. It's the best-preserved medieval wall in Europe—it nearly got demolished in the 19th century because it was thought to stifle urban expansion. Fortunately, the plan was abandoned. You can walk along 1,700 meters of the wall walk.

On the wall itself, the Cathedral of the Savior. It gave architectural vocabulary the term “fortress-cathedral”. Its apse, nicknamed the Cimorro, literally forms part of the defensive system—it's one of the rampart towers, pierced with arrow slits. Spain's first Gothic cathedral, begun around 1170 by Master Fruchel, a Burgundian architect influenced by Saint-Denis. Built in oxblood-red sandstone that gives it its unique color. Inside, the main altarpiece by Pedro Berruguete and Juan de Borgoña, the tomb of El Tostado (the bishop and writer who published 50 volumes in 25 years and died in 1455).

Outside the walls, five minutes on foot from Puerta del Alcázar, the Basilica of San Vicente is one of Spain's finest Romanesque buildings. Built between the 11th and 13th centuries on the site where saints Vincent, Sabina, and Christeta were allegedly martyred in 304 under Diocletian. The stone tomb-cenotaph at the nave's center recounts their martyrdom in moving sculpted bas-reliefs: flagellation, torture, embalming by a converted Jewish lady. West façade with its grand portico, historiated capitals, golden light in the morning. A stop on the Camino del Sur.

You cannot understand Ávila without Teresa. Born here in 1515 to a family of converted Jewish merchants, she reformed the Carmelite order, founded 17 monasteries, wrote The Interior Castle, and became the first female Doctor of the Church in 1970. Her birthplace was transformed in the 17th century into a convent and baroque basilica. The adjoining museum displays some strange relics: a finger of the saint preserved in a monstrance, her cane, autograph manuscripts. More moving: the Monastery of the Incarnation, outside the walls, where she lived for 27 years and experienced the famous “transverberation” (a vision in which a seraph pierces her heart).

For the postcard photo of Ávila, exit through Puerta del Carmen and follow the road northwest toward Salamanca for 1.5 km on foot to the Cuatro Postes. Four Doric columns topped by a cross, erected in 1566 on the path where, according to legend, young Teresa was caught by her uncle while running away with her brother to seek martyrdom among the Moors. Panoramic view of the illuminated ramparts, especially late in the day. That's where you take the best photos of Ávila.

activities.text: Sample yemas de Santa Teresa, an Ávila specialty since 1860. Small round balls made of beaten egg yolk and sugar, slowly cooked, presented in paper cups. Too sweet for many, but they define the city's sweet treats. The places to try: La Flor de Castilla confectionery, and the keeper of the original recipe's secret, Antigua Confitería La Talavera. Three yemas are enough—they're dense.

Dine on chuletón de Ávila—the charcoal-grilled beef rib steak that is the province's emblem. Cattle of the avileña-negra ibérica breed are raised in the mountains of the Sierra de Gredos and produce marbled meat; they are slaughtered at an average age of 5–6 years (versus 18–24 months elsewhere). It's one of Spain's most tender meats. Restaurant El Almacén or Las Cancelas for the classic version, served rare. Allow €60 for two. If you happen upon the Jornadas Medievales in early September, the city transforms into a medieval market for three days.

visits.text: Walls plunge several hundred metres above the río Mundo from the Mirador del Diablo, 1.5 km from Ayna on the CM-3203—a few steps in the rock bring you to a platform overlooking the complete canyon, the village, and its orchards. Locals have called Ayna the 'Suiza Manchega' for so long it's become official. Stop the car in the parking on the road; the climb to the stairs takes 3 minutes.

The Cueva del Niño, on the outskirts of Ayna, shelters Paleolithic rock art dated to around 16,000 BC, according to published archaeological studies. Ask at Ayna's tourist office for access arrangements—the cave is not freely accessible and may require reservation or a guide.

activities.text: Follow the ruta de los miradores: five viewpoints dot Ayna's casco urbano, including the Mirador de los Picarzos and the Sidecar (a nod to the motorcycle from the film 'Amanece que no es poco'). The loop is walkable in under an hour. On the way down, try the 'suspiros'—local cakes sold at the bakery on the main street.

days_plan.itin_title: Castilla-La Mancha: Windmills and Sierra in 11 days

visits.text: Baeza is one of the two towns inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2003 for their Renaissance ensembles. But before becoming a 16th-century jewel, it was a stronghold of the Reconquest: Ferdinand III conquered it in 1227, and it became Castile's forward base facing the Kingdom of Granada for two centuries. Begin at Plaza del Pópulo, the civic heart of the town. The Fuente de los Leones (Lion Fountain), which resembles the one in the Alhambra, is actually an Ibero-Roman remnant from the ancient city of Cástulo. Around the square, the old slaughterhouse (Antigua Carnicería) and the Villalar Arch complete a harmonious ensemble.

Climb to Plaza de Santa María, the religious and educational heart of Baeza. The Cathedral of the Nativity, rebuilt in the 16th century on a former mosque, blends Gothic, Renaissance, and Baroque. Its main façade is sober, but the interior surprises with the brightness of its vaults and the richness of its chapels. Just opposite, the Palacio de Jabalquinto is Baeza's most photographed monument: its Isabelline façade, covered with carved stone diamond points, is a masterpiece of stone lacework from the 15th century. It now houses the headquarters of the International University of Andalusia.

The Old University of Baeza, founded in 1538, is an austere Renaissance building with a beautiful arcaded courtyard. The poet Antonio Machado taught French there between 1912 and 1919—his classroom has remained intact, with his desk, blackboard, and student benches. It was here that he wrote part of his Campos de Castilla. On the wall, a plaque quotes his verses: “En estos campos de la tierra mía...” Entry is free and the emotion is real.

Finish with a walk along the Paseo de la Constitución and the ramparts, from where the view embraces the olive fields stretching to the horizon. The sunset over this green and silver sea is a daily spectacle that Baeza's inhabitants never tire of watching.

activities.text: Baeza is a town of tapas and olive oil. The bars around Plaza de la Constitución and Calle San Pablo serve generous portions drizzled with Sierra de Cazorla PDO olive oil. Try the ochíos (olive oil bread typical of Jaén), pipirrana (cold salad of tomato, pepper, and cucumber), and revuelto de ajetes (scrambled eggs with tender garlic). Olive oil here isn't a condiment—it's a main ingredient.

visits.text: Balouta is the last village in León province before the border with Galicia and Asturias. With about twenty inhabitants, this Ancares hamlet preserves the highest concentration of pallozas in the entire region—those circular houses with schist walls and woven rye-straw roofs that look like giant haystacks. Pallozas date back at least to the Middle Ages; their round shape helped them withstand the winds and snows of these mountains at an elevation of over 1,000 meters. Some once sheltered both people and animals under the same roof, the livestock's body heat warming the dwelling. One old palloza has been restored and now serves as a bar—make sure to go inside to see the interior. Book your casa rural well in advance; accommodations are very scarce.

The neighboring village of Suarbol, 4 km away, has only seven permanent residents (around thirty in summer). The road between the two villages follows the floor of the Ancares valley, framed by slopes covered in oak and chestnut trees. You will also find a small church, with a noble family's coat of arms on one of the neighboring façades—one of the few reminders of the valley's former prosperity.

activities.text: Hiking in the Ancares Biosphere Reserve. Marked trails from Balouta lead to the brañas—high-altitude pastures—where views sweep across several valleys at once. Wildlife is remarkable in this seldom-visited area: brown bears (presence confirmed), wolves, deer, and a remarkably high density of birds. Bring hiking boots and water—there are no services outside the village.

Watch the sunset from the heights above Balouta. The late-day light on the rye-thatched palloza roofs and green slopes creates one of the Ancares' most striking images. Bring a flashlight for the return.

places.name: Banos De La Encina

visits.text: The road south from Almagro crosses the Sierra Morena through the Despeñaperros gorge—the natural frontier between Castile and Andalusia. This narrow pass between quartzite cliffs has been the gateway to Andalusia for centuries: Roman armies, Visigoths, Moors, and Christian armies all passed through. Stop at the viewpoint for a view over the gorges, then detour to the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa Interpretation Centre in Santa Elena. On 16 July 1212, the Christian coalition led by Alfonso VIII of Castile crushed the Almohad army here—a battle that reversed the course of the Reconquest and definitively opened Andalusia to the Christian kingdoms.

Baños de la Encina appears among the olive groves, dominated by the spectacular silhouette of Castillo de Burgalimar. This Caliphate fortress, built in 968 on the orders of Caliph Al-Hakam II of Córdoba, is one of the best-preserved Muslim fortresses in Europe. Its 14 towers and its wall of tapial (rammed earth, lime, and stone) still stand at their original height—a millennium later. A 15th tower, the Keep, was added by the Christians after the reconquest. It's called 'the fortress of seven kings' because seven monarchs passed through, from Alfonso VII to Ferdinand the Catholic. Climb the 18-metre keep: the panorama over the endless sea of olive trees is one of the most striking images in the province of Jaén.

Coming down from the castle, stroll through the streets of Baños de la Encina. Unlike Andalusia's white villages, here the façades are ashlar stone—16th and 17th-century manor houses with carved coats of arms line the streets. The Church of San Mateo (15th century), in late Gothic style, dominates the main square. Don't miss the anthropomorphic tombs carved into the rock near the Molino del Santo, vestiges of a Visigothic past.

activities.text: Baños de la Encina sits at the heart of the world's largest olive grove—the province of Jaén alone produces about 20% of the world's olive oil. Local operators offer visits to olive groves and oil mills with tastings. You'll learn to distinguish the Picual variety (the most planted here, intense and fruity) from Arbequina, and to recognise a “virgen extra” from a simple “virgen”. It's an experience that permanently changes your relationship with olive oil.
