places.name: Cangas De Onis

visits.text: The so-called “Roman” bridge of Cangas de Onís actually dates from the 13th century and was built on ancient foundations. Its raised central arch, flanked by two smaller asymmetric arches, spans the Sella River. A replica of the Cross of Victory has hung from it since 1939.
Steps from the bridge, the Hermitage of Santa Cruz conceals a megalithic dolmen beneath its altar. This small edifice founded in 737 covers one of the oldest funerary monuments in Asturias.

Take the winding road to the Sanctuary of Covadonga, birthplace of the Reconquest. The neo-Romanesque basilica in pinkish limestone, built between 1877 and 1901, raises its twin spires above the steep-sided valley.

Descend into the Santa Cueva, a cave carved into the cliff face that houses the statue of Our Lady of Covadonga and the tomb of King Pelayo. Beneath the rocky vault, a waterfall plunges into a pool of green water. Below, the Fuente de los Siete Caños invites the superstitious: drinking from all seven spouts supposedly promises marriage within the year.

Cangas de Onís was the first capital of the Kingdom of Asturias until 774. On the central square, a bronze statue of Pelayo the Conqueror commemorates the victory of 722 that launched eight centuries of Reconquest.

activities.text: Set off on a canoe trip down the Sella, a popular route. The river runs through landscapes of green hills, dense forests and small Asturian villages.
Try the fabada asturiana in one of the town's restaurants. This hearty stew of white beans, chorizo, morcilla, and bacon is Asturias' signature dish.
On Sunday mornings, Cangas de Onís market takes over the square with stalls of Cabrales cheese, heather honey, artisan cider, and smoked mountain charcuterie.

days_plan.itin_title: Asturias Road Trip: Cantabrian Coast and Picos de Europa

map_keywords: Ermita Santa Cruz Cangas de Onís

visits.text: From Granada, expect about an hour's drive to reach Lanjarón, the gateway to the Alpujarras. This small spa town is famous for its mineral water (Spain's best-selling brand) and its ruined Arab castle, the last Moorish stronghold to fall in 1500. Make a quick stop to refill your water bottle at one of the public fountains and grab a coffee on the plaza before continuing.

Pass through Órgiva (the valley's main town, market day on Thursdays) and climb towards the Barranco de Poqueira, the spectacular gorge where the three most famous villages of the Alpujarras cascade down the mountainside. First stop: Pampaneira (1,058 m), the lower village. Its 340 inhabitants live among whitewashed houses with flat roofs (the “terraos”), sloping lanes, covered passages (the “tinaos”) and spring-fed fountains. On the main square, taste the water from the San Antonio fountain - legend says it helps you find love. Pampaneira is also the Alpujarras' artisan village: the “jarapas”, those colorful rugs woven from recycled fibers, are the local specialty. Step into a weaving workshop.

Climb to Bubión (1,296 m), 2 km higher up - on foot via the old mule track (30 minutes) or by car. This is the quietest of the three villages, a member of Spain's "slow tourism" network. The Berber architecture is best preserved here: cubic houses with flat slate roofs, cylindrical chimneys topped with a stone cap. At the Museo Casa Alpujarreña, you'll see how the inhabitants lived in the past - kitchen, bedroom and workshop recreated in a traditional house. Don't miss the Artesa de los Moros, a large 2-meter stone whose original purpose remains mysterious.

Capileira (1,436 m) is the highest of the trio, at the gates of Sierra Nevada National Park. From the Mirador de Perchel, the view is vertiginous: to the north, the peak of Veleta (3,396 m); to the south, the rooftops of Bubión and Pampaneira cascading below; and on clear days, the Mediterranean and even the Rif mountains of Morocco on the horizon. This is where the trails begin towards the highest peaks of the Iberian Peninsula, including Mulhacén (3,479 m). The water from the public fountains comes directly from the Sierra Nevada's snowmelt - it's ice-cold even in midsummer.

activities.text: If you have the time and energy, the circular hike linking the three villages via the old mule tracks is the best way to discover the valley. Allow 3 to 4 hours for the complete loop, through chestnut groves, walnut trees, terraced olive groves and irrigation channels inherited from the Moorish era. You might spot Iberian ibex on the slopes.

In the evening, dine in Capileira or Bubión on a "plato alpujarreño" - the local dish: potatoes, fried egg, blood sausage (morcilla), ham and peppers. It's hearty and perfect after a day in the mountains. Pair it with a local Alpujarras wine.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Granada: Alpujarras, Guadix and the Sierras
Al-Andalus: From the Mezquita to the Alpujarras in 10 days

visits.text: You're leaving Andalusia for the Murcia region. Caravaca de la Cruz is the fifth holy city of Christianity, along with Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago de Compostela and Santo Toribio de Liébana. This privilege, granted by Pope John Paul II in 1998, allows a perpetual Jubilee to be celebrated every seven years. Everything revolves around the Vera Cruz, a relic containing fragments of Christ's cross. According to legend, in 1231, the Moorish king Abou Zeïd asked a captive priest to celebrate mass in the castle. Since a cross was missing, two angels brought one from heaven - and the Moorish king converted to Christianity.

Climb to the Castillo via the steep paved lane that runs through the medieval quarter. The fortress, of Moorish origin (10th-11th century), was enlarged in the 15th century by the Templars then taken over by the Order of Santiago. Fourteen towers guard the walls. Inside stands the Sanctuary of the Santísima y Vera Cruz, built from 1617 onwards - its baroque facade in red marble from Cehegín is spectacular. The interior museum displays the chasuble of the priest Chirinos at the moment of the legendary apparition, as well as paintings dedicated to the miracle. From the ramparts, the view embraces the entire town and the mountains of northwestern Murcia.

Descend into the center to see the El Salvador church, considered the pinnacle of Murcian Renaissance art. The Carmelite convent, founded by Saint John of the Cross in 1586, is a place of calm and contemplation. On calle Mayor and calle Rafael Tegeo, admire the manor houses with wrought-iron balconies. The Templete (or Bañadero) is a small hexagonal baroque building where, every May 3rd, the relic of the Vera Cruz is bathed in water - a ritual celebrated since 1384.

activities.text: Late in the day, go relax at the Fuentes del Marqués, a natural area just outside town: an abundant spring surrounded by poplars and plane trees, with shaded paths, caves carved by Arab settlers (once used for tanning hides) and the Torre de los Templarios. It's the locals' favorite walking spot.

If you visit between May 1st and 5th, you'll witness the fiestas of the Santísima y Vera Cruz, declared of International Tourist Interest. On May 2nd, the Caballos del Vino (Horses of Wine) gallop up the castle slope, sumptuously harnessed - a unique spectacle. The Moors and Christians reenactments in the following days are equally colorful.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Granada: Alpujarras, Guadix and the Sierras
Murcia Coast and Hinterland: 13 days from La Manga to Cuenca

visits.text: The fortress of Cardona dominates the Cardener valley at 589 meters, perched on a pinnacle no attacker ever took by force—hence its nickname the "unconquered fortress." Built in 886 by Wilfred the Hairy, Count of Barcelona, it held out during the War of Succession until September 18, 1714, capitulating after Barcelona fell on September 11—this Barcelona date became Catalonia's national Diada. The castle is now a luxury Parador, but the historic spaces can be visited (€5).

The collegiate church of Sant Vicenç, inside the fortress, is an absolute masterpiece of Catalan Lombard Romanesque—consecrated in 1040, it predates the churches of the Vall de Boí. Three naves, dome on squinches, intact crypt beneath the high altar. Exceptional acoustics: Jordi Savall has recorded most of his discography here over the past 30 years, and Orson Welles shot scenes from Falstaff here in 1965. Visit included in the castle ticket.

The Torre de la Minyona, a Romanesque keep 15 meters tall and 10 meters in diameter, takes its name from the legend of Adélaïs, the viscount's daughter locked here by her father in the 11th century to prevent her marrying a Moorish lord. Partially dismantled in 1794 by French troops to deprive the fortress of its key defensive piece. Now open at the top, 360° views over the saline valley below—the orange-red color of the salt is visible even from a distance.

The Gothic church of Sant Miquel, in the old town below, merits a quick detour for the contrast with the austere Romanesque of the castle. Built in the 13th-14th centuries, single nave, late Baroque altarpieces. The medieval center has been a cultural asset of national interest since 1992: arcaded houses on Plaça del Mercat, cobbled lanes leading to the old fortified gate. An hour's stroll suffices.

activities.text: Guided tour of the Salt Mountain Cultural Park—descent by vehicle to 86 meters underground in the Nieves mine, exploited until 1990. Cardona's mine is Spain's deepest, 1,310 meters at its lowest point, 300 km of galleries in total. Beneath your feet, the red salt diapir descends 2 km—visible at the surface for only 120 meters, it's the tip of a mineral iceberg. The illuminated galleries reveal the salt's folds like a Baroque fresco. €18, duration 90 minutes, booking essential.

Evening at the castle Parador—even if you're not staying, the courtyard bar serves Reus vermouth at €4, to sip on the ramparts at sunset. For dinner, restaurant La Volta in the village offers hearty Catalan cuisine around €30: simmered escudella, rabbit with Sant Antoni mustard. Cardona's violet salt, sold in village shops, makes a fine souvenir at €6 a jar.

days_plan.itin_title: Catalonia - Complete 24-Day Grand Tour
Catalonia Wine Route - 7 Days from Penedès to Priorat

visits.text: The red clay of the ramparts burns in late-morning light. Carmona has perched on a promontory since the Bronze Age. Its two monumental gates—Seville to the west, Córdoba to the east—have Punic foundations reinforced by Rome, then modified by the Umayyads. Three civilizations stacked in the same stone.

The Alcázar del Rey Don Pedro, at the eastern tip of the promontory, is an Arab-origin fortress transformed by Pedro I of Castile in the 14th century. Now a luxury hotel, the mirador entrance is still free—the view from the battlements over the Sevillian plain is worth the stop alone.

Climb into the Alcázar de la Puerta de Sevilla to understand Carmona from its gateway. The terraces overlook the city and farmland, while alterations to the fortification tell the story of successive occupations. Leave your car outside the old town, enter through the Puerta de Sevilla, and continue on foot through the narrow streets after visiting the fortress.

The city of the dead begins beyond Carmona’s narrow streets, at the Necrópolis Romana. The burial chambers and preserved remains shift the focus from panoramic views to ancient practices; some spaces can only be viewed from outside. Start with the open-air sections during the cooler hours, then view the burial chambers from the designated paths.

activities.text: Two centuries before Christ, Carmona buried its dead outside the walls in underground chambers carved into bedrock, some fitted with niches for cinerary urns. The 1st-century Roman necropolis, which yielded the Tomb of the Elephant and the Tomb of Servilia, is one of the peninsula's best-preserved Roman burial complexes. Allow 90 minutes. Closed Mondays.

days_plan.itin_title: Al-Andalus: From the Mezquita to the Alpujarras in 10 days
Algarve, Andalusia, and Alentejo Road Trip in 20 Days

places.name: Carrion De Calatrava

visits.text: Calatrava la Vieja closes the loop: here, on the banks of the Guadiana, the Order of Calatrava was born in the 12th century before moving south. The Umayyad fortress, documented as early as 785, controlled the route between Córdoba and Toledo. The 750-meter moat and pentagonal towers are still visible.

The site forms part of the Parque Arqueológico de Alarcos-Calatrava. Systematic excavations since 1984 have uncovered the medina, alcázar, suburbs, and Bronze Age remains. Guided tour included with admission, about 1.5 hours.

activities.text: In June and October, dramatized tours recreate the site's history with costumed actors. The rest of the year, silence reigns and the Meseta light carves the walls. The site is 13 km northeast of Ciudad Real.

days_plan.itin_title: Campo de Calatrava and Valle de Alcudia in 5 Days

map_keywords: Calatrava la Vieja Carrión de Calatrava

visits.text: The Roman theater of Carthago Nova, 7,000 seats, built between 5 and 1 BC under Augustus - and rediscovered in 1988 by pure chance during construction work. It had slept beneath the cathedral quarter for twenty centuries. Museum by Rafael Moneo, opened in 2008. Allow 1h30 for museum and theater. Closed Mondays.

Behind a plain wall in the city center, a Punic wall from 227 BC - the one Hasdrubal the Fair had built when he founded Qart Hadasht on this site. Scipio Africanus stormed it in 209 BC. The interpretation center lets you walk on the original stones. Only Carthaginian remains visible in Spain in the open air.

Roman stones emerge everywhere in the Barrio del Foro Romano—beneath the lanes and in the walls of houses. The city has twenty-two centuries of superimposed layers. Sections of colonnade can be seen in the Molinete district. Free walk, information panels, 30 minutes.

activities.text: Walk along the naval harbor before catching your train or getting back on the road - the Cartagena naval base is one of Spain's three main bases, along with Rota and Ferrol. The moored submarines are visible from the public quay. Strange contrast with yesterday's beaches. Coffee in Paseo Alfonso XIII to digest three thousand years of history.

The Museo Naval de Cartagena, on the harbor, traces 2,000 years of maritime military presence in this natural harbor - one of the best protected in the western Mediterranean. Raised Roman wrecks, models of Punic galleys, history of the Peral submarines built here in 1888. Free entry. Open mornings Tuesday to Sunday.

days_plan.itin_title: Murcia Road Trip: Baroque Splendor & Costa Cálida
Murcia Coast and Hinterland: 13 days from La Manga to Cuenca
Wild Coast: Málaga to Cartagena in 9 Days

places.name: Castillo De Loarre

visits.text: The Castle of Loarre, built from 1020 by King Sancho III of Navarre on a rocky spur at an altitude of 1,071 meters, is the best-preserved Romanesque fortress in Europe. Its 172-meter perimeter wall, flanked by eleven towers, dominates the plain of the Hoya de Huesca. The site served as a filming location for “Kingdom of Heaven” and “The Name of the Rose.”

Pass through the Romanesque portal adorned with a checkerboard pattern in the Jaca style, then climb the barrel-vaulted staircase. The Crypt of Santa Quiteria, to the left, served as a burial site. Two narrow staircases lead to the Church of San Pedro, a marvel of Romanesque art: its 26-meter-high dome crowns a semicircular apse with capitals carved with biblical and fantastical motifs.

The keep, 22 meters high with five floors, was linked to the castle by a drawbridge. The Torre de la Reina, above the entrance to the military section, offers a dizzying panorama over the Pyrenean foothills and the farmland below.

In 1071, King Sancho Ramírez transformed the fortress into an Augustinian monastery. The Church of Santa María, predating the monastery, preserves alabaster windows whose white, milky light bathes the nave in an unexpected softness in this military setting.

From the parking lot, before entering the castle, take time to admire the fortress silhouette that seems to spring from the rock itself. The winding road leading up crosses a landscape of scrubland and limestone cliffs where griffon vultures nest.

activities.text: Walk the trail that circles the castle's outer ramparts, added in the 13th century. The path offers varied perspectives on the towers, walls, and cliffs that naturally protect the fortress's southern side.

The limestone cliffs around Loarre shelter a colony of griffon vultures. From the castle's surroundings, look up: these raptors with nearly 3-meter wingspans circle above the rock faces, carried by thermal currents.

The Collegiate Church of Santa María de Bolea, about twenty kilometers away, deserves a detour for its monumental 15th-century Hispano-Flemish altarpiece. This 16-meter-high altarpiece, with exquisitely painted panels, is considered one of Aragon's most important.

days_plan.itin_title: Aragon Tour: Zaragoza and Mudéjar Villages

map_keywords: Iglesia de San Pedro Castillo de Loarre
Torre del Homenaje Castillo de Loarre

places.name: Castro Urdiales

visits.text: The Church of Santa María de la Asunción sits enthroned on the rocky promontory above the harbor. Built from the 13th to 15th centuries in rose-colored stone, it is the finest example of Cantabrian Gothic. Its flying buttresses and soaring naves rival French cathedrals.
The Castle of Santa Ana, a 12th-century fortress, houses a lighthouse installed in 1853 in its southeast tower. In the courtyard, a Roman milestone bears witness to the ancient road to Flaviobriga.
Cross the medieval bridge—locally nicknamed the 'Roman bridge'—to reach the hermitage of Santa Ana, perched on a rock battered by the waves. At high tide, the sea surges beneath the arches.
Plaza del Ayuntamiento is ringed by arcades and dominated by the town hall with its crenellated tower. Café terraces come alive from aperitif hour onward.
The lanes of the Puebla Vieja, declared a Historic-Artistic Ensemble in 1978, preserve their wooden-balconied houses and medieval facades.
The Palacio de Ocharan, with its Greek-inspired columned portico, illustrates 19th-century bourgeois splendor. Its gardens open onto the sea.

activities.text: Castro Urdiales is a working fishing port. Grilled sardines, preserved anchovies and bonito stew are the specialties to savor beneath the harbor arcades.
Walk along Avenida de la Constitución, parallel to the sea, then descend to Brazomar beach. The golden sand stretches at the harbor's foot, facing the cliffs.
The pintxo bars in the center show Basque Country influence from nearby. Order at the counter and pair with a chilled txakoli overlooking the harbor.

days_plan.itin_title: Cantabria Road Trip: Atlantic Bays and Picos de Europa

map_keywords: Iglesia Santa María de la Asunción Castro Urdiales
Castillo-Faro de Santa Ana Castro Urdiales
Ermita de Santa Ana Castro Urdiales

visits.text: A former flour mill converted into the Museo del Turrón: the building alone is worth a visit, with its original machinery. Four themed rooms trace the development of the turrón industry since the late 19th century. Opened in 2005. Calle Huertos 46, free admission.

If you have time, head to the Centro de Interpretación de la Naturaleza La Serena y Sierras Periféricas, in the same building as the Museo del Turrón. Models, information panels, local fauna. A useful introduction before exploring the comarca.

Walk through the streets of Castuera's historic centre: white façades, glimpses of patios, the atmosphere of a prosperous farming town. Bars and shops cluster around the Plaza de España. Allow twenty minutes for a full circuit.

activities.text: Castuera turrón, the forgotten cousin of Jijona's, has been made here since the late 19th century with Marcona almonds and sierra honey. Four factories still operate, the largest exporter being Rey. Buy directly in town, it's half the price.

At the Centro de Interpretación de la Naturaleza, panels identify birds of prey found in the comarca: griffon vultures, golden eagles, lesser kestrels. Useful before the stops at Cabeza del Buey and Puebla de Alcocer, two birdwatching spots.

days_plan.itin_title: La Siberia and La Serena: Secret Extremadura in 6 Days

visits.text: Explore the archaeological site of Cástulo, 5 kilometres from Linares, one of the most important Ibero-Roman settlements on the peninsula. This ancient city was the capital of Oretania and a strategic point in the wars between Rome and Carthage, with remains spanning from the Bronze Age to medieval times.

activities.text: Walk through the archaeological excavations where exceptional Roman mosaics, walls, necropolises, and public buildings have been discovered. The site continues to reveal treasures and offers a unique glimpse into life in ancient Hispania.

days_plan.itin_title: Jaén Province Tour: Renaissance and Olive Trees

visits.text: The road from Úbeda to Cazorla crosses a sea of olive trees stretching as far as the eye can see—the province of Jaén has over 66 million olive trees. Cazorla is a white village clinging to a hillside at the foot of the natural park. Plaza de Santa María, one of the two main squares, is built around the spectacular ruins of the Iglesia de Santa María—a 16th-century Renaissance church bombed during the Civil War and never rebuilt. Its open-air arches, with the mountain backdrop, create a unique theatrical setting.

The Castillo de la Yedra (Ivy Castle), of Arab origin then enlarged by the Christians, dominates Cazorla from its rocky spur. It houses the Museo de Artes y Costumbres Populares del Alto Guadalquivir—an ethnographic museum tracing rural life in the sierras. From the ramparts, the view plunges over Cazorla's rooftops and the first forests of the natural park. It's also an excellent spot to watch griffon vultures soaring above the gorges.

Two kilometres from Cazorla, the village of La Iruela has one of the most spectacular sites in the province: a castle perched on a rocky pinnacle so narrow it seems to defy gravity. The adjoining ruined church, clinging to the same rock, reinforces the vertiginous impression. The climb is short but steep—the view from the summit embraces the entire Cerezuelo valley and the distant sierras.

Full day in the Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y las Villas Natural Park—at 210,000 hectares, it's Spain's largest protected area and Europe's second largest. Declared a Biosphere Reserve by UNESCO in 1983, it's home to over 2,170 plant species including 34 endemics (Cazorla violet, the world's smallest narcissus, a carnivorous plant). Wildlife includes ibex, deer, wild boar, mouflon, griffon vultures, golden eagles, and the rare bearded vulture.

The Río Borosa hike is the park's flagship trail - and one of the most beautiful in Andalusia. From the Torre del Vinagre visitor centre, reached by car from Cazorla along the Tranco mountain road (A-319), the trail follows the Borosa, the first major tributary of the Guadalquivir, for about 10 km one way. You first pass through the Cerrada de Elías, a narrow gorge where the path is cut into the rock above turquoise water - wooden walkways span the torrent. Higher up, the path crosses forests of century-old pines before reaching two mountain lakes, the Laguna de Aguas Negras and the Laguna de Valdeazores. Allow 6 to 7 hours return. Bring water, food and good shoes - there is no supply point along the trail.

activities.text: Cazorla is the ideal starting point for exploring the natural park, but it's also a town where you eat well. The restaurants around Plaza de la Constitución serve game (deer, wild boar), Segureño lamb, seasonal mushrooms, and of course Sierra de Cazorla PDO olive oil on everything. Rin-ran (cod, tomato, and pepper salad) is the local speciality. Dine early—mountain restaurants close earlier than in the city.

If you prefer a less strenuous option, local operators offer 4x4 excursions through the park, with stops at viewpoints and wildlife observation spots. The Tranco road runs along the great dam and crosses pine forests with spectacular views. You can also go kayaking on the embalse del Tranco - the artificial lake at the heart of the park, a day's round trip from Cazorla. It is from the lake that you have the best chance of seeing deer come down to drink at dusk.

days_plan.itin_title: Madrid to Cazorla: La Mancha, the Sierras of Jaén, and the Forgotten Renaissance
Madrid to Cazorla: La Mancha, the Sierras of Jaén, and the Forgotten Renaissance
Jaén Province Tour: Renaissance and Olive Trees

visits.text: The Fuenfría Valley Interpretation Center unveils the natural and cultural history of the valley. Permanent exhibitions showcase flora, fauna, and human heritage. Try the "Treasure of La Tuerta" scavenger hunt to discover the park's riches.
The Calzada Romana (Antonine Way XXIV) once linked Toledo to Segovia. Restored in 2009, this ancient section reveals the original Roman route. Informative panels line the path, marked by metal posts.

The 18th-century Puente del Descalzo spans the Arroyo de la Fuenfría. Three granite arches with stone benches built into the pillars. Commissioned by Philip V to connect the Royal Palace of La Granja.

Dense forests of Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris)—the best preserved in the Central System—rise on all sides. Oak, cherry, maple and ash mix near the Arroyo de la Venta. Clearings open to vast panoramas.
Puerto de la Fuenfría at 1,796 meters marks the boundary between Madrid and Segovia. A crossroads of historic paths where Calzada Romana, Calzada Borbónica and modern roads converge.

activities.text: Follow the Calzada Romana up to Puerto de la Fuenfría. A gentle ascent through pine forests, 641 meters of elevation over 7.9 km. Track the green circles painted on trees to stay on course.
The Camino Schmidt, laid out in 1926 by mountaineer Eduardo Schmidt, traces the base of Siete Picos. Mature Scots pine forests alternate with meadows. Follow white circles marking the way.
Return via the scenic mountain train (Cercanías C-9). This historic line snakes through the Sierra with spectacular views of valleys and peaks. Departs from Cercedilla station.

days_plan.itin_title: Sierra de Guadarrama Road Trip: Castles and Forests

visits.text: Castillo de Chinchilla, built by the Marquis of Villena in the 15th century on a hill that was Roman before being Islamic, served as a prison for three centuries. César Borgia was imprisoned there—in the highest tower, apparently. Only the exterior is freely accessible; the views over the Manchego plain from the ramparts justify the ascent. BIC status since the 19th century.

Two cannons mutilated by French troops in 1812 lie in front of the Baroque Ayuntamiento on Plaza Mayor de Chinchilla—it was the former provincial capital before Albacete snatched the title in 1833. The plaza hosts the Iglesia de Santa María del Salvador (14th-16th century), the Casino with glazed gallery, and the neoclassical Clock Tower. Free stroll.

days_plan.itin_title: Castilla-La Mancha: Windmills and Sierra in 11 days

visits.text: The road to Chulilla seems to lead nowhere—and that's exactly why you should go. The 400-inhabitant village perched on the Turia canyon is one of the region's most renowned climbing destinations, with routes opened on limestone cliffs over 200 meters high.

activities.text: The Turia canyon here is quite different from Valencia's: wild, steep-sided, populated by griffon vultures. The hanging bridges trail (pasarelas) connects two cliffs over a 3km easy walk. Start and finish from the Chulilla parking lot, total duration 2 hours with photo stops.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Valencia Road Trip: 10 Days of Villages

places.name: Ciudad Real

visits.text: The Catedral de Santa María del Prado surprises visitors with its extraordinarily long title: Priory of the Four Military Orders, basilica, and cathedral all rolled into one. Its single nave, 34 meters high, is the second-largest in Spain after Girona's. The altarpiece by Giraldo de Merlo, completed in 1616, is worth a look. Free admission.

Look for the Puerta de Toledo, a surviving remnant of the medieval walls. The double-arched Mudéjar gateway dates from the 14th century and marks the northern entrance to the old town. The city was founded in 1255 by Alfonso X the Wise under the name Villa Real.

The Museo del Quijote, right in the city center, offers an interactive journey through Cervantes' universe. Rooms recreate scenes from the novel using animatronics and projections. Free entry, closed Mondays.

activities.text: Sample pisto manchego in a downtown taberna: tomatoes, peppers, zucchini, and onions sautéed in olive oil, served with a fried egg. It's the region's signature dish, and every cook has their own version.

days_plan.itin_title: Campo de Calatrava and Valle de Alcudia in 5 Days

map_keywords: Santa María del Prado Cathedral Ciudad Real

visits.text: Santa Maria Cathedral, built between 1300 and 1365 in Catalan Gothic style, replaces a former mosque. Baroque altarpiece and an accessible bell tower.
Plaça des Born gathers 17th-century aristocratic palaces around a central obelisk commemorating the resistance against the Turks in 1558.
Ciutadella's harbor cuts inland like a fjord between the cliffs. Low quays lined with colorful facades and terraces facing the boats.
Palau Salort occasionally opens for guided tours. Aristocratic interiors, period furniture, and shaded patios.
Museu Palacio Can Saura displays ethnographic and archaeological collections. Remains of an Andalusian necropolis lie beneath the building.
Carrer Ses Voltes, lined with arcades, is home to shops and restaurants. Cobbled medieval streets of the historic center.

activities.text: The Sant Joan festival, on June 23 and 24, features black Menorcan horses rearing up among the crowd.
Chocolate-filled ensaimadas and formatjades can be enjoyed at bakeries in the old town.
The terraces of Plaça des Born come alive at dusk. Drinks facing the illuminated palaces and town hall.

days_plan.itin_title: Menorca Road Trip: Harbors, Whitewashed Villages & Coves

visits.text: El Capricho de Gaudí, built between 1883 and 1885, is one of the architect's rare works outside Catalonia. Its watchtower, sunflower ceramics and columned portico draw on oriental art.
The neo-Gothic Sobrellano Palace was commissioned by the Marquis of Comillas. Beside it, the chapel-pantheon in matching style houses the family tombs.

Climb toward the Pontifical University. This imposing neo-Gothic edifice with Mudéjar influences crowns the hill of La Cardosa. Its red-orange brick stands out against the green of the surrounding hills.
Comillas cemetery, enclosed by medieval walls, is crowned by the Ángel Exterminador, a modernist sculpture keeping watch over the graves facing the sea.
Descend to Plaza del Corro de Campios, the old town's heart. Mansions built by 'Indianos'—émigrés who returned wealthy from the Americas—line the cobbled streets.
The small fishing harbor and sandy beach nestle at the village's foot. The ocean horizon opens onto the dunes of Oyambre Natural Park.

activities.text: Savor octopus, baby squid and shellfish at the harbor restaurants. Cantabrian cuisine celebrates raw ingredients, simply cooked.
Follow the coast toward Oyambre Natural Park. The trail crosses dunes, cliffs and marshes rich in birdlife, with views over wild beaches.
Head to Oyambre beach in the late afternoon. The dunes gilded by the setting sun offer one of the most beautiful panoramas on the Cantabrian coast.

days_plan.itin_title: Cantabria Road Trip: Atlantic Bays and Picos de Europa

visits.text: Twelve white silhouettes on the Cerro Calderico ridge: Consuegra's mills all bear names from the Quijote—Chispas, Mambrino, Caballero del Verde Gabán. Five retain their original mechanism. Molino Rucio still grinds wheat; Bolero houses the tourist office. Free access to the ridge; guided interior visits from €8.

Castillo de la Muela crowns the same ridge, right next to the mills—a medieval castle whose walls witnessed, according to local tradition, the death of El Cid's son during the battle of 1097. The Cid's son dying in a windmill castle: La Mancha's history loves the melodramatic. Guided tours offered by the town.

Head down to the casco histórico to discover Plaza Mayor, the archaeological museum, and Casa de la Tercia. A tip from the tourist office: drive up to the ridge via the south-slope road (less crowded), and walk back down via the senda—4 km round trip, view over the entire La Mancha plain.

activities.text: Head to Cerro Calderico late afternoon. The golden light illuminates the white mills against endless plains—the perfect moment to photograph this icon of La Mancha.
The Consuegra region is one of the main terroirs for Spanish saffron. Local cooperatives offer tastings of olive oil and Manchego saffron.
Climb on foot from the parking at the bottom of the hill (20 min). The gradual ascent reveals the mills and castle one by one, adding suspense to the panorama.

days_plan.itin_title: La Mancha Road Trip: Don Quixote's Windmills and Cuenca
Castilla-La Mancha Route: In the Footsteps of Don Quixote
Castilla-La Mancha: Windmills and Sierra in 11 days

visits.text: The Mezquita-Cathedral of Córdoba is, without exaggeration, one of the most extraordinary monuments on the planet. Begun in 785 by Abd al-Rahman I on the site of a Visigothic basilica, enlarged three times over two centuries, then transformed into a cathedral after the Reconquest of 1236, it layers civilizations within a single 23,400 m² space. Upon entering, you're seized by the forest of more than 850 columns of marble, jasper, and granite—some salvaged from Roman and Visigothic ruins—connected by red-and-white bicolor arches that unfold as far as the eye can see. Push on to Al-Hakam II's mihrab: its golden and blue mosaics, created by artisans sent by the Byzantine emperor, rank among the finest in Islamic art. Then discover the Renaissance cathedral planted in the middle of the mosque—Charles V, who had authorized it, reportedly regretted upon visiting the works: 'You have destroyed what was unique to build what can be seen everywhere.' Arrive at 8:30 AM for free entry (until 9:30 AM)—after that, the queue grows quickly.

Leaving the Mezquita, lose yourself in the Judería, the medieval Jewish quarter that's part of Córdoba's UNESCO listing. Its whitewashed lanes so narrow you can touch both walls with outstretched arms, its patios glimpsed through half-open doors, its pots of geraniums clinging to facades—this is the image of Córdoba you'll take home. Don't miss the Calleja de las Flores, a tiny dead-end alley that opens onto a perfect perspective of the Mezquita's bell tower framed by flowers. The synagogue (14th century), one of only three preserved in Spain along with those in Toledo, can be visited in 15 minutes—it's small, but the Mudéjar stuccowork is remarkable.

The Alcázar de los Reyes Cristianos, built in 1328 by Alfonso XI on the ruins of a Moorish palace, is especially famous for its terraced gardens—rectangular pools bordered by clipped hedges, cypresses, and orange trees that descend toward the Guadalquivir. This is where Ferdinand and Isabella planned the conquest of Granada and where Christopher Columbus presented his project for a voyage to the Indies in 1486. The interior is sober—vaulted halls, Roman mosaics, and Arab baths—but the gardens at sunset are worth the visit.

Cross the Puente Romano, Córdoba's Roman bridge—331 meters, 16 arches, built in the 1st century BC under Augustus, rebuilt several times since. In the middle, pause before the statue of the Archangel Raphael, patron of the city. On the other side, the Torre de la Calahorra (12th century), a former Arab fortified gate, houses a small museum on the Córdoba of three cultures (Muslim, Jewish, Christian). But above all, turn around: the view of the Mezquita and the historic center from the bridge, especially in late afternoon, is the finest in Córdoba.

Devote the morning to Medina Azahara (Madinat al-Zahra), the caliphal city that's been a UNESCO site since 2018. Eight kilometers west of Córdoba, at the foot of the Sierra Morena, Abd al-Rahman III ordered in 936 the construction of an entire palatine city to serve as the seat of the Caliphate of Córdoba. Over 75 years, 10,000 workers built a city of 112 hectares on three terraces—royal palaces at the top, gardens and administration in the middle, mosque and dwellings at the bottom. Then, in 1010, the civil war that ended the caliphate reduced it to ashes. It remained buried for a millennium, until its rediscovery in 1910. Today, only 10% has been excavated, but the Salón Rico (official reception hall), with its arches and carved stone panels of insane delicacy, conveys the measure of what this 'Andalusian Versailles' once was. The museum at the base of the site is excellent—start there to understand what you're about to see. Allow at least 2.5 hours.

Back in the city in the afternoon, visit the Palacio de Viana, nicknamed the 'Museum of Patios.' This aristocratic palace built between the 14th and 18th centuries has 12 patios and a garden—each with its own style, fountains, columns, and vegetation. It's the best way to understand Córdoba's patio culture, inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list since 2012 (Festival of the Patios, in May). If you're there in May, the private patios of the San Basilio and Alcázar Viejo neighborhoods open to the public—it's a spectacle of flowers, colors, and popular pride.

Push on to the Roman Temple on Calle Claudio Marcelo—the eleven Corinthian columns of this 1st-century temple, dedicated to imperial cult, recall that Córdoba was the capital of Roman Baetica and the birthplace of Seneca and Lucan. Just beside it, the remains of the Roman theater (the largest in Spain in its time) are visible in the cellars of the Archaeological Museum.

Return to Córdoba for the final day, devoted to the less touristy neighborhoods. Start with the Plaza del Potro, mentioned by Cervantes in Don Quixote—the inn bordering it is where Sancho Panza supposedly lodged. The square houses the Museo de Bellas Artes (in the former Hospital de la Caridad, 15th century) and the Museo Julio Romero de Torres, dedicated to the most popular Córdoban painter of the early 20th century, famous for his portraits of Andalusian women with intense gazes.

Head up toward the San Lorenzo neighborhood, one of the most authentic in Córdoba. The church of San Lorenzo (13th century), with its Gothic rose window and arcaded portico, is one of the 'Fernandine churches' built after the Reconquest of 1236—Ferdinand III had 14 parishes constructed in the reconquered city. The neighborhood is calm, residential, with flowery patios you'll only glimpse by craning your neck through half-open doors—this is the Córdoba of Córdobans, far from the tourist groups of the Judería.

Finish with the Palacio de la Merced (18th century), an imposing Baroque building that now serves as the seat of the Provincial Council. Its two-level cloister, with pink marble columns and azulejos, is one of the finest Baroque spaces in Córdoba. Entry is free and the place is rarely mentioned in guidebooks.

A cathedral in the middle of a former mosque: the Mezquita-Catedral de Córdoba makes you examine the site’s layers. The rows of arches and the central Christian space create different perspectives, making this a monument that cannot be understood from a single vantage point. The contrast speaks for itself, without a stream of figures about the columns. Book a cultural visit on the official website, check worship times, and allow plenty of time to explore the areas open to visitors.

Allow time for the gardens of the Alcázar de los Reyes Cristianos after the more confined spaces of downtown. The pools and plantings are part of the route, while the accessible rooms and towers offer another way to understand the fortress. Access may vary depending on construction work and visiting conditions. Plan to see the gardens during the first hours after opening and bring water, especially if you continue afterward through the streets of the Judería.

A small room is enough to bring a change of scale at the Sinagoga de Córdoba. In the narrow streets of the Judería, its decoration preserves another trace of the city’s religious history, distinct from the large neighboring complexes. The visit is short, but the inscriptions and details reward unhurried attention. Include the synagogue in your walk through the Judería and examine the wall inscriptions before heading back toward the mosque-cathedral.

Medina Azahara is worth the trip for its landscape as much as its remains. The terraces of this palatial city, commissioned by Abd al-Rahman III, place caliphal power beyond Córdoba’s narrow streets; preservation and access vary across the site. The interpretation center helps you understand the structures that have disappeared. Start at the interpretation center, then head to the ruins; allow for the return to Córdoba within the same sightseeing window.

The Puente Romano de Córdoba draws your attention above all to the two riverbanks. From the pedestrian crossing, the silhouette of the Mezquita-Catedral takes its place in the Guadalquivir landscape, while the opposite bank offers a different perspective on the city. The bridge has undergone changes throughout its history: its name does not tell the whole story of what you see. Come as the light fades, then spend some time on the riverbank instead of immediately crossing back.

activities.text: In the evening, settle into the taverns of the San Basilio neighborhood or the Plaza de la Corredera for a tapas crawl. Córdoba is a city of generous tapas: salmorejo (cold tomato soup thicker than gazpacho, served with ham and hard-boiled egg), flamenquines (breaded ham and pork roll), berenjenas con miel (fried aubergines with honey), and a glass of Montilla-Moriles, the local fortified wine that resembles sherry but with its own character. The Plaza de la Corredera, the only enclosed square plaza in Andalusia (17th century), is perfect for starting.

If you're in Córdoba between May and June, don't miss the flamenco shows in the peñas flamencas of the Santiago and San Lorenzo neighborhoods—more intimate and authentic venues than the tourist tablaos. Córdoba's flamenco guitar tradition is distinct, inherited from Paco Peña and Vicente Amigo.

For your final evening, treat yourself to dinner in the Plaza de las Tendillas or San Miguel neighborhood, where the tapas bars are frequented by locals rather than tourists. Order a salmorejo (the Córdoban version is the most authentic in Andalusia), rabo de toro (braised oxtail, Córdoba's emblematic dish), and a glass of Montilla-Moriles amontillado. From Córdoba, you can take the AVE back to Madrid, Seville, or Málaga, or continue by car toward Jaén (our 'Madrid to Cazorla' itinerary) or toward Granada.

If you want to walk between two reserved visits, the Judería de Córdoba offers a compact loop. Its narrow streets connect small squares and buildings whose patios are sometimes visible, but the patio festival and regular opening arrangements follow different rules. Choose patios with organized visits and leave private courtyards to their residents. Set out on foot from the mosque-cathedral area, enjoy the shade, and respect private entrances.

places.name: Coria

visits.text: Start the day at the Monastery of Yuste, a European Heritage site nestled in the Sierra de Gredos foothills near Cuacos de Yuste. This is where Charles V—Charles I of Spain and V of the Holy Roman Empire, the most powerful man in the world—chose to retire after abdicating in 1556 in favor of his son Philip II. He arrived on February 3, 1557, with an entourage of about sixty people. His chamber was positioned against the church choir so he could attend mass from his bed—he suffered from terrible gout that confined him to his litter. He died here on September 21, 1558, at age 58, from malarial fevers. The visit shows both cloisters (one Gothic, one Renaissance), the 15th-century church, and the emperor's apartments—surprisingly austere for the man who'd ruled an empire where the sun never set.

Head to Coria in the afternoon. This town is the ancient Caurium of the Vettones, which later became a Roman municipality. Its Roman walls, built between the third and fourth centuries, form a remarkable ensemble: more than 1,100 meters of ramparts with around twenty square towers and four gates, including two of Roman origin (Puerta del Sol and Puerta de la Guía). In places the walls are 8 meters thick. Walk around them—the circuit takes about 30 minutes, and it's striking to think that these stones have stood here for 1,700 years.

Coria Cathedral, built between the fifteenth and eighteenth centuries on the remains of a Visigothic church, combines Gothic, Plateresque and Baroque styles. Its Plateresque façade is remarkable, as is its Churrigueresque tower with fine views over the town and countryside. The cathedral houses an extraordinary relic: what is said to be the tablecloth of Christ's Last Supper, mentioned in a papal bull of 1404. Tourist visits are closed on Mondays.

Don't miss the bridge without a river—Coria's most surreal image. This five-arched stone bridge, built in the 16th century probably on earlier Roman foundations, spanned the Río Alagón. But the river changed course—likely gradually following floods, worsened by the 1755 Lisbon earthquake—and now flows several hundred meters away. Result: a bridge without a river and a river without a bridge. Walk under the arches for the best photo, especially late afternoon.

If you still have daylight, plan a drive from Coria to Granadilla, a fascinating ghost village. This fortified town of Almohad origin (ninth century), which governed 15 municipalities in the Middle Ages, was emptied of its inhabitants in 1955 when the Franco regime decided to build the Gabriel y Galán dam. Cruelly, the water never reached the village. Declared a Conjunto Histórico-Artístico in 1980, it has been partly restored through an educational program. You can explore the cobbled lanes, the circular wall, and the fifteenth-century castle built by the Duke of Alba, whose terrace has striking views over the reservoir and hills.

activities.text: In the evening in Coria, try dulces de las monjas—cloistered convent sweets. The town's convents sell handmade pastries (quemados, dulces de yema) through a rotating hatch, without seeing the nuns who make them. It's a typically Spanish tradition that persists in Extremadura's small towns.

visits.text: The Corralejo Dunes Natural Park stretches across 2,600 hectares. These white dunes, formed from disintegrated seashells and marine organisms, contrast with the dark volcanic rock.
Climb Montaña Roja, a 314-meter volcano at the park's southern edge. The summit rewards you with 360-degree panoramas over the dunes, the ocean, and Lobos Island.
The Grandes Playas stretch for 10 kilometers. Immaculate white sand, turquoise waters, and unobstructed views toward Lobos and Lanzarote. Stone wind shelters called corralitos protect from the wind.
Flag Beach draws surfers and kitesurfers. The steady Atlantic winds create ideal conditions for water sports.

activities.text: Take the ferry to Lobos Island, a 6-square-kilometer protected nature reserve. Once home to a colony of sea lions, the island now shelters the Punta Martiño lighthouse and preserved volcanic landscapes.
Swim in the shallow lagoons sheltered by reefs. Watch for strong currents in certain areas—check the flags.
The Kite Festival in November draws participants from across the globe. Multicolored kites dance across the natural park's skies throughout an entire weekend.

days_plan.itin_title: Fuerteventura Road Trip: Dunes, Lagoons & Villages

visits.text: The Jameos del Agua, about thirty minutes' drive from Costa Teguise, are César Manrique's first major work on Lanzarote, opened to the public in 1966. The site lies in a lava tunnel formed by the eruption of the Corona volcano around 4,000 years ago - a 6 km tube of which 1.5 km continues under the ocean (the Atlantis Tunnel). You descend through the Jameo Chico to an underground saltwater lake, fed by the Atlantic, home to blind albino crabs (Munidopsis polymorpha) 1 cm long, endemic to this spot. Do not throw any coins into the water - the rust kills them. The visit continues to the Jameo Grande, an open-air cave with a turquoise pool and an auditorium seating 600 people. Book your ticket online to avoid the queue.

Cueva de los Verdes lies minutes from Jameos—it's the same Corona volcanic tube, but here the roof remained intact for nearly a kilometre. The guided tour (mandatory) takes you through geological formations lit by a system designed by Manrique that enhances colours without altering the rock. The cave was used in the 17th century as a refuge by locals fleeing pirates. The visit also hides a visual surprise: prepare for a memorable optical illusion that guides never reveal in advance.

Jardín de Cactus in Guatiza is César Manrique's final major work, inaugurated in 1990—he built it in a former abandoned quarry as a vegetable amphitheater. The garden houses about 4,500 cactus specimens from 500 species originating from five continents, planted on black volcanic stone terraces. The area was historically dedicated to prickly pear cultivation for cochineal dye. At the entrance, an 8-meter cactus sculpture signed by Manrique welcomes you. Allow 45 minutes for the visit.

activities.text: Detour to the César Manrique Foundation in Tahíche. The artist built his house directly on the lava flows of 1730, incorporating five natural volcanic bubbles into the architecture. Since his death in 1992, it has been a museum showing his works and those of international contemporaries. This is where his philosophy is best understood: art and nature must coexist without one crushing the other.

Volcanic malvasía tasting at one of La Geria's vineyards, en route to Costa Teguise. This protected designation of origin produces white wine from grape varieties planted in pits dug into volcanic lapilli, surrounded by semicircular stone walls (zocos) that protect from wind. The landscape is so singular that a photo of La Geria was exhibited in 1964 at New York's MoMA in the “Architecture Without Architects” exhibition.
A late-afternoon swim on one of Costa Teguise's beaches. Or head up to Haría and the Valley of a Thousand Palms - a green oasis in the northern hills, about thirty minutes' drive from Costa Teguise.

days_plan.itin_title: Lanzarote & La Palma: Volcanoes and the Art of César Manrique

visits.text: The Cova des Culleram, a Punic sanctuary dedicated to goddess Tanit, hides at 150 m altitude in the mountain. Discovered in 1907, the site yielded hundreds of terracotta figurines now displayed in Eivissa's museum. The atmosphere inside remains striking.

activities.text: Allow 20 min walk from parking on a steep, rocky trail. The sanctuary opens April to October, Tuesday to Sunday, 10:30 AM–1:30 PM, free entry. Bring a flashlight to see inside.

days_plan.itin_title: Ibiza & Formentera by Scooter: Calas & Beaches in 7 Days

places.name: Covarrubias

visits.text: The Collegiate Church of San Cosme y San Damián, a 15th-century Gothic gem, houses the tombs of Count Fernán González and his wife in 4th-century Hispano-Roman sarcophagi. The 16th-century cloister preserves the sepulcher of Princess Kristina of Norway, who journeyed from Scandinavia in 1257 to marry a Castilian prince.

Step inside the Collegiate Treasury Museum to admire the Adoration of the Magi triptych, a polychrome wooden masterpiece attributed to Gil de Siloé. Also on display: a Virgin painting attributed to Van Eyck, a canvas by Pedro Berruguete, and the 1620 organ—the oldest still functioning in Castile.

The Torreón de Fernán González, a 10th-century Mozarabic defensive tower, rises at the end of half-timbered streets. Its stone walls are the oldest remnants of the fortified enclosure that once protected the capital of the first County of Castile.

Enter the old town through the arch of the Archives of the Adelantamiento de Castilla, a 16th-century Renaissance building adorned with Philip II's coat of arms. In front of the arch stands a Gothic stone calvary.

Wander around Plaza de Doña Urraca, bordered by the town hall housed in the former palace of Fernán González. The cobbled streets around the square reveal half-timbered houses built with juniper wood on stilts, like the Casa del Obispo Peña with its carved corbels and the house of Doña Sancha with wooden balconies.

The Church of Santo Tomás, dating from the 15th century, preserves a Renaissance pulpit and beautiful altarpieces. Less visited than the collegiate church, it's worth a look for its peaceful atmosphere and quality woodwork.

activities.text: Walk down to the banks of the Arlanza for a riverside stroll. The path follows the remains of the old walls and offers a sweeping view of the village and its tiled roofs.
The Arlanza Valley produces wines under the AO Arlanza designation. Pair them with local sheep's cheese and valley cherries, a village specialty for centuries.

At the end of the day, the half-timbered façades take on golden hues in the setting sun. Plaza de Doña Urraca and the surrounding lanes provide a fine setting in which to appreciate the village's medieval atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Castile and León Road Trip: Cathedrals and Villages

Archivo del Adelantamiento de Castilla Covarrubias

visits.text: First shock on arrival: the houses cling to the void. The Casas Colgadas date from the 14th-15th centuries, their wooden balconies projecting over a hundred-meter gorge with no apparent support. Originally there were dozens running along the cliff; only three remain. Two have housed the Spanish Abstract Art Museum since 1966—a magnificent juxtaposition of late Gothic and works by Tàpies or Saura. The best vantage point isn't from the houses but from the iron bridge of San Pablo opposite: a slightly vertiginous footbridge, avoid if you're prone to vertigo.

Cuenca's cathedral is more discreet but surprising: begun in the late 12th century after the reconquest, it's one of Spain's rare examples of Anglo-Norman Gothic, with a neo-Gothic façade rebuilt in 1902 after the tower collapsed. Note the modern stained glass by Henri Dechanet, Bonifacio Alfonso and Gustavo Torner, installed in the 1990s: a quite successful dialogue with the medieval stone. Combined ticket for cathedral, treasury and Tribuna del Pontifical, around €6.

Climb to the Castillo at the northern tip of the old town. Almost nothing remains of the Arab fortifications, but the entrance arch and especially the viewpoint beyond give the most complete view of the upper city's layout, with the two V-shaped gorges on either side. Well windswept, allow twenty minutes to climb without rushing. Descend via Calle San Pedro and its old ochre-façaded houses—one of the city's most beautiful stepped streets.

activities.text: If you're here during Holy Week, don't miss Las Turbas on Good Friday at dawn: hundreds of hooded figures parade drumming and blowing trumpets, their lamentations echoing through the canyon from 5:30am. The tradition dates back at least to the 17th century. Outside this period, the Hoz del Huécar can be walked, a marked trail of about 4 km from the bridge below, return by the stairs—good idea just before sunset for the colors on the cliff.

Dinner at Figón del Huécar, former home of singer Plácido Domingo transformed into a restaurant: terrace hanging over the gorge, well-executed Castilian cuisine (pickled partridge, morteruelo, ajoarriero—a local cod pâté). Try the resolí, local coffee and herb liqueur, as a digestif. Reservations recommended on weekends.

visits.text: Tiny and nearly forgotten, Culla nonetheless appears in Spain's national roster of most beautiful villages. Fewer than 50 permanent residents, limestone-white lanes, and the ruins of a 12th-century Templar castle. The visit takes 90 minutes—take your time finding the house with red geraniums, which is the bakery.

If the sky is clear, the panorama from the old watchtower rewards the 10-minute climb. On fine days you can make out the Columbretes Islands to the east—a spectacle that locals reserve for curious visitors who ask the way. The tower isn't signposted: it's just behind the church.

places.name: Daimiel

visits.text: Small (just 3,030 hectares), Tablas de Daimiel National Park is the last representative of Spain's 'fluvial table' wetlands—two rivers with different salinities (the Guadiana and the Cigüela) meet here, creating a unique ecosystem. The wooden walkways of the Ruta de la Isla del Pan (2 km circular) let you advance into the heart of the reeds without damaging the ground. Free entry.

Classified a National Park in 1973, then a Ramsar site in 1982, Tablas de Daimiel shelters purple heron, common crane, and white-headed duck. The Ruta de la Laguna Permanente (1.5 km) offers water and ducks in all seasons. Start at the Molino de Molemocho Visitor Centre for free context.

activities.text: If you arrive at dawn, the aquatic warbler sings in the carrizos and cranes take off above the water mirror—the visual spectacle is well worth the rough wake-up. Sunset is equally effective. Avoid summer afternoons: heat, midges, birds gone to shade. Binoculars recommended.

places.name: Daroca

visits.text: Final stop: Daroca, in the Jiloca valley. This town of 2,000 inhabitants has one of Spain's longest fortified circuits: 4 km of walls bristling with 114 towers, built from the 9th century by the Arabs and enlarged after the Christian conquest by Alfonso I the Battler in 1120. Enter through the Puerta Baja (14th century), an impressive tunnel-like gate that also served as a drain for the river - note the Fuente de los Veinte Caños (Fountain of the Twenty Spouts) just outside. Walk up the Calle Mayor, the town's backbone, between brick Mudéjar churches (San Miguel, San Juan, Santo Domingo) and noble palaces.

The Basilica of Santa María de los Sagrados Corporales, at the town's heart, is one of Aragon's most remarkable. It houses the relics of a Eucharistic miracle that occurred in 1239 during the Battle of Chío, when six consecrated hosts supposedly survived intact wrapped in the corporals despite the heat of battle. The main altarpiece, the Chapel of the Corporals, and the adjacent museum merit careful attention. Exit through the Puerta Alta (15th century), adorned with Charles V's coat of arms.

activities.text: Climb up to the Castillo Mayor via the path that follows the ramparts. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for the return walk. The wall walk lets you visit several towers in succession and offers views down over the town squeezed between the two ridges and the Jiloca valley. From the castle, the panorama takes in cereal fields, red clay hills and, on clear days, the sierras of the Iberian System. Bring good shoes and water – there is no shade on the ramparts.

From Daroca, you can continue towards Teruel (1 hour 30 minutes to the south) to join the “Aragonese Pyrenees and Lower Aragon” itinerary (UNESCO Mudéjar towers), or head back up to Zaragoza (1 hour 15 minutes to the north). Daroca is also a starting point for visiting the village of Anento (15 km), a member of Spain's Most Beautiful Villages, with its waterfall and hanging gardens.

places.name: Deltebre

visits.text: The Ebro Delta, 320 km² of rice paddies, lagoons, and beaches, is the second-largest delta in the western Mediterranean after the Rhône Delta. A natural park since 1983, it shelters over 300 bird species including 30% of Spain's flamingos—approximately 4,000 overwintering birds. The first shock upon arrival: no hills, not a tree, just water and rice paddies as far as the eye can see, crossed by irrigation canals inherited from the Moors. A feeling of being at the edge of the world. The best approach: explore it by bike.

The Ecomuseu del Delta in Deltebre is an essential stop for understanding the delta—600 m² of exhibits on its formation (created over 1,500 years by Ebro sediments, but receding since the construction of upstream dams that retain 99% of the silt), rice cultivation (planted in April, harvested in September), and eel fishing. A small aquarium with local species. Allow 1 hour, €4. Combine with a traditional boat ride (perxana) for €6—the last boat used by rice farmers before motorization.

The Far del Fangar, at the tip of the delta's northern peninsula, is an 1864 lighthouse (24 m high), reached along a 6 km sandy track. Shifting white dunes reaching 8 m, nesting birds (plovers and terns), and giant shells along the shore. A protected site, accessible only on foot. Views over Fangar Bay (oyster and mussel farming); sample the oysters and mussels afterward at the mussel farms in Deltebre. Strange, flat, sublime.

activities.text: Rise before 7am: that's when flamingos arrive by the hundreds at the Encanyissada and Tancada lagoons. Watch from the free viewing platforms; binoculars are useful. Avoid Mosquéro (fierce insects). The complete delta bike loop covers 50 flat kilometers—rental at Bicicletes del Delta (Deltebre) for €15 per day. Paved paths along the canals, little shade; bring 3 liters of water per person in July–August. Rice is harvested in September, with a golden landscape ideal for photos.

For lunch, arròs negre—black rice with cuttlefish ink—or arròs a banda (rice cooked in fish broth, served separately) are delta classics. Casa Nuri in Riumar is one of the leading names; expect €25–30 for the set menu. Delta rice (Bahia or Bomba variety, Arròs del Delta PDO) holds up perfectly during cooking—an inimitable texture. Ask for a bottle of Terra Alta, a little-known neighboring PDO.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Catalonia in 10 Days: Tarragona, Priorat & the Ebro Delta
