map_keywords: Trabucador Beach Sant Carles de la Ràpita

visits.text: A UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy since 2015, Dénia earned its stripes through its celebrated red prawn—the gamba roja—and its rice dishes rooted in Arab tradition. The 11th-century Almohad castle watches over the sea from its hilltop: built by successive occupiers, its walls blend Moorish architecture with Renaissance additions. Climb early in the morning when the raking light over the bay is at its finest. Paid entry, audioguide available.

The salt air, the brightly painted wooden hulls, the tightly packed fishermen's houses: the Baix la Mar quarter captures everything Dénia has managed to preserve despite the tourism. Squeezed between the castle and the twin marinas, this little maze takes thirty minutes to walk through but deserves longer. Finish with a coffee on the Paseo de Cervantes watching the ferries depart for Ibiza—the closest mainland port to the Balearics.

activities.text: Touristy without excess, the Montgó (753 m) towers over Dénia and Jávea in a way that makes you want to put away the beach towels. Several marked trails allow you to explore the park, ranging from 1h40 to 6h of walking. In summer, set off before 8am and carry at least two liters of water - the park rangers stress this.

days_plan.itin_title: Costa Blanca & Alicante Hinterland: 12 days

visits.text: Don Benito doesn't appear in any mainstream guidebook, and that's just as well. The Plaza de España is vast, lined with café terraces and dominated by the Iglesia de Santiago Apóstol, an imposing 16th-century Gothic-Renaissance building with a baroque-Herrerian façade. It's the natural starting point for entering La Serena.

The Iglesia de Santiago Apóstol, dating from the 16th century, blends late Gothic interiors with baroque-Herrerian exteriors. Large, austere, tourist-free. Remodelled in 1965, it lost some charm but kept its imposing bulk. Free entry, open in the morning.

The Museo Etnográfico smells of waxed wood and raw wool. Opened in 2000 thanks to donations from locals, it brings together 19th- and 20th-century objects: farming tools, costumes, kitchen utensils. Small but sincere. Calle Pedro Granada, behind the Palacio Municipal.
Make a detour to the Museo del Automóvil Clásico, near the station. Over 200 vintage cars, from the 1900s to the 1970s. Unexpected in an Extremaduran town, but well maintained. Allow 30 minutes.

activities.text: Start at the Plaza de España late morning: the bars serve café con leche and the tapa of the day for next to nothing. The monument to water and earth at the centre sums up the town's agricultural identity. Local atmosphere guaranteed.
Locals call La Velá their most popular festival, in September. If you're visiting off-season, the Ruta del Aperitivo offers a bar crawl with local tapas. Ask at the tourist office, Plaza de España.

days_plan.itin_title: La Siberia and La Serena: Secret Extremadura in 6 Days

places.name: Donana

visits.text: Doñana National Park, created in 1969, spans 54,000 hectares of marshlands, shifting dunes, pine forests, and Mediterranean scrub at the mouth of the Guadalquivir. Designated a Biosphere Reserve and UNESCO World Heritage site, it is home to Western Europe's largest wetland and over 360 bird species.

Off-road vehicle tours cover 70 kilometers through the park's four ecosystems in 4 hours: beach and shifting dunes reaching 30 meters high, flooded marshlands, wooded reserves, and the banks of the Guadalquivir. Guides identify flamingos, imperial eagles, deer, fallow deer, and marsh horses.

The village of El Rocío, with its packed-earth streets and low white houses, seems frozen in another era. The Ermita del Rocío, a Marian sanctuary, draws over a million pilgrims each spring during the Romería, one of Spain's largest pilgrimages.

El Acebuche Visitor Center, the park's main gateway, offers marked walking trails and bird observatories. The more remote José Antonio Valverde Visitor Center, accessible by 4x4, has a large window overlooking the marshlands, through which flamingo colonies can be observed at water level.

Palacio del Acebrón, near the Arroyo de la Rocina, houses an exhibition on the park's ecosystems. A circular trail through gallery forest allows you to interpret animal tracks and discover plant species endemic to Doñana.

activities.text: Rise before dawn for a birdwatching session. Doñana sits at a migratory crossroads between Europe, Africa, and Asia: over 500,000 waterbirds winter here annually. Flamingos, spoonbills, storks, glossy ibises, and gray herons create a constant spectacle.

With a little patience and a lot of luck, you may catch a glimpse of the Iberian lynx. Around twenty individuals live in the park or on its outskirts. The wooded areas crossed towards the end of the day on the 4x4 tour are the most promising.

For over five centuries, Almonte ranchers have held the Saca de las Yeguas on June 26: hundreds of mares and foals cross the park in a spectacular seasonal migration. At other times, horseback rides in the park's peripheral areas offer immersion in the dune and forest landscapes.

days_plan.itin_title: Cádiz Road Trip: Jerez, Bodegas and White Villages
Huelva, the Forgotten Land: Doñana to Faro in 7 Days

map_keywords: Centro de Visitantes El Acebuche Doñana

visits.text: The scent of warm stone rises from the cobbled lanes of Dalt Vila as soon as you pass through the Portal de ses Taules, flanked by two headless Roman statues. This Renaissance fortress, a UNESCO site since 1999, commands the harbor from atop Puig de Vila. Arrive early morning or after 6 PM to escape the scorching heat.

Founded by the Phoenicians around 654 BC, the necropolis of Puig des Molins contains over 3,000 visible Punic tombs. The adjacent museum displays terracotta figurines and Egyptian scarabs unearthed on site. Closed Mondays, €3 entry.

Push open the door of the Museu d'Art Contemporani, housed in an 18th-century bastion at the summit of Dalt Vila. The collection blends local artists with international pieces, but it's the terrace with its plunging harbor views that steals the show. Free on Wednesdays.

Touristy by night, but Eivissa's harbor remains photogenic with its colorful llaüts and Dalt Vila glowing in the background. Quayside restaurants charge premium prices: duck into a backstreet for better value.

activities.text: On selected summer evenings, the Las Dalias night market, around 28 km from Eivissa, a 35-minute drive, offers handmade jewellery, dyed clothing and live music in a garden lit by lanterns. The atmosphere remains resolutely hippie.
Take time for dinner on a terrace in La Marina quarter, below the ramparts. The tapas bars on Carrer de la Verge serve generous portions at fair prices, far from the tourist traps by the harbor.

days_plan.itin_title: Ibiza & Formentera by Scooter: Calas & Beaches in 7 Days

visits.text: Two kinds of goat, one denomination: El Bosque's payoyo cheese is the pride of the sierra gaditana. The small local Museo del Queso explains production in 20 minutes. The village itself is modest, but its position on the Majaceite river makes it the greenest gateway to the Grazalema park.

The El Castillejo botanical garden, on the village edge, brings together the endemic species of the natural park in a few hundred meters - potted pinsapos, cistus, local medicinal plants. Small but educational, and free. A good introduction before entering the sierra.

activities.text: The green waters of the Majaceite flow between reeds as tall as a person — the riverside trail from El Bosque to Benamahoma (about 10 km and 3 hours round trip) is the most popular in Grazalema Natural Park, and for good reason: it is almost flat, shaded all year round, with trout visible in the pools. Swimming is prohibited, but the cool air is enough.

days_plan.itin_title: White Villages: Arcos, Grazalema, Ronda - 6 Days

places.name: El Cotillo

visits.text: El Cotillo's lagoons (Playa de los Lagos) stretch from the village to the lighthouse. These natural swimming pools, protected by coral reefs, offer immaculate white sand and crystalline waters.
The Torre del Tostón, an 18th-century circular fortress, once defended the port from pirate raids. Thick local stone walls, a drawbridge, and quarters designed for 12 men.

The Faro del Tostón lighthouse complex includes three structures built in 1897, 1955, and 1986. The site houses the Museum of Traditional Fishing, chronicling the village's historic bond with the sea.
Playa de La Concha curves like a crescent moon of white sand. Shallow emerald waters make it perfect for families. Despite its proximity to the village, the beach retains a wild character.
Explore the old fishing harbor with its colorful boats. Fishermen continue their traditional activities, delivering fresh fish daily to local restaurants.

activities.text: Feast on grilled fish and seafood at the harbor restaurants. Fresh squid, vieja parrotfish, and fish stew are the local specialties.
The surf spots south of the village draw surfers, windsurfers, and kitesurfers. Powerful Atlantic waves and steady winds.
Watch the sunset from the old harbor or lighthouse. El Cotillo faces due west, offering spectacular views over the Atlantic Ocean.

days_plan.itin_title: Fuerteventura Road Trip: Dunes, Lagoons & Villages

map_keywords: Playa de La Concha El Cotillo
Playa de los Charcos El Cotillo

visits.text: The fishermen of El Palmar served this rice dish with duck and eels long before Valencia claimed it. The Albufera is a coastal lagoon of around 2,800 hectares separated from the sea by a strip of dunes—the ecological birthplace of Valencian rice cultivation. Arrive at sunset to watch the lake turn red-orange.

activities.text: If you rent a barco, skirt the reed beds to the north: ducks and grey herons are denser there and local guides avoid that corner. Boat trips from El Palmar or El Saler, duration 1 hour, guide not compulsory but useful for identifying birds.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Valencia Road Trip: 10 Days of Villages

visits.text: Transition stop in the heart of the Catalan Pyrenees. El Pont de Suert (841 m altitude) is the capital of Alta Ribagorça, midway between Lleida and Vall de Boí. Mentioned as early as 1016, the town developed at a crossroads between valleys—hence its role as a historic market. Plaça Major and Plaça del Mercadal form the medieval center, and Església Vella (Romanesque origin, modified in the 18th) warrants a quick detour. Not touristy, sincere yes: we sleep here because it's on the route, not for anything else.

Small curiosity 3 km south, on the road to La Pobla: the ruins of Lavaix monastery on the edge of the Escales reservoir. Founded in the 11th century, abandoned in the 19th, it was partially submerged by dam waters from 1950—when the level drops, the vestiges reappear. Photos guaranteed if you hit the right season.

activities.text: Dinner at Hotel Cotori or Lavaix, two village institutions. No-fuss mountain cuisine: wild boar stew, river trout, Alta Ribagorça cheese. Good bill for €25-30. Typical Pyrenean family welcome, and after a day on the road it feels good.

days_plan.itin_title: Catalonia - Complete 24-Day Grand Tour

visits.text: A ghost town 51 weeks out of 52, a city of hundreds of thousands of pilgrims during Pentecost week. The streets are sandy—not from neglect, but because horses still travel along them. In front of every house with a veranda: rings for tethering horses. The Ermita de Nuestra Señora del Rocío, facing the lagoon, is open year-round.

Flamingos landing on the lagoon beside the village, just meters from the first restaurants—that's what makes El Rocío distinctive. The Doñana marshes begin here. Take time to walk along the shore early in the morning, before tourists arrive for the day.

Sand replaces paving underfoot around the Ermita del Rocío. The shrine forms the center of a community shaped by pilgrimage, with broad streets suited to horses. Enter quietly if the church is open, and avoid timing this brief stop to coincide with a major celebration.

The Plaza del Acebuchal offers a different sense of scale in El Rocío, defined more by greenery than monuments. Its name refers to the wild olive trees in the square: a simple stop after the shrine. Stay on the public paths and enjoy the trees’ shade before getting back on the road to Seville.

activities.text: Follow the sandy streets on foot or on horseback: horses can be rented from the ranchos on the village edge. The outing to the lagoon viewpoint takes 30 minutes. Bring water. In intense heat, flamingos move deeper into the park—morning remains the best time.

Walk along the Paseo Marismeño to look for birds without entering the protected areas. This marsh edge offers a window onto Doñana, but water conditions and the species you can see vary with the season. Bring binoculars and check access; this short walk replaces a long guided excursion.

days_plan.itin_title: Huelva, the Forgotten Land: Doñana to Faro in 7 Days
Algarve, Andalusia, and Alentejo Road Trip in 20 Days

visits.text: The UNESCO-listed palm grove, designated in 2000, unfolds its fronds in the heart of the city—a landscape laid out in the late 10th century during construction of the Islamic settlement. More than 200,000 palms across 144 hectares, half of them date palms. It's the largest palm grove in Europe, and the irrigation practice inherited from al-Andalus—the tandeo system—remains active today.

activities.text: Gardeners call it the tandeo, this water distribution system inherited from the Arab period: each orchard receives water in turn, according to a thousand-year-old calendar. The Municipal Park, at the heart of the palm grove, offers guided tours (inquire at the tourist office). The Alcudia museum and its Iberian collections round out the day nicely. Elche is also the capital of Spanish footwear—factory outlets abound.

days_plan.itin_title: Costa Blanca & Alicante Hinterland: 12 days

visits.text: Ibiza's first official nudist beach and a pioneer in Spain, Es Cavallet stretches 1,100 m of white sand between dunes and pine forest. The central section is naturist, the northern tip draws celebrities to Chiringuito, and the south hosts the gay-friendly scene. On clear days you see Dalt Vila and Formentera.

activities.text: Dunes ripple between pines and salt basins in shifting colors: the scooter ride through the marshes to reach Es Cavallet is an attraction in itself. Stop to photograph the roadside mountains of salt.

days_plan.itin_title: Ibiza & Formentera by Scooter: Calas & Beaches in 7 Days

places.name: Falset

visits.text: Falset, capital of the Priorat comarca, preserves its medieval center around Plaça de la Quartera. Its 3,200 inhabitants live from wine and it shows: stone farmers' houses, sloping lanes and a 12th-century castle at the top. The partly ruined castell belonged to the Counts of Prades. This is where people say “I am going to Priorat” even when they are already there.

Falset's cooperative winery (1919), designed by Cèsar Martinell, a student of Gaudí, is one of some forty Modernist "wine cathedrals" he built in Catalonia between 1917 and 1923; seven have been nationally protected cultural assets since 2002. Exposed brick, Catalan fan vaults, interior air stays at a constant 16°C in summer. Tour and tasting €12, two cooperative wines included—Étim Verema Tardana in white, harvested in late November, is remarkable. Allow 75 minutes.

The Castell de Falset-Museu Comarcal occupies the former castle of the Counts of Prades at the top of the town. Its rooms present the history of Priorat, from prehistory through the Iberian, Roman, medieval and modern periods, using objects from the Centre d'Estudis Falsetans and interactive displays. A temporary exhibition completes the route. The visit also explains the castle's role in the birth of Falset.

The Scala Dei Charterhouse, 25 km from Falset, is the cradle of Priorat viticulture. Founded in 1194 by Carthusian monks from Provence on the orders of King Alfonso II, this is where the first vines were planted and where the word "priorat" takes its meaning—the entire region depended spiritually and economically on this charterhouse. The majestic ruins, partially restored, include a monk's cell reconstructed identically. Entry €5, French audioguide included.

Siurana is perched at 737 meters on a vertiginous limestone spur. It has around thirty year-round residents and was the last Moorish fortress in Catalonia to fall, in 1153. Legend says that Abdelazia, the last Moorish queen, threw herself from the cliffs with her horse rather than surrender, and visitors are still shown a hoofprint in the rock. The 12th-century Romanesque church of Sant Pere overlooks the turquoise reservoir below. Allow for a return trip during the day from Falset.

Porrera, to the southeast, is the village of sundials—14 sundials from the 18th-19th centuries are painted on facades, identifiable via a 45-minute marked route. It's also Priorat's most northerly terroir, where the tautest grenaches grow. Virtually empty on weekdays, perfect for a pause after winery visits. The Vinícola del Priorat cooperative shop open Tuesday to Saturday, free tasting.

activities.text: Head to Gratallops, Priorat's most emblematic village—200 inhabitants, perched at 312 meters above the vines. Tour and tasting at Buil & Giné or Saó del Coster (€35-45 depending on estate), booking essential the day before. The llicorella soil, crushed black slate, gives the reds their signature mineral and smoky character—record concentration in grenache and carignan, sometimes from 80-year-old vines. 90 minutes on site, plus time to understand why these wines are so difficult to produce: yields of 5-10 hl/ha versus 50 elsewhere.

Dinner at Brichs in Falset, a creative dining room in an old stone house—inventive Mediterranean cuisine exclusively from Priorat products, menu €38 + wine pairing €22. The sommelier opens bottles directly in the cellar. Dishes to try: pasture-raised lamb roasted with Montsant herbs, Siurana DOP almond tart. Booking essential, capacity 25 covers.

Hike in the Serra de Montsant Natural Park, created in 2002, where 1,100-meter limestone cliffs rise above the Priorat vineyards. From La Morera de Montsant, the camí dels Graus climbs toward the Serra Major via the grau de l'Agnet, a steep passage for walkers who are comfortable on rugged terrain. Griffon vultures nest on the ledges and often soar above the massif. Bring water and allow for a return trip during the day from Falset.

Before returning to Falset, comparative tasting at Mas Doix in Poboleda (€45, by reservation)—family estate owning carignan vines planted in 1902, among Spain's oldest. Winemaker Valentí Llagostera recounts his family like a saga since 1850. Five wines served, including Doix Costers de Vinyes Velles, regularly ranked among the world's 50 finest wines. To finish: coffee at Lotus Priorat in Falset, shaded terrace on Plaça de la Quartera.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Catalonia in 10 Days: Tarragona, Priorat & the Ebro Delta
Catalonia - Complete 24-Day Grand Tour
Catalonia Wine Route - 7 Days from Penedès to Priorat
Catalonia Wine Route - 7 Days from Penedès to Priorat

map_keywords: Scala Dei Charterhouse La Morera de Montsant

visits.text: The Dalí Theatre-Museum is the only work of architecture that Dalí designed himself, from start to finish. He built it on the ruins of the municipal theater of Figueres, which burned down at the end of the Civil War in 1939. Dalí wanted to make it “the largest surrealist object in the world” - and he was not wrong: giant eggs crown the walls, loaves decorate the façade, and a geodesic glass dome tops the central hall. The museum opened on 28 October 1974. Dalí is buried in its crypt, beneath the stage, against his wishes - he wanted to rest in Púbol beside Gala.

The Sant Ferran fortress is 18th-century Europe's largest bastioned fortification: 32 hectares, 3.2 km perimeter, 9 million liters of water capacity in its underground cisterns. Built from 1751 under the reign of Fernando VI to block a potential French invasion, it nevertheless capitulated twice without fighting - to French troops in 1793 and again in 1808. Salvador Dalí did his military service here. Allow at least 2 hours, including the cistern tour if available.

Salvador Dalí's birthplace, at 6 Carrer Monturiol, is open to the public with an audio-visual tour tracing his childhood in Figueres. It's the intimate complement to the Theatre-Museum spectacle: here, you understand where the man came from before measuring the myth.

activities.text: The Rambla de Figueres, with its cafes and neoclassical and modernist buildings, is the city's commercial heart. Stop here for lunch with Empordà products: Alt Empordà anchovies are among Spain's finest. The markets on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday at Plaça del Gra are an opportunity to buy olives, Empordà AOC oils, and local cheeses.

Wine tasting of AOC Empordà wines at one of the downtown bodegas or in the surroundings: Empordà vineyards produce powerful reds and mineral whites influenced by the tramontana. The region also produces an excellent sweet fortified wine, Garnatxa d'Empordà.

days_plan.itin_title: Barcelona and Costa Brava Road Trip: Coves and Villages

places.name: Fisterra

visits.text: Cape Finisterre—Fisterra in Galician—was the end of the world for the Romans, who called the place Finis Terrae (“end of the earth”). A 138 m granite cliff plunging into the Atlantic, constant winds, the feeling of standing at the edge of a cosmic precipice. The 1853 lighthouse marks the unofficial finishing point of the Camino—many pilgrims continue from Santiago for an extra 90 km to reach it. Tradition (controversial) of burning your socks at sunset on the rocks: a gesture of breaking with the past, journey's end. Now forbidden but still practised in secret.

The Pedras Santas, 200 m below the lighthouse, are rounded granite rocks, a Celtic-Roman solar cult site predating Christianity—hence the nickname Costa da Morte (coast of death). Pilgrims came here for purification before Christianity, a ritual later co-opted by the Church. The main flat rock still serves for end-of-Camino ceremonies. Feasts, meditation, sometimes symbolic weddings—tolerated as long as nature isn't degraded. Strange atmosphere, more pagan than Christian.

The igrexa de Santa María das Areas, in Fisterra village 3 km from the cape, is the official spiritual stop for pilgrims—a 12th-century Romanesque sanctuary housing the Cristo de la Barba Dourada, a medieval Christ with a gold-painted beard that supposedly floated ashore according to legend. Church open only during Mass times, usually noon and 7pm. Small Atlantic cemetery attached—gravestones facing the ocean, some very recent. Allow 30 minutes.

The Costa da Morte, stretching 200 km from Malpica to Fisterra, owes its ominous name to more than 600 shipwrecks recorded since antiquity. Winds, fog, invisible cliffs; HMS Serpent lost 172 English sailors at Camariñas in 1890. English Cemetery (Cemiterio dos Ingleses): allow for a round trip within the day from Fisterra, then a moving 1-hour walk on site. Mar de Fora beach, 2 km from Fisterra, is unsuitable for swimming (deadly currents) but sublime for walking. Ideal at dusk.

activities.text: For dinner, Fisterra's port serves what the trawlers brought in that afternoon. O Centolo (del Puerto street) has been the institution since 1957—percebes (goose barnacles) at €60 per 200 g portion, whole spider crab (centola) at €30/kg, clams in white wine at €18. Booking essential at weekends. For limited budgets, A Marina at the port serves a fisherman's menu at €18 with the day's fish dish. Bottle of Pazo de Señorans Albariño at €22.

For a morning off the beaten track, the lighthouse trail (Camiño dos Faros) - a 200 km coastal route from Malpica to Fisterra - can be explored on foot along its final section, between Mar de Fora beach and the Fisterra lighthouse. The route climbs Monte do Facho, with views of the rocky coast and the Atlantic, before reaching the cape. Choose a section suited to your fitness and return the same way. Walking poles are useful; bring water and a windproof jacket. The coastal sections require good shoes and suitable weather.

days_plan.itin_title: Castile and León and Galicia: 21 days from Roman aqueducts to the Atlantic
Galicia: Complete 10-Day Circuit

map_keywords: Santa María das Areas Church Finisterre

visits.text: You'd swear it's the Caribbean, except it's 25 min by ferry from Ibiza: Ses Illetes unfurls its white and pink sand along the Es Trucadors peninsula, in the heart of UNESCO-listed Ses Salines Natural Park. The water is so clear fish swim in your shadow.

The Es Trucadors peninsula stretches a few hundred meters wide between two seas: the west side's sand faces the sunset, the east faces Ibiza. At low tide, you can almost walk to the islet of Espalmador.

activities.text: Rent a bicycle at La Savina port as soon as you disembark the ferry: Ses Illetes is 4 km away on a flat road. In summer, motorized access is restricted and charged (€4–6), bikes pass free.

If you walk to the northern tip of Es Trucadors, you'll see Espalmador within reach. Some cross on foot through the shallows (knee-deep water), but currents are treacherous: prefer the water taxi running the shuttle.

days_plan.itin_title: Ibiza & Formentera by Scooter: Calas & Beaches in 7 Days

visits.text: Fornells, a village of 1,000 inhabitants, stretches along a four-kilometer bay. A traditional fishing port and whitewashed houses.
The Torre de Fornells, built in 1801 under British rule, stands at the mouth of the bay.
From the top of the tower, a panoramic view over the sheltered bay, the village, and Cap Cavalleria. An exhibition on the island's defensive history.
Sant Antoni Abad Church dates from the 17th century. Austere architecture at the heart of the fishing village.
Remnants of Sant Antoni Castle, built in the 17th century and later dismantled, dot the area around the village.

activities.text: Caldereta de langosta, a stew simmered with freshly caught lobster, is served in the restaurants around the harbor.
The sheltered bay, four kilometers long, offers ideal conditions for kayaking. Rental outfitters available at the harbor.
The Northern Marine Reserve's seabed invites snorkeling among posidonia meadows teeming with Mediterranean biodiversity.

days_plan.itin_title: Menorca Road Trip: Harbors, Whitewashed Villages & Coves

visits.text: Frías is considered Spain's smallest “city”—it received this title in 1435 and today has only about a hundred inhabitants. It has been a member of Spain's Most Beautiful Villages since 2014. Viewed from the bottom of the Tobalina valley, the castle stands atop the limestone outcrop called La Muela: built between the 12th and 15th centuries on Alfonso VIII's orders, it contains 13th-century Romanesque capitals depicting warriors on horseback and fantastical birds. The panoramic view over the valley from the keep is worth the climb. Buy the ticket at the tourist office before heading up.

Along the slope below the castle, Frías's medieval lanes reveal the 'hanging houses'—half-timbered constructions clinging to the cliff edge, upper floors jutting out into space above the gorge. Descend to the medieval bridge over the Ebro (143 meters, 9 arches) with its 14th-century defense tower. The San Vicente church is also notable: its original Romanesque portal was detached and shipped to New York when the tower collapsed in 1904—it's now in an American museum.

About 49 km from Frías, a 1-hour drive, Puentedey takes its name from its geology: this village of 50 inhabitants is built on a natural limestone bridge carved by the Nela River over 85 to 90 million years. It is the most photographed image in the province of Burgos after the cathedral. From the suspended San Andrés viewpoint, the panoramic view of the natural bridge and the houses perched on it is striking. On the arch itself, San Pelayo Church (Romanesque elements from the 11th century) and the Brizuela Palace (15th century, two rectangular towers with their coats of arms) are worth a stop.

activities.text: Walk the pebble-paved lanes climbing toward the castle. The town's medieval layout is evident in the tangle of passages and stairs.
Go down to the bridge to photograph Frías from the opposite bank. The silhouette of the village and its castle stands out against the sky.

days_plan.itin_title: Castile and León: Ramparts, Canyons and Peaks

visits.text: Frigiliana earns its reputation: the Barribarto is a real Moorish labyrinth, not a reconstructed film set. Steep cobbled lanes, whitewashed houses adorned with flowerpots, azulejos tiles telling the story of the Moorish revolt of 1570. Declared a Historic-Artistic Ensemble in 2014. Avoid midday in summer: the alleys offer little shade.

The old cane honey mill El Ingenio occupies the palace of the Counts of Frigiliana - it's still operational, the last of its kind in Andalusia. Short visit possible. Local cane honey (miel de caña) is sold at the village entrance, cheaper and better than what you'll find in Nerja.

activities.text: Climb to the last alleys before the path tips over into the sierra. The El Fuerte trail begins there - 2 km out for sea views. Bring closed shoes: wet cobbles are slippery. Return via the upper road for variety.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Coast: Málaga to Cartagena in 9 Days

places.name: Fromista

visits.text: Frómista, 800 inhabitants, sits on the flat land of Tierra de Campos—the Castilian grain-growing plateau where the sky fills three-quarters of the landscape. A stop on the Camino Francés since the 12th-century Codex Calixtinus, the village has lived off passing pilgrims for a thousand years. The main street, Calle Mayor, is actually the Camino de Santiago itself: yellow arrows painted on the ground, shells in the paving, pilgrim guesthouses, municipal hostels. A village that probably wouldn't have survived the 20th century if the Camino hadn't been revived in the 1980s.

The Church of San Martín de Frómista is the reason to stop here. Founded in 1066 by Doña Mayor, Countess of Castile and widow of Sancho the Great of Navarre, as part of a Benedictine monastery. The building seen today dates from around 1100. A basilican plan with a barrel-vaulted nave and two barrel-vaulted aisles, three circular apses, a polygonal lantern tower above the transept crossing, and two circular towers flanking the façade. The purity of its geometric form makes it the prototype of Castilian Romanesque.

Inside San Martín, the capitals hold your attention. More than fifty, carved with fantastic animals, biblical scenes, and representations of medieval vices and virtues. The two-tailed mermaid, the miser strangled by his purse, contorted acrobats—the complete iconography of the 11th-century Romanesque imagination. Above the altar, a late-13th-century Gothic sculpture of Christ crucified, in polychrome wood, preserved in place. The restoration carried out between 1894 and 1904 by architect Aníbal Álvarez removed all later additions to restore the building's original Romanesque form—a controversial decision at the time, since endorsed.

The Canal de Castilla runs through Frómista—an 18th-century hydraulic engineering project designed to transport Castilian wheat to the northern ports. Launched in 1753 under Ferdinand VI, completed only a century later, and already made obsolete by the arrival of the railroad. But the locks and towpaths remain. In Frómista, the four-stage lock—a 14-meter change in level spread across four chambers—is one of the most spectacular along the route. A walk along the canal, a tourist barge in season.

activities.text: Dinner in the village, simple but authentic—Frómista isn't a gastronomic hotspot, but its Castilian cuisine is worth the detour. Mesón Hostería de los Palmeros (a converted 12th-century hospital for pilgrims) or Restaurante San Telmo: lechazo asado (oven-roasted suckling lamb), morcilla de Burgos, queso de Burgos, wines from nearby Cigales and Ribera del Duero. Allow €25 per person. The atmosphere is that of a pilgrim village: unpretentious, welcoming, with scallop shells carved into the woodwork.

A quiet evening in the village. About 65 km north of Frómista, a 45-minute drive, Aguilar de Campoo has the world's greatest concentration of Romanesque art—more than one hundred 11th–12th-century Romanesque churches in the north of the province. If you have time, detour to the Monastery of Santa María la Real in Aguilar (12th century, partly converted into a hotel and school of Romanesque studies), another major stop with exceptional heritage.

days_plan.itin_title: Castile and León Road Trip: Cathedrals and Villages
Castile and León and Galicia: 21 days from Roman aqueducts to the Atlantic

map_keywords: Church Santa María del Castillo Frómista

places.name: Fuente

visits.text: The Fuente Dé cable car climbs 753 vertical meters in just 4 minutes. From the lower station at 1,094 m, the glass cabin rises to 1,823 m into the heart of the central massif of the Picos de Europa.
The Mirador del Cable at the top offers a sweeping panorama over the glacial cirque of Fuente Dé, the Liébana valley and, on clear days, the Cantabrian Sea to the north.
Before or after the cable car, detour to Mogrovejo. This stone-built village boasts a medieval tower and spectacular views of the Picos.

The monastery of Santo Toribio de Liébana, 3 km from Potes, can be reached from Fuente Dé: allow for a return drive during the day. It houses what tradition regards as the largest fragment of the Cross. It is one of Christianity's holy places.

Potes, the capital of Liébana, approximately 23 km from Fuente Dé, a 25-minute drive, spreads its arcaded houses and bridges along the rio Quiviesa. The Torre del Infantado has overlooked the small town since the 15th century.

activities.text: Take the PR-PNPE 24 trail, the Ruta de los Puertos de Áliva. From the upper station, a descending path crosses high pastures and karst landscapes down to Espinama.
Picnic facing the peaks. The high mountain pastures, dotted with shepherds' huts, provide an ideal setting between June and September.

In Potes, approximately 23 km from Fuente Dé, a 25-minute drive, try cocido lebaniego, a stew of chickpeas, cabbage and compango typical of the valley. Orujo de Liébana, the local spirit, accompanies dessert.

days_plan.itin_title: Cantabria Road Trip: Atlantic Bays and Picos de Europa

map_keywords: Puertos de Áliva Picos de Europa
Monasterio de Santo Toribio de Liébana

visits.text: The Palau Ducal dels Borja dates from the 15th century and was the Borgia family's residence before Francis Borgia became a Jesuit and was canonized. The palace is remarkably well preserved, with a gilded gallery and rooms decorated with Manises ceramics. 45-minute guided tour, available in Spanish and Valencian.

activities.text: Gandia's beach stretches five kilometers of fine sand, separated from the town centre by a residential zone. Less dense than Benidorm, still managed on a human scale. The north section of the beach, near the fishing port, stays quieter and retains a few chiringuitos without amplified music.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Valencia Road Trip: 10 Days of Villages

visits.text: Ochre, white, turquoise. Three colours for a landscape you'd swear belongs on another planet. The Barrancos de Gebas are badlands of argillaceous marls deposited 10 million years ago, when Sierra Espuña was an island. Protected since 1995, the site covers over 2,000 hectares. The viewpoint (built in 2002) offers an overview from the road. The hike down to the turquoise lake of Algeciras reservoir is 8 km round trip, with no shade—bring water.

days_plan.itin_title: Murcia Coast and Hinterland: 13 days from La Manga to Cuenca

visits.text: The Balenciaga Museum occupies a contemporary black building adjoining Aldamar Palace. Architectural dresses, clean lines, and flowing fabrics. The collection traces the career of the couturier, who was born here in 1895.
Head down to Getaria’s harbor. Colorful boats return with the day’s catch. Restaurants grill fish over wood fires on terraces facing the sea.

San Salvador Church towers over the village. A 15th-century Gothic building with a paved floor that follows the natural slope and a gilded Baroque altar. From here, enjoy views of the harbor and Mount San Antón.
Mount San Antón forms a mouse-shaped peninsula. A trail climbs through the pines, offering panoramic views of the Cantabrian coast.
Stroll through the cobbled streets of the historic center. Fishermen’s houses with colorful facades, vaulted passageways, and shaded squares. Getaria has retained its village soul despite its fame.

activities.text: Visit a txakoli winery in the hills. Terraced vineyards, hand harvesting, and fermentation in stainless steel tanks. Taste the sparkling wine paired with local cheese.
Head out on a morning fishing trip with a local skipper. Traditional techniques, seagull watching, and a return to port around 11 a.m.
Follow the coastal trail to Zarautz. 5 kilometers of cliffs, wild coves, and maritime pines. Constant views of the ocean and the Basque mountains.

days_plan.itin_title: Spanish Basque Country Tour: Bilbao and San Sebastián

visits.text: Climb into the Cimadevilla district, an old fishing quarter perched on a promontory between sea and harbor. Its cobbled alleys lined with colorful houses and cider bars lead to the Revillagigedo Palace, an imposing 17th-century baroque building now serving as a cultural center.

At the summit of Cerro de Santa Catalina, the Elogio del Horizonte overlooks the Cantabrian Sea. This monumental 10-meter-high sculpture—two pillars bearing a concrete arch—was inaugurated in 1990 and has become Gijón's icon.

Descend to the Campo Valdés Roman Baths, late 1st-century public baths discovered beneath the esplanade of San Pedro church. The underground museum displays hypocaust heating systems and remnants of the Roman wall that once protected the Cimadevilla peninsula.
San Lorenzo beach unfurls over a kilometer of golden sand along the bay. Its seafront promenade, bordered by 19th-century villas, connects the historic quarter to residential neighborhoods.

On Plaza de Jovellanos, the birthplace of the Enlightenment writer and politician houses the municipal museum: memorabilia, paintings, and sculptures in a handsome 16th-century building at the heart of Cimadevilla.

activities.text: Hop on a bike and follow the cycling path that runs along the San Lorenzo promenade to the marina. The flat route offers constant views of the bay and Cimadevilla's cliffs.
Walk along the paths of the Cerro de Santa Catalina, above Cimadevilla. Around the Elogio del Horizonte, you can admire the Cantabrian Sea and San Lorenzo bay from this headland laid out as a park.
Sit down in a harbor chigre for an escanciado of cider accompanied by grilled sardines, cachopo (breaded cutlet stuffed with ham and cheese), or chorizo a la sidra.

days_plan.itin_title: Asturias Road Trip: Cantabrian Coast and Picos de Europa

places.name: Girona

visits.text: Girona Cathedral dominates the city from its monumental staircase of 91 steps. Begun in the 11th century and completed in the 18th, it boasts the world's widest Gothic nave: 23 meters, surpassed only by St. Peter's Basilica in the Vatican. Inside, don't miss the Tapestry of Creation, a 12th-century Romanesque embroidery depicting the medieval calendar - a unique textile masterpiece in Europe. Game of Thrones fans will immediately recognize this staircase: Jaime Lannister rode up it in season 6.

From the ramparts of the Passeig de la Muralla - a 3 km free walk along 9th-century Carolingian walls - you'll have plunging views over the old town's rooftops and, on clear days, the Pyrenees ridges on the horizon. It's Girona's best vantage point, and entry is free.

The Jewish Quarter of El Call is one of the best preserved in Europe. The Jewish community lived here for over 600 years before being expelled in 1492. The stepped alleyways, stone arches, and tightly packed houses have changed function but retained their exact medieval morphology. The Museum of Jewish History, installed in one of the Call houses, presents Hebrew inscriptions and ritual objects recovered during excavations.

The colorful houses along the Onyar River are Girona's most photographed image. These ochre, pink, and yellow facades reflecting in the river have been painted in the tones mandated by local tradition. For the best angle, position yourself on the Pont de Ferro - yes, the one designed by Eiffel's workshops, the same Gustave Eiffel, delivered in 1877 before his Parisian tower was built.

activities.text: In the morning, visit the Arab Baths (built in 1194 following the model of Roman baths, despite their name) and the 12th-century Benedictine monastery of Sant Pere de Galligants - two stops that are unremarkable from the outside but whose interiors are truly worth seeing. The Baths were transformed into a Jewish mikveh in the 13th and 14th centuries.

For Game of Thrones fans, free guided tours of the season 6 filming locations are organized from the tourist office. More than 11 series sets were filmed in Girona between the cathedral (Great Sept of Baelor), the Jewish quarter, and the Arab Baths (House of Black and White). Even if you've never watched the series, the tour is a good excuse to explore the old town thematically.

In the evening, Plaça de la Independència and its terraces are the favorite meeting place for Gérone residents having an aperitif. Order a glass of Catalan cava and some xuixos - fried cream-filled pastries that are a local specialty. Do not leave without trying at least one.

map_keywords: City Walls Passeig de la Muralla Girona

visits.text: The Alhambra is the last Nasrid palace in Spain—and Al-Andalus's final breath. Built from 1238 by Mohammed I, expanded under Yusuf I and Mohammed V in the 14th century, surrendered on January 2, 1492, by Boabdil to the Catholic Monarchs. The Court of the Lions (124 white marble columns, fountain carried by 12 stone lions), the Hall of the Two Sisters with its muqarnas (stucco stalactites) defying the laws of statics, the Court of the Myrtles and its reflecting pool—everything is designed to demonstrate that only God is eternal, and earthly beauty is but a metaphor. Mandatory reservation 2-3 months in advance, imposed time slot for the Nasrid Palaces. 19 euros.

The Generalife, summer palace of the Nasrid sultans built around 1319, completes the Alhambra visit. Patio de la Acequia with its 50 crisscrossing water jets, terraced gardens, orange and cypress orchards. This is where the sultans came to escape Granada's heat in July-August—it's always 3-4°C cooler than downtown. Included in the general ticket.

12 km south of Granada, on the Motril road, lies the Puerto del Suspiro del Moro—'the Pass of the Moor's Sigh.' This is where Boabdil reportedly cast a final look at Granada, which he had just surrendered on January 2, 1492, and burst into tears. His mother Aisha then reportedly launched the famous phrase: 'Weep like a woman for what you could not defend like a man.' The pass today is a parking lot on the N-323 with a modern statue and a restaurant—the staging is basic, but the panorama of the Alhambra from afar is striking.

The Royal Chapel, adjoining the Cathedral, houses the tombs of Isabella the Catholic and Ferdinand of Aragon—the two monarchs who toppled Granada, expelled the Jews, and financed Christopher Columbus, all in 1492. Carrara marble funeral sculptures commissioned by Charles V from Domenico Fancelli. But the real shock is the crypt below: the lead coffins of the two monarchs and their daughter Joanna the Mad and her husband Philip the Fair are visible, placed on the ground, sealed. Austere to the point of severity. 6 euros.

The Madrasa Yusufiyya, on the square adjoining the Cathedral, is the last Quranic school of Al-Andalus still standing—founded in 1349 by Yusuf I. The original mihrab with its stucco arabesques has survived, now embedded in a baroque building. After 1492, the Catholic Monarchs transformed it into a city hall, which explains its preservation. Small, 3 euros, but striking in contrast: Islamic architectural grammar encircled by Christian baroque.

The Albaicín, the former Moorish quarter preserved almost intact, climbs opposite the Alhambra on the facing hill. White sloping alleys, cármenes (houses with flowered patios hidden behind blind walls), fountains, old ladies still sweeping their doorsteps. UNESCO since 1994 as complement to the Alhambra. Morisco residents (forcibly converted Muslims) were expelled in 1568 after the Alpujarras revolt—the quarter was repopulated by Christians from other regions, but the Arab urbanism hasn't budged.

The Mirador de San Nicolás offers Granada's most famous view: the Alhambra face-on, at the same altitude, with the snow-capped Sierra Nevada in the background. Bill Clinton stopped here in 1997 and declared it 'the most beautiful sunset in the world'—the phrase is engraved on a plaque. Always packed at sunset, with itinerant musicians, djembe players, beer vendors. Go in the morning instead for the photo, or to the Mirador de San Miguel Alto just above, quieter.

The Huerta de San Vicente, 1.5 km from downtown in Parque García Lorca, is the summer house where Federico García Lorca spent every summer of his life between 1926 and 1936. This is where he wrote the majority of his late work—'Blood Wedding,' 'Yerma,' 'The House of Bernarda Alba.' The piano, the desk, annotated manuscripts, the room where he spent his last night on August 16, 1936, before his arrest. Frozen atmosphere, few tourists. 3 euros, guided tour every 30 minutes.

The Barranco de Víznar, 8 km north of Granada in a pine forest of the Sierra de Alfacar, is one of the great memorial sites of the Civil War. Federico García Lorca was shot here at dawn on August 19, 1936, by the Nationalists, along with Republican schoolteacher Dióscoro Galindo and two anarchist bullfighter banderilleros—Joaquín Arcollas and Francisco Galadí. His body has never been found despite repeated excavations since 2009. Discreet memorial in the middle of the pine forest, ceramic plaques with the names of the executed. About 3,000 Republicans executed here between 1936 and 1939, mass grave still not exhumed. Powerful place, imposed silence.

Sacromonte, the hill parallel to the Albaicín, is Granada's former gypsy quarter—troglodyte dwellings carved into rock since the 16th century. Still inhabited today (200 occupied caves), zambras (family flamenco shows) in the evening. The Sacromonte cave museum gives access to several restored cave-houses, 5 euros, panoramic view of the Alhambra from the top of the hill.

Slowing down is the right way to experience the Palacios Nazaríes de la Alhambra. The courtyards, water features, and ornamentation reveal different perspectives just a few steps apart; tightly framed photographs do little to convey this sequence. Entry is tied to a specific time slot, separate from the overall time spent in the monumental complex. Buy tickets on the official website, check which documents are required, and allow extra time before entering the palaces, even if you are already on-site.

The sound of water accompanies your walk through the Generalife, above Granada. The gardens and courtyards of this residence complement the Alhambra palaces, with a more open relationship to the plantings and landscape. They are not a detour to improvise at the last minute if your ticket already sets out your admission arrangements. Check the included route and plan this visit around your palace time slot, allowing time to get between sites.

The Mirador de San Nicolás brings the Alhambra and the hills behind the city into a single view. The vista explains its popularity, but the square can become crowded when everyone seeks the same shot at sunset. The neighborhood is still residential, and its streets offer other perspectives too. Come earlier if you want to take in the view peacefully, then continue on foot without blocking residents’ entrances or the narrow streets leading to the square.

A large Renaissance cathedral near the old narrow streets: the Catedral de Granada brings a change of pace. Its light-filled spaces and the arrangement of its chapels offer a different way to understand the city from the Nasrid palaces. The neighboring Capilla Real is a separate visit; save the Albaicín for another half-day.

If you want to understand Granada’s political transition, add the Capilla Real de Granada. The tombs of Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon put faces to this chapter of history, in a space whose scale contrasts with the neighboring cathedral. The collections add context to the tombs when the rooms are accessible. Pair the chapel with the neighboring cathedral, reaching both in a single walk from the downtown streets instead of making a round trip to the Alhambra.

activities.text: Dinner at Bodegas Castañeda (calle Almireceros), taberna since 1929, steps from the cathedral. Barrels of house vermouth, old saint paintings, daily specials in chalk. Specialty: the tabla de variados—board of ham, lomo, cheese, salchichón. Free tapas with each drink, old-school style—Granada practice maintained here, rare elsewhere. 20-25 euros per person.

Nighttime stroll on the Paseo de los Tristes, at the foot of the Alhambra on the Carrera del Darro side. This is where funeral processions passed toward the Sacromonte cemetery in the 16th century—hence the name ('walk of the sad ones'). Illuminated Alhambra viewed from below, 1 km along the Darro.

Dinner at Cunini (Pescadería 14), Granada institution for fish—Granada is 1 hour from the sea (Motril), daily catch. Specialty: pijota frita (small fried hake eaten whole with fingers), urta a la roteña (red mullet in Rota tomato sauce). 40-55 euros per person. Fancier than yesterday's tabernas.

Zambra in Sacromonte. Family flamenco show in a cave, more authentic than downtown tablaos. Addresses: Cueva de la Rocío, Cueva los Tarantos, Cueva María la Canastera. Count on 25-30 euros, duration 1 hour, bring a layer (caves are cool).

Explore the Albaicín by linking its small squares rather than heading only for an overlook. Houses with gardens, known as cármenes, are part of the neighborhood’s identity, but an open door does not make them public spaces. The slopes and cobblestones also call for a different pace than downtown. Wear good shoes, bring water, and choose a loop that gradually descends toward the city, avoiding repeated climbs between viewpoints.

If you want to see flamenco, Sacromonte is an option to consider during your stay in Granada. The neighborhood is associated with cave dwellings and performance venues, whose programs and arrangements vary. Compare the duration and what the ticket includes before booking; also plan your return to your accommodation, since an evening out changes the pace of the next day’s visits.

visits.text: Grazalema receives exceptionally heavy rainfall for Andalucía: geography explains this paradox. More than 2,000 mm falls here on average each year — Atlantic weather fronts hit the sierra and release their rain. At an altitude of 812 m, the white houses are a response to the summer heat, not the rain. Plaza de España and Calle Las Piedras sum up the atmosphere: compact, clean and slightly austere.

Grazalema's weavers have been making wool blankets for centuries. The mantas grazalemeñas - heavy hand-carded blankets - continue to be produced in the village workshops with traditional equipment. Several shops sell the real thing, made from local wool. Touch alone is enough to tell them apart from imitations.

The Aurora church, a sober 18th-century building in the village heart, houses a penitent brotherhood that once sang auroras every Saturday at dawn. The tradition endured here when it died out everywhere else in the province. View over Peñón Grande from the forecourt.

Grazalema’s white houses cluster at the foot of mountains that put the village’s scale into perspective. The narrow streets and squares make for a compact stop without turning this stage into a full day of hiking. Park away from the narrow passageways and bring an extra layer for changes in the weather in the sierra.

activities.text: The pinsapar forest deserves the detour: it's one of the few remaining pinsapo forests (Abies pinsapo, an endemic fir relic from the Tertiary era) surviving in Europe. To enter the strict reserve zone of the Sierra del Pinar, a free permit is mandatory - request it from the Grazalema or El Bosque tourist office. In summer, visits with accredited guides only.

Garganta Verde, a canyon more than 400 meters deep inside the park, is one of the sierra's signature hikes, with griffon vultures soaring overhead. Access is regulated: a permit is mandatory, following the same procedure as for the pinsapar. It is not suitable for all ability levels.

If you would like to walk without devoting the day to the park, choose the Sendero de los Charcones. This route near Grazalema gives you access to the sierra landscape rather than the major regulated routes of the Pinsapar. Ask the tourist office about the day’s conditions and turn back according to the time you have available.

visits.text: Perched at 595 meters, Guadalest is reached through a tunnel carved into the rock—the sole entrance to this village of fewer than 250 inhabitants. The castle of San José dates from the 11th century, partially destroyed by the earthquakes of 1644 and 1748, then further damaged during the War of Succession in 1706. Declared a Historic-Artistic Site in 1974. Castle access via Casa Orduña, €4.

The turquoise lake gleams brightly in the valley, 200 meters below the castle. This reservoir built in 1971 supplies water to the entire Marina Baixa. The view from Plaza de San Gregorio takes your breath away—locals call it 'el corazón esmeralda' (the emerald heart). A marked trail loops around it if you have two hours to spare.

days_plan.itin_title: Costa Blanca & Alicante Hinterland: 12 days

visits.text: The Real Monasterio de Guadalupe (14th century) weaves together Gothic, Mudéjar, Renaissance, and Baroque. This UNESCO site was patronized by the Catholic Monarchs and visited by Christopher Columbus in 1486 and 1492.
The Claustro Mudéjar (1389–1405) ranks among Spain's finest. Red and white bricks, horseshoe arches, and a small terracotta pavilion with a fountain at the center.
The Gothic-Mudéjar basilica houses the Camarín de la Virgen. This dazzling Baroque chapel (stucco, marble, bronze, frescoes) displays the Virgin of Guadalupe carved in cedar (12th century).
The Baroque Sacristía (1638-1647) preserves eight canvases by Zurbarán depicting the life of Hieronymite monks. Known as the 'Sistine Chapel of Extremadura.'
The Museo de Bellas Artes displays three paintings by El Greco, a late Goya, works by Pedro de Mena, and a 16th-century ivory crucifix attributed to Michelangelo.
Wander through the village's whitewashed lanes. Half-timbered houses with flower-filled balconies rise in tiers around the monastery.
The Arco de Sevilla and Arco del Chorro are two medieval Mudéjar gateways. They once marked the entrance to the fortified enclosure.

activities.text: Climb up to the mirador del Humilladero (2 km from the town center). This Gothic-Mudéjar chapel offers panoramic views of the monastery nestled in the valley and the Sierras de las Villuercas.
Hiking in the Sierra de las Villuercas. Marked trails through holm oaks, cork oaks, and quartzite outcrops.
Savor migas extremeñas (bread fried with garlic and pimentón) and morcilla de Guadalupe. Shepherds' specialties served in the village inns.
Visit a hand-hammered copper workshop. Guadalupe preserves this Moorish craft tradition: pots, platters, and decorative pieces shaped by hand.

days_plan.itin_title: Extremadura Road Trip: Cáceres, Mérida & Trujillo

places.name: Guadix

visits.text: Guadix is one of Andalusia’s most striking towns. Founded as Acci by the Iberians, colonised by the Romans (Julius Caesar is said to have founded Julia Gemella Acci in 45 BC), then ruled by the Moors as Wadi-Ash, it retains traces of all these civilisations. What will stay with you, though, is the Barrio de las Cuevas: some 2,000 cave houses still inhabited across 200 hectares, forming a vast cave-dwelling district. The first caves were dug around 1452 by Moors seeking refuge in the clay hills. Today 45% of the population lives here, with Wi-Fi, heating and fitted kitchens—and a year-round temperature of 18–20°C.

Start at the Mirador del Cerro de la Magdalena for a sweeping view: white chimneys rising from ochre hills, the contrast between the cave district and the old town, and Sierra Nevada beyond. Then walk down through the cave district, past whitewashed facades and rainbow-colored doors. Visit the Cueva Museo (cave museum) on Plaza del Padre Poveda; it recreates life inside a cave house with period furniture and an informative film. If a resident invites you into their cave home (it sometimes happens when you show interest), accept: it is the best way to understand this way of life.

In the historic center, the Cathedral of the Incarnation is a surprising monument - built from the 16th to 18th centuries on a former mosque, itself built on an even older temple, it blends Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque and Neoclassical styles. Its red sandstone facade is particularly beautiful in late afternoon light. Right next door, the ruins of the Roman theater, discovered in 2008, date from Emperor Tiberius' reign. The Alcazaba, an 11th-century Arab fortress on the hill, offers the best views of the town and Sierra Nevada - but it's only partially open.

Don't miss the church of Santiago, declared a national monument, with its facade richly sculpted with figures, masks and demons - a striking contrast between the white walls and the reddish-brown ornaments. And if cinema interests you, know that Guadix served as location for "For a Few Dollars More" (1965), "Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade" and "Doctor Zhivago". The lunar landscapes around the town are an open-air studio.

activities.text: Sleep in a cave house - several are converted into guesthouses, and the experience is worthwhile. The silence is total, the temperature ideal, and you'll wake up understanding why these people don't want "normal" houses. If you're in Guadix in September, don't miss the Cascamorras, a wild festival where a character covered in black grease tries to cross the crowd to retrieve a statue - it's the ancestral rivalry between Guadix and Baza.

Late in the day, make a detour to Purullena, the neighboring village, known for its handmade pottery shops along the roadside. Further on, La Calahorra castle deserves a stop if you have time: this 15th-century fortress, with massive round towers, conceals an Italian Renaissance courtyard built in Italian marble by Florentine craftsmen - an Italian palace hidden within a Castilian fortress.

visits.text: The Tree of Gernika stands in the garden of the Casa de Juntas. The current oak, planted in 2015, continues a thousand-year-old lineage. Beneath this tree, the kings of Castile swore to uphold the Basque fueros.
Enter the Casa de Juntas. The neoclassical assembly chamber still houses the Parliament of Biscay. The glass ceiling, installed in 1985, casts golden light over the carved wooden seats.

The Peace Museum recounts the bombing of April 26, 1937. Videos of survivors, a reconstruction of a destroyed house, and reflections on Picasso’s Guernica make for a moving and educational experience.
Visit the traditional market on Monday morning. Smoked Idiazabal cheeses, red peppers, and Basque cakes await. The bustle is in full swing by 8 a.m.
The Urdaibai reserve stretches around the estuary. Salt pans, dunes, and oak forests. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site as a biosphere reserve.

activities.text: Taste Idiazabal at a local farm. This smoked sheep’s milk cheese matures in a cellar for at least two months. Its woody flavor pairs perfectly with txakoli.
Walk toward the Urdaibai marshes. Marked trails through the reed beds, a birdwatching observatory. Herons, spoonbills, and wigeons inhabit the wetlands.
The Peace Museum offers interactive workshops on mediation and reconciliation. Accounts from descendants of German pilots who came to ask for forgiveness.

days_plan.itin_title: Spanish Basque Country Tour: Bilbao and San Sebastián

places.name: Haro

visits.text: Haro's Barrio de la Estación is seven century-old bodegas concentrated on a few streets around a station built in 1880. The history is straightforward: French merchants, driven out by phylloxera in Bordeaux, came down here with their barrels, and the bodegas set up as close as possible to the railway wagons to export north. It's the birthplace of the modern Rioja style. Start with a walking tour of the neighborhood before entering the first cellar.

Bodegas Muga, founded in 1932—a family winery, and one of the few still making its own barrels on site. The tour is very technical: you see the cooperage in action and the coopers at work, and smell the heated wood. Rare in Rioja today. The Reserva Selección Especial is the winery's ultimate benchmark—at the tasting, discover why French oak changes everything. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for the tour, around €20.

R. López de Heredia Viña Tondonia: here, you step into another era. Founded in 1877, the winery maintains a tradition of long aging in old oak. Tours are for professionals only; the public can visit the shop, without tastings. You can buy bottles there and discover the reception pavilion designed by Zaha Hadid. The white Tondonia Reserva is an oxidative, complex white wine. This stop lets you discover the winery without planning to descend into its cellars: the contrast between 19th-century tradition and 21st-century architecture is already visible from the pavilion.

activities.text: Two wineries in a day, no more - otherwise your palate becomes overloaded and the visits blur together. After Muga in the morning, have a simple lunch in one of the bars in the Barrio: a bocadillo de jamón and a glass of Crianza. That is Rioja too.

Dinner in Haro at Restaurante Atamauri or Las Duelas: Basque-Riojan cuisine, oven-roasted milk-fed lamb, a perfect pairing with a house Reserva. Both restaurants are in the historic center, a 5-minute walk away.
