visits.text: Millennia on 16 metres of wall: the Abrigo Grande de Minateda, on the outskirts of Hellín, contains Levantine and schematic rock paintings dated between 6,000 and 1,500 BC—more than 500 recorded figures, classified UNESCO World Heritage in 1998. Free guided tours offered by Hellín's tourist office on the last Sunday of the month; reservation required. For other days, enquire at 967 541 500.

activities.text: The Tolmo de Minateda, neighbouring rock platform, is a first-rate archaeological site: Iberian, Roman, Visigoth, Islamic—the layers stack up on this natural promontory that was a crossroads of routes. Excavations have shown continuous occupation for over two millennia. Guided tours organised occasionally by Hellín Council—check the calendar on culturahellin.com.

days_plan.itin_title: Castilla-La Mancha: Windmills and Sierra in 11 days

visits.text: Few tourists find their way to Herrera del Duque, and those who arrive all say the same thing: they didn't know Badajoz was hiding this. The 15th-century Almohad castle, perched on the Sierra Chamorro at 745 m, dominates the town and the comarca. Guided tours are available through the tourist office.

Naturalists can spot a Cruziana in the keep of the Castillo de Herrera del Duque: a trilobite trace fossil 360 to 570 million years old, embedded in the stone of the second level. Ask the guide to show it to you. Lesser kestrels also nest in the ramparts.

Head down to the historic centre for the Iglesia de San Juan Bautista and the viewpoints: Puerto de Consolación (stone and wood), Las Víboras (a balcony overlooking the valleys), Puerto de las Navas (towards the Cíjara reserve). Each offers a different angle on the dehesas and sierras.

activities.text: In autumn, the bellowing of stags echoes through the Reserva Regional de Cíjara, a few kilometres away. The Observatorio de la Berrea is the official spot to observe deer, wild boar, and fallow deer without disturbing them. Bring binoculars and patience.

The pedanía of Peloche, on the edge of the Embalse de García de Sola, has two river beaches with clean, warm water. Quiet spot to finish the road trip with a swim. Access by road from Herrera, 10 minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: La Siberia and La Serena: Secret Extremadura in 6 Days

places.name: Hervas

visits.text: Devote the morning to the Valle del Jerte, one of Extremadura's most spectacular landscapes. The name comes from Arabic "xerete"—crystalline river—and that's exactly what it is: a deep V-shaped valley framed by the Sierra de Tormantos and the Traslasierra mountains, where dozens of gargantas (gorges) run with mountain water. The valley holds 1.5 million cherry trees whose simultaneous flowering, usually late March to early April, transforms the slopes into a vast white mantle—this is the Cerezo en Flor festival, declared a National Tourist Interest celebration. In summer, the gargantas become natural swimming spots of rare beauty.

The valley's jewel is the Reserva Natural de la Garganta de los Infiernos, 7,000 protected hectares since 1994—Extremadura's second most-visited natural area. The circular trail (about 7 km, 2 hours) starts from the Interpretation Center and descends to Los Pilones—giant's kettles carved into granite by water over centuries, forming natural pools of crystalline water where you can swim in summer. The path threads through oak, chestnut, and cherry forests, with waterfalls at every turn. Motor access is forbidden—tour operators offer trips in authorized 4x4s to the trailhead.

Heading down the valley, stop at Cabezuela del Valle, whose historic center is classified as a Conjunto Histórico-Artístico. Its narrow streets with half-timbered chestnut houses, overhanging balconies, and heraldic doorways make it one of the valley's prettiest villages. The church's detached tower and the Plaza de la Independencia deserve a photo stop.

In the afternoon, head to Hervás in the neighboring Valle del Ambroz. This village has one of Spain's best-preserved juderías—classified as Conjunto Histórico-Artístico since 1969. The Jewish community settled here after the 1391 pogroms, welcomed by the Duke of Béjar. At its peak in the 15th century, nearly 50 Jewish families lived here. Walk down Calle Abajo, the main street of the barrio judío: the adobe and timber-framed chestnut houses, streets so narrow you could touch both walls with outstretched arms (Travesía del Moral is 55 cm wide—one of Spain's narrowest), Stars of David carved on facades, and street names like “Amistad Judeo-Cristiana” all testify to a past that remains very present.

Finish at the Puente de la Fuente Chiquita, a sturdy medieval granite bridge spanning the Río Ambroz at the foot of the judería. It's one of Hervás's most photographed images, especially in autumn when the chestnuts turn golden. At number 19 Calle Rabilero, a building wider than the others occupies the site of the old synagogue. In July, the Fiesta de los Conversos reenacts medieval life and the 1492 expulsion in an open-air performance by the river.

activities.text: Hervás and Valle del Ambroz cuisine centers on the chestnut—which provides timber for houses, autumn fruit, and accompaniment to many dishes. In autumn (late October through December), the Otoñada celebrates chestnuts with markets, tastings, and walks through centuries-old chestnut groves. The rest of the year, try dulces sefardíes (Sephardic-inspired pastries) that some Hervás restaurants offer on themed menus.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Extremadura: From Plasencia to Zafra Through Valleys and Dehesas

map_keywords: Garganta de los Infiernos Valle del Jerte

visits.text: You expect a classic Andalusian port city and instead encounter a British mining town: the Barrio Reina Victoria, built in 1916 by the Rio Tinto Company Limited for its English workers. Seventy-one houses with wooden gables, gardens and lawns, gable roofs—in the middle of Andalusia. Declared a site of historical interest in 2002.

In Huelva, the Monumento a Colón stands at the confluence of the Tinto and Odiel rivers. This monumental sculpture by Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney, inaugurated in 1929, overlooks the river mouth through which the caravels reached the Atlantic in 1492. From the foot of the monument, you can admire the two rivers merging and the landscape of the estuary.

activities.text: The blood-red waters of the Río Tinto arrive here, at Muelle del Tinto, the old wrought-iron pier used to load ore onto ships. The smell of iron and acidic water lingers at the pier's end. The sunset over the estuary, between the orange reflections of the river and the Atlantic on the horizon, is one of the strangest in all Andalusia.

days_plan.itin_title: Huelva, the Forgotten Land: Doñana to Faro in 7 Days

places.name: Huesca

visits.text: The church and cloister of San Pedro el Viejo, a national monument since 1885, form one of Aragon's most important Romanesque complexes. The 1149 cloister preserves 18 original capitals sculpted by the Master of San Juan de la Peña, depicting the life of Christ. The Chapel of San Bartolomé houses the royal pantheon of kings Alfonso I the Battler and Ramiro II the Monk.

Huesca's Gothic cathedral, erected on the former mosque, houses the monumental alabaster altarpiece by Damián Forment, a masterpiece of the Aragonese Renaissance. Its high vaults and stained glass filter soft light onto the side chapels.

Facing the cathedral, the Town Hall occupies a 16th-century Renaissance palace. This is where the bloody events of the “Bell of Huesca” legend are said to have taken place: King Ramiro II supposedly beheaded rebellious nobles and arranged their heads in the shape of a bell to impose his authority.

The Provincial Museum of Huesca occupies the former Sertoriana University, adjoining the Palace of the Kings of Aragon. Explore its archaeological collections tracing the history of the province, then walk through the galleries of its octagonal courtyard.
Stroll through Huesca's old town, among arcaded squares and medieval lanes.

activities.text: Parque Miguel Servet, Huesca's green lung, features paths shaded by century-old plane trees, fountains, and sculptures. It's the Huescans' favorite place for a stroll, especially pleasant at the end of the day.

Sample the specialties of Upper Aragon: sheep's milk cheeses from the Pyrenean valleys, longaniza de Graus, chiretas (tripe stuffed with rice and meat), and ternasco, the roast suckling lamb that is the region's gastronomic emblem.

Around August 10, the Fiestas de San Lorenzo, designated a festival of national tourist interest, transform Huesca into a community celebration where white and green fill the streets. Off-season, the outdoor seating on Plaza de la Catedral lets you enjoy the evening bustle.

days_plan.itin_title: Aragon Tour: Zaragoza and Mudéjar Villages

map_keywords: Monasterio San Pedro el Viejo Huesca

visits.text: Dalt Vila—a fortified citadel—has towered over Ibiza Town since the 16th century. UNESCO-listed, it features Renaissance ramparts, bastions, and cobbled lanes offering panoramic views of the harbor.
Portal de ses Taules opens onto Dalt Vila. This monumental gateway flanked by Roman statues is the upper town's main entrance.
Santa María Cathedral was erected in the 14th century atop the former mosque. Its Gothic character gained Baroque additions in the 18th century.

The Archaeological Museum in Dalt Vila is closed, but the Puig des Molins necropolis museum, at the foot of the upper town, remains open. A UNESCO World Heritage site, the necropolis displays Phoenician, Punic and Roman remains, and a path winds across the hill riddled with rock-cut tombs.
Ibiza's coves shine an unreal turquoise. Cala Comte, Cala d'Hort facing Es Vedrà and Cala Salada are among the most spectacular, each about thirty minutes' drive from Ibiza town.
Eivissa harbor pulses day and night. Yachts, fishing boats, and Formentera ferries line the marina.
Ses Salines Natural Park extends between Ibiza and Formentera. This UNESCO site harbors flamingos, traditional salt pans, and pristine beaches.

activities.text: Ferries reach Formentera in 30 minutes. The neighboring island unveils white-sand beaches and crystalline waters worthy of the Caribbean.
Cala Comte, about thirty minutes' drive from Ibiza town, offers the finest sunsets on Ibiza. The sun sinks behind the rocky islets while beach bars play chill music.
Dalt Vila's lanes come alive in the evening. Art galleries, bohemian boutiques, and outdoor terraces share a laid-back atmosphere.
The hippy markets of Las Dalias and Punta Arabí, about thirty minutes' drive from Ibiza town, offer crafts, jewelry and bohemian clothing. Live music and a relaxed atmosphere reign beneath the pines.

days_plan.itin_title: Majorca Road Trip: Serra de Tramuntana and Coves

places.name: Jaca

visits.text: Jaca was the first capital of the Kingdom of Aragón in the 11th century and a major stopping point on the Camino Aragonés to Santiago de Compostela. Begin with the Cathedral of San Pedro, the first Romanesque cathedral built in Spain - construction began in 1077, almost simultaneously with Santiago de Compostela. The tympanum of the western portal features a Chi-Rho flanked by two lions, one protecting a repentant sinner, the other crushing a serpent. Inside, the dome on squinches above the transept crossing is the oldest in Spain. Note the checkerboard pattern (ajedrezado jaqués), created here and later adopted throughout Romanesque churches along the Way of Saint James.

Don't miss the Diocesan Museum of Jaca, housed in the cathedral's cloister - it's an underrated gem. The museum preserves Romanesque frescoes recovered from small churches throughout the Aragonese Pyrenees - some were detached from walls to save them from abandonment and looting. The Romanesque painting gallery, with its figures sporting enormous eyes and intense blue backgrounds, is worth the visit alone. Take the guided tour (included in the ticket price), which lasts about an hour and reveals details invisible to the naked eye.

The Ciudadela de Jaca is the only pentagonal fortress in Spain that is still fully preserved. Designed by the Italian engineer Tiburzio Spannocchi in 1592 on the orders of Philip II to defend the border with France, it has a perfect star-shaped plan with five bastions linked by wall walks, a deep moat (now home to deer) and a drawbridge. Walk around the ramparts to appreciate the perfect geometry of the plan. Inside, the chapel and the powder magazine are open to visitors, and the Museum of Military Miniatures recreates battles with 32,000 lead soldiers.

activities.text: If you have time at the end of the day, drive 20 minutes southwest to reach the Monastery of San Juan de la Peña, one of Aragón's most spectacular monuments. This 11th-century monastery is semi-troglodytic, wedged beneath an enormous rocky overhang that serves as its natural roof. It was the pantheon of the early kings of Aragón and one of the kingdom's cultural centers. The Romanesque cloister, carved directly beneath the rock, features historiated capitals of extraordinary fineness.

days_plan.itin_title: Aragonese Pyrenees and Lower Aragón: From Ordesa to Teruel

map_keywords: Monasterio San Juan de la Peña

visits.text: Vandelvira had a problem: Jaén Cathedral is too large for the city that contains it. The architect's last great 16th-century work, it became the formal template for many Latin American cathedrals. On the UNESCO indicative list. Its twin-towered façade, 63 meters high, dominates from any point in the city.

The Castillo de Santa Catalina, an Arab fortress dominating Jaén from 330 meters elevation, is now partly a parador. The terrace is freely accessible and offers the widest view over the sea of olive trees covering the province—millions of trees as far as the eye can see. Drive up recommended, 15 minutes from downtown.

activities.text: Beneath the slabs of a 16th-century palace, 450 square meters of interconnected rooms—cool, dark, perfumed with damp stone. The Arab baths of the Palacio de Villardompardo, built in the 11th century, are the most extensive you can visit in Spain. A viceroy of Peru buried them beneath his palace in the 16th—a fortunate mistake. Free entry. Closed Mondays.

days_plan.itin_title: Al-Andalus: From the Mezquita to the Alpujarras in 10 days

places.name: Javea

visits.text: Locals simply call it 'el cap'—and that says it all. Cabo de la Nao is the easternmost point in Alicante province, marking the end of the Gulf of Valencia. Its octagonal lighthouse stands 122 meters above the sea and is visible from 23 nautical miles away. On clear days, Ibiza appears on the horizon. The winding road from Jávea offers breathtaking views over the coves of Portixol and La Granadella. Free parking at the cape.

Twenty kilometers of coastline, yet not a single dull beach along this stretch. The fortified church of San Bartolomé in the historic center—Gothic and massive like a castle disguised as a church—contrasts sharply with the bustling marina. The old town, two kilometers from the sea, unfolds through medieval streets built to withstand pirate raids of the 16th and 17th centuries.

activities.text: Arrive at La Granadella before 10am to enjoy a quieter atmosphere. This little gem of white rock and turquoise water is also a renowned diving site. Kayak rentals are available at La Granadella and Portixol for exploring the sea caves. Allow 3h for a kayak trip to the cape and back. Avoid July and August after 11am: access becomes difficult and the car park gets crowded.

days_plan.itin_title: Costa Blanca & Alicante Hinterland: 12 days

map_keywords: Cap de la Nau lighthouse Jávea

places.name: Jerez De La Frontera

visits.text: The Alcázar of Jerez, a 12th-century Almohad fortress, contains nearly every feature of a Moorish palace: vaulted halls, Arab baths lit through star-shaped openings, a small mosque converted into a chapel, and an old oil mill. From the top of the tower, the view extends over the cathedral and Jerez's rooftops.

San Salvador Cathedral rises on a platform where a mosque once stood. It mingles Gothic, Renaissance, and neoclassical styles. The bell tower, probably a former minaret, forms a beautiful ensemble with the Alcázar, illuminated at nightfall. Inside, a Zurbarán painting depicts the Virgin Mary as a child meditating.

Step inside a sherry bodega to understand the solera and criaderas system: American oak barrels are stacked in tiers, and the wine slowly moves from youngest to oldest, creating a perpetual blend. The salty air from the Atlantic, 12 km away, gives fino its characteristic salinity.

The Royal Andalusian School of Equestrian Art, founded in 1973, occupies a 19th-century palace. Its 1,600-seat riding arena hosts the show “Cómo bailan los caballos andaluces”: a ballet of Andalusian horses in 18th-century costumes, accompanied by traditional Spanish music.

Wander through the Santiago quarter, birthplace of Jerez flamenco, with picturesque alleys lined with colorful buildings and flower-filled patios. The Gothic church of San Miguel rises at the end of a square where flamenco peñas keep the bulería tradition alive.

An old mosque inside a fortress: the Alcázar de Jerez offers this unexpected combination. The baths and gardens round out your understanding of its Almohad heritage, offering far more than a simple tour of the walls. Choose the areas included in your ticket and check access to the camera obscura separately.

The exterior of the Catedral de Jerez de la Frontera also deserves your attention. It combines several architectural influences, while its bell tower stands apart from the main building—a detail easily missed if you head straight to the ticket office. First walk around the square in front, then check the sightseeing hours.

activities.text: Join a guided tasting of different sherry types: dry, saline fino; amber amontillado with hazelnut aromas; dark, powerful oloroso; and rare, complex palo cortado. Jerez, El Puerto de Santa María, and Sanlúcar form the “sherry triangle”.

Attend the equestrian show on performance days. Riders perform classical dressage routines and doma vaquera, the traditional horsemanship of Andalusian herders, on purebred Spanish horses selected for their grace and power.

In the evening, settle into a tabanco in the old town. These traditional sherry bars serve wine straight from the cask, accompanied by tapas: chicharrones, tortillita de camarones, and cheese from the Sierra de Cádiz.

Choose the Real Escuela Andaluza del Arte Ecuestre if a performance coincides with your visit. The work of the horses and riders takes the form of an equestrian ballet, with a schedule separate from tours of the facilities. Book the specific program you want and arrive before the announced start time.

If you prefer wine to the spectator stands, book a tour of the bodegas in Jerez. Sherry aging and the solera system give the tasting a clear theme that goes beyond the glass served at the end of the tour. Choose a short tour and plan who will drive after the tasting.

places.name: Jerez De Los Caballeros

visits.text: Jerez de los Caballeros is the final stop on this itinerary—and what a finale. Birthplace of Vasco Núñez de Balboa, the first European to sight the Pacific Ocean in 1513, it has a spectacular historic center dominated by the silhouettes of its baroque towers. The Templar fortress, built in the 13th century when the Knights Templar controlled this frontier with Muslim Andalusia, overlooks the town from a hilltop. It's in the Torre Sangrienta (Bloody Tower) that Jerez's last Templars were supposedly massacred in 1312 during the dissolution of the order. The legend is probably exaggerated, but it fits the mood of the place.

Jerez's two baroque churches are among Extremadura's finest. The Iglesia de San Bartolomé has a bell tower covered in colorful azulejos that recalls Seville's bell towers—it's the town's iconic image. The Iglesia de La Encarnación, with its own slender baroque tower, completes an urban landscape you'd swear was Andalusian. Climb the sloping streets to discover the noble palaces, carved coats of arms, and flower-filled patios that built the reputation of this conquistador town.

On Plaza de Vasco Núñez de Balboa, a statue honors the town's most famous son. Born here around 1475, Balboa sailed for the New World in 1500 and crossed the Isthmus of Panama in 1513 to become the first European to see the Pacific Ocean. The plaza also offers fine views over the surrounding hills covered in holm oaks—the dehesa landscape that characterizes all of Lower Extremadura.

activities.text: Jerez de los Caballeros sits at the heart of the jamón ibérico de bellota production zone—the world's finest ham. Black Iberian pigs roam free in the dehesas, feeding on holm oak acorns during the montanera (autumn). If you're passing October through February, you'll see the pigs under the oaks—a unique landscape. Regional tour operators offer visits to ham-curing facilities with tastings. Even out of season, every bar in Jerez serves hand-sliced jamón ibérico—it's the best way to close this Extremadura journey.

places.name: La Alberca

visits.text: La Alberca became the very first village in all of Spain to be declared a Historic-Artistic Site—in 1940, by decree of September 6, published in the BOE on the 18th of the same month. This pioneering title is well deserved: its granite houses with ground floors topped by upper stories in adobe and timber forming warm half-timbering are the perfect model of serrana architecture. The village name comes from the Arabic 'Al-Bereka,' meaning pond or water place—the numerous fountains dotting the lanes are its legacy. The Plaza Mayor, with its irregular layout, granite arcades, and flower-decked balconies, displays an 18th-century cross carved with symbols of the Passion.

The Church of Nuestra Señora de la Asunción, built in 1730 by Manuel de Larra Churriguera (architect of Salamanca Cathedral), is a baroque jewel in this medieval setting. Its grand tower was erected in 1518 by the first Dukes of Alba—their coat of arms still visible on one corner. Inside, ask to see the Cristo del Sudor, attributed to Juan de Juni, and the 16th-century polychrome wooden altarpiece.

Walk down to the Puente del Arroyo, the old granite bridge spanning the stream below the village—a classic view of serrana architecture. Along the way, you'll pass the Hornacina de las Ánimas, a wall niche where each evening a local woman comes out with her bell (esquila) to recite a prayer for the souls in purgatory. This nighttime tradition is still alive.

The Casa Museo Sátur Juanela, adjacent to the square, preserves the interior of a typical serrana house as it was in the early 20th century—farmyard, wine cellars on the ground floor, kitchen under the eaves. It's the most concrete way to understand how mountain villagers lived.

activities.text: Each year in the village, a pig is released into the streets on June 13 (Saint Anthony's Day) and fed by residents until January 17, when it's raffled off. Proceeds now go to an NGO. If you visit outside this period, you'll still find the statue of the marrano de San Antón at the church corner. This tradition reaches back to the Middle Ages and is one of the most photographed in Spain.

The route into Parque Natural Las Batuecas-Sierra de Francia starts from La Alberca. The Batuecas Path descends into a steep, secret valley where Neolithic cave paintings and a Carmelite monastery survive. Count on a half-day for the round trip to the valley floor.

On the square, sample the obleas and artisan turrones sold in local shops—La Alberca's sweet specialties found throughout the region. Local markets also offer a good opportunity to buy honey, cheese, and sierra cured meats.

visits.text: Two seas on either side—one calm as a millpond, the other open to the swell—that's the strange promise of La Manga. This 24 km sand spit separates the Mar Menor, Europe's largest saltwater lagoon, from the Mediterranean. Formed over millennia by currents and volcanic reefs, the place is both a beach resort on steroids and a nature reserve. Avoid July-August when the population explodes from 10,000 to 200,000.

activities.text: Explore La Manga by bike in sections, between the Mediterranean beaches and those of the Mar Menor. The Venetian bridge is at the northern end, while Calblanque Park requires a separate trip to the south, beyond the sandbar. Bike rentals are available at the main access points.

days_plan.itin_title: Murcia Coast and Hinterland: 13 days from La Manga to Cuenca

places.name: La Seu D Urgell

visits.text: On the way from Lleida, stop at Coll de Nargó, approximately 23 km from the town for this stage, a 35-minute drive. The village is home to the Romanesque church of Sant Climent, but above all to its palaeontological site: one of Europe's most important deposits of dinosaur eggs, dating back 70 million years, was discovered here. The Dinosfera centre lets you see fossilised nests and reconstructs the ecosystem of the late Cretaceous. An interesting detail: Coll de Nargó was also the birthplace of Ramon Lambard, the architect who completed the cathedral of La Seu d'Urgell. Allow 1 hour here.

Arguably the centrepiece of Catalan Romanesque art: the cathedral of Santa Maria d'Urgell, the only fully Romanesque cathedral left in the region. Work began in 1116 under Bishop Saint Ot and was finished in 1183 under Ramon Lambard. A basilican plan with a nave and two aisles, a transept with five apses and, above all, that Italianate gallery above the facade – a detail found nowhere else in Catalonia. The very thick walls hide another truth: the cathedral doubled as a fortress, which is why it has stood for eight centuries. All the carved decoration is concentrated on the central doorway.

The adjoining cloister is slightly trapezoidal in plan, an oddity you notice from the entrance. Three 12th-century Romanesque galleries with historiated capitals – plant motifs, human figures, monsters; the fourth was redone in the 17th century. It provides a passage to the church of Sant Miquel and the diocesan museum. The museum is worth the detour for one piece alone: the Beatus of La Seu d'Urgell, an illuminated Mozarabic manuscript of the Commentary on the Apocalypse, early 10th century. One of the oldest preserved in the world.

The Carrer dels Canonges, the old town's main street, runs along the former defensive moats filled in during the 16th century. A row of stately houses: Cal Tarragona, Cal Calçot, Cal Patalín. Originally, this was the street of the cathedral canons. Today, cheese shops (La Seu d'Urgell is Catalonia's cheese capital), artisan shops, cafés with terraces. The Tower of Solsona, isolated from the rest of Castellciutat's walls, is a 5-minute walk above town and offers the best view of the cathedral.

activities.text: The Parc Olímpic del Segre, built for the canoe-kayak events of the 1992 Barcelona Olympics, still runs whitewater rafting and kayaking on the artificial channel and the natural river. The world championships have been held here several times. A good option for an afternoon of adrenaline if you would rather save the wilder Noguera Pallaresa for tomorrow. Morning or afternoon sessions, from 35 euros a run.

Cheese tasting in La Seu. The region produces formatge de l'Alt Urgell i la Cerdanya, a PDO cheese made from the milk of dairy cows grazing on high-altitude pastures, with a washed rind and soft texture. Several cheese shops. Combine it with a tasting of local vermut or ratafia (a green walnut liqueur typical of the Catalan Pyrenees). More original than the usual evening meal of paella.

days_plan.itin_title: Catalan Pyrenees - 6-Day Discovery
Catalonia - Complete 24-Day Grand Tour
Catalan Pyrenees and Romanesque Art in 8 Days: Lleida, Pallars, Vall de Boí and Val d'Aran

map_keywords: Sant Miquel de la Seu d'Urgell

visits.text: Lake Enol is the first lake to appear around a bend in the road, at an altitude of 1,070 meters. This glacial lake reaches a depth of 25 meters. Beneath its waters lies a replica of the Virgin of Covadonga, raised to the surface every September 8 by divers.

Two kilometers farther up, Lake Ercina rests at 1,108 meters. Smaller than Enol, it's surrounded by pastures where Asturian cattle and horses graze freely. In the background, the summit of Peña Santa de Enol rises to 2,486 meters.

The Pedro Pidal Visitor Center, near the Buferrera parking lot, traces the glacial geology of the lakes and the history of the national park. Nearby, the old Buferrera manganese mines bear witness to the area's mining past.

Stop at the Mirador de la Reina on the road uphill: on clear days, the panorama sweeps from the Cangas de Onís valley all the way to the Cantabrian Sea. The Mirador Entrelagos, on the hill between the two lakes, offers a simultaneous view of both Enol and Ercina.

activities.text: Complete the lakes circuit (PR-PNPE-2), a 5 km circular hike starting from the Buferrera parking lot. The marked trail takes in viewpoints, high-altitude meadows, and beech forests of the western Picos massif.
Keep your eyes and ears open: chamois, griffon vultures, and golden eagles frequent the limestone ridges above the lakes. The tinkling of bells from free-roaming herds accompanies the walk.
Set up for a picnic facing Lake Enol with views of the snow-capped peaks. The Vega de Enol, a vast high-altitude meadow dotted with shepherds' barns, is the perfect spot.

days_plan.itin_title: Asturias Road Trip: Cantabrian Coast and Picos de Europa

places.name: Laguardia

visits.text: The Guggenheim in Bilbao, opened in 1997 on the banks of the Nervión, literally saved a city in industrial decline. It is about 113 km from Laguardia, a 1-hour 20-minute drive. 24,000 m² of titanium, limestone and glass designed by Frank Gehry—and a solid permanent collection, from Richard Serra to Jeff Koons. If you only have 2 hours, head straight to the Serra gallery: the Torqued Ellipses sculptures stand 4 meters high and swallow you up. Admission around €18, free on Tuesday evenings after 6 pm.

Crossing the Sierra de Cantabria from Bilbao brings a dramatic shift you won't forget. In 20 minutes of climbing, the green, humid Atlantic landscape abruptly gives way to the Ebro plain: vineyards as far as the eye can see, a drier sky, different light. It's the curtain falling on Rioja. Stop at the pass to take in the sheer scale—on clear days, you can spot Logroño 60 km away.

Laguardia is tiny—1,500 inhabitants—and that's handy, because the medieval alleyways can be explored on foot in an hour. Nearly intact fortified walls, the church of Santa María de los Reyes with its polychrome 14th-century portal (unique in Spain in this state of preservation), and beneath every house: cellars carved into the rock, some dating back to the 12th century. To see them, ask your host.

Founded in 1858, Marqués de Riscal was one of the first wine producers to introduce Bordeaux techniques to Rioja. But frankly, people come mainly for the architectural shock: the hotel designed by Frank Gehry in 2006 sits amid the vineyards like a sculpture of pink and gold titanium that landed there by mistake. €75 million invested, and it shows. The winery tour (2 hours, €30–40) covers the history, the wine cellars and a tasting. The Reserva remains the benchmark cuvée; for larger budgets, the Gran Reserva.

A complete contrast in the afternoon with Bodegas Ysios, designed by Santiago Calatrava in 2001. The aluminum roof undulates, precisely following the outline of the Sierra de Cantabria just behind it—a calculated and successful composition. The wines are more modern and fruitier than those of the great historic wineries. The tour takes about 1 hour 30 minutes, and is much more accessible than Riscal in terms of price and availability.

activities.text: Spending your first evening at a pintxos bar in central Laguardia is a must. No strict rules: order a glass of local Crianza, point to whatever takes your fancy on the counter, repeat. Basque cuisine is already here—anchovies, ham, mushrooms, tortilla. It's simple, effective, and clearly better than most sit-down dinners in the area at the same price.

Twilight walk along Laguardia's ramparts with views over the vineyards. The sun descends behind the Sierra de Cantabria, the rows of Tempranillo turn orange - it's free, takes 30 minutes, and is probably the best photo of the trip.

Gourmet lunch at the Marqués de Riscal restaurant (1 Michelin star, chef Francis Paniego). It's the full experience—contemporary Basque-Riojan cuisine, a dizzying wine list, a dining room overlooking the vineyards and the Gehry sculpture. Budget €80–120 per person. If your budget doesn't stretch that far, Hector Oribe in Páganos, 5 minutes away by car, is excellent and half the price.

Dinner on the terrace at Restaurante Amelibia in Laguardia, with direct views of the vineyards at sunset. Short menu, local ingredients, well-thought-out wine pairings. Book 48 hours in advance in season.

places.name: Laguna Negra De Urbion

visits.text: The Laguna Negra is one of the most impressive natural destinations in the province of Soria: a glacial lake nestled at an altitude of 1,750 meters, surrounded by granite cliffs and pine forests. Its name comes from the dark color of its waters, reflecting the cliffs around it. The Natural Park of the Lakes and Glacial Cirques of Urbión, created in 2010 across 4,617 hectares, protects this landscape. From the Paso de la Serrá parking area (mandatory access in high season), reach the lake on foot or by shuttle when it is operating, then take the stone-paved path to the wooden boardwalk beside the lake.

activities.text: The loop hike from Paso de la Serrá to Pico de Urbión (2,228 m) via Laguna Negra and Laguna Helada is one of the most beautiful in the entire Iberian System. Allow about 4 hours for the 12 km route with 664 m of elevation gain—rated difficult on AllTrails with a 4.6/5 score. From the summit, you'll see the plains of Castile to the south, La Rioja and the Ebro to the north. This summit is also where the Duero River rises. Wear high-cut footwear: the rocky gully above the lake is steep. In winter and spring, hard snow may be present.

days_plan.itin_title: Castile and León: Ramparts, Canyons and Peaks

map_keywords: Pico de Urbión Sierra de Urbión

visits.text: Lanjarón water has a taste: light, cold, slightly mineral—the water sold in bottles all over Spain comes from this town's springs at the gateway to the Alpujarras. The ruined castle on the northern promontory, called the 'Moors' castle,' offers a panorama over the valley. According to legend, its last defender threw himself from the tower rather than surrender to the Catholic Monarchs in 1490. An hour is enough here.

The Balneario de Lanjarón, a thermal establishment open since the 19th century, uses water from the town's six sulfurous and bicarbonate springs. A day pass to the baths (basic thermal circuit) is offered without an overnight stay requirement—a good break before climbing into the Alpujarras.

activities.text: The Mirador del Castillo, a few minutes' walk from the center, gives the clearest overview of Lanjarón and the Guadalfeo valley toward the sea. A marked trail from the main street climbs to the castle ruins in 20 minutes—rocky path but no difficulty.

days_plan.itin_title: Al-Andalus: From the Mezquita to the Alpujarras in 10 days

visits.text: From O Cebreiro, you descend into the Bierzo, leaving Galicia behind. The road passes through Villafranca del Bierzo, a charming town on the Camino de Santiago with Romanesque churches and a medieval bridge. Stop for a coffee on the Plaza Mayor before continuing to Ponferrada. Allow for a drive from Las Médulas to visit Villafranca del Bierzo and Ponferrada. Ponferrada's Templar Castle (12th–13th century) is one of Spain's largest Templar fortresses—its towers and ramparts dominate the town and the river Sil. It was built to protect pilgrims on the Camino de Santiago and enlarged in the 15th century by the counts of Lemos.

End your itinerary at Las Médulas, the ancient Roman gold mines listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. This site is already covered in another ORT itinerary—it's your connection point with Castile. The landscape of red earth pinnacles sculpted by Roman hydraulic engineering (the ruina montium, which involved exploding the mountain with water pressure) is spectacular from the Mirador de Orellán.

activities.text: If you have time, follow the Senda de Las Valiñas from the village of Las Médulas, among chestnut trees and the red-earth formations of the former Roman mine. The route leads towards La Cuevona and La Encantada, but access to the caves is restricted because of rockfall risks: stay on the open sections and respect the barriers, without entering the galleries.

Before leaving the Bierzo, try the botillo—the region's emblematic charcuterie, a casing stuffed with pork ribs and smoked tail, served with potatoes. It's the Bierzo's winter dish, hearty and delicious. Bierzo wine, based on Mencía like in the Ribeira Sacra, rounds out the picture perfectly.

days_plan.itin_title: Castile and León: Ramparts, Canyons and Peaks
Inland Galicia: From Ourense to the Ribeira Sacra

places.name: Las Negras

visits.text: Cala San Pedro takes some effort to reach: an hour's walk from Las Negras along a coastal path overlooking the Mediterranean. The ruins of a 15th-century castle guard the entrance to this isolated cove, a former pirate hideout. A freshwater spring—the only one in the park—gushes out at the beach's edge.

Las Negras takes its name from Cerro Negro, the dark volcanic mass that dominates the village. About 350 people live here year-round, including many foreigners drawn by the tranquility. Fishing boats still beach on the black pebble shore each evening.

Take the road to Rodalquilar, a former mining village that has found a new role. The ruins of the gold mines, worked until 1966, are open to visitors to explore independently. The Jardín Botánico El Albardinal showcases the park's semi-arid flora.
The Playazo de Rodalquilar offers a striking contrast to the coves hemmed in by cliffs: 400 meters of golden sand bordered by an 18th-century fortification. The water here is calm and shallow.
From the trail above Cerro Negro, viewpoints offer spectacular vistas of black cliffs plunging into the sea and, in the distance, the silhouette of Isleta del Moro.

activities.text: Hike from Las Negras to Cala San Pedro via the coastal trail. The route crosses a semi-arid landscape punctuated by red and yellow cliffs before dropping down toward the turquoise cove.
Kayak along the volcanic cliffs from Las Negras. Rental shops offer guided outings that pass alongside caves and rock formations inaccessible by land.
Snorkeling in the coves around Las Negras. The volcanic rocky seabeds create varied habitats for Mediterranean marine life.
Evening drinks facing the sea on the Las Negras promenade. The village's bohemian vibe carries through to the small waterfront bars.

days_plan.itin_title: Almería Road Trip: Volcanic Coves and Tabernas Desert
Wild Coast: Málaga to Cartagena in 9 Days

places.name: Las Palmas De Gran Canaria

visits.text: The Cathedral of Santa Ana has dominated Vegueta since the 16th century. Four centuries of construction blend late Gothic, Renaissance, and Neoclassical styles. Its nave and two aisles, all of equal height in a “hall church” arrangement, rise on slender fluted columns whose ribs fan out into palm-shaped vaults.

Step through the door of the Casa de Colón, just behind the cathedral. Built on the exact site where the city was founded in 1478, its green stone façade opens onto colonial courtyards. The museum traces the connections between the Canaries and the Americas.

The Museo Canario, founded in 1879, is the archipelago's most important archaeological museum. Its pre-Hispanic collections evoke the culture of the Guanches—the islands' first inhabitants—through ceramics, mummies, and idols.

Stroll down Calle Triana, a long pedestrian street bringing together all the city's architectural styles: Modernist façades from 1900–1910 alternate with Neoclassical, Neo-Baroque, and Art Nouveau buildings.

Playa de Las Canteras stretches three kilometers through the heart of the city. A natural rocky barrier protects swimmers and creates a turquoise lagoon sheltering a marine reserve. Blue Flag beach since 1989.
The Teatro Pérez Galdós, Italian-inspired, has been the city's cultural emblem for over a century. Flanked by a contemporary extension, it hosts opera, concerts, and dance year-round.

activities.text: Put on your mask and snorkel at Las Canteras: waters protected by the rocky barrier shelter a wide variety of fish in a protected natural area, accessible right from the sand.

The Mercado de Vegueta, in operation since 1854, comes alive each morning with spectacular displays of tropical fruits, fresh fish, and Canarian cheeses. On Sundays, a craft market sets up in Plaza del Pilar Nuevo.
Stay on the Las Canteras promenade for sunset. The Auditorio Alfredo Kraus stands at the end of the beach, closing off the view, its silhouette outlined against the Atlantic horizon.

visits.text: The Las Tuerces labyrinth resembles a ghost town sculpted by water: over millions of years, karst erosion of Upper Cretaceous limestone has created a tangle of giant stone mushrooms, natural arches, dead-end corridors and shaded galleries. You feel like you're on another planet—with free access and no lines. The site is accessed from the village of Villaescusa de las Torres. Set off without a fixed route and explore paths at random.

activities.text: At the foot of the labyrinth, the Cañón de la Horadada is a gorge carved by the Pisuerga River with vertical walls over 40 meters high. The trail from Mave descends into the gorge along the old greenway, passes the former hydroelectric plant and reaches a rock face where you can climb back up for an overview. The loop combining Las Tuerces and Cañón de la Horadada from Aguilar de Campoo covers 9.5 km and takes about 2 hours 30 minutes. The site is included in the “Las Loras” UNESCO Global Geopark.

days_plan.itin_title: Castile and León: Ramparts, Canyons and Peaks

places.name: Ledesma

visits.text: Ledesma is built on a rocky spur between two meanders of the Tormes—a naturally defensive position inhabited since prehistoric times. The Romans called it Bletisama in honor of Consul Bleto (93 AD). Medieval repopulation dates to 1161, when Fernando II raised the walls and fortress. In 1462, Enrique IV handed lordship of Ledesma to Don Beltrán de la Cueva, his favorite, who made it a city of splendor in the 15th century. Classified as a historic site in 1975, Ledesma preserves fragments of Roman and medieval wall.

Ledesma's castle, partially demolished, has kept what matters: its entrance gate with a Gothic arch of keystones founded directly in bedrock, flanked by a semicircular cube and a polygonal one. It's the most eloquent entrance to the walled enclosure. Inside, the lanes lead to the Gothic church of Santa María la Mayor and the Casa de las Almenas—a 15th-century palace with cloister and interior garden, one of the province's finest noble residences.

The Mocho Bridge, of Roman origin, spans the Ribera de Cañedo north of Ledesma. The ancient oak forest bordering the road to the bridge is a remarkable habitat where you may see griffon vultures and black kites in flight. A plaque recalls that Mesta herds crossed this passage for centuries, paying the portazgo (toll) to the lord of the town.

activities.text: The route to the Mocho Bridge, waymarked from the town, crosses a centuries-old oak forest. Birdwatchers can easily spot black storks, kites and vultures from the higher ground above the bank. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for the return walk.

Ledesma is renowned for its thermal mud baths—the aguas termales have been known since Roman times. Wellness establishments still exploit the springs. If you have fatigue from the miles in your legs, it's a welcome break.

days_plan.itin_title: Sierra de Francia Medieval Villages Route

map_keywords: Église Santa María la Mayor Ledesma

visits.text: León Cathedral, called Pulchra Leonina ("the Beautiful Leonese") in Latin, has 1,800 m² of stained glass - one of the world's largest glass surfaces, alongside Chartres and Sainte-Chapelle. Three rose windows and 134 bays from the 13th to 20th centuries, some depicting medieval peasant scenes: harvest, grape picking, boar hunting. The structure is so fragile it was dismantled stone by stone then reassembled in the 19th century to save it from collapse. Entry €7, audioguide included. Best in mid-morning for light on the south windows.

The Royal Pantheon of the Basilica of San Isidoro is called the "Sistine Chapel of Romanesque art" - and it's no exaggeration. Vault entirely painted in early 12th century, Apocalypse scenes, agricultural calendar, Last Supper. Exceptional preservation because the paintings were never covered or restored before the 20th century. Twenty-three kings and queens of León rest here, including Ferdinand I the Great, founder in 1063. Combined entry basilica + pantheon + museum €6.

The chalice of Doña Urraca, preserved in the San Isidoro museum, caused a scandal in 2014: two historians, María Margarita Torres and José Manuel Ortega del Río, published a book claiming it was the Holy Grail, the cup of the Last Supper, brought from Egypt in the 11th century. Agate cup set in gold, offered to the monastery by Queen Urraca of León around 1100. Thesis contested by most medievalists, who date the agates to roughly the Roman period without confirming their provenance. True or false Grail, the piece is beautiful, and the museum is rich beyond: 300 codices, carved ivories, cloisonnés.

Casa Botines, steps away, is one of Antoni Gaudí's three works outside Catalonia - built in 1893 for two textile merchants. Neo-Gothic façade with corner turrets, statue of Saint George above the door. When workers attempted to demolish it in 1955, they found Gaudí's original plans in a bottle sealed by himself inside Saint George's statue - true story. Today a museum, entry €5, allow 45 minutes.

The San Marcos convent, converted into a 5-star Parador in 1965, stretches its Plateresque façade over 100 meters - one of the longest of the Spanish Renaissance, carved like a picture book. Construction began in 1513 to create a hospital for pilgrims to Santiago de Compostela and the headquarters of the Military Order of Santiago.

MUSAC, Museum of Contemporary Art of Castile and León, is an exploded cube of 37 glass panels in the 37 colors of the cathedral's stained glass - avant-garde building by Mansilla and Tuñón that won the Mies van der Rohe prize in 2007. Over 1,650 works, emphasis on Spanish art from the 1990s to today. Architecture alone worth the detour if contemporary art doesn't attract you. Entry €5, free Sunday afternoons.

Castrillo de los Polvazares, approximately 57 km west of León, a 1-hour drive, is the village of the arrieros - muleteers who carried goods and news between the coast and Madrid before the railway. Reddish stone houses, streets paved with rounded cobbles, 70 residents. Its 250-meter, car-free main street has served as a setting for several films. A unique specialty is cocido maragato, a dish served in reverse order, with meat first and soup last. Try it at Mesón Casa Coscolo (€28); booking is essential.

activities.text: Tapas tour in the Barrio Húmedo, the "wet quarter" - labyrinth of lanes around Plaza San Martín, nicknamed thus because of the dozens of taverns that make it perspire every evening. Leonese specialty: the tapa is free with each drink, sometimes substantial (piece of cecina, croquette, tortilla). Three or four glasses and you've had dinner. Reliable addresses: Bar La Bicha (house cecina), El Rebote (tortilla), El Tizón (cod croquettes). Figure €12-18 for a real tour.

If you are there in July, do not miss the free concerts in Plaza San Marcelo alongside the early music festival. Otherwise, end the evening in Plaza de Regla, in front of the illuminated cathedral - the backlighting makes the stained-glass windows glow from outside. A good place for a mojito with a cathedral view is Cafetería La Catedral, with a terrace at number 5.

Excursion to the Valporquero caves, approximately 44 km north of León, a 1-hour drive, in the Cantabrian Mountains natural park - a 3 km karst system, 1.3 km of which is open to the public. Stalactites, underground lakes and the Fairy Chamber with its 30-metre-high ceiling. The temperature is a constant 7°C, so bring a coat even in July. One-hour guided tour, departures every 30 minutes, €11. Closed from December to February; the approach road has hairpin bends and the final kilometre is narrow.

Gourmet evening in Castrillo or return to León for pulpo a la feria - Galician-style octopus, present everywhere since the province is adjacent - at Mesón Jabugo in Barrio Romántico. Single dish €16, wash down with a glass of Bierzo, local wine AOC on the rise made from mencía grape. El Bierzo, 30 km west of León, now produces reds that rival those of Ribera, at still reasonable prices.

visits.text: Lerma appears in the distance like an ocean liner perched on a hill. The Palacio Ducal dominates the Plaza Ducal—one of Spain's largest squares at 6,862 m². This 17th-century palace, built between 1601 and 1617 by architect Francisco de Mora, is the work of the Duke of Lerma, favorite of Philip III and the most powerful man in Spain at the time. The duke, so influential he dared add four towers to his palace (a privilege normally reserved for kings), made Lerma a parallel court with six monasteries, a collegiate church, and secret passages connecting everything. Its austere façade has 210 balconies and 35 windows. You can visit the cloister and covered inner courtyard.

Take the Pasadizo del Duque, the covered passage the duke built to attend Mass without stepping into the street. It connected the palace to the Collegiate Church of San Pedro (early 17th century), an austere temple whose interior preserves a gilded bronze praying statue of Archbishop Cristóbal de Rojas, the duke's uncle. From the Mirador de los Arcos at the end of the passage, the view plunges over the vega of the Arlanza—the agricultural plain stretching as far as the eye can see.

Cross through the Arco de la Cárcel, the only preserved medieval gate from the old walls. It now houses the headquarters of the DO Arlanza regulatory council. Around the square, visit the convents: San Blas (where Dominican nuns sell hand-painted ceramics), La Ascensión (where the infanta Margarita, daughter of Philip III, was baptized), Santa Teresa (now city hall and interpretation center). Lerma had six monasteries in the 17th century—a village of 600 inhabitants surrounded by convents, that's Habsburg Castile.

activities.text: Use the afternoon for an excursion to Santo Domingo de Silos, 35 km southeast of Lerma. The Benedictine monastery, founded in the 10th century, houses an 11th-century Romanesque cloister considered one of Europe's finest. The carved capitals and corner pillar bas-reliefs are exceptionally refined. The monks still chant Gregorian chant at services.

days_plan.itin_title: Duero Castile: From Valladolid to Cuenca via Ribera and Alcarria

visits.text: No tourists, no pretence: Letur's casco árabe was declared a Historic-Artistic Ensemble in 1983, and it's the best-preserved medieval layout of Moorish origin in Albacete province. Labyrinthine callejuelas coil around a white stone outcrop at 740 metres altitude. The Arco de las Moreras, in natural stone, marks the entrance to the old walled enclosure—it's both a triumphal arch and a geological phenomenon. Free stroll.

Water springs from everywhere in Letur: fountains, irrigation channels, the río Segura below. The Charco de las Canales, a natural rock pool in the heart of the casco histórico, is one of the best-known in the Sierra Segura. Check it's open before coming (reopening varies depending on the riverbed condition after floods). In summer, arrive early to find a spot.

days_plan.itin_title: Castilla-La Mancha: Windmills and Sierra in 11 days

visits.text: Liétor literally hangs in balance: the village is perched about 100 metres above the río Mundo canyon, houses jutting right onto the rock, like an extension of the cliff. Classified casco histórico, narrow streets of Islamic origin, coats-of-arms façades. The miradores of the barrio morisco (Calle Portillo) offer a view of the río Mundo that few places in Spain can match.

The Ermita de Nuestra Señora de Belén is worth the climb: it's one of the most memorable scenes in the film 'Amanece que no es poco' (1989) by director José Luis Cuerda, shot here. Inside, a curiosity: everything is painted in trompe-l'oeil, from the altarpieces to the curtains. If it's closed, the frescoes are visible through the grille.

days_plan.itin_title: Castilla-La Mancha: Windmills and Sierra in 11 days

places.name: Linares

visits.text: Visit the Archaeological Museum of Linares, housed in the former 17th-century Casa del Torreón Palace. Discover a fascinating collection of artefacts from the Cástulo excavations, including the famous Ibero-Roman sandstone lion originally from the northern wall of the ancient city.

Explore the Hospital of the Marquises of Linares, an impressive neo-Gothic building constructed between 1904 and 1917, commissioned by José de Murga and Raimunda de Osorio. Admire its Victorian architecture with gargoyles on the entrance columns and visit the Marquises' crypt with life-size sculptures.

Discover El Pósito, home to the Raphael Museum, one of the main cultural attractions in the singer's hometown. Admire his countless awards, records, and film costumes, including a very rare uranium disc from 1980 that only artists like Michael Jackson or Queen have received.

Admire the Church of Santa María la Mayor, the oldest building in Linares, built on the site of a mosque in the 13th century. Built in a Gothic-Renaissance style with contributions from architect Andrés de Vandelvira, it was raised to the status of a basilica by Pope Francis in 2016.

activities.text: Stroll along the Paseo de Linarejos, a pleasant boulevard lined with green spaces where locals enjoy tapas and gather. It begins at the white marble Constitution Fountain and ends at the statue of guitarist Andrés Segovia, one of the city's most illustrious figures.

Visit the Andrés Segovia House Museum in the 17th-century Orozco Palace. View the guitars that belonged to the maestro, the medals honouring his achievements, and the crypt where his remains lie. In November, it hosts the International Guitar Meetings.

days_plan.itin_title: Jaén Province Tour: Renaissance and Olive Trees

map_keywords: Hospital of the Marquis of Linares

visits.text: The historic center of Llanes preserves about 300 meters of 13th-century wall. The Torreón, a five-story circular crenelated tower, served as a watchtower and defense against seaborne invasions. It adjoins the Casino, an elegant 'Indiano' building from 1910.

The Basilica of Santa María del Conceyu, begun in the 13th century, is a fine example of the Romanesque-Gothic transition. Its distinctive feature: it was funded by a tax paid by all inhabitants, making it a church of the people rather than of the clergy.

Walk down to the fishing harbor to behold the Cubos de la Memoria. More than 200 concrete blocks on the breakwater were painted by Basque artist Ibarrola between 2001 and 2006: abstract figures, ancestral symbols, and vivid colors change in appearance with the light and tides.
Toró beach, 500 meters from the center, is distinguished by its erosion-sculpted rocks that rise from the sand like sentinels. At low tide, natural pools form between the boulders.
Head to Barro beach, accessible by a short road from Llanes. More sheltered than Toró, it offers a long stretch of fine sand framed by green meadows sloping down to the water.

activities.text: Follow the Paseo de San Pedro, a coastal path laid out along the cliffs. The path overlooks the sea and offers views of Sablón beach, the rocks of Toró and the Sierra del Cuera in the background.
The municipality of Llanes boasts more than thirty beaches. Sample a smoked Gamoneu or a cave-aged Cabrales accompanied by cider in a harbor bar—mountain cheeses are the local pride.
Stay until sunset at Punta de Toró or the Llanes lighthouse (1860) at the end of the San Antón promenade. Ibarrola's colored cubes blaze in the low-angle light.

days_plan.itin_title: Asturias Road Trip: Cantabrian Coast and Picos de Europa

places.name: Lleida

visits.text: The Seu Vella crowns the hill that gives Lleida its skyline, and it is the silhouette you can pick out from the Pyrenees on a clear day. Begun in 1203 by Pere de Coma on the remains of a mosque, consecrated in 1278 and finished in 1431 with its bell tower – more than two centuries of building work. It is regarded as the last great Romanesque cathedral in Europe, already showing Gothic elements. Then in 1707 Philip V closed it to worship and turned it into an army barracks for 240 years. Now restored to its role as a heritage site, it can be visited along with its huge cloister – one of the largest in Europe – and the Gothic bell tower. 238 steps up a spiral staircase for the view.

Atop the Turó, just above the cathedral, the Castell del Rei – la Suda – overlooks what remains of a Muslim castle documented since 882. Palace of the kings of Aragon from the 12th to 16th centuries, destroyed during the 18th-century wars and finished off by an explosion during the Napoleonic wars. Less than a quarter survives, but the interpretation centre housed in the royal hall tells the story of how Lleida shifted from al-Andalus to the Crown of Aragon. A hillside lift makes the site accessible to those with reduced mobility – rare for this type of monument.

Below it, the Catedral Nova on Carrer Major went up between the 18th and 19th centuries to replace the confiscated Seu Vella. Neoclassical, with a plainer facade. Inside, the Virgin of Blau bears a mark on her forehead: the legend says a sculptor jealous of his apprentice's work tried to smash the statue with a hammer; the hammer bounced back and killed him, leaving the Virgin with the bluish bruise that gave her her name. The first name Blau, still common in Lleida, comes from this.

The Palau de la Paeria, on the square of the same name, is Lleida's town hall – and one of the finest Gothic civic buildings in Catalonia. Built in the early 13th century by the lords of Sanaüja and handed to the city in 1383 as its municipal seat, it has two facades: civic Romanesque on the square side, neoclassical on the Segre side. The archives hold the Charter of the People, one of the earliest known urban constitutions, dated to the 12th century. Free to visit on weekdays.

One last detour before the break: the Dipòsit del Pla de l'Aigua, nicknamed the “water cathedral”. Built in the late 18th century, it's simply the city's first drinking water reservoir – 25 stone pillars, 6 barrel vaults, a capacity of 9 million litres. Closed then forgotten for decades, it is now open to visitors. Don't miss the acoustics: clap beneath the vault, the sound returns eight times.

activities.text: Walk along the Segre at sunset. The river cuts through the city and the banks have been developed—bike paths, picnic areas, even kayak and canoe launches. From here you get the finest view of the Seu Vella lit up after nightfall. Locals come for their evening jog, giving a strangely provincial feel to a city of 140,000. Sample caracoles a la llauna or xató at an old-town tavern to finish.

On the first Saturday of the month, the market in and around Plaça Sant Joan is one of the most authentic in inland Catalonia. Producers from Urgell, cheeses from the Pyrenees, arbequina olive oil, mountain honey and coca de recapte (Catalan focaccia with toppings). It is also a chance to hear Western Catalan, slightly different from the Catalan spoken in Barcelona.

places.name: Logrono

visits.text: Calle Laurel in Logroño is some fifty pintxos bars over 100 meters - and each has had its specialty for decades. Bar Soriano has served only garlic-grilled mushrooms for decades. A single item on the menu, lines spilling onto the sidewalk, and it's perfectly justified. Next door, Bar Sebas for stuffed eggs, Tastavin for wine selections by the glass. Count on at least two hours to do the street properly.

The Cathedral of Santa María de la Redonda is a curiosity: two 18th-century Baroque towers placed on a 15th-century Gothic collegiate church, all in the center of a lively square. The interior hides a copy of Michelangelo's Calvary, a Crucifixion from the early 16th century long attributed to Michelangelo, now considered to be from his circle. Free entry, 20 minutes is enough.

Bodegas Ontañón on the outskirts of Logroño: the tasting room is decorated with stained glass, sculptures and mosaics—the owner is an art patron, and it shows as soon as you enter. It's a good introduction to the contemporary Reserva style, more accessible than the great wineries of Haro. Tour + 4 wines, €25. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

The Paseo del Espolón in central Logroño: century-old plane trees, a bandstand and benches that are always occupied. This is where the people of Logroño take their evening stroll, and you will inevitably meet Camino de Santiago pilgrims with their walking sticks and shells - Logroño is a major stop on the route.

Briones is perched on a promontory above the Ebro, one of the best-preserved villages in Rioja Alta. It is about 34 km from Logroño, a 30-minute drive. At its foot is the Vivanco Museum of Wine Culture—probably the best wine museum in the world, and that is no empty phrase. Four floors, from Roman presses to Greek amphorae, works by Picasso, Miró and Sorolla acquired by the Vivanco family, and the archaeology of viticulture stretching back 8,000 years. Allow at least 3 hours, really. Ticket €17, tasting costs extra. Do not rush it.

San Vicente de la Sonsierra, about 35 km from Logroño, a 35-minute drive: the medieval bridge over the Ebro and the castle overlooking the village since the 10th century. An intact winegrowers' village, sloping streets and cellars beneath every house. A 15-minute stroll is enough, but the stop is worthwhile - and Bodegas Sierra Cantabria is right there.

Bodegas Sierra Cantabria, owned by the Eguren family—the same family behind the hugely celebrated Viñedo de San Vicente and Teso La Monja in Toro. Plan a same-day round trip from Logroño. This final tasting is a good overview of the week: precise wines expressing their terroir, unlike anything else. Buy a few bottles to take away—winery prices are well below retail.

activities.text: An evening walk along the full length of Calle Laurel: the classic route starts at the east end of the street and heads west, stopping at each bar that catches your eye. Order a glass of Rioja Crianza or a txakoli if you want to keep things light. The atmosphere picks up around 9 pm.

Logroño's covered market in the morning (Mercado de Abastos): fruit, vegetables from Rioja's market gardens, cheeses, cured meats. The piquillo peppers from Navarre are here, the artichokes from Tudela too. Excellent for putting together a picnic or understanding what you've been eating for two days.

Lunch at the Vivanco Museum restaurant, with a terrace facing the vineyards and the Ebro plain. Plan a same-day round trip from Logroño. Classic Riojan cuisine, paired with the family's wines. This is one of the few museum restaurants whose menu deserves your time.

One last evening visit to Calle Laurel in Logroño, with a farewell glass of a Reserva you'll have chosen yourself after five days of tasting. It's time to compare it with what you thought you knew about Rioja before arriving.

visits.text: From the terrace of the Fortaleza del Sol, the whole Guadalentín valley spreads out at an altitude of 640 m. This 52,000 m² fortress (640 m long, one of Spain's largest) was the Christian outpost facing the Nasrid kingdom of Granada for over 250 years after the conquest of 1244. The Alfonsine Tower, commissioned by Alfonso X the Wise, and the Torre del Espolón dominate the complex. The medieval judería—unique in Murcia—was discovered during excavations when the neighbouring Parador was built.

Descending from the castle, Baroque Lorca takes over: the church of Santiago, Palacio de Guevara, and a Semana Santa declared Festival of International Tourist Interest for its embroideries and processions rivalling Seville. The Teatro Guerra (1861), Murcia's oldest theatre still in operation, deserves a look.

activities.text: Go down into the castle's judería: excavations uncovered 12 houses and a 14th-15th century synagogue, the only one ever found in the Region of Murcia. Access to the synagogue is included in the fortress ticket (around €6). Theatrical evening tours (available seasonally) recreate medieval life in a very vivid way.

places.name: Los Llanos De Aridane

visits.text: Los Llanos de Aridane is the most populous town on La Palma, set in the green Aridane valley on the western slope - a microclimate warmer and sunnier than the capital. The historic centre is home to the Museo de La Calle, a permanent open-air exhibition of contemporary art: since 1999, murals painted directly on the town's blank walls by recognised artists have covered up to 140 m² of wall. Stroll through the lanes to find them.

The Benahoarita Archaeological Museum traces the life of La Palma's prehistoric inhabitants, the Benahoaritas—a people of Berber origin who arrived on the island before the Spanish conquest. Reconstructions of their habitat, beliefs, and crafts help understand how they lived in this volcanic environment before being expelled in the 15th century.

Tajogaite volcano—also called Cumbre Vieja—erupted on September 19, 2021 and flowed for 85 days until December. The flow covered 1,218 hectares, destroyed 1,345 houses and 73 km of roads, and expanded the island by 47 hectares into the sea. From Los Llanos, Mirador de Tajuya offers the best view of the entire lava field and the new volcanic cone. Guided 5 km trails allow you to approach the crater's base from Llano del Jable.

Fuencaliente, at the southern tip of La Palma, is a land of volcanoes. Allow half a day from Los Llanos de Aridane, including the drive. The San Antonio volcano (430 m) erupted in 1677 and its crater is freely accessible, with an interpretation centre tracing the history of Canarian volcanism. Right next to it, Teneguía spewed lava as recently as October 1971 - less than 55 years ago. You can walk on its still-warm slopes and watch the vegetation gradually recolonising the lava. Do not miss the Fuencaliente lighthouse at the end of the cape: from the point, you get a view of both coasts of the island at once.

Fuencaliente's vineyards merit a stop. As in Lanzarote, vines grow here in volcanic soils on terraces—but the landscapes are even more dramatic because Teneguía's lava fields descend right to the vineyards. The La Palma appellation produces volcanic malvasía and red wines from listán negro whose reputation far exceeds the island.

If the weather allows, drive up to the Roque de los Muchachos (2,426 m), the island's highest point, about 1 hour 30 by road from Los Llanos de Aridane. The road winds through Canary pine forests and alpine zones to the summit, home to the domes of the astrophysical observatory - one of the most advanced observation centres in the world, benefiting from the island's low light pollution. On a clear day, you can see Mount Teide on Tenerife from the summit.

activities.text: Hike the Route of the Volcanoes (Cumbre Vieja) from the El Pilar refuge. This GR-131 trail follows the volcanic ridge where all the island's historic eruptions occurred—1949 (Hoyo Negro), 1971 (Teneguía), and 2021 (Tajogaite). The panorama from the ridges embraces the entire Aridane valley on one side and the Atlantic on the other. Start early: wind can be fierce and heat intense on this shadeless terrain.

Relaxation at Puerto de Tazacorte, a colourful fishing port 10 minutes from Los Llanos. Waterfront restaurants serve the day's catch—grouper, vieja (parrotfish), and local prawns. The sunset from the terrace facing the Atlantic is one of La Palma's finest. Boat trips to observe dolphins and whales depart from this port.

Tasting at Casa Museo del Vino Las Manchas, which traces La Palma's winemaking history and offers local wine tastings. The island produces malvasía, listán negro, and several Canarian grape varieties that exist nowhere else.

A swim at Charco Verde beach, on the west coast of La Palma, two kilometres south of Puerto Naos. This small black-sand cove, lined with cliffs and banana plantations, is sheltered by rocks that calm the sea, which makes it pleasant even with children. A kiosk with a terrace serves food and drinks on site. Check the weather before setting off, as the Atlantic swell can be strong.

Market or end-of-trip stroll in Los Llanos de Aridane. The town is also the finish line of the Transvulcania, one of the world's best mountain races. The lively pedestrian centre and cafe terraces offer a final immersion in local life before heading to the airport.

Closing lunch with La Palma specialties: potaje de berros (watercress soup), pork in mojo sauce, and bienmesabe for dessert. The island is renowned for exceptional agricultural products—avocados, bananas, and palmero PDO cheese that you can bring home vacuum-sealed.

visits.text: Lucena is one of Spain's great Sephardic unknowns: a majority-Jewish city between the 9th and 12th centuries under Al-Andalus, nicknamed Eliossana—'God has saved us.' Capital of Andalusian Judaism for 300 years, renowned Talmudic school. Its population fled before the Almohad invasions of 1146-1148, which forced conversion or death. The Castillo del Moral, where Boabdil was reportedly imprisoned after his defeat at Lucena in 1483, is now the municipal museum—the episode is minor in the Reconquista timeline but narrated locally as a great feat.

The Jewish necropolis of Lucena, discovered in 2006 during roadworks, is the largest known on the Iberian Peninsula: 346 graves dating from the 9th to the 11th century. Inscriptions in Hebrew and Arabic - evidence of a linguistic coexistence that is unimaginable today. Modest but moving.

activities.text: Coffee-tapas break at La Casa del Vino, on Plaza Nueva. Montilla-Moriles wines (neighboring DOC), regional specialty of draft fino. Tapas of salmorejo and Iberian salchichón. Good spot to catch your breath before hitting the road to Granada.

days_plan.itin_title: Dark Andalusia: 10 Days from Seville to Málaga

visits.text: Lugo, a 2,000-year-old city. Founded in 13 BCE under the name Lucus Augusti—“sacred grove of Augustus”—derived from the Celtic deity Lugh, to whom a sacred grove on the site was dedicated. And the city boils down to one thing absolutely unique in the world: its Roman wall. A circumference of 2,117 meters, 71 towers preserved out of the original 85, 10 gates (5 Roman, 5 added later). Built between 260 and 320 under Constantine I. It's the only Roman wall in Europe to have preserved its entire perimeter, which earned it UNESCO listing in 2000. The wall walk, 4 meters wide, can be followed on foot or by bike—free, open 24/7.

Inside the walls, the Cathedral of Santa María. Construction began in 1129 on the orders of Alfonso VII and continued century after century in every style: a Romanesque nave, Gothic ambulatory, baroque west façade, neoclassical cloister. The standout feature: the Chapel of the Virgin of the Large Eyes (Virxe dos Ollos Grandes), spectacular Galician baroque. And a unique privilege in Spain: Lugo Cathedral has kept the Blessed Sacrament on perpetual display since the 14th century, following a Eucharistic miracle. It's depicted in the city's coat of arms—a chalice with a host.

Beneath a pedestrian street in the center, the Casa dos Mosaicos is a recently opened archaeological site (2011): the remains of a 3rd-century Roman domus, with mosaics in situ. You see them through a glass floor. The rooms retain their layout: tablinum, oecus, peristylium. Digital reconstructions on screens. Small, surprising, free, never crowded. Five minutes away is Praza do Campo, a former Roman forum that became a medieval market, now the heart of tapas evenings.

Outside the walls, 300 meters to the south, the ancient Roman baths are incorporated into the Balneario de Lugo hotel building—iron- and bicarbonate-rich water at 43°C that has flowed continuously since antiquity. The 1st-century changing room and cold-bath room have been preserved. You can bathe in the spa (allow €25 for admission; it is a proper spa). The Ponte Vello, which spans the Miño right next door, is also Roman in origin—rebuilt in the 12th century.

activities.text: A gastronomic tour. The official slogan “For food, Lugo” is no empty boast: the city has an exceptional concentration of starred or recommended restaurants. Local specialties: lacón con grelos (ham hock with turnip greens), pulpo a feira, tarta de Mondoñedo, Galician churrasco, PDO tetilla cheese. Don't miss a small draft beer of Estrella Galicia—a regional beer brewed in A Coruña—with a slice of empanada. Reliable places: Mesón Alberto, Paprica, Don Mansito.

If you catch Arde Lucus (the weekend closest to the summer solstice, in mid-June), it's the event not to miss. For three days, the city transforms into ancient Rome: 600 costumed participants, legionaries, senators, slaves, gladiators, Roman weddings, banquets, reenacted battles in the forum. Over 300,000 visitors in three days. A Festival of National Tourist Interest since 2007.

days_plan.itin_title: Castile and León and Galicia: 21 days from Roman aqueducts to the Atlantic
Galicia: Complete 10-Day Circuit

visits.text: Begin your Madrid stay along the Paseo del Arte, Europe's most concentrated museum triangle. The Prado Museum, founded in 1819 in a neoclassical building by Juan de Villanueva, houses over 8,000 paintings—only a fraction of which are on display. Velázquez's Las Meninas (1656), Hieronymus Bosch's Garden of Earthly Delights (circa 1500), Rubens's The Three Graces, and Goya's Black Paintings await you in the main galleries. Allow at least 2 hours for the major works, longer if you're a painting enthusiast. Arrive at opening time to avoid the queues—they lengthen quickly after 11am.

A ten-minute walk south along the Paseo del Prado brings you to the Reina Sofía Museum, housed in the former 18th-century San Carlos Hospital. The museum opened in 1992 and covers Spanish art from 1881 onwards. The absolute star is Picasso's Guernica (1937)—7.76 metres wide, painted in response to the bombing of the Basque village by the German Condor Legion during the Civil War. The room is always crowded, but the canvas is so immense you can see it well from anywhere. Don't miss Dalí's The Great Masturbator and Miró's canvases on the upper floors.

To catch your breath between museums, cross the street to the Parque del Retiro - 125 hectares of greenery right in the centre of Madrid. The park was created in the 17th century as the garden of the Buen Retiro palace, residence of Philip IV. Rent a rowing boat on the Estanque Grande, facing the monument to Alfonso XII.

Devote the morning to the Royal Palace, official residence of the Spanish monarchs—though the royal family no longer lives there. Built between 1738 and 1764 on the site of the former Habsburg Alcázar destroyed by fire, it's the largest palace in Western Europe by floor area: 135,000 m² and 3,418 rooms. You'll visit the state rooms—the Throne Room with its Tiepolo frescoes, the Gala Dining Room with its 140-seat table, and the Royal Armoury, one of the world's most complete collections with armour belonging to Charles V and Philip II. Allow 1.5 to 2 hours.

Leaving the palace, cross Plaza de la Armería to the Almudena Cathedral. Begun in 1883, it wasn't completed and consecrated until 1993 by Pope John Paul II—over a century of construction. The interior is surprisingly modern, with brightly painted ceilings that contrast sharply with the sobriety of the neoclassical façade. Climb to the dome for views over the palace and Casa de Campo.

Walk down to Plaza Mayor via Calle Mayor. This arcaded rectangular square, completed in 1619 under Philip III, was the scene of Inquisition autos-da-fé, bullfights, and public executions. Today, the terraces beneath the porticos are tourist traps—just admire the architecture and the equestrian statue of Philip III at the centre, then head to Mercado de San Miguel, just next door. This covered market from 1916, with its iron-and-glass structure, has become a gourmet temple: oysters, jamón ibérico, churros, vermouth, and creative tapas.

Head up to Gran Vía, Madrid's main commercial artery, cut through between 1910 and 1929. The Edificio Metrópolis (1911), at the corner of Calle de Alcalá, with its gilded dome and winged Victory, is the city's postcard image. Continue west to the Templo de Debod, an authentic Egyptian temple from the 2nd century BC, gifted by Egypt to Spain in 1968 in thanks for its help saving the Nubian temples threatened by the Aswan Dam. At sunset, the temple's reflections in the pool with Casa de Campo in the background offer one of Madrid's most beautiful views.

activities.text: In the late afternoon, head to Plaza de Santa Ana for a tapas crawl through the Las Letras neighbourhood—the literary quarter where Cervantes, Lope de Vega, and Quevedo lived in the 17th century. The tapas bars around the square and along Calle de las Huertas serve generous portions of tortilla, croquetas, and jamón ibérico. Wash it down with a glass of Ribera del Duero or a vermut de grifo (vermouth on tap), Madrid's traditional aperitif drink.

If you're in Madrid on a Sunday morning, don't miss El Rastro, Spain's largest flea market. It spreads out every Sunday from 9am to 3pm around Calle de la Ribera de Curtidores, in the La Latina neighbourhood. Antiques, vintage clothing, books, vinyl, curiosities—it's a joyful bazaar that attracts Madrileños as much as visitors. After the market, the tapas bars of La Latina are mobbed—it's Madrid's Sunday ritual.

In the evening, catch a flamenco show. Madrid isn't Andalusia, but the city has a historic flamenco scene—many Andalusian artists have settled here since the 19th century. Tablaos in the La Latina and Lavapiés neighbourhoods offer intimate performances with singing, guitar, and dance. Allow 1 to 1.5 hours for a show.
