visits.text: En route southeast, cross the Sierra de Cardeña y Montoro Natural Park—the highest in Córdoba province. The Mediterranean forest of holm oaks and cork oaks is dense, and the wildlife rich: Iberian lynx (reintroduced), wolf (last Andalusian populations), otter, Spanish imperial eagle. The Río Yeguas trail crosses spectacular granite rock landscapes. Allow 2 to 3 hours for a hike in the park before descending toward Montoro.

Montoro is a surprise. This village of 10,000 inhabitants, classified as a Historic-Artistic Ensemble since 1969, sits on a promontory encircled by a spectacular meander of the Guadalquivir—almost a peninsula. What strikes you first is the color: the monuments are built in piedra molinaza, a local red sandstone that gives the church, ducal palace, and manor façades terracotta hues. The church of San Bartolomé (15th century), in the center on Plaza de España, has a red sandstone bell tower nicknamed 'the Red Giralda' for its resemblance to the Sevillian campanile. Opposite, the Ducal Palace of the Casa de Alba (16th century), now the town hall, presents Mudéjar elements in piedra molinaza.

Descend toward the Puente de las Donadas, built in 1498 by Enrique Egas—one of the finest bridges in the province. Its name ('bridge of the women who gave') comes from the fact that the women of Montoro sold their jewelry to finance its construction, and the king granted them in exchange the privilege of no longer having to lodge or feed troops. From the bridge, the view of the Guadalquivir's meander encircling Montoro is the village's emblematic image. Before leaving Montoro, seek out the Casa de las Conchas—a house whose façade and interior patios are entirely covered with seashells, 45 million in total, accumulated over 50 years by a passionate local.

activities.text: Montoro is at the heart of Córdoba's olive-growing zone—the surrounding olive groves produce PDO Montoro-Adamuz olive oil. Cooperatives offer visits and tastings. Local gastronomy reflects the terroir: ajo sopeao (tomato, pepper, and garlic stew), tortilla de faisanes (bean omelet), perdices en salsa (partridge in sauce), and tortas de manteca for dessert.

days_plan.itin_title: Córdoba and the Sierra Morena: From the Caliphate to the Dehesas of Los Pedroches

visits.text: The monastery of Santa Maria de Montserrat clings to a ledge at 720 meters altitude, anchored to a massif of weirdly sculpted conglomerate. Founded in 1025, it still houses a hundred Benedictine monks. But it's the Black Madonna—the Moreneta—that draws 2.3 million visitors annually: a 12th-century Romanesque statue, patron saint of Catalonia since 1881. The queue to touch her can exceed two hours in high season. Arrive before 9:30 AM or after 5 PM—it's the only way.

The Museu de Montserrat is the site's big surprise—a collection of 1,300 works including Caravaggio, Picasso, Dalí, El Greco, Monet, and Miró, plus an archaeological section on the biblical Near East with an actual mummy. Built through private donations since the 19th century, it's now one of Catalonia's most important collections outside Barcelona. Allow an hour, entry €8. Almost deserted at midday when everyone's queuing for the Virgin.

At 1 PM on weekdays and noon on Sundays, the Escolania choir sings for 15 minutes in the basilica. One of Europe's oldest boys' choirs, documented since the 14th century, with some fifty resident boys. Remarkable acoustics—Jordi Savall records in the neighboring chapels for this reason. Arrive 30 minutes early for a seat. No singing in July or during Christmas holidays.

Next to the basilica, the Santa Cova funicular descends in 5 minutes to the cave chapel built where, according to legend, shepherds discovered the statue in 880. The walk from the station takes 20 minutes along the Way of the Cross, punctuated by 14 Modernist sculptures by the great Catalan architects of the early 20th century, including Gaudí and Puig i Cadafalch. The path is free, easy trail, plunging views over the valley. Round-trip funicular: €4.50.

activities.text: The Sant Joan funicular climbs in 7 minutes to 1,000 meters altitude—average gradient of 65%, one of Europe's steepest. At the top, five marked trails head toward hermitages and peaks. Most accessible: the Sant Joan loop, 2.7 km in 1 hour, no serious elevation gain, returning with views above the monastery. For seasoned hikers, Sant Jeroni at 1,236 meters, the summit: 4 hours round trip, 360° views to the Pyrenees on clear days.

Buy mató at the monastery exit—fresh Catalan goat cheese, sold for €5 a pot by local farmers, eaten drizzled with Pyrenean honey. A tradition for every pilgrim since the Middle Ages. For dinner, the restaurant at Hotel Abat Cisneros, attached to the monastery, serves honest Catalan cuisine at €35. Booking advised on weekends. Absolute calm after the tour buses depart at 6 PM—one of the benefits of staying overnight.

days_plan.itin_title: Catalonia Wine Route - 7 Days from Penedès to Priorat

visits.text: The scent of pine resin and salt rises through the alleyways: Moraira has kept its fishing village proportions despite the second-home tourism that has settled here. The 18th-century Castillo de Moraira sits on l'Ampolla beach, built to repel pirates. The Cap d'Or tower (11 meters) watches over the port at the opposite end. On Friday mornings, the market spreads along the entire promenade.

activities.text: Climb up to the Cap d'Or tower to take in the sweep of Moraira bay—on clear days the Peñón de Ifach looms to the south. The SL-CV51 trail starts from El Portet beach and takes 1h round trip. Back at sea level, Cala del Moraig merits a stop for diving or swimming in deep water. Closed-toe shoes essential on the rocky path.

days_plan.itin_title: Costa Blanca & Alicante Hinterland: 12 days

visits.text: Moratalla is a hilltop village in northwestern Murcia, dominated by a medieval castle with fine views of the mountains and pine forests. Narrow lanes climb through whitewashed houses to the fortress, giving the village a remote feel. Moratalla is also known for its rock art: the surrounding area has several shelters decorated with prehistoric paintings, included in the UNESCO-listed Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. The abrigos del Cañaíca del Calar contain hunting scenes dating back millennia. Book a visit to these shelters through the Casa de Cristo interpretation center; the interior of Moratalla castle is temporarily closed to visitors.

From Moratalla, the road to Lorca crosses dry mountain landscapes. The Cañón de los Almadenes, reached from Calasparra or Cieza, requires a separate detour from Moratalla; allow for a return trip if you want to see it. Lorca, your exit point towards Murcia, is overlooked by a fortress and its two towers, Alfonsina and Espolón - this site is already covered in another ORT itinerary.

activities.text: From Moratalla, allow for a return trip towards Calasparra or Cieza for this activity. Operators offer canoe or kayak trips through the Segura gorges between Calasparra and Cieza, passing through the Cañón de los Almadenes. Allow 2 to 3 hours for a relaxed descent past rock walls and moderate rapids. This activity suits beginners and makes a nature-filled end to the trip.

Before leaving northwestern Murcia, try Calasparra rice, a rice with protected designation of origin. Grown on terraces irrigated by the Segura since the Arab period, it is smaller and firmer than other Spanish rice varieties, ideal for paellas and caldero dishes (fish and rice cooked in a pot).

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Granada: Alpujarras, Guadix and the Sierras
Murcia Coast and Hinterland: 13 days from La Manga to Cuenca

places.name: Morella

visits.text: The castle of Morella crowns the rocky outcrop at an altitude of 1,070 meters. Built in the 13th century, it witnessed battles involving El Cid and sheltered Pope Luna in 1414.
The ramparts stretch for 2.5 kilometers and have protected the town since the 14th century. Their 14 towers and 6 gates testify to Morella's strategic importance.

The Basilica of Santa María la Mayor displays its Gothic portals—the Portal of the Apostles and the Portal of the Virgins—carved in the 14th and 15th centuries. The spiral staircase leading to the rood screen is entirely covered with painted reliefs.

The aqueduct of Santa Llúcia dates from 1338. Its two surviving Gothic arches once carried water from the springs to the town. The trail alongside offers panoramic views across the Els Ports countryside.
The Torres de San Miguel form the main gateway. These twin octagonal towers from the 14th century house a collection of medieval games and offer stunning views over Morella's rooftops.
Step inside the San Francisco convent to see the Dance of Death, an enigmatic 14th-century fresco showing nobility, clergy, and common people face to face with death.
Walk through the arcades of Blasco de Alagón and along the stepped alleys. Aristocratic houses—Ciurana, Piquer, Rovira, Cardinal Ram—punctuate the route.

activities.text: Morella is the kingdom of black truffles. Restaurants offer menus and tastings from November through March, accompanied by local cheeses aged in cellars.
The Paseo de la Alameda circles the mountain. This shaded promenade offers changing perspectives on the ramparts and the surrounding countryside.
Textile workshops keep alive a centuries-old tradition. Some artisans open their doors to demonstrate old-fashioned weaving techniques.
The cave paintings of Morella La Vella lie 6 kilometers away. These UNESCO-listed hunting scenes can be visited in small groups on weekends.

days_plan.itin_title: Castellón and Maestrazgo Route: Castles and Coves
Northern Valencia Road Trip: 10 Days of Villages

map_keywords: Basilique Santa María la Mayor Morella

visits.text: The Cathedral of Saint Mary blends a soaring Gothic interior with a baroque façade designed by Jaime Bort in 1751. Its 95-meter tower—Spain's second tallest—offers sweeping views over Murcia's vast orchards and market gardens.

Step through the doors of the Real Casino. The Moorish patio glitters with 20,000 sheets of gold leaf, the neo-baroque ballroom displays allegorical ceiling paintings celebrating the arts, and the English library is adorned with wrought-iron flamingos.
Plaza de las Flores fills with terrace cafés by 5 PM. Cross the Puente de los Peligros over the Segura River, where a statue of the Virgin has stood watch since the 18th century.
The Salzillo Museum showcases the baroque processional sculptures of Francisco Salzillo. Polychrome wood, hauntingly lifelike faces, meticulous detail in every gesture.
The Episcopal Palace unfurls an exuberant rococo façade across the Plaza del Cardenal Belluga.

activities.text: Go on a tapas crawl around Plaza Julián Romea. Marineras (anchovy toasts), michirones (spiced fava beans), pasteles de carne (savory meat pies).
Paparajotes are lemon-tree leaves dipped in sweet batter and fried—a Murcian specialty served for dessert.
The Teatro Romea stages concerts, operas, and comedies in a stunning 19th-century hall with remarkable acoustics.

days_plan.itin_title: Murcia Road Trip: Baroque Splendor & Costa Cálida
Murcia Coast and Hinterland: 13 days from La Manga to Cuenca

places.name: Muxia

visits.text: The Sanctuary of Nosa Señora da Barca, built in the 18th century on a rocky headland, marks the spiritual terminus of the Fisterra pilgrimage route.
The Pedra de Abalar rocks and sways when storms batter the coast. The Pedra dos Cadrís is said to cure back pain if you crawl beneath it nine times.
The A Ferida monument commemorates the 2002 Prestige oil spill disaster. Two granite blocks separated by a fissure symbolize the wound inflicted on the coast.

Cabo Vilán raises its white lighthouse 105 metres above the waves. Spain’s first electrified lighthouse in 1896, it marks the dangers of the Costa da Morte. Located about 28 km from Muxía, it is a 40-minute drive.
The English Cemetery, near the cape, contains the graves of the 172 sailors from HMS Serpent who were shipwrecked in 1890. Plan a round trip during the day from Muxía.

activities.text: Hike the coastal trail from Muxía to Monte Corpiño for sweeping views across the Ría de Camariñas and out to Cape Vilán.
The Atlantic-battered cliffs draw cormorants and kittiwakes. Bring binoculars to watch the seabird colonies wheel and dive.
The sunset viewed from the sanctuary illuminates the polished granite rocks.

days_plan.itin_title: Galicia Road Trip: Santiago de Compostela and the Coast of Death

map_keywords: Sanctuaire Nosa Señora da Barca Muxía
Cimetière des Anglais Costa da Morte

visits.text: The roar precedes the vision: water bursts from the Cueva de los Chorros at between 80 and 100 metres high, plunging into successive pools before forming the río Mundo. During the phenomenon called 'El Reventón', after heavy rains, the flow multiplies spectacularly and impressively. The trail to the mirador runs 1.5 km from the Chorros parking. Swimming banned in the pools near the source.

activities.text: If you come after heavy rain, watch for the Reventón: a torrential flow bursts from the rock with a force that completely transforms the landscape—locals describe it as a spectacle in its own right. Otherwise, an approximately 8 km return hike from Puerto del Arenal climbs to the upper viewpoint. Drones are not permitted above the waterfall.

days_plan.itin_title: Castilla-La Mancha: Windmills and Sierra in 11 days

visits.text: Navacerrada Pass (Puerto de Navacerrada) sits at 1,860 meters, straddling Madrid and Segovia provinces. A natural crossroads between Siete Picos to the west and Bola del Mundo to the east, the latter crowned by rocket-shaped television antennas.
Gaze across Cuerda Larga, a mountain ridge stretching toward the horizon. Scots pines (Pinus sylvestris) cling to the slopes, alpine meadows burst with wildflowers come summer.
Bola del Mundo peaks at 2,258 meters, crowned by historic antennas that once broadcast television across the Iberian Peninsula. From the summit, panoramas unfold in every direction.
The Siete Picos massif arrays seven granite peaks in a dramatic line. The seventh summit reaches 2,138 meters, offering 360° views across the Sierra de Guadarrama.

activities.text: Hike to Siete Picos via the PR-M trail. The rocky ridge demands some easy scrambling. With 764 meters of elevation gain, spectacular panoramas are guaranteed every step of the way.
The Guarramillas chairlift operates in summer. Ride up for panoramic views to Bar La Bola, a high-altitude establishment at 2,000 meters—the highest point in the Community of Madrid.
In winter, the ski resort offers family-friendly slopes and breathtaking views. Light, dry snow characteristic of high altitude. Snow cover typically arrives in January.

days_plan.itin_title: Sierra de Guadarrama Road Trip: Castles and Forests

visits.text: The people of Navajas call it their back garden—the Cascada del Brazal lies in the wooded valley of the Salto de la Novia, a 10-minute walk from the village. This short 2-hour stop is ideal for stretching your legs between Montanejos and Sagunto. The trail is signposted and can be walked in sneakers.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Valencia Road Trip: 10 Days of Villages

visits.text: On January 12, 1959, five teenagers were looking for bats and punched a hole in the rock wall - that's how the Cueva de Nerja was discovered. Inside: in the Hall of the Cataclysm, a limestone column 32 meters high and 13 meters in diameter, listed in the Guinness Book of Records since 1989 as the world's largest known underground column. Allow 1h30. Book ahead in summer - visitor numbers are capped.

Salt air thick at the end of the promontory, the sea on either side - the Balcón de Europa lives up to its name. Alfonso XII christened it so in January 1885 during a visit after the earthquake that devastated the region. A bronze statue marks the moment, leaning on the railing. Five minutes is enough, but you'll stay longer.

activities.text: If you are staying in Nerja, head down to Burriana before 9 a.m.: the beach is still empty and the chiringuitos are just beginning to open. You will find fresh-fish restaurants there. Espetos of sardines grilled over a wood fire.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Coast: Málaga to Cartagena in 9 Days

places.name: O Cebreiro

visits.text: The road from Monforte to O Cebreiro crosses the mountainous heart of Lugo province—chestnut forests, meadows, stone hamlets where time seems to have stopped. O Cebreiro (1,300 m altitude) is the gateway to the Camino de Santiago in Galicia for pilgrims coming from Castile on the Camino Francés. The village has barely a handful of houses, a pilgrims' hostel, and a church—but the atmosphere is extraordinary, especially when fog rises from the valley and wraps around the pallozas.

The pallozas are the very reason for visiting O Cebreiro. These pre-Roman dwellings—circular or oval stone houses with conical thatched roofs—were inhabited until the mid-20th century. They descend directly from pre-Roman Celtic constructions (the castros). Several have been restored, and one houses a small ethnographic museum showing how peasant families lived: a single room shared with animals, a central hearth with no chimney (smoke escaped through the thatched roof). These structures are unique to this mountainous zone of Galicia and the Bierzo.

The church of Santa María la Real in O Cebreiro, pre-Romanesque (9th century), is one of the oldest in Galicia still standing. It's also the site of the 'Miracle of O Cebreiro': in the 14th century, a priest who doubted transubstantiation saw the bread and wine literally transform into flesh and blood during Mass. The chalice and paten from the miracle are still preserved in the church—and it's precisely these that are said to have inspired the legend of the Holy Grail in Wagner's Parsifal. The simple, moving Romanesque chalice is displayed in a case to the left of the altar.

activities.text: Walk a section of the Camino de Santiago from O Cebreiro—even if you're not a pilgrim, the descent to the village of Liñares then Hospital da Condesa (4 km, 1 hour) gives you a taste of what walkers experience: a dirt path between stone walls, birch forests, views of the Lugo mountains. You'll encounter pilgrims of all nationalities carrying their scallop shells and walking sticks.

If you continue by car to the Alto do Poio (1,337 m), the highest point of the Camino de Santiago in Galicia, you'll cross a landscape of moorland and peat bogs that recalls Scotland or Ireland. It's also excellent territory for spotting wild Galician horses (garañóns). In the evening, dine at O Cebreiro on caldo gallego and empanada—Galician mountain cuisine is simple and comforting.

days_plan.itin_title: Inland Galicia: From Ourense to the Ribeira Sacra

map_keywords: Iglesia Santa María la Real O Cebreiro

visits.text: The scent of citrus rises from the huertas before you even enter the valley. The Valle de Ricote, the last Moorish stronghold in the Spanish Levant until the expulsion of 1610, has preserved its Arab irrigation systems and century-old palm trees. In Abarán, the Noria Grande - almost 12 m in diameter and Europe's largest operating noria - still turns in the Segura. The village of Ojós (500 inhabitants) is a peaceful Murcian village.

activities.text: In Abarán, Europe's largest operating noria has been turning in the Segura for centuries. The Ruta de las Norias (4 km) follows the river between dense orchards and waterwheels. The Mirador del Alto de Bayna, a 30 m metal walkway above the river, offers a broad view over the valley. Rafting or canoeing and kayaking are available from several local operators.

days_plan.itin_title: Murcia Coast and Hinterland: 13 days from La Manga to Cuenca

places.name: Olite

visits.text: The Royal Palace of Olite was commissioned in 1402 by Charles III the Noble. Over 22 years rose one of Europe's most important Gothic civil buildings, complete with seven towers, gardens, and mudéjar decoration.
The royal chambers cluster around the central core. The splayed bay windows in the Queen's chamber overlook the orange tree courtyard.
Climb the Tower of the Three Crowns to discover one of the most breathtaking views of the complex. This tower was allegedly built for the king's children.
The church of Santa María la Real stands adjacent to the castle. Its Gothic sculpted portico displays balanced figures, fantastical animals, and vegetal motifs.
The church of San Pedro retains its octagonal bell tower. Inside, admire the main altarpiece and the baptismal fonts.
Wander the cobblestone lanes of the medieval center. The palace occupies a full third of the old town's surface area.

activities.text: Local bodegas offer tastings of Navarre DO wines. The wine region produces celebrated reds and rosés.
At the foot of the Tower of the Three Crowns, observe the reconstruction of a medieval ice well eight meters deep, once used as a refrigerator.
Head to the ramparts at sunset to watch the towers silhouette themselves against the golden light.
The Chapitel Tower, on Carlos III Square, housed one of the first public clocks on the peninsula.

days_plan.itin_title: Navarre Road Trip: Castles, Irati Forest & the Camino

map_keywords: Tower of the Three Crowns Olite
Santa María la Real Church Olite

places.name: Olvera

visits.text: Olvera's silhouette appears from afar: 12th-century Arab castle and neoclassical church side by side, on the ridgeline, photographed in every Andalusian brochure without ever growing stale. Up close, the medieval alleys preserve the typical interlacing of the Nasrid frontera. Declared a Conjunto Histórico-Artístico in 1983.

Olvera castle's Torre del Homenaje can be visited and gives a panorama over the sierra gaditana as far as Grazalema in clear weather. The climb is short. The church of Nuestra Señora de la Encarnación, right beside it, is neoclassical and closes early - check opening times at the village entrance.

activities.text: 36 km of disused railway track converted into a cycle path, through 30 tunnels and 4 viaducts - the Vía Verde de la Sierra crosses sierra landscapes that the road bypasses. Departing from the old Olvera station (converted into a discovery center) toward Puerto Serrano. Bike rental on site. Even an hour round trip through the first tunnels is worthwhile.

days_plan.itin_title: White Villages: Arcos, Grazalema, Ronda - 6 Days

map_keywords: Vía Verde de la Sierra Olvera

visits.text: Locals have come here every summer since the Clariano River carved these pools into the limestone. Six natural swimming holes bear specific names: Pou dels Esclaus, Pou Clar, Pou Gelat, Pou de la Reixa, Pou Fosc, Pou dels Cavalls. The walking or cycling circuit from Ontinyent passes through Mediterranean vegetation of agaves and carob trees. Pedestrian access only in high season—parking closes.

days_plan.itin_title: Costa Blanca & Alicante Hinterland: 12 days

places.name: Orbaneja Del Castillo

visits.text: Orbaneja del Castillo is perhaps Spain's most improbable village: a 25-meter waterfall emerges directly from the Cueva del Agua, flows through the village dividing houses into two quarters, and plunges into the Ebro below. Along the way, the water has formed terraced pools with turquoise reflections surrounded by green moss—the contrast is striking. The village, declared a historic site in 1993, has about fifty inhabitants and stone lanes where time seems frozen. Park at the lot outside the center.

The Cueva del Agua, from which the waterfall springs, is a karst cave you can visit on a guided tour in summer and on weekends. From the upper part of the town, climb to Orbaneja's natural viewpoint for a view down into the Ebro canyon—the limestone walls form rocky silhouettes that locals compare to African profiles. Also look for the natural arch that the river has sculpted in the cliff above the village.

activities.text: The Ebro canyon (Hoces del Alto Ebro y Rudrón) offers spectacular hikes from Orbaneja. The circular route linking Orbaneja del Castillo to Valdelateja follows the canyon for 17 km—allow a good half-day. If you prefer something shorter, the GR-99 between Pesquera de Ebro and Manzanedo offers the best gorge views in 2-3 hours.

days_plan.itin_title: Castile and León: Ramparts, Canyons and Peaks

map_keywords: Cueva del Agua Orbaneja del Castillo

visits.text: A Blue Flag beach in the middle of Extremadura, 200 km from the sea: the Playa de Orellana (called Costa Dulce) was the first inland beach in Spain to win this label. Clean water, eucalyptus, fine sand. A marina and a sendero azul complete the facilities.

The Castillo-Palacio de los Altamiranos, a 15th-century fortress transformed into a palace in the 16th, dominates the village. Lesser kestrels nest in its walls in spring. The building can be visited from outside; the interior is closed to the public.

Head to the 16th-century Convento de San Benito, in the village centre. The Iglesia de la Inmaculada Concepción, from the same century, completes the tour. Austere architecture, no frills. Allow ten minutes for each visit.

activities.text: The warm water of Orellana Lake is inviting for windsurfing, kayaking, and sailing. A boating club organises competitions and offers equipment rental. In summer, the chiringuitos on the Costa Dulce serve fried freshwater fish.

If you're into birdwatching, the Orellana reservoir is classified as a ZEPA (Special Protection Area for Birds). Cranes in winter, raptors all year. The marked trail around the lake offers observation points without disturbing the species.

days_plan.itin_title: La Siberia and La Serena: Secret Extremadura in 6 Days

visits.text: Orihuela often goes unnoticed on the road to Murcia, which is a mistake. Its historic center, declared an artistic monument in 1969, brings together El Salvador Cathedral (begun in the 14th century on the ruins of the Aljama mosque, elevated to cathedral in 1564), the convent of Santo Domingo, and the castle on Mount San Miguel. The cathedral preserves a Velázquez painting, The Temptation of Saint Thomas, in its sacred art museum.

activities.text: The market runs along the Segura amid the gentle scent of fruit and vegetables from the Vega Baja - the fertile plain already cultivated by the Romans. The house museum of poet Miguel Hernández, born in Orihuela in 1910, is worth 45 minutes for anyone interested in 20th-century Spanish poetry. Orihuela lies inland: allow for a day return trip to reach the beaches of Orihuela Costa.

days_plan.itin_title: Costa Blanca & Alicante Hinterland: 12 days

visits.text: Ourense—the city takes on a different face as you enter Galicia. The Romans founded it at the end of the 1st century BCE under the name Aquae Urentes (“burning waters”) or Auriense (“city of gold”), for its thermal springs and the gold then found in the Miño. Today it is Galicia's third-largest city and one of the few in Europe with thermal waters in the heart of the city. Its focal point is As Burgas, three springs that gush out at 67°C with a flow of 300 liters per minute. The Romans had already built a thermal sanctuary dedicated to the nymphs here—the excavations are visible.

Five minutes' walk away, the Cathedral of San Martiño dates from the 12th–13th centuries. Built on a 6th-century Suevic church. The centerpiece is the Pórtico do Paraíso: a later copy (13th century) of Santiago's Pórtico da Gloria by Master Mateo, but one that has preserved its original polychromy—exceedingly rare, since the original in Compostela was stripped. Here you see what Romanesque portals must have looked like before centuries wore away their colors. Inside, the Cristo de Ourense, a 14th-century polychrome sculpture with human hair, is the object of local devotion.

The Ponte Vella spans the Miño with its seven arches, the central arch rising 40 meters above the water. Roman foundations from the reign of Augustus, medieval reconstruction in 1230 by Bishop Lourenzo, restorations in the 17th and 19th centuries. Today closed to cars, it's Spain's oldest bridge to have retained such a uniform silhouette. Beside it, the Ponte do Milenio (2001) provides a contemporary architectural counterpart—a pedestrian walkway suspended 22 meters above the river, accessible by stairs. Panoramic view of both banks.

The San Francisco cloister, behind the former convent, is considered Galicia's finest Gothic cloister. Built in the 14th century, 63 pointed arches, 76 double columns, 120 different capitals—each carved with a unique motif: foliage, fantastic animals, anthropomorphic scenes. The Franciscan convent was dismantled in the 19th century, the cloister transferred stone by stone to its current location to save it from destruction. Absolute calm, free access, few visitors.

activities.text: The small thermal tourist train leaves from Plaza Mayor. Since January 2026, it has operated only on Saturdays and Sundays and serves A Chavasqueira and O Tinteiro. The thermal promenade follows the Miño and is also pleasant on foot. Outariz offers the most complete experience, with pools at different temperatures and Zen gardens. It is quieter on weekdays.

A tapas crawl in the Vinos area—the streets Viriato, Fornos, and San Miguel have been home to clusters of tapas bars since the 1950s. In Ourense, tapas are still served free with your drink. Specialties: pulpo a feira (octopus with paprika), bolo de pote (a kind of Galician bread), filloas (local crêpes). Regional wines—Ribeiro and Valdeorras—are mineral white wines that are beginning to be discovered outside Galicia. Three to four bars are enough for a full dinner.

days_plan.itin_title: Inland Galicia: From Ourense to the Ribeira Sacra
Castile and León and Galicia: 21 days from Roman aqueducts to the Atlantic
Galicia: Complete 10-Day Circuit

visits.text: San Salvador Cathedral blends flamboyant Gothic with pre-Romanesque roots. Its single tower dominates the city center and once served as a compass for pilgrims on the Camino Primitivo. Inside, three rib-vaulted aisles converge on an imposing main altarpiece.

Step through the door of the Cámara Santa, a 9th-century chapel built by Alfonso II the Chaste. Six pairs of apostles carved as Romanesque statue-columns support the vault. The treasury holds the Cross of the Angels (808), Oviedo's emblem, and the Cross of Victory (908), symbol of Asturias—both made of chased gold and set with cabochons.

Climb Mount Naranco to Santa María del Naranco, the palace of Ramiro I consecrated in 848. This rectangular 20 × 6-meter two-story structure is the finest example of European pre-Romanesque architecture. The upper floor reveals a barrel vault with transverse arches, triple-arched loggias, twisted colonnettes, and medallions carved with animals and horsemen.

A hundred meters away, San Miguel de Lillo preserves only a third of the original church, but its door jambs carved with Roman circus scenes and stone lattice screens remain unique in 9th-century religious architecture. Both monuments have been UNESCO-listed since 1985.
Descend to Plaza del Fontán, an arcaded square that hosts Oviedo's covered market. Asturian cheeses, canned fabada, local cider—the stalls overflow with regional products.

Detour to La Foncalada, a 9th-century fountain built under Alfonso III the Great. Still functioning today, it's the only hydraulic engineering monument from the early Middle Ages with UNESCO status in Spain.

activities.text: Push open the door of a sidrería in the Casco Antiguo and order a culín. The server pours the cider from high above to aerate it—the escanciado, an unmissable Asturian ritual.
Wander through Parque San Francisco, the green lung of downtown. Its shaded paths shelter free-roaming peacocks and contemporary sculptures scattered among century-old trees.
Follow Oviedo's urban sculpture trail: dozens of bronze statues line the pedestrian streets of the center, from La Maternidad to the seated silhouette of Woody Allen on Calle Milicias.

days_plan.itin_title: Asturias Road Trip: Cantabrian Coast and Picos de Europa

visits.text: La Seu Cathedral has overlooked the bay since the 13th century. Its nave rises to 45 meters. The 14-meter Gothic rose window is among the largest in the world.
Almudaina Palace was built in the 14th century on the site of a former Arab alcazaba. The official residence of the King of Spain in Majorca, it houses the Chapel of Saint Anne and state rooms.
Parc de la Mar stretches beneath the ramparts. Its artificial lake reflects La Seu in a photographic composition emblematic of Palma.
Old town lanes wind between flower-filled patios and ochre facades. The quarter hides Baroque churches, noble houses, and shaded squares.
Step through the doors of the Arab Baths, dating to the 10th century. Their barrel vaults and columns bear witness to Moorish occupation.
Bellver Castle crowns a hill 3 kilometers away. This circular 14th-century fortress offers a panorama over the whole bay.
Passeig del Born is Palma's elegant thoroughfare. Lined with plane trees and modernist facades, it connects Plaça de la Reina to the waterfront.

activities.text: The bike path follows the bay for several kilometers. It runs along the waterfront between Parc de la Mar and the city beaches.
Ensaimada can be enjoyed in traditional pastry shops. This spiral brioche dusted with powdered sugar is the emblem of Majorcan baking.
Settle in at Bellver Castle toward the end of the day. The sun sinks behind Palma while the city lights come on.
Olivar Market overflows with local produce. Fresh fish, sobrassada, Mahón cheese, and Majorcan vegetables crowd the stalls.

days_plan.itin_title: Majorca Road Trip: Serra de Tramuntana and Coves

places.name: Palos De La Frontera

visits.text: Columbus stayed at this Franciscan monastery, La Rábida, several times—notably in 1485 and 1491, when he was seeking backers for his project. The monks sheltered him, interceded at court, and introduced him to Martín Alonso Pinzón, a local shipowner. On August 3, 1492, the three ships left the port of Palos with 90 men. The monastery preserves Vázquez Díaz's frescoes on the discovery.

On the Río Tinto, the three full-scale replicas of the Pinta, Niña, and Santa María have floated since 1992, built for the 500th anniversary. You can visit the interiors: the cabins are cramped and the bunks unthinkable for a 90-day crossing. Allow 1.5 hours. The river carrying them is already orange—the mine water begins here.

activities.text: Moguer residents will tell you that Platero is as famous as Columbus in the region. Juan Ramón Jiménez, born here in 1881, received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1956 for his collection about the white donkey. The birthplace is now a museum. Moguer is 7 km from Palos—a 30-minute detour worth the stop.

days_plan.itin_title: Huelva, the Forgotten Land: Doñana to Faro in 7 Days

map_keywords: La Rábida Monastery Palos de la Frontera

visits.text: Pampaneira is touristy. We know it, and we don't care: at 1,058 meters in the Poqueira gorge, this Morisco village classified as a historic ensemble keeps its flat roofs in slate slabs, its tubular chimneys, and its Mudéjar church Santa Cruz, the finest of the three gorge villages. The architecture resembles Rif and Atlas villages—same Berber heritage.

The Santa Cruz church in Pampaneira, built in the 16th century in Mudéjar style, has preserved its coffered ceiling in mulberry wood. Inside, sober and cool. The San Antonio fountain on the square, called the bachelors' fountain, is said to help those who drink from it find a partner—the tradition is still cited seriously by elders.

activities.text: Shops selling jarapas (Alpujarran weavings made from recovered fabric scraps) line Pampaneira's alleys. It's not high craft, but it's authentically local and cheap. The Hilacar workshop, in operation for several decades, is one of the few still weaving on traditional looms—visits are free.

days_plan.itin_title: Al-Andalus: From the Mezquita to the Alpujarras in 10 days

visits.text: Santa María Cathedral shelters the alabaster tomb of Charles III the Noble and his wife Eleanor. Sculptor Janin Lomme personalized the faces of the recumbent figures and varied the poses of the 28 mourners.
The Gothic cloister dates from the 14th and 15th centuries. Its elegant Gothic bays topped with gables lend remarkable lightness to the entire ensemble.
Walk along the 5 kilometres of ramparts listed as a National Monument. The pentagonal citadel of 1571 was designed by Giacomo Palearo.
Pass through the Portal de Francia with its still-operational drawbridge. Pilgrims on the Camino have crossed this gateway for centuries.
The old town preserves its medieval layout, born from the 1423 merger of three rival boroughs: the Navarrería, San Cernin, and San Nicolás.
The Church of San Cernin houses the chapel of the Virgen del Camino, featuring a 12th-century statue set within a spectacular baroque altarpiece dripping with gilt.

activities.text: Join the terraces along Calle Estafeta for pintxos. This narrow street becomes the running route for the encierros during the San Fermín festival.
Taconera Park offers shade and cool respite. Its French-style gardens date from the 19th century.
The Museum of Navarre displays Romanesque capitals salvaged from the former cathedral and the Holy Sepulchre reliquary gifted by Saint Louis in 1258.
Climb to the Portal Nuevo viewpoint for sweeping vistas over the fortified city and the distant Pyrenees beyond.

days_plan.itin_title: Navarre Road Trip: Castles, Irati Forest & the Camino

places.name: Parque Natural De Arribes Del Duero

visits.text: The Arribes del Duero Natural Park stretches along nearly 100 kilometers of canyons carved by the Duero River through granite, forming the natural border between Spain and Portugal. The cliffs plunge up to 500 meters—the deepest gorges in the entire Iberian Peninsula. The Mirador del Fraile, at Aldeadávila de la Ribera, offers the most vertiginous viewpoint: a walkway overhangs the canyon directly, not recommended if you have a fear of heights. From there, the Duero's waters seem motionless because they're so far below. Bring water as the trails are exposed.

The Pozo de los Humos is one of the peninsula's most spectacular waterfalls: the Uces River plunges into the canyon from a height of over 50 meters, creating a permanent cloud of spray that gave it its name (“well of smoke”). The trail from Masueco is short (2.3 km round trip) and accessible to all, but the stones are slippery during the wet season. In summer, the flow can be low depending on the year's rainfall—choose spring or fall to see the falls at full force.

Make a detour to Fermoselle, a town designated a historic and artistic site, perched on high ground. The town is nicknamed “the town of 1,000 cellars”—cellars carved into the rock beneath the houses to store wine from the Arribes area, a developing appellation of origin with eleven terraced vineyards. The castle and Escaleras viewpoints are worth a stop.

activities.text: Walk along the GR-14, the long-distance trail that follows the Duero from its source to Porto. In the Arribes area, several sections above the gorges can be walked in 1 to 3 hours. The microclimate, warmer than in the rest of Castile due to the deep gorges trapping heat, allows olive trees, almond trees and vines to grow at this latitude. Look up: golden eagles, griffon vultures and black storks nest in the rock faces.

places.name: Parque Natural De Las Lagunas De Ruidera

visits.text: The Lagunas de Ruidera natural park strings together 15 lagoons over 20 km along the upper course of the Guadiana, separated by natural travertine barriers. The total elevation drop of 128 meters creates a succession of waterfalls between each basin.
Start at the Cascada del Hundimiento, the park's highest waterfall, just steps from the village of Ruidera. It's the starting point of the left-bank trail, the wildest and best-preserved route.
The Laguna del Rey is the park's deepest lagoon. From the Mirador de la Laguna del Rey, the view sweeps across its turquoise waters bordered by reeds. A developed beach allows swimming in summer.

The Laguna Colgada ('hanging' lagoon) extends into a tongue of land that advances into the water. At its tip, small waterfalls feed the Laguna de Batana below—a bucolic landscape typical of tufa formations.
The Laguna Lengua offers the park's most spectacular colors: deep blue and emerald green. The limestone rock barriers and waterfalls carving their way through create an almost surreal setting.

The Cueva de Montesinos, a cave mentioned by Cervantes in Don Quixote, opens onto the plateau of Campo de Montiel. This is where the errant knight claimed to have spent three days in an enchanted palace.

activities.text: Paddle a kayak on the Laguna del Rey or Laguna Colgada. The calm, crystal-clear waters allow you to glide along the travertine cliffs and access beaches and caves unreachable on foot.
Hike the left-bank trail between the Cascada del Hundimiento and Laguna Redondilla. The path crosses shaded zones and offers plunging views over the successive lagoons.
At dawn, the lagoons attract grey herons, coots, ducks and raptors. The marsh reeds and quiet shores of the park make excellent terrain for birdwatching.
Set up a picnic in the designated areas by the lagoons. The turquoise waters and birdsong compose an ideal setting for a nature lunch break.

days_plan.itin_title: La Mancha Road Trip: Don Quixote's Windmills and Cuenca

visits.text: Head to Brihuega, approximately 53 km from Pastrana, a 55-minute drive, nicknamed the “Garden of the Alcarria”. If you come in July, the spectacle of the flowering lavender fields around the village is breathtaking - hectares of purple as far as the eye can see. Outside the flowering season, the village is still worth visiting: its medieval walls with the fortified gates of the Cadena and Cozagón, three beautiful 13th-century Romanesque churches (Santa María de la Peña, San Miguel, San Felipe) and the former Real Fábrica de Paños, a royal cloth factory founded in the 18th century by Charles III.

Discover Pastrana, the “ducal town” of the Alcarria, listed as a Historic Ensemble since 1966 and a member of Spain's Most Beautiful Villages. The Ducal Palace, designed by Alonso de Covarrubias in the 16th century with a façade reproducing that of the Alcázar of Toledo, is inseparable from the Princess of Éboli - Ana de Mendoza y de la Cerda. One-eyed (she wore an eye patch), beautiful and scheming, first Duchess of Pastrana and then mistress of Antonio Pérez, Philip II's secretary, she ended up imprisoned by the king in the palace's east tower (the Cámara de la Reja Dorada) from 1581 until her death in 1592. Look at the barred window from the Plaza de la Hora - that is where she watched the world.

Don't leave Pastrana without visiting the Tapestry Museum in the collegiate church of the Asunción. The six 15th-century Flemish-Gothic tapestries, woven in Tournai from cartoons attributed to Nuño Gonçalves, depict the conquest of North African cities by King Afonso V of Portugal. They rank among the world's most important tapestries from this period. The collegiate church itself, of Templar origin (12th century), holds paintings by El Greco and Carreño de Miranda. The Princess of Éboli is buried in the crypt.

activities.text: Pastrana is also linked to Saint Teresa of Ávila, who founded two convents of Discalced Carmelites here in 1569 - one for women (San José) and the other for men (del Carmen), where Saint John of the Cross was master of novices. The convent del Carmen houses a small Teresian museum and a natural history museum. Walk through the lanes of the upper town, between Princess of Éboli Street, lined with stately houses, and Palma Street, with the House of the Inquisition and the House of the Knight of Calatrava.

days_plan.itin_title: Alcarria and Guadalajara: Between Madrid and Aragon
Duero Castile: From Valladolid to Cuenca via Ribera and Alcarria

visits.text: Pedraza is the best-preserved medieval village in Castile and León—perhaps in all of Spain. Declared a historic site in 1951, it has only one entrance gate (made of wood dating from the 16th century), cobbled lanes lined with houses bearing noble coats of arms, and an arcaded Plaza Mayor ranking among the region's most beautiful. Park in the lot outside the village and enter on foot. To avoid weekend crowds, choose a weekday or arrive before 10am.

Pedraza's castle occupies a rocky outcrop at the village's edge. Built in the 13th century, transformed into a Renaissance palace in the 16th-17th centuries, it was saved from ruin by painter Ignacio Zuloaga who made it his residence and studio. Its keep now houses a museum with some of his works. A little-known historical anecdote: the sons of King Francis I of France were imprisoned in this castle in 1526 as hostages to guarantee the Treaty of Madrid—they stayed four years. Book tickets online.

Pedraza's medieval prison (Cárcel de la Villa), a 13th-century building rebuilt in the 16th, is one of Spain's best preserved. Guided tours recreate medieval prison life. If you're there on the evening of the first or second Saturday in July, do not miss the Noche de las Velas under any circumstances: electric lights are turned off and thousands of candles illuminate the lanes while concerts take place outdoors.

activities.text: Stroll along Calle Mayor past houses bearing coats of arms and noble residences from the 16th–17th centuries, testaments to the village's textile prosperity.
Savor cordero asado, lamb roasted in a wood-fired oven that earned Pedraza its culinary reputation. In 2024, Britain's The Times ranked El Soportal among the 28 best Mediterranean restaurants.
Attend the Candlelight Nights on the first two Saturdays of July. Thousands of candles illuminate lanes, balconies and squares as classical music concerts fill the air.

days_plan.itin_title: Castile and León: Ramparts, Canyons and Peaks

visits.text: Pedroche is the village that gave its name to the entire comarca. Perched on a hill, it's the former capital of the Siete Villas de los Pedroches—the seven villages that governed themselves in the Middle Ages. The landmark monument is the Torre de Pedroche, a 56-meter-high bell tower that dominates the entire landscape. Begun in the 15th century, it was completed by Hernán Ruiz II—the same architect as at Hinojosa, the Mezquita, and the Giralda. Four superimposed sections (square, octagonal, square, cylindrical) rise above the church of El Salvador (Gothic-Mudéjar). Climb to the top if access is open—the view embraces the entire dehesa as far as the eye can see. Around the Plaza de las Siete Villas, the narrow lanes with granite houses preserve the atmosphere of a medieval Sierra Morena market town.

Drive 15 minutes east to Dos Torres, whose historic center is classified as a Property of Cultural Interest. This village was born from the merger of two medieval settlements—Torrefranca and Torremilano—in 1839. The Pedroches granite architecture is best preserved here: manor houses with dark stone façades highlighted with white lime, carved coats of arms, wrought-iron balconies. The Centro de Interpretación de la Arquitectura Popular explains local construction techniques. Don't miss the Plaza de Toros integrated into the urban fabric and the Pozo de la Nieve (snow well), where ice was stored in winter.

Push 10 minutes south to Añora, the smallest village in Los Pedroches. Its dark granite houses striped with white bands create a unique architectural style in the comarca. The church of San Sebastián (16th century) is considered one of the purest examples of Mudéjar art in Los Pedroches. The village is tiny—30 minutes suffices to tour it—but the end-of-the-world atmosphere is total.

activities.text: The Valle de los Pedroches is classified as a Starlight Reserve by UNESCO for its night sky quality—very little light pollution in this rural area. If you stay a night in Pedroche or Pozoblanco, take advantage of it to observe the stars. Operators offer astronomical observation sessions with telescopes, especially in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Córdoba and the Sierra Morena: From the Caliphate to the Dehesas of Los Pedroches

places.name: Penafiel

visits.text: Two hours from Barajas, and suddenly the landscape tips: goodbye Sierra de Guadarrama, hello Castilian plateau. Wheat fields stretching forever, sparse trees, endless sky. This is Ribera del Duero—a fertile desert at 800 meters altitude, and that's precisely why the grapes here are exceptional.

Peñafiel Castle is absurd—in the best possible way. 210 meters long, 20 meters wide, perched on a cerro (an oblong hill), locals say it looks like a ship at anchor. The 34-meter Torre del Homenaje spirals upward to views across three valleys (Duero, Duratón, Botijas). Built from the 10th century onward, rebuilt in the 14th-15th centuries by Don Pedro Girón, declared a National Monument in 1917. Since 1999, the southern courtyard houses the Provincial Wine Museum, a modern and pedagogical journey through Valladolid province's five DOs. Ticket €6.60, closed Mondays.

Plaza del Coso de Peñafiel: one of the few wooden bullfighting squares still active in Castile. Rectangular, surrounded by houses with wooden balconies that serve as stands during the ferias. Outside festival season, it's simply a beautiful medieval plaza where old men gather in the shade. The neighboring collegiate church of San Juan Bautista dates from the 15th century.

Pago de los Capellanes in Pedrosa de Duero, about 15 km from Peñafiel, a 15-minute drive - the name comes from a chaplaincy that existed on this land in the 13th-14th centuries and was confiscated during the 1855 disentailments, but local people continued to call the place by its historic name. The estate was re-established in 1996 by the Rodero Villa family. One hundred hectares of Tempranillo, mainly trellis-trained. The value for money is excellent at every level - Crianza, Reserva and Parcela El Nogal. Tour and tasting €25, welcoming staff and genuine teaching about the soils of the Ribera.

Watch the sunset from the bridge over the Duero at Quintanilla de Onésimo, about 25 km from Peñafiel, a 25-minute drive. The river is wide, the vines run down to the bank, and the late-day light in May or September turns the valley golden. It is not a monument. It is simply beautiful and deserves 20 minutes.

The village of Pedrosa de Duero, about 15 km from Peñafiel, a 15-minute drive, has 600 inhabitants, an 18th-century Baroque church and several stone manor houses that the 19th-century disentailment did not completely break up. One of the many Ribera villages where Castilian vernacular heritage - granite, slate and inner courtyards - survives between two ultra-modern wineries.

activities.text: Welcome dinner at Mesón Las Carrigüelas or any asador in Peñafiel for lechazo: Castilian milk lamb, roasted at 180°C in a wood-fired clay oven, served by the quarter with a few potatoes and nothing else. This is Ribera's totem dish. Pair it with a Crianza from Protos or Pesquera—you can't go wrong.

Comparative tasting at Bodegas Protos in Peñafiel—one of the DO's oldest cooperatives (1927). The modern winery, designed by Richard Rogers (architect of Centre Pompidou), plays with ceramic vaults. Tour + 3-wine tasting, around €20. Good warm-up to calibrate your palate for the coming days.

Have lunch in Pedrosa, about 15 km from Peñafiel, a 15-minute drive, after the Pago de los Capellanes tour, in any village bar. If nothing opens at 2 p.m. on a Tuesday - which happens in Castile - head to Pesquera or Peñafiel. Flexibility is the main skill required when travelling in Ribera del Duero.

Closing tasting of the Golden Mile at Bodegas Pago de Carraovejas in Peñafiel. The estate, founded in 1987, is one of the most serious in the Peñafiel zone—Pago de Carraovejas Reserva is the reference cuvée. The tour includes underground cellars beneath the vineyard. Around €30.

places.name: Penalba De Santiago

visits.text: To reach Peñalba de Santiago, you must cross the entire Valley of Silence by a single-lane road once called “la senda de los monjes”—the monks' path. Perched at 1,100 meters in the Aquilanos mountains, this village of about fifty inhabitants is one of Spain's most beautiful: stone and slate houses with wooden balconies, lanes so narrow they seem never to have changed since the 10th century. Park in the lot at the entrance—the lanes are impassable by car.

The Mozarabic church of Santiago de Peñalba is the only remnant of the monastery founded by San Genadio in the 10th century, completed in 937 by Abbot Salomón. It's a jewel of Spanish Mozarabic architecture—a style born from the fusion of Visigothic traditions and Arab influences. Enter through the double door with horseshoe arches supported by three marble columns: inside, the horseshoe arches divide the nave, and remnants of medieval wall paintings survive on the walls. This is where the body of San Genadio rests.

From the village, a half-hour walk on the old monks' path leads to the Cave of San Genadio, carved into a vertical rock face at the very entrance to the Valley of Silence. The Bishop of Astorga retreated here to meditate in the 9th century. A local legend says he ordered the Oza River to be silent so as not to disturb his prayer—and the river disappeared underground at that spot.

activities.text: The Valley of Silence also offers an appealing setting for hiking, with forests of oak, chestnut and walnut crossed by the Oza River. The trail climbing to the Monastery of San Pedro de Montes (founded in the 7th century by San Fructuoso, rebuilt in the 12th–13th centuries) is one of the region's most beautiful. Allow 3 hours round trip from Peñalba.

visits.text: Playa de Sotavento stretches for kilometers, famous for its lagoon that forms at low tide. Shallow turquoise waters, ever-shifting sandbanks, and spectacular vistas make this beach a photographer's paradise.
The Faro del Matorral lighthouse, standing 60 meters tall, visually divides Playa del Matorral into two zones. It's a prime observation point for watching sunsets over the Atlantic.
The Saladar de Jandía, a protected wetland, is a salt marsh of scientific interest for the conservation of a rare salt-tolerant plant.

Head for the Punta Jandía lighthouse at the southwestern tip, built in the 19th century to guide ships toward Africa. Allow a full day for the return trip from Morro Jable, as the last stretch runs along an unpaved track. A spectacular drive through the Jandía Natural Park, desert landscapes and cliffs pounded by the waves.
Stroll through Morro Jable village, once a fishing port. The marina now welcomes up to 300 yachts, while narrow streets shelter boutiques and restaurants serving fresh fish.

activities.text: Relax on Playa del Matorral's 4 kilometers of golden sand, equipped with beach bars, restrooms, sun loungers, and lifeguards. Perfect for families seeking comfort and safety.
Kitesurf and windsurf at Playa de la Barca. Constant Atlantic winds make Sotavento one of the world's premier spots, hosting international competitions.
Join a boat excursion to observe dolphins and whales. Success rates run 50-70% depending on conditions. Curious and playful dolphins often approach boats.
Hike to Pico de la Zarza (807m), Fuerteventura's highest peak. The summit reveals panoramic views over the wild Cofete beach and the entire Jandía Peninsula.

days_plan.itin_title: Fuerteventura Road Trip: Dunes, Lagoons & Villages

visits.text: The castle of Peñíscola has dominated the rocky promontory since 1307. Built by the Knights Templar atop an Arab alcazaba, it became the palace of Pope Benedict XIII—Papa Luna—after 1411.
Step through the Portal de San Pedro to enter the old town. Cobbled lanes climb between whitewashed facades all the way up to the castle's parade ground.
Renaissance ramparts wrap around the peninsula for 2 kilometers. From the muralla del Olvido, you can take in the entire coastline and the old town spread out below.
The church of Santa María occupies a former mosque converted in the 14th century. Its bell tower has served as a landmark for sailors for centuries.
The Casa de las Conchas boasts a facade entirely covered in seashells—a unique decoration commissioned by a local family in the 19th century.
Walk out to the lighthouse built in 1899, still keeping watch over the Mediterranean horizon. The surrounding seaside garden offers a cool haven.
The Artillery Park spreads out at the foot of the castle. Its terraced gardens host bird-of-prey shows and give access to the casemates.

activities.text: Playa Norte stretches for 2 kilometers of fine sand. Its calm waters are perfect for swimming with views of the castle perched above.
Rice with cuttlefish turns the plate a deep black. This signature dish can be enjoyed at the restaurants along the harbor or the seafront promenade.
Find a spot on the rock late in the day. The sun drops behind the castle while the lights come on across the old town.
Want to see the castle from another angle? Rent a kayak to follow the base of the rock and discover its sea caves.

days_plan.itin_title: Castellón and Maestrazgo Route: Castles and Coves
Northern Valencia Road Trip: 10 Days of Villages

visits.text: Plasencia keeps its treasures close to the chest. Founded in 1186 by King Alfonso VIII of Castile, it boasts a unique quirk in Spain: two cathedrals stuck side by side. The Catedral Vieja, begun in the 13th century, is a fine example of Romanesque-Gothic transition—sober, compact, with a baroque altarpiece and a stunning ivory Christ. The Catedral Nueva, started in the 15th century, was never finished—but what exists is breathtaking: soaring ribbed vaults, a magnificent altarpiece attributed to Gregorio Fernández, and a heady mix of flamboyant Gothic, Renaissance, and Baroque. They're visited together—don't choose, see both.

The Plaza Mayor of Plasencia has been the beating heart of the city since medieval times. Irregularly shaped and ringed by soportales (arcades) lined with bars and restaurants, it hosts a market every Tuesday that's been running uninterrupted since the 12th century. Grab a terrace seat and watch the unhurried rhythm of this 40,000-soul town that carries itself like a regional capital.

Plasencia is part of the Red de Juderías de España—the network of Spain's historic Jewish quarters. The Jewish community settled here from the city's founding in 1186. Traces survive in two neighborhoods: the old judería de la Mota (around today's Parador, a former San Vicente Ferrer convent built on the site of the first synagogue confiscated in 1477) and the “new judería” around Calle Trujillo and Calle Zapatería. In these alleys, plaques set into the pavement bear the names of Jewish families who lived here—Yuçe Alaçán, Abraham Almale, Samuel... Don't miss the Jewish cemetery of El Berrocal outside the walls: it's the only preserved Jewish burial ground in Extremadura, with about twenty anthropomorphic tombs carved into rock, facing Jerusalem.

Walk the circuit of Plasencia's medieval ramparts, still well-preserved along much of their length. You'll pass through the Trujillo, Coria, and Berrozana gates and cross paths with the acueducto—a restored medieval aqueduct running through the San Antón neighborhood. The Palacio del Marqués de Mirabel, built on the site of the old judería de la Mota in the 15th century, is worth a look for its facade and garden (visible from the street).

activities.text: Northern Extremadura's cuisine is generous and underrated. Try Torta del Casar—a creamy soft-paste cheese eaten with a spoon—migas extremeñas (fried breadcrumbs with chorizo and pimiento), jamón ibérico de bellota, and Valle del Jerte cherries in season. The Plaza Mayor and surrounding streets are packed with tapas bars where you'll eat well and abundantly.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Extremadura: From Plasencia to Zafra Through Valleys and Dehesas

visits.text: At 2.5 km, Playa d'en Bossa is Ibiza's longest beach. The southern end is notably quieter than the club strip in the center. The airport sits 5 min away—planes roar overhead, atmosphere guaranteed.

activities.text: Loud, commercial, but the beachfront energy is infectious: Ushuaïa and Hï Ibiza face off across the road, and beach clubs run DJ sets from noon onwards. Expect €30–60 club entry.
Walk south along Playa d'en Bossa in late afternoon: beyond the beach club sunbeds, the shoreline meets the entrance to Ses Salines Natural Park with views over salt marshes and flamingos.

days_plan.itin_title: Ibiza & Formentera by Scooter: Calas & Beaches in 7 Days

places.name: Ponferrada

visits.text: The Templar Castle of Ponferrada is one of the most impressive medieval fortresses in northwest Spain. In 1178, the kings of León ceded the town to the Order of the Temple to protect pilgrims on the Camino. The Templars remained until 1312, when the Order was dissolved. The castle spreads over 8,000 square meters with a complex system of courtyards, barbicans, and towers—the original twelve reproduced constellations. In 1850, the town council sold the walls as a quarry—it took designation as a National Monument in 1924 to halt the destruction. Climb the rampart walk for views over the city and the Bierzo mountains.

The 16th-century Renaissance Basílica de la Encina houses the statue of the Virgin of La Encina—patroness of El Bierzo. According to legend, the Templars found her hidden in an oak trunk (encina) during the Reconquista. Right next door, the Renaissance Clock Tower and the Baroque Town Hall form one of the city's best-preserved civic ensembles.

Peñalba de Santiago is perched at an altitude of 1,110 meters at the far end of the Valle del Silencio—a valley so deeply enclosed in the Aquilanos mountains that the water of the río Oza briefly disappears underground, hence the name. Saint Genadio, bishop of Astorga, retired here in 920 to live as a hermit until his death in 936. He had founded a monastery of which only the Mozarabic church of Santiago remains, completed in 937 by Abbot Solomon—one of the few surviving examples of Spanish Mozarabic art, and one of the most beautiful. Its south doorway, with a double horseshoe arch resting on three marble columns with Corinthian capitals, is exceptionally graceful. The interior contains early medieval wall paintings uncovered during recent restorations. The village itself, with its stone and slate houses and wooden balconies, has been listed as a Property of Cultural Interest since 1998. Plan for the road—it is narrow and winding and may be closed in winter. Allow for a day trip from Ponferrada.

From the village, a 30-minute walk leads to the Cueva de San Genadio, the cave hollowed into the vertical rock face at the entrance to the valley where the saint withdrew each night to pray. The view from the cave over Peñalba's slate roofs below is the emblematic image of the Valle del Silencio. Allow for a day trip from Ponferrada to reach the village, then follow the trail on foot.

activities.text: Visit the Bierzo Museum. It traces the natural and human history of the comarca, with a remarkable room devoted to Roman mines—Ponferrada lies at the heart of the area surrounding Las Médulas, the most productive gold mine in the Roman Empire.

A late-day stroll along the Río Sil. The riverbank has been turned into a tree-lined promenade; it's locals' favorite spot for jogging and aperitifs. The illuminated castle viewed from the riverbanks in the evening is the city's signature photo opportunity.

Hiking in the Valle del Silencio from Peñalba: the trail continues beyond the Cueva de San Genadio toward the monastery of San Pedro de Montes, founded in the 7th century by Saint Fructuoso and restored by San Genadio in 895. The complete round-trip hike from Peñalba covers around 10 km, taking half a day through oak woodland. Allow for a day trip from Ponferrada to reach Peñalba, in addition to the hike itself.

places.name: Pontevedra

visits.text: Pontevedra is a revelation. A city of 80,000 inhabitants, the provincial capital, and above all: a listed historic center that has been entirely pedestrianized since 1999. Not a single motor vehicle in the entire old town—one of Spain's most radical urban mobility projects, recognized with several international awards. The result: quality of life, café terraces everywhere, children playing in the streets, an almost zero accident rate. The center is organized around five interconnected squares: Ferrería, Curros Enríquez, Leña, Verdura, Teucro.

25 km north of Pontevedra, an excursion to Cambados is a must for anyone interested in Galician wine. The town is the capital of Albariño, the fresh, mineral white wine that has become one of Spain's great whites in thirty years. The center is clustered around Praza de Fefiñáns, designated a national monument: the Renaissance Pazo de Fefiñáns (1535–1647) with its baroque arch spanning the street, the late Gothic Church of San Bieito, and the 14th-century defensive tower. Uneven cobblestones, wine merchants under the arcades. Sublime at sunset.

In Cambados, on Monte da Pastora hill 10 minutes from the center, the ruins of Santa Mariña Dozo. A 16th-century Gothic church abandoned in the 19th century and left to fall into ruin. But the ground between the collapsed arches still serves as the parish cemetery: tombstones set in the grass between broken columns, vaults open to the sky, lichens, moss. The most photogenic place in all of Galicia, and one of the most moving. Freely accessible, never crowded. View over the Ría de Arousa.

The Church of La Peregrina, at the entrance to the historic center, has a unique shape: an octagonal cross plan, with angles of 45° rather than 90°. Built in the 18th century (1778), its style is midway between baroque and neoclassical. Its symbolic shape: the scallop shell. Pontevedra was a stop on the Camino Portugués, and La Peregrina is the patron saint of the Portuguese Way. The interior is equally unexpected—small, centrally planned, bright. An 18th-century statue of the Virgin in polychrome wood, venerated by sailors.

The Basilica of Santa María la Mayor, overlooking the Lérez River, has a Plateresque façade carved by Cornelis de Hollanda (1541–1559)—Renaissance ornamentation with the delicacy of a goldsmith's work. Inside, a late Gothic hall-church plan, baroque altarpieces, and the curious “capilla del Cristo del Buen Viaje”—Christ of the Good Voyage, an object of devotion for sailors heading out to sea. Funded by the sailors' guild at the height of Pontevedra's commercial prosperity in the 16th century. The city was then larger than Vigo or A Coruña.

The Museum of Pontevedra is one of Galicia's best museums—six interconnected buildings, free admission. Archaeology collection: the Caldas treasure (Bronze Age gold, 12 kg), Roman funerary stelae. Fine arts: Castelao (cartoonist and painter, Galician cultural hero), Sotomayor, Flemish painting. A room containing the intact cabin of the frigate Numancia, the first ironclad ship to circumnavigate the world (1865–1867). Allow 2 hours to see everything. Free admission. Often nearly empty.

activities.text: The Pazo de Fefiñáns in Cambados houses the oldest Albariño winery, founded in 1904 by the Marquis of Figueroa himself. A guided tour of the Renaissance palace, a tasting of the winery's three signature Albariños and pomace brandies. One hour, around €18. Here you understand the wine's identity: granite soils, Atlantic climate, hand harvesting, plots of less than one hectare divided among hundreds of winegrowers. Over a hundred producers in a few square kilometers.

A tour of the five squares. Ferrería (former blacksmiths, café terraces), Curros Enríquez with its fountain, Leña (the most picturesque, a vegetable market in the morning), Verdura (shopping street), Teucro (the most aristocratic, 18th-century palaces). Each square has its own atmosphere: Leña for morning coffee, Ferrería for a predinner drink, Verdura for shops. Pontevedra is a city where you happily waste time—it's rare.

A tapas dinner around Praza da Leña—Ribadavia, Casa Fidel, Eirado da Leña (fancier). Pontevedra has an excellent network of traditional bistros that haven't given in to tourist trends. Specialties to try: empanada de zamburiñas (pie with a characteristic small scallop), berberechos al natural (cockles), tarta de Mondoñedo (almond and cider cake). Wines: Albariño, Rosal, Condado do Tea—all the Rías Baixas appellations are represented.

Galicia: Complete 10-Day Circuit

Ruins of Santa Mariña Dozo Cambados

visits.text: Three coves form the small beach resort of Portinatx: S'Arenal Gran for families, S'Arenal Petit for quiet, and Es Port for diving. The atmosphere is the opposite of the clubbing south: here, people dine early and rise for hiking.

activities.text: Take the coastal trail to Punta Moscarter lighthouse, the Balearics' tallest with its spiraling black-and-white tower. The walk lasts 30–40 min along cliffs, with views over the north coast. Do it at sunset for golden light.

days_plan.itin_title: Ibiza & Formentera by Scooter: Calas & Beaches in 7 Days

visits.text: From the keep of the Castillo de Puebla de Alcocer, the Embalse de La Serena stretches out like an inland sea. This dam, the largest in Spain (3,220 hm³), could contain the city of Madrid within its perimeter of 530 km of shoreline. The 13th-century castle, remodelled in the 15th by the Master of Alcántara, is open for guided tours.

The old folk of Puebla tell of a secret passage linking the castle to the nearby village of Galizuela, repopulated by Galicians after the Reconquest. No one has found it, but the story keeps evening conversations going. The other local celebrity: Agustín Luengo, born here in 1826, stood 2.35 m tall.

The Iglesia de Santiago, a former mosque converted in the 15th century, blends Gothic and Mudéjar with a Plateresque portal. Inside, 13th-century frescoes sit alongside later additions. Look for the funerary slab of Fray Fernando de Moraga, tireless traveller.

Look for the Ermita de la Cueva, nestled on the castle hill. Its white bell tower gives it away. Spaniards know the nursery rhyme "Que llueva, que llueva, la Virgen de la Cueva": tradition places it here.

activities.text: If you arrive at sunset, climb to the castle viewpoint: reflections on the Embalse de La Serena and the Zújar turn orange. Sunrises are equally spectacular. Parking at the foot of the village, walk up.

The Palacio de los Duques de Osuna, in the centre, now houses the library and cultural centre. A fine manor house, free entry. Also look out for the Casa de la Inquisición and the Casona de San Juan, reminders of the town's judicial and religious past.

days_plan.itin_title: La Siberia and La Serena: Secret Extremadura in 6 Days

visits.text: Puebla de Sanabria is one of Spain's most beautiful villages—an official designation—perched at 960 meters at the confluence of the Tera and Castro, 20 km from the Portuguese border. In the 13th century, it was one of the Kingdom of León's most important military strongholds facing Portugal. The Counts of Benavente owned it for four centuries. The main cobbled lane winds uphill between houses with stone coats of arms, flowering gardens, and wrought-iron balconies. You can cross the center in 30 minutes, but you'll spend the morning there.

The Counts of Benavente's castle crowns the town—15th century, square plan, multistory keep nicknamed “El Macho”. One of Castile's best-preserved castles. Restored, it now houses an interpretation center on fortifications across four levels: models, videos, interactive games about the military history of the Portuguese-Castilian border. Ideal for children. From the keep, a panoramic view over the Sierra de la Culebra and—on clear days—as far as the peaks of Portugal.

On Plaza Mayor, the Church of Nuestra Señora del Azogue—late 12th century, transitional Romanesque and Gothic. Three semicircular apses, a 13th-century baptismal font adorned with carved figures, a Renaissance altarpiece. “Azogue” comes from the Arabic name for the market held here. The Virgin of Victories, inside, is the town's patron saint—feast day on September 8, with a procession through the medieval streets featuring giants and big-headed figures. Less conspicuous: the Museum of Giants and Big-Headed Figures next door displays processional figures dating from the 19th century onward.

activities.text: An excursion to Lake Sanabria, 12 km north—the Iberian Peninsula's largest glacial lake, 369 hectares, 50 meters deep, formed 100,000 years ago by retreating glaciers. It even has small “waves” in strong winds, like an inland sea. Sandy beaches are an option in summer (Viquiella and Custa Llago). Outside summer, hike to Laguna de los Peces—a high-altitude lake at 1,707 meters—or to the Sotillo waterfalls. The water is icy all year, even in August.

15 minutes south, the Iberian Wolf Center in Robledo (Centro del Lobo Ibérico) takes in injured wild wolves and wolves born in captivity. Several observation trails in natural surroundings, with viewing huts, let you see the packs from a distance without disturbing them. The neighboring Sierra de la Culebra is home to Western Europe's largest wolf population. Open only at certain hours for guided tours; reservations are required in season. Moving, especially for children.

days_plan.itin_title: Castile and León and Galicia: 21 days from Roman aqueducts to the Atlantic
Castile and León - 14-Day Grand Tour

places.name: Puente Del Congosto

visits.text: Puente del Congosto owes its name and existence to a single feature: the bridge over the Tormes. This strategic crossing on the Cañada Real Soriana Occidental—the great transhumance route descending toward Extremadura—generated enough toll revenue to finance castle, church, and village. The old bridge, built on orders of the Catholic Monarchs around 1500, is solidly founded on granite bedrock and counts 13 arches; it still retains one of its two original defensive towers. Declared a Site of Cultural Interest with historic site status in 2019, it's the last village in the province to receive this title.

The Dávila Castle, on the left bank of the Tormes, was built in the 14th century to defend and control the strategic bridge crossing. In 1393, King Enrique III ceded the lordship of Puente del Congosto to Gil González Dávila, who rebuilt the fortress. In 1539, the Duke of Alba bought it from Charles V and added a second twin tower. Beautifully restored, it's now private property and can only be viewed from outside—but the silhouette from the bridge is remarkable.

Don't leave without walking the riverside path along the Tormes—the crystalline waters and natural swimming holes make Puente del Congosto a popular summer stop. The entire setting, declared a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 2006, is ideal for spotting European bee-eaters and grey herons along the banks.

activities.text: For whitewater enthusiasts, the Tormes upstream from Puente del Congosto offers rafting sections navigable in spring and early summer. Local outfitters offer 2- to 3-hour trips on the river's rapids. Inquire at the tourist office.

Come evening, the menu del día in village bars invariably features hornazo—a savory pie with ham and hard-boiled eggs, a Salamanca specialty you'll find throughout the province. Also try the cured meats from the Sierra de Béjar.

places.name: Puerto De La Cruz

visits.text: Lago Martiánez covers 100,000 m² of seawater pools, gardens, and terraces. Designed by César Manrique in 1977, the complex integrates volcanic rock, sculptures like Las Raíces al Cielo (eucalyptus trees planted upside down), and a giant volcanic stone fountain supplying 27,000 m³ of seawater.
The La Orotava Botanical Garden was founded in 1788 by order of King Charles III. Across 20,000 m², more than four thousand tropical species from around the world flourish among fountains and ponds.

Head to Plaza del Charco, the beating heart of the old town, then walk down to the old harbor where fishing boats dock early in the morning with their fresh fish. The Hermitage of San Telmo, built in 1780, watches over sailors from the waterfront.

The Castillo de San Felipe, a former defensive fortress, marks the entrance to Playa Jardín—a trio of black volcanic sand beaches landscaped by César Manrique with gardens of endemic species and waterfalls.
The Church of Nuestra Señora de la Peña de Francia, built in 1684 on the site of an older hermitage, dominates the main square. Its tower dates from 1898. Inside, paintings by Canarian masters.

activities.text: Climb to Mirador de La Paz for sweeping views of the Atlantic, Martiánez beach, the Lago, and the La Orotava Valley with Teide in the background. On clear days, the island of La Palma can be seen in the distance.
Martiánez beach, with 350 meters of black sand beneath the cliffs, draws surfers. Waves form here year-round, and the atmosphere is laid-back.

Sample volcanic wines from the Tacoronte-Acentejo appellation at a guachinche, one of the typical temporary restaurants that also serve papas arrugadas, rabbit in salmorejo sauce, and grilled vieja fish.

places.name: Puerto Del Rosario

visits.text: The city has transformed into an open-air museum with over 150 sculptures scattered throughout its streets. Juan Bordes' snail-shaped works line the coastal promenade.

The Iglesia Nuestra Señora del Rosario, a 19th-century neoclassical edifice, houses a sculpture of the Virgin of the Rosary and remarkable red stone stained glass windows. The square bell tower commands the historic quarter.
Visit the Casa Museo Miguel de Unamuno, the former hotel where the Spanish philosopher lived in exile in 1924. Period furniture, photographs, and writings chronicle his island wanderings.
The lime kilns (Hornos de Cal) stand as monuments to the city's economic past. In the 18th century, Puerto del Rosario became the “Port of Lime,” exporting burned limestone to England.
Playa Chica, recently expanded, offers an urban beach right in the heart of the capital. Showers and facilities make swimming easy.

activities.text: Stroll along Calle Primero de Mayo, the main pedestrian street lined with boutiques and terraces. This is where locals and visitors meet.
Browse the weekly artisan market for PDO Majorero cheese, aloe vera products, and traditional crafts.
Sample vieja (local parrotfish) grilled or fried, roasted goat, and papas arrugadas with mojo sauce. The island's goat cheese carries a protected designation of origin.
