visits.text: Puertollano is an industrial town with little charm, but it marks the start of the route toward the Valle de Alcudia. The Museo Municipal displays local Carboniferous fossils and traces the area's mining history. Quick stop.
If you're passing outside museum hours, fill up and take the road west. The N-420 cuts through dehesa and holm-oak landscapes that already hint at Extremadura.

days_plan.itin_title: Campo de Calatrava and Valle de Alcudia in 5 Days

places.name: Rascafria

visits.text: The Monastery of Santa María del Paular was founded in 1390 by Enrique II of Castile. Castile's first Carthusian monastery blends Gothic and Baroque styles. An exceptional cloister, intricately worked high altar retable, and transparente await inside. Architects Jean Goas and Juan Gil de Hontañón left their mark.

The 18th-century Puente del Perdón crosses the río Lozoya in three granite arches. Stone benches on the pillars once allowed witnesses to watch trials. The condemned could receive pardon on this bridge—their last hope before the Casa de la Horca (House of the Gallows).

The Purgatory Waterfalls cascade down the Arroyo del Aguilón. Two spectacular drops: the first plunges 10 meters and is accessible by platform, the second falls 15 meters and requires scrambling. Carthusian monks once meditated here to purge their sins.

The Lozoya Valley, dubbed the "Jewel of Guadarrama," unfolds in forests of oak, pine and birch. Crystal-clear waters of the Lozoya wind through verdant meadows. Panoramic views stretch to Cuerda Larga and the Montes Carpetanos.
Explore the village of Rascafría, whose name derives from “carrasca fría” (cold oak). Traditional mountain architecture, cobbled lanes leading toward forest trails.

activities.text: Hike to the Purgatory Waterfalls. Start from the monastery, cross the Puente del Perdón, then follow the Arroyo del Aguilón through oak groves. About 6 km one way with 250 meters of elevation gain.
Discover Las Presillas, natural swimming pools in the río Lozoya. Cool, clear waters, shaded picnic areas. Very popular in summer, ideal for cooling off after a mountain hike.
Wildlife watching in the forests: red deer, wild boar, squirrels. Raptors soaring above the valleys. Early morning or late afternoon offer the best chances for sightings.

days_plan.itin_title: Sierra de Guadarrama Road Trip: Castles and Forests

map_keywords: Monasterio Santa María del Paular Rascafría

visits.text: Valencians simply call it 'la Villa'—Requena's Medieval Quarter, built by the Arabs at the top of the hill between the 8th and 11th centuries, has been a BIC since 1966. Access via the Cuesta del Castillo under a stone arch. Inside: cobbled alleys, Palacio del Cid, Torre del Homenaje, and Gothic churches (Santa María, El Salvador). Free stroll.

The Cuevas de la Villa, under the Plaza de la Villa, form a Moorish-era underground labyrinth (12th-18th centuries): 22 galleries that served as wine cellars, silos, and wartime shelters. Entry €4 (reduced €3). Tuesday-Thursday and Sun 9:30 a.m.-2 p.m. The guide explains how the hill's topography allowed these galleries—fascinating for 45 minutes.

activities.text: Take time for a tasting in the bodegas of the DO Utiel-Requena before leaving town: the Bobal variety (documented from the 15th century in the region according to Jaume Roig) produces frank, fruity rosés and reds here, unlike anything found in France. The tourist office directs you to bodegas with visits and tastings, including those in historic underground galleries.

days_plan.itin_title: Castilla-La Mancha: Windmills and Sierra in 11 days

visits.text: Antoni Gaudí was born in Reus in 1852—the house where he was born has disappeared, but the Gaudí Centre, opened in 2007 on Plaça del Mercadal, reconstructs his childhood and his obsessions with form. Three floors, interactive models, French audio guide included. The most moving item: his last pair of glasses, found on him after the 1926 streetcar accident. Small but well done; allow 1 hour, about €9. Combine with coffee on Plaça del Mercadal right in front—shaded terraces and rows of modernist facades.

Casa Navàs, on the same Plaça del Mercadal, is Lluís Domènech i Montaner's masterpiece in Reus—built in 1901–1907 for a textile wholesaler, it's the only modernist house in Spain entirely preserved with its original furniture. Stained glass by Rigalt, mosaics by Mario Maragliano, marquetry by Gaspar Homar. The 1938 bombing destroyed the tower but spared the interior. Guided tour required, 50 minutes, €16—not cheap, but unparalleled. Advance booking essential, limited time slots.

The Institut Pere Mata, on Reus's northern edge, is Domènech i Montaner's least-known project—a private psychiatric hospital built in 1898 within a 25-hectare park, still operating today. The Distinguidos pavilion (for wealthy patients) is open to visitors: ceramics, mosaics, stained glass, floral sculptures. Freer and more experimental than Casa Navàs—a laboratory before the construction of Barcelona's Hospital de Sant Pau. Guided tour €6, Saturday mornings only. Niche but sublime.

The Modernisme Route in Reus connects 26 buildings over 2 km in the city center—Casa Rull, Casa Gasull, Casa Pinyol, Casa Anguera. Free map at the tourist office, downloadable audio guide. Reus was Catalonia's second-largest city by population after Barcelona in the 18th–19th centuries, its fortune built first on the trade in spirits (the expression “Reus, Paris, London” referred to the three markets where their global price was set), then on vermouth, viticulture, and textiles. Industrialists competed through extravagant facades. An ideal stroll in late afternoon when sunlight gilds the ceramics. Allow 2 leisurely hours.

activities.text: Reus is also the birthplace of Catalan vermouth—the city where Yzaguirre, Miró, and Rofes began distilling it in the 19th century. The Museu del Vermut, a bar-museum on Carrer Sant Joan, displays 6,000 different bottles from five continents and serves the customary glass for €4–5. Guided tasting for €12 with a reservation. Reus locals still say “Anem a fer un quinzet”—let's have a quinzet (15 cl), an expression born here. At noon or aperitif time—a difficult choice.

The central market at Plaça de la Llibertat, built in 1949 in a neo-modernist style, buzzes every morning except Sunday. Stalls selling nuts (Reus is Spain's hazelnut capital, PDO Avellana de Reus), fish from Cambrils, and cured meats from the hinterland. Tapas bars in the upper gallery: toast with anchovies and roasted peppers, €6. Noisy, local atmosphere, ideal between 10am and noon.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Catalonia in 10 Days: Tarragona, Priorat & the Ebro Delta
Catalonia - Complete 24-Day Grand Tour

visits.text: First stop: Celanova, south of Ourense, about 37 km from Ribadavia, a 45-minute drive. San Salvador Monastery, founded in 936 by San Rosendo (a Galician bishop and saint), is one of the most important in Galicia. The church, rebuilt in Baroque style in the 17th and 18th centuries, impresses with its monumental façade and regularly laid-out cloister. But Celanova's treasure is hidden behind the monastery: San Miguel Chapel, a tiny 10th-century Mozarabic oratory, one of the few pre-Romanesque buildings in all of Galicia. Its horseshoe arches and miniature proportions transport you to an era when Christians and Muslims shared an architectural vocabulary.

Continue to Allariz, about 47 km from Ribadavia, a 30-minute drive. This medieval village on the Arnoia River received the European Town Planning Award in 1994 for its exemplary restoration. Stroll along the river, cross the stone bridges, and climb into the historic centre, where the granite lanes retain the atmosphere of a medieval Galician town. The Romanesque church of Santiago (12th century) and Santa Clara Convent (which houses a rare medieval rock-crystal crucifix) are worth a stop. Allariz is also a village for food lovers, known for its artisan bakeries.

End the day at Ribadavia, the former capital of the medieval province of Ribeiro. The historic centre preserves one of Galicia's best-preserved Jewish quarters—the quarter is laid out around narrow lanes, with houses bearing coats of arms and the former synagogue (identifiable by its floor plan). After the expulsion of the Jews in 1492, the quarter was gradually absorbed, but the architectural traces remain visible. The castle of the Counts of Ribadavia dominates the village, and the Praza Maior, lined with granite arcades, is the perfect place to enjoy a glass of Ribeiro—Galicia's oldest white wine, produced here since Roman times.

activities.text: If you visit Ribadavia on the last Saturday of August, you will encounter the Festa da Istoria—a medieval re-enactment in which the whole village dresses up, the streets become a medieval market, and life in the Jewish quarter is recreated. It is one of Galicia's most authentic historical festivals.
Sample Ribeiro wine at the bars in Praza Maior—it's a light, fresh white, perfect with fish tapas and Galician empanadas. Several wineries in the region offer tours and tastings.

days_plan.itin_title: Inland Galicia: From Ourense to the Ribeira Sacra

places.name: Ribeira Sacra

visits.text: Welcome to the Ribeira Sacra, one of Spain's most spectacular yet least-known regions. Canyons 500 metres deep carved by the Sil and Miño rivers, Romanesque monasteries clinging to the canyon walls, and vertiginous terraced vineyards where harvesters sometimes work secured by ropes. The name Ribeira Sacra (Sacred Shore) comes from the concentration of monasteries founded between the 6th and 12th centuries along these gorges. Begin at the Mirador de Balcones de Madrid, one of the most vertiginous viewpoints: you overlook the Sil canyon from more than 300 metres above, with terraced vineyards plunging towards the river like a natural amphitheatre.

Descend to the Monastery of Santo Estevo de Ribas de Sil, founded in the 6th century and rebuilt in the 12th–13th centuries. Its three superimposed cloisters—Romanesque, Gothic, and Renaissance—are a lesson in architectural history in a single place. The monastery has been converted into a national Parador (state-run hotel)—even if you're not staying, you can enter to visit the cloisters and have coffee in the gallery overlooking the canyon. The Romanesque church preserves the tombs of nine bishops who retired here in the Middle Ages.

Continue to San Pedro de Rocas Monastery, the oldest monastic site in Galicia (founded in the 6th century). Three chapels are carved directly into the granite rock—a unique example in Galicia. Inside, a rare medieval world map painted in fresco is partially preserved. The place is isolated, deep in a chestnut forest, and the silence is complete.

activities.text: The catamaran cruise through the Sil canyons is the signature experience of the Ribeira Sacra. For 1.5 to 2 hours, you glide up the gorge between 500-metre walls covered with oaks and terraced vineyards. Several embarkation points exist (Santo Estevo, Abeleda). Book ahead in summer—places fill up quickly.

If you're a wine lover, visit a Ribeira Sacra bodega. The terraced vineyards, some with gradients of 50–60%, produce reds based on Mencía—an indigenous grape variety that yields elegant, fruity wines. Harvesting is done by hand, sometimes with ropes to prevent slipping. It's one of the most heroic vineyards in Europe.

map_keywords: Mirador de Balcones de Madrid Ribeira Sacra

visits.text: Riópar Viejo was abandoned in the 18th century when Carlos III authorised Viennese engineer Johann Georg Graubner to exploit the zinc mines in 1772—the workers left to settle in the new industrial town below. What remains today is a small restored stone hamlet, with the ruins of the 13th-century Muslim castle, a cemetery in the parade ground, and the Iglesia del Espíritu Santo whose façade hides recently rediscovered 15th-century frescoes. Free access, free visit; road from Riópar (6 km).

days_plan.itin_title: Castilla-La Mancha: Windmills and Sierra in 11 days

places.name: Roa De Duero

visits.text: Valbuena de Duero, about 30 km from Roa, a 30-minute drive, is home to the estate most steeped in mythology in Spanish wine. Vega Sicilia was founded in 1864 by Eloy Lecanda, who returned from Bordeaux with 18,000 vine plants in his luggage - Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Malbec - to plant alongside the local Tinto Fino. The Álvarez family bought the estate in 1982, the very year the Ribera del Duero DO was created. Coincidence or destiny? The first wines (Único and Valbuena) date from 1915. Único, the flagship wine, can spend ten years in barrels before bottling - a degree of patience required by almost no other great producer in the world. Annual production does not exceed 200,000 bottles.
Bodegas Alión, 10 minutes from Vega Sicilia, is the Álvarez family's second estate. The style is more modern and more approachable, with excellent value for money.

The Castilla Termal hotel in Valbuena is about 30 km from Roa, a 30-minute drive, and occupies a former 12th-century Cistercian monastery converted into a Relais & Châteaux property. Even if you are not staying here, the architecture is worth a look: the cloister, the vaults and the gardens facing the Duero. Stop for lunch at the restaurant if your budget allows.

The Dane arrived in 1995, found 4 hectares of old Tinto Fino vines at Quintanilla de Onésimo, about 35 km from Roa, a 35-minute drive, rented a garage and made his first wine. Peter Sisseck named the wine 'Pingus', his childhood nickname. Robert Parker tasted it at the March 1996 en primeur tastings and wrote on the cover of his Wine Advocate that it was one of the greatest young wines he had ever tasted. Production of the first vintage: 325 cases of 12 bottles. The cargo crossing the Atlantic to the United States sank in November 1997 - almost all the American allocation of the 1995 was lost. Today, fewer than 500 cases are produced each year and sold en primeur before bottling. Visits by appointment only and highly restricted.

Hacienda Monasterio in Pesquera de Duero, about 20 km from Roa, a 20-minute drive - the estate Peter Sisseck has managed since 1990, before Pingus even existed. This is where he learned about the Ribera, and the atmosphere is much more relaxed than at his personal project. Certified organic, with 30 rooms in a former abandoned monastery. Tour and tasting €30. Reserva Especial is the benchmark wine, complex and approachable.

Bodegas Aalto, in the municipality of Quintanilla de Arriba, about 25 km from Roa, a 25-minute drive. Mariano García made his first vintage at Vega Sicilia in 1968 - he was 22. He left 30 years later, in 1998, and founded Aalto the following year with Javier Zaccagnini. The stated aim was to make a wine that would reach the level of the world's best within 15-20 years. Many believe it has. The winery controls 130 hectares of old vines across 9 municipalities in Burgos province, planted exclusively with Tinto Fino. PS (Pagos Seleccionados) is the flagship single-parcel wine, with fewer than 10,000 bottles a year.

Bodegas Emilio Moro in Pesquera de Duero, about 20 km from Roa, a 20-minute drive - three generations of the same family on the same terroir. Its distinctive feature: Malleolus de Valderramiro is made from vines planted in 1924, exactly a century ago. Each of these vines produces less than a kilo of grapes, but with a concentration that outclasses all young plantings. The tour (€30) is well designed, informative and educational without being patronizing - a good introduction if this is your first encounter with the Ribera.

Roa de Duero, seat of the DO's Consejo Regulador since 1982, is also a medieval town with a secret beneath its cobblestones: over 150 cave cellars dug from the 13th century onward to store wine at stable temperatures. The galleries form a network running beneath almost every house. Some are open to the public via the tourism office (Bodega de la Coopérative, private caves by appointment), others remain privately owned—their owners still keeping a few barrels down there. The contrast is striking: steel and concrete bodegas on the surface, an 800-year-old underground network just below.

The church of Asunción de Roa, 15th-century Gothic, and the remains of medieval ramparts merit a tour. The mirador at the edge of the old town offers views across terraced vineyards descending toward the river. This is the landscape that explains why Roa is here and not elsewhere.

activities.text: Lunch at Restaurante Liturgia in Quintanilla de Onésimo—revisited Castilian cuisine, pleasant dining room, terrace. Without excessive gastronomic pretension, but sincere and well-executed. 10 minutes from the bodegas.

Take a late-afternoon walk along the Duero between Valbuena and Quintanilla, about 35 km from Roa, a 35-minute drive. The riverside path runs beside the vines, and the river is wide and calm at this latitude. It is the kind of walk that makes you understand why so many people wanted to make wine here.

Have lunch between the two afternoon visits in Pesquera de Duero, about 20 km from Roa, a 20-minute drive - Asador Mesón La Vid for another lechazo, or simply croquetas and Castilian cured meats in a village bar. Rioja cuisine loses out here to food that is simpler and more direct.

Dinner in Roa at Restaurante Asador Nazareno: cordero lechal in traditional wood-fired oven. This is the most authentic version you'll find in the zone—no white tablecloths, no menu in French, just an oven and a few tables. Reservations advised on weekends.

Have lunch in Pesquera, about 20 km from Roa, a 20-minute drive, after the Emilio Moro tour - Asador Mesón La Vid if you have not already tried it, otherwise any village bar for pinchos and a glass poured from the tap. There is something very wholesome about eating roast lamb standing up in a bar in a village of 300 inhabitants after visiting a winery that produces 800,000 bottles a year.

Guided tour of Roa's underground caves with the local tourism office—about 1.5 hours. The guide explains the medieval technique of digging into limestone rock, the natural ventilation system, and shows some caves still used for aging. Book the day before or two days ahead.

places.name: Roncesvalles

visits.text: The Collegiate Church of Santa María at Roncesvalles is a major example of French Gothic in Navarre. Built in the 13th century on the orders of Sancho VII the Strong, it follows the model of Notre-Dame de Paris.
The square Gothic cloister replaced in 1600 its predecessor that had collapsed under snow. Its galleries provide access to the chapel of San Agustín.

In the chapel of San Agustín lies King Sancho VII the Strong in a 2.3-meter tomb corresponding to his height in life. The chains taken at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa adorn the coat of arms of Navarre.
The Chapel of the Holy Spirit, or Silo de Charlemagne, from the 12th century is the oldest building. According to legend, Roland planted his sword here after the defeat of 778.
The museum displays Charlemagne's Chessboard, a gilt and enameled silver reliquary, a 12th-century evangeliary, and Miramamolín's emerald taken from the Moorish king.
Since the 10th century, Roncesvalles has welcomed pilgrims after the arduous Pyrenean ascent. For many, it marks the starting point of the Camino de Santiago in Spain.

activities.text: Walk a short stage of the Camino toward Zubiri through beech and oak forests. Yellow waymarkers line the path.
Restaurants serve river trout and local sheep's cheeses. Pyrenean gastronomy marries products of livestock farming and fishing.
Ascend to the Ibañeta Pass at 1,057 meters elevation where the original fortress once stood. A modern chapel commemorates the 778 Battle of Roncesvalles.
At twilight, watch the raking light sweep across the Lindus and Ortzanzurieta mountains, which rise above 1,000 meters. Silence reigns over the high-altitude pastures.

places.name: Ronda

visits.text: Ronda sits astride a 100 m deep canyon—el Tajo—that cuts the city in two. The Puente Nuevo, completed in 1793 after 40 years of construction, is the mythical bridge linking the two banks. During August 1936, the Republicans of Ronda who controlled the city threw hundreds of Nationalists alive from the top of the Tajo—the episode is recounted by Ernest Hemingway in chapter 10 of 'For Whom the Bell Tolls' (1940), who had lived in Ronda. A few months later, the Nationalists recaptured the city and executed in turn. The bridge today serves as a postcard; the toll of both purges remains a sensitive local subject.

The Plaza de Toros in Ronda, completed in 1785, is the birthplace of modern bullfighting on foot. Before 1726, bulls were killed from horseback. Francisco Romero, from Ronda, invented bullfighting on foot with a muleta here, later codified by his grandson Pedro Romero (1754-1839), who is said to have killed more than 5,000 bulls without suffering a single injury during his career. Capacity of 5,000, with two levels of golden-stone arcades. Bullfighting museum inside, open except on bullfight days. 9 euros.

The Arab Baths of Ronda, built in the 13th century in the Moorish quarter of San Miguel downhill, are the best-preserved Arab baths in Spain. Classic three-room plan (cold, warm, hot), vaults pierced with star-shaped skylights for light, still-visible functional hypocaust. Public baths from Al-Andalus times, abandoned after 1485 (reconquest of Ronda). 4 euros, closed Mondays.

The Palacio de Mondragón, former Nasrid palace remodeled in the 16th century after the reconquest, preserves three Mudéjar patios with original azulejos. Now houses the municipal archaeology museum, with Bronze Age objects found in the Sierra de Grazalema. Spectacular view from the terrace over the sierra and plain. 4 euros.

The Casa del Rey Moro, on the edge of the Tajo, never housed a Moorish king despite its name—it's an 18th-century palace built on Nasrid foundations. Its centerpiece: the Mina, a staircase carved into rock in the 14th century that descends 231 steps to the bottom of the gorge to reach the Guadalevín River. During sieges, Christian prisoners were forced to haul water up in jugs. Very narrow, dim light, not for the claustrophobic. 8 euros.

The gorge cuts sharply through the landscape beneath Ronda’s Puente Nuevo. The bridge connects the two parts of the city, but its significance becomes fully apparent when you view it from the overlooks. Take in the views from each side and check access routes before considering a descent into the Tajo.

Head down to the Baños Árabes de Ronda for a change of atmosphere after the overlooks. The cold, warm, and hot rooms reveal how the historic baths worked; openings in their vaulted ceilings create a distinctive light. Wear shoes suitable for steep slopes and check opening hours before leaving the center.

The architecture warrants a visit to the Plaza de Toros de Ronda, regardless of whether a performance is taking place. The galleries and arena offer a more intimate sense of scale than the sweeping landscapes of the Tajo; the museum provides context for the bullfighting tradition. Start with the galleries, then view the arena from the stands before walking to the Tajo overlooks.

activities.text: Dinner at Tragatá (calle Nueva 4), inventive tapas by Benito Gómez—double Michelin-starred chef with Bardal 100 m away. Tragatá is the informal version, gently priced: liquid potato tortilla, baby squid croqueta, fried sea anemones. 25-35 euros per person. No reservations, line at 8 PM.

Sunset at the Mirador de Ronda (paseo Blas Infante, just in front of the bullring). Plunging view over the sierra, golden light on the old town's white walls. Classic Tajo photo accessible from the edge by walking 200 m.

visits.text: Climb into the Maestrazgo mountains. Cantavieja, the comarca's capital, perches on a limestone rock at 1,300 m altitude. This triangular-plan village was a Templar commandery from 1169, then passed to the Hospitallers after the dissolution of the Order of the Temple. The medieval streets converge on the Plaza Porticada, one of the province's most beautiful arcaded squares, dominated by the imposing Baroque church of the Asunción and the town hall. The Carlist War Museum traces the battles of the 'Tiger of Maestrazgo,' General Ramón Cabrera, who made Cantavieja his headquarters in 1836.

Descend south (1h mountain drive) to Rubielos de Mora, in the Gúdar-Javalambre comarca. Nicknamed the 'Court of the Sierra' for the number of nobles who settled here in the 16th-17th centuries, this town at 1,000 m altitude possesses a remarkable collection of Renaissance mansions and palaces. The Excolegiata Santa María la Mayor (16th century) houses a large 15th-century International Gothic altarpiece dedicated to the life of the Virgin. The Casa Consistorial (town hall) is a fine Renaissance building. Rubielos is part of the Cittaslow (slow cities) network - a label that suits it perfectly.

activities.text: Enjoy Rubielos de Mora's peaceful atmosphere at day's end. Stroll beneath the arches of the Portal del Carmen and Portal de San Antonio, the two medieval gates still standing. The convents of the Discalced Carmelites and Augustinians are open for visits. In the evening, the Plaza de la Villa gently comes alive with its terraces - this is deep Spain, without tourists, where time seems to slow down.

days_plan.itin_title: Aragonese Pyrenees and Lower Aragón: From Ordesa to Teruel

visits.text: Fifteen lagoons linked by travertine waterfalls over 30 kilometres: the Lagunas de Ruidera shift colour with the light—turquoise to the west, emerald green to the east. The Natural Park straddles Albacete and Ciudad Real. The CR-650 road runs alongside the lower lakes; stop at each viewpoint. Avoid August: area is packed. Spring and autumn offer the clearest waters.

In the Quijote, Cervantes sets the episode of the Cueva de Montesinos here: Don Quixote descends 80 metres into a cave and sleeps three days (outside, only two hours pass). The cave still exists, accessible to the public with fitted stairs—a strange, dark place inhabited by bats. Ideal if you're reading Cervantes en route.

Castillo de Peñarroya marks the lower entrance to the park, on the edge of the reservoir lake of the same name. The partly ruined medieval fortress dominates the lake: from its ramparts, the entire chain of lower lakes becomes visible. Free access. Budget 20 minutes to walk around it.

activities.text: You can rent a kayak in Ruidera to explore Laguna del Rey, where swimming is permitted. Rental operators are available locally (check during the season).

days_plan.itin_title: Castilla-La Mancha: Windmills and Sierra in 11 days

visits.text: Locals call this spot the birthplace of the city: the Phoenician site of Sa Caleta, a UNESCO listing since 1999, preserves the foundations of a village founded around 654 BC and abandoned half a century later. The ruins perch above the cliff, the panorama over the salt flats is striking.

Es Bol Nou beach (Sa Caleta) is closed by the authorities because of the risk of rockfalls: do not enter the fenced-off area. Sa Caleta restaurant and the nearby interpretation centre remain accessible; take the opportunity to view the cove from authorised areas and discover the Phoenician site.

activities.text: Head to the Sa Caleta interpretation centre and follow one of the outdoor routes devoted to the Phoenician village and the 20th-century military installations. The ruins occupy the headland above the sea; stay on authorised paths and do not enter Es Bol Nou beach, which is closed because of the risk of rockfalls.

days_plan.itin_title: Ibiza & Formentera by Scooter: Calas & Beaches in 7 Days

visits.text: Hannibal besieged Sagunto for eight months in 219 BC—the episode that triggered the Second Punic War with Rome. The hill still bears the traces of that clash: Iberian enclosure, then Roman, then Arab, all superimposed in readable strata. Allow a good hour for the full circuit.

From the castle summit, the plain spreads to the sea and the chimneys of Valencia port point southward. The 2nd-century Roman theatre, controversially restored in the 1990s, still hosts summer performances. Tickets available on the municipal website.

places.name: Sajazarra

visits.text: Sajazarra's castle-palace has stood since the 15th century, with its rectangular keep flanked by four octagonal turrets. The Velasco family, lords of the town, had it built when the town became their fief. Privately owned, it cannot be visited, but you can walk around its entire perimeter.

The church of Santa María de la Asunción, dating from the 12th–13th centuries, stands a few meters from the castle. Founded with the Cistercian monastery in 1171, it houses a statue of the Virgen de la Antigua.
Wander the cobbled lanes of this village of 120 inhabitants, listed among Los Pueblos más Bonitos de España. Stone houses bear coats of arms and pointed arches.
Pass under the restored medieval archway that pierces the remnants of the ramparts. This gate once marked the fortified entrance to the medieval town.
Walk down to the banks of the Río Ea. This stream borders the village and irrigates the surrounding vineyards.

activities.text: Visit a small family estate for a tasting. Sajazarra's winemakers cultivate their parcels on the slopes of the Montes Obarenes.
Settle on a village bench at sunset. The hillsides turn golden and the castle stands in silhouette.
Walk among the vines that surround Sajazarra. Rows of Tempranillo roll toward the Río Tirón, which flows into the Ebro.

visits.text: Salamanca's Plaza Mayor is considered Spain's most beautiful baroque square—and it's hard to argue. Commissioned in 1729 by Philip V in gratitude to the city for its support in the War of Succession, designed by Alberto de Churriguera, completed in 1755. 88 arcades on three sides, the fourth occupied by the town hall. Look for the stone medallions in the spandrels: Christopher Columbus, Cervantes, Cortés, Franco (yes, removed and restored depending on the era). The local sandstone turns orange at sunset—hence the nickname "golden city."

The University of Salamanca, founded in 1218 by Alfonso IX of León, is Spain's oldest university and Europe's fourth oldest (after Bologna, Paris, Oxford). Christopher Columbus defended his project here in 1486; Antonio de Nebrija published the first Spanish grammar here in 1492. The Plateresque façade of the Escuelas Mayores (1529) is so finely carved it looks like a goldsmith's work in stone. The challenge: find the lucky frog on one of the three skulls in the pediment. Students say you'll pass your exams if you spot it on your own. Hint: on the right, on the rightmost skull. Tell no one.

Salamanca has two adjoining cathedrals. The Romanesque Catedral Vieja, dating from the 12th century, preserves in its apse an altarpiece of 53 panels painted by Nicolás Florentino around 1445—one of Spain's largest Gothic ensembles, completed by a fresco of the Last Judgment. The late Gothic and later baroque Catedral Nueva was begun in 1513 without destroying the old one—a rare occurrence. A curiosity: on the north façade (Puerta de Ramos), an astronaut and a faun eating ice cream were carved in 1992 during a restoration. Look closely.

Facing the university, the Casa de las Conchas—"House of Shells." Built between 1493 and 1517 by Don Rodrigo Maldonado de Talavera, university professor and knight of the Order of Santiago. The façade is adorned with 365 carved scallop shells (one for each day of the year), symbol of the order to which he belonged. Today a public library, free access to the interior courtyard and first floor. According to a legend at least four centuries old, one of the shells hides an ounce of gold. No one has ever found it. And no one has the right to look underneath.

The Convent of San Esteban, ten minutes from Plaza Mayor, is one of Salamanca's finest Plateresque buildings—a 30-meter-high stone façade resembling an altarpiece, carved by Juan de Ribero between 1524 and 1610, with a relief depicting the Stoning of Saint Stephen. A Dominican convent where Christopher Columbus stayed in 1486 during negotiations with university theologians. The church's main altarpiece by José de Churriguera (1693) is a 27-meter-high baroque explosion. The Renaissance cloister, by Juan de Álava, is a haven of calm.

Right next door, the Convent of Las Dueñas has an irregular pentagonal cloister. Built in the 16th century for Dominican nuns, it is still home to 9 cloistered sisters who sell pastries through a revolving hatch (you speak through the wall, put the money in the hatch, it turns, and the cookies arrive). Above all, the cloister capitals: grotesque sculptures, demons and monsters, unusual for a convent—scholars still disagree about their meaning.

Casa Lis, above the Tormes against the old walls, houses the Museum of Art Nouveau and Art Deco, one of Spain's best. The house itself, built in 1905 by modernist Joaquín de Vargas, is a marvel—multicolored stained glass flooding the hall, floral ironwork, marble and bronze staircase. Collection: 19,000 pieces including porcelain dolls by Bru and Jumeau, bronzes by Demêtre Chiparus, Émile Gallé furniture. Very intimate visit, never crowded.

The Roman Bridge—Puente Mayor del Tormes—dates from the 1st century CE and was part of the Vía de la Plata, the Roman road linking Mérida to Astorga. The southern half was rebuilt in the 17th century after a flood. At the bridge's end, a pre-Roman sculpture—perhaps a Vettonian verraco, perhaps an Iberian bull—over 2,000 years old. The bridge is pedestrian, perfect for photographing both cathedrals from the other bank. Lazarillo de Tormes, Spain's first picaresque novel (1554), begins precisely when Lazarillo's master forces him to ram his head against this stone.

activities.text: A tapas crawl along Calle Van Dyck or around Plaza Mayor. Salamanca is one of Spain's tapas capitals—here tapas are still served free with your drink, unlike in Madrid or Barcelona. Try the hornazo (meat pie with serrano ham, chorizo and hard-boiled egg), chanfaina (ratatouille with rice and beef tongue), and especially the ibérico ham from Guijuelo, 30 km from Salamanca—one of Spain's best PDO products, from pigs raised on acorns in the oak groves of the Sierra de Béjar.

Head out for the evening. Salamanca has 30,000 students among its 145,000 inhabitants. Student bars cluster around the Calle Bordadores barracks and Plaza de San Juan Bautista; for mojitos and a young party crowd, head to Calle Compañía. For something more intimate, try Calle Quintana, where the tradition of the tuna (student singing in medieval costume, with a lamp and guitar) still survives—one of the last places in Spain where it's still alive rather than folklore staged for tourists.

If the sky is clear, a hot-air balloon flight at sunrise over Salamanca—the outing starts around 6 a.m., lasts one hour, and offers an unmatched view of the two cathedrals and the Tormes plain. Several operators (Aerotours Castilla, Globos Boreal), from €175. The whisper of the burner, low sunlight on the sandstone, and traditionally a countryside brunch with cava on your return. Reservations are essential in season.

Walk in Barrio del Oeste, behind the train station. Post-Franco working-class neighborhood that has metamorphosed into an open-air street art gallery since 2013—Galería Urbana festival. Over 100 murals by international muralists: Kraser Tres, Phlegm, Borondo. It's the perfect antithesis to the golden sandstone of the center. Pick up the free map at the Plaza Mayor tourist office.

visits.text: From a distance, the castle seems to crush the village - up close, it's what saved it. Originally a Phoenician fortress, rebuilt by the Romans, then transformed into a Nasrid palace. The Hall of the Sultans preserves its stucco work. Entry €4. Ticket includes the archaeological museum below. Allow 1h.

The mirador at the village summit opens onto a double panorama: the Mediterranean on one side, the sugar cane plain on the other. These fields between Salobreña and Motril are the last in Andalusia - cultivation dates back to the Arabs and has survived thanks to the Costa Tropical's subtropical microclimate. Five-minute walk from the castle.

activities.text: The whitewashed limestone lanes hold the cool even in high summer - the Arabs designed it well. La Bóveda, an underground passage that once linked the Albaicín to the medina, is still traversable. Short but striking: the acoustics are those of a cellar. Allow 30 minutes for a tour of the center.

places.name: San Carlos Del Valle

visits.text: It is called the “Vaticano de La Mancha”: the Plaza Mayor of San Carlos del Valle, built between 1713 and 1729, forms a rectangle measuring 53 meters by 21 meters, lined with Tuscan columns and wooden galleries. The church of Santísimo Cristo del Valle dominates the ensemble with its dome and four towers topped by Madrid-style capitals. Listed as a Bien de Interés Cultural since 1993.

The church interior stuns with its proportions: the octagonal dome rises over 28 meters, and the spire reaches 47 meters. Late Baroque with neoclassical touches. The village has no more than 1,100 residents, which makes the building's immense scale all the more striking.

activities.text: Sit under the plaza's arcades and observe: the rectangular space, designed like a Baroque theater, once hosted performances and public ceremonies. The three brick arches leading into the square frame the landscape of La Mancha beyond.

places.name: San Felices De Los Gallegos

visits.text: San Felices de los Gallegos encapsulates the turbulent history of the Spanish-Portuguese frontier. The castle was built in 1296 by King Denis I of Portugal, who had just occupied the town. The annexation by Portugal was confirmed in 1297 at the Treaty of Alcañices. In 1326, San Felices returned to Castilian control as a royal marriage dowry. But that was far from the end of sovereignty exchanges: the town was retaken by the Portuguese during the Castilian War of Succession in the 15th century, then pillaged again during the Portuguese Restoration War in 1646. Its castle is the best-preserved of the four in Arribes del Duero Natural Park.

The Puente de los Franceses (Bridge of the French) spans the Águeda River below the village—the only crossing point of the Arribes de l'Águeda. According to tradition, it was built by Gauls settled in the region, whose name may be the origin of 'Gallegos' in the village name. The descent to the bridge crosses steep slopes of the riverbank with dense Mediterranean vegetation (olive trees, cork oaks) characteristic of the Arribes microclimate.

The Arribes del Duero form one of Spain's most spectacular landscapes: 200-meter-deep canyons carved by the Duero and its tributaries on the Portuguese border. The viewpoint at Mesa del Conde (Table of the Count), accessible from San Felices, offers a vertiginous panorama over the gorges. In 1476, the inhabitants of San Felices revolted against their tyrant lord Gracián de Sessé and hanged him from the tower arch—legend says the shadow of the hanged man stretched all the way to the square.

activities.text: The marked trails of the Arribes del Agueda departing from San Felices offer impressive views of the gorges and colonies of griffon vultures, black storks, and Bonelli's eagles. The avifauna here is among Spain's richest. Choose a morning outing for the best observation conditions.

The AOC Arribes del Duero wines, produced from centuries-old vines on terraces exposed to the gorges' Mediterranean microclimate, are a discovery for many visitors. The heat reflected from the rock walls produces powerful reds based on Juan García and Rufete. A visit to one of the local estates is a must.

places.name: San Jose

visits.text: Mónsul beach is the natural park's most famous stretch. Enormous black lava tongues frame its golden sand—this is where a scene from Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade was filmed. At the beach's center, a massive wind-sculpted rock serves as a landmark.

Want a kilometer of pristine sand? Los Genoveses beach stretches across a bay bordered by dunes, with no buildings. The seabed slopes gently beneath the shallow water, making it ideal for swimming. In summer, vehicle access is limited to a few cars per day.

The Arrecife de las Sirenas, at the tip of the cape, owes its name to the monk seals that sailors once mistook for mermaids. Dark volcanic chimneys rise from the turquoise water, right at the foot of the Cabo de Gata lighthouse, built in 1863. Plan a round trip by car from San José for this visit.
The village of San José serves as the park's main gateway. Its white houses and small fishing port follow the rhythm of the seasons. Restaurants with terraces facing the sea serve fresh fish dishes.

The Cabo de Gata salt pans cover 400 hectares between the road and the sea. More than 80 bird species frequent these shallow basins, including flamingos that can be seen from the observation points set up along the site. Plan a round trip by car from San José for this visit.
Climb up to Mirador de La Amatista for a view down over the volcanic cliffs and Pico de los Frailes, the park's highest point. The violet-hued rocks give the viewpoint its name.

activities.text: Coastal hike between Genoveses and Mónsul along the ridges. The trail follows the cliffs and crosses several deserted little coves with colorful geological formations—white, orange, gray.
Snorkeling in the clear waters around San José. Posidonia seagrass meadows shelter rainbow wrasses, seabream, and octopuses among the volcanic rocks.
Flamingo and black-winged stilt watching at the salt pans, ideally late in the day when the low-angle light colors the basins pink and gold. Plan a round trip by car from San José for this activity.

places.name: San Millan

visits.text: The monastery of Suso has clung to the flank of the Sierra de la Demanda since the 6th century. Hermit disciples of San Millán carved these caves, which became the cradle of the Castilian language. The Glosas Emilianenses, 10th-century annotations in Castilian and Basque, were written here.

At the monastery of Yuso, built downhill in the 11th century and rebuilt between the 16th and 18th centuries, marvel at the Baroque frescoes in the sacristy and the 11th-century ivory caskets holding San Millán's relics.
The library at Yuso preserves medieval manuscripts and illuminated codices. Its scriptorium was one of the most distinguished in medieval Spain.
Climb to the burial chamber at Suso. The founder's 12th-century black alabaster tombstone rests in the dim light beneath the Romanesque vaults.
Look up at Yuso's bell tower and slate roofs dominating the Cárdenas Valley. The Sierra de la Demanda rises in the background, with its San Lorenzo peak (2,262 m).

activities.text: Hike in the Iregua valley, which winds between oak trees and vineyards, planning a same-day round trip by car from San Millán. The marked trails lead to secluded hermitages in the hills.
Photograph Yuso's Renaissance facades at dusk. The low light carves out the reliefs of the 1661 Baroque portal.
Settle in for a picnic at the edge of the vineyards. The silence of the monastic valley is broken only by birdsong.

days_plan.itin_title: La Rioja Tour: Wine Route and Monasteries

map_keywords: Sierra de la Demanda San Millán

visits.text: La Concha Bay forms a perfect crescent between Monte Urgull and Monte Igueldo. 1,350 meters of golden sand, calm waters, and a white Art Deco balustrade. One of Europe’s most beautiful urban beaches.
Get lost in the Parte Vieja. Narrow streets, colorful facades, and pintxos bars every ten meters. San Vicente Church dates from the 16th century and is the oldest in the city.
Head up Monte Igueldo on the century-old funicular. From the summit, views down over the bay, Santa Clara Island, and the Basque mountains. A retro amusement park occupies the plateau.
The Aquarium showcases Cantabrian marine life in a 360° underwater tunnel. Rays, sharks, and schools of sardines swim above visitors.
The fishing harbor comes alive as the boats return. A morning fish auction, drying nets, and the briny scent of the sea. The aroma of fresh fish on the grill fills the quays.

activities.text: Reserve an evening at a gastronomic society. These private clubs sometimes welcome visitors to cook together. A menu of your choice, market ingredients, and a convivial atmosphere around the stoves.
Take an early morning swim at Ondarreta. Quieter than La Concha, this beach attracts local swimmers. Sheltered waters with few waves.
Rent a paddleboard to paddle along the bay. From the water, a unique perspective on the Belle Époque promenade, the white buildings, and Chillida’s sculptures at Ondarreta.
Explore the pintxos bars of the Parte Vieja. Gilda (anchovies, olives, chili peppers), txangurro (brown crab), kokotxas (hake cheeks). Three or four establishments are enough for a full meal.

places.name: Sanlucar De Barrameda

visits.text: Santiago Castle has dominated Sanlúcar since the 15th century. Built by the Dukes of Medina Sidonia to control the mouth of the Guadalquivir, it retains the Puerta de la Sirena, a carved Gothic arch. From the top of its Torre del Homenaje, the panorama takes in the white houses, the river, and Doñana's marshlands on the opposite bank.

Magellan set sail from Sanlúcar in 1519 on the first circumnavigation of the globe. The “Legua Cero” monument at Bajo de Guía marks this historic departure point. In the former Fábrica de Hielo, now Doñana's visitor center, a replica of the Nao Victoria tells the story of the expedition.

Climb from the Barrio Bajo to the Barrio Alto through zigzagging lanes inherited from the Muslim era. The 14th-century Gothic church of Nuestra Señora de la O features a richly carved Mudéjar portal. The Palace of the Dukes of Medina Sidonia, built in the 16th century on the remains of the old Andalusian alcázar, houses exceptional historical archives.

Plaza del Cabildo, Sanlúcar's heart, buzzes around its central fountain and tapas bar terraces. Whitewashed facades and wrought-iron balconies create an authentic Andalusian setting, far from the tourist routes.

Visit a manzanilla bodega to discover this dry white wine, unique in the world, whose saline taste comes from moisture the vines absorb from Atlantic breezes. The cathedrals of manzanilla, vast cellars with high ceilings, preserve centuries of winemaking tradition passed down from generation to generation.

activities.text: Board a traditional barge from Bajo de Guía to cross the mouth of the Guadalquivir toward Doñana National Park. The 3-hour cruise heads upriver along marshlands populated by flamingos and gray herons.

Settle into a restaurant in Bajo de Guía facing the Guadalquivir and Doñana. This former fishing quarter has become one of Andalusia's leading seafood destinations: Sanlúcar langoustines, white shrimp, coquina clams, and tortillita de camarones, all washed down with well-chilled manzanilla.

In August, Sanlúcar hosts Spain's oldest beach horse races, documented for over 200 years and formalized in 1845. At sunset, riders send their mounts racing across the sand of Las Piletas beach, with Doñana as a backdrop.

places.name: Santa Cruz De La Palma

visits.text: Santa Cruz de La Palma was founded on 3 May 1493 by Alonso Fernández de Lugo. In the 16th century it became the third port of the Spanish Empire after Seville and Antwerp - the riches of the American colonies passed through here. This prosperity left a historic centre listed as a Historic-Artistic Ensemble, with 17th- and 18th-century palaces and mansions, colourful façades and carved wooden balconies overlooking the Atlantic. Start with the Avenida Marítima: its 17th-century wooden balconies, full of flowers and each different from the next, make up one of the most photogenic promenades in the Canaries. Note that these enclosed balconies (ajimeces) were inspired by Arab architecture and served to cool the houses thanks to the sea breeze.

Walk up Calle Real—also called Calle O'Daly, named after an Irish banana merchant who lived there. This long cobbled pedestrian street concentrates palaces, craft shops, and small squares. Plaza de España, in the city's heart, is one of the Canaries' finest Renaissance ensembles: the arcaded town hall, public fountain, and El Salvador Church (whose origins date to 1500) form a setting seemingly preserved for five centuries. Casa Salazar, a bit further, is the city's most remarkable Baroque palace—built in the second half of the 17th century, its patio surrounded by wood-balconied galleries is open to the public through temporary exhibitions.

On the port esplanade, don't miss the Barco de La Virgen—a full-scale replica of Christopher Columbus's Santa María, housing the city's naval museum. Just beside it, Castillo de Santa Catalina, a 16th-century fortification, defended the port against corsair attacks. From the esplanade, the view of the Avenida balconies and the castle facade is Santa Cruz's iconic photo.

The Caldera de Taburiente is La Palma's national park - protected since 1954, one of the first in Spain. This gigantic erosion crater, 8 km across and 1,500 metres deep, is covered with Canary pine forests and cut by ravines. If you do not want to hike, the Mirador de La Cumbrecita (1,287 m), about forty minutes' drive from Santa Cruz de La Palma and reachable by car subject to a permit between 8:30 am and 4 pm, offers a dizzying view into the caldera. From up there, the walls rising to more than 2,000 m make you feel as if you are at the bottom of a natural amphitheatre.

For those who want to enter the caldera on foot, the PR-LP 13 trail from Los Brecitos is the most popular (16 km, about 6 hours, -700 m descent). It goes down through Canary pine forests to the riverbed and passes the Cascada de Colores - a 6-metre waterfall whose rocks are naturally stained yellow, orange and red by the iron dissolved in the ferruginous water of the Barranco de las Angustias. The green comes from algae and mosses. The sight changes with the season and the flow. Bring plenty of water - there are no services inside. Allow a full day from Santa Cruz de La Palma, including the drive.

Roque Idafe, a basaltic monolith rising in the caldera's heart, was venerated by the Benahoaritas—La Palma's prehistoric inhabitants—who attributed supernatural powers to it. It stands at the confluence of the Almendro Amargo and Limonero ravines, just before the Cascada de Colores. If you hike here, take a break at this spot: the view of the caldera walls is breathtaking.

activities.text: Lunch in the historic quarter around Calle Real. La Palma's cuisine revolves around palmero cheese (PDO) and bienmesabe - an almond cream you will find in every dessert. Pair it with a glass of malvasía wine, produced in the island's vineyards.

The city is small and entirely walkable in 2 to 3 hours. Late afternoon, climb to Mirador de la Concepción for a panoramic view over the city, colorful balconies, and port. It's the best time of day: the low light ignites the yellow and ochre facades.

Swim in a natural pool on the coast near Santa Cruz, depending on sea conditions. Volcanic pools are numerous on La Palma's east coast—check with your hotel about conditions, as Atlantic swells can be strong.

Guided hike into the caldera from Los Brecitos: several operators offer accompanied descents in small groups, with a 4x4 bus to reach the starting point from Los Llanos de Aridane. It's the recommended option if you don't know the trail, as ravines can be slippery and weather changes fast inside.

Stargazing from La Palma's heights. The island obtained UNESCO's first Starlight Reserve status worldwide in 2011—no light pollution, perfectly stable skies. Roque de los Muchachos (2,426 m), the island's summit, houses one of the world's most important astronomical observatories. Outside observatory visiting hours, the mountain roads are freely accessible for night observation.

Picnic at the Playa de Taburiente camping area, inside the park. This sandy riverbed with small natural pools is one of the Canaries' only permanent streams. The water is cold and clear—a welcome break after the descent.

places.name: Santa Cruz De Tenerife

visits.text: The Tenerife Auditorium rises in a wave of white concrete facing the Atlantic. Designed by architect Santiago Calatrava and inaugurated in 2003, its roof reaches 58 meters. The 1,800-seat main hall is clad in crystalline wood paneling shaped for acoustics.

Walk through Parque García Sanabria, the largest urban park in the Canary Islands. Inaugurated in 1926, its 67,000 m² are home to outdoor sculptures from an international exhibition, century-old ficus trees, and Art Deco fountains.

La Concepción Church was built in 1500, then reconstructed after a 17th-century fire. Its bell tower dominates the historic center—a triangle bounded by Plaza de España, Plaza de Candelaria, and Plaza de Weyler.
Step into the Palmetum, a botanical garden created on a former landfill transformed into a collection of palms from around the world. The view looks down over the port and the ocean.
Plaza de España opens onto the waterfront with its pool designed by Swiss architects Herzog and de Meuron. Terraces overlook the cruise port.

activities.text: Head to Las Teresitas beach, north of the city. Its golden sand—imported from the Sahara—stretches 1,300 meters beneath the fishing village of San Andrés.
Mercado Nuestra Señora de África has operated since 1944 under its North African–style arcades. Tropical fruits, goat cheeses, flowers, and fresh fish crowd the stalls.
Try gofio, the toasted grain flour that accompanies Canarian soups and desserts. Pair it with papas arrugadas and either mojo rojo or mojo verde.

visits.text: Climb the Camí de Missa to the fortified church of Puig de Missa, consecrated in 1568. At 52 m altitude, the panorama embraces the east coast and wooded hills. The Museu Etnogràfic, in the 300-year-old farmhouse Can Ros, displays traditional tools and costumes.

Ibiza's third-largest town, Santa Eulària feels different from the rest of the island: a palm-lined promenade, a peaceful marina and decent restaurants without tourist traps. The riu (river) runs through the town.

activities.text: The paseo runs along the sea, lined with palm trees and terraces: have a coffee at Passion on the promenade.

days_plan.itin_title: Ibiza & Formentera by Scooter: Calas & Beaches in 7 Days

visits.text: After a short boat crossing from Santa Pola, the bustle disappears. Tabarca is the only inhabited island in the Valencian Community, fortified in the 18th century by Charles III with Genoese people freed from captivity in Tunisia. Its walls, three gates (San Gabriel, San Miguel, San Rafael) and church, declared a national monument in 1964, remain. No cars. Nine streets, two squares and a few fish restaurants.

activities.text: The marine reserve of 1986: Spain's first designated as such. Beneath the surface, Tabarca's seabeds are remarkably rich. Mask and snorkel suffice from the coves—snorkeling is free and accessible. Equipment rental available on the quay upon arrival. Departure from Santa Pola: boats roughly every hour, round trip from €9.

days_plan.itin_title: Costa Blanca & Alicante Hinterland: 12 days

visits.text: The Magdalena Palace commands the peninsula of the same name. Built between 1908 and 1912 for the royal family, it blends English and French influences across 2,500 square meters.
Wander through the 30 hectares of Magdalena Park. Coastal trails wind past a small marine zoo housing penguins and seals, while viewpoints at the peninsula's tip overlook the bay.
The Centro Botín, designed by Renzo Piano, appears to hover above the bay on its stilts. Its 270,000 pearlescent ceramic discs shimmer with the ever-changing Cantabrian light.
Step inside Santander Cathedral, rebuilt after the 1941 fire. Its Gothic cloister and the Cristo crypt shelter Roman-era remnants.
El Sardinero beach sweeps in an arc of fine sand facing the Piquío gardens. A fashionable resort since the Belle Époque, it retains its elegant facades.
The Museum of Prehistory and Archaeology of Cantabria gathers artifacts from the Paleolithic to the early centuries. French-language commentary is available.

activities.text: Board a cruise around Santander Bay. From the water, the silhouette of the Magdalena Palace and the cliffs of Cabo Mayor reveal their full drama.
The Mercado de la Esperanza spreads its stalls across two floors: fish and shellfish below, cheeses and cured meats above. Sample Cantabrian anchovies and rabas (crispy fried squid).
Follow the coastal path to Cabo Mayor lighthouse. The cliffs plunge into the Atlantic, and the sunset here is breathtaking.
The Puertochico quarter brims with pintxo bars and terraces overlooking the harbor. Grilled sardines, rabas and Cantabrian wines make for the perfect local aperitif.

days_plan.itin_title: Cantabria Road Trip: Atlantic Bays and Picos de Europa

places.name: Santiago De Compostela

visits.text: Santiago Cathedral rises at the end of the Praza do Obradoiro and takes the breath away even of committed atheists. Its first stones were laid in 1075, during Alfonso VI's reign, over the supposed tomb of the Apostle James, discovered by the hermit Pelayo in 813. The current Baroque façade dates from 1750—Fernando de Casas Novoa placed it like a mask over the original Romanesque structure. Pilgrims arriving on foot still embrace the statue of St James above the high altar and descend to the crypt to see the silver reliquary. Allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes, more if there is a noon Mass with the giant botafumeiro.

The Pórtico da Gloria, behind the western façade, is arguably Europe's finest Romanesque portal—sculpted by Master Mateo between 1168 and 1188, with over 200 polychrome figures restored in 2018 after a ten-year project. The original colouring, nearly erased by centuries of smoke and touching, has been partially revealed—greens, reds, golds. Guided visit compulsory, €18, 30-minute slots, limited to 25 people. Booking essential 2–3 days ahead, especially during pilgrimage season. The cathedral's highlight, to see before anything else.

The Cathedral Museum occupies the ground floor and the cloister at the rear of the cathedral. Three floors of medieval goldwork, Goya tapestries copied by Bayeu, and the star piece: the 1851 botafumeiro (53 kg, 1.6 m tall), the giant censer that swings across the transept crossing at 70 km/h on feast days, suspended 25 m high. Rope-and-pulley system operated by 8 tiraboleiros. The legend of its origin: to mask the stench of filthy medieval pilgrims. Still true today? More than ever. Allow 1 hour, €12 combined ticket.

The Praza do Obradoiro, the vast cobbled square west of the cathedral, is the backdrop for the iconic photo of exhausted pilgrims collapsing on the ground after 800 km. Flanked by the Hostal dos Reis Católicos (1499, former pilgrims' hospital, now a 5-star parador), the Pazo de Raxoi (city hall) and the Colexio de San Xerome. Continuous action: musicians, gaiteros (bagpipers), tearful pilgrims, reunions of strangers who became friends. Not just a place—a stage. Best in late afternoon when the light gilds the granite stone.

The Mosteiro de San Martiño Pinario, just north of the cathedral, is Spain's second-largest monastery after El Escorial—20,000 m², a 110 m-long façade. Benedictine since 912, rebuilt between 1590 and 1750 in restrained Baroque style. The church altarpieces, by Casas Novoa and Romay, feature gilding, chubby angels and Solomonic columns. Today an active seminary and accommodation for pilgrims. Entry €4, allow 1 hour. Church accessible separately from the main visit, free at certain times.

The Museo do Pobo Galego, in the former Santo Domingo de Bonaval convent, tells the story of 2,000 years of Galician culture—Celtic rock carvings, Galician fest-noz costumes, ancient gaitas (bagpipes), reconstructed peasant interiors. The architectural highlight: the triple spiral staircase, carved in granite by Domingo de Andrade in 1700—three helical flights with no central pillar, a technical feat unique in Europe. Restored in 2019. Entry €3, allow 1 hour 30 minutes. Perfect for rainy days.

The Colexiata de Santa María a Real do Sar, 1 km south of the centre, is a 12th-century Romanesque church out of a nightmare—columns tilted 15° outward, as if the building's leaning backwards. Cause: foundations laid on loose ground sank from the 15th century, but the structure's held for 800 years with emergency flying buttresses added externally. Dizzying effect inside. Adjacent cloister with 12 sculpted capitals. Entry €2, almost never crowded. Strange and magnificent.

The Cidade da Cultura de Galicia, perched on Monte Gaiás 4 km from the centre, is Spain's most controversial architectural UFO—Peter Eisenman's project launched in 1999, never completed. Six buildings with wave-shaped granite roofs reproducing the old town's topography, budget ballooning from 100 million to over a billion euros. Construction abandoned in 2013 after partial inauguration. The library, archives and museum are operating. Unexpected urban stroll, sunset view over Santiago. Bus C11 from the centre, €1.20.

activities.text: The Mercado de Abastos, Santiago's second attraction after the cathedral, buzzes Tuesday to Saturday from 8am to 2pm. Neo-Romanesque building from 1937 with eight themed halls. Fish stall: live octopus in a tank, percebes (goose barnacles) at €80/kg, navajas (razor clams) piled high. Several market restaurants cook what you buy there—€5 extra per item. Mariscadas Abastos 2.0 remains the benchmark; expect €30–40 per person. Booking advised for Saturday lunch.

For dinner, the rúa do Franco has a 50-metre stretch of tapas bars—crowded, noisy, with orders chalked up on a slate. Pulpo a feira (octopus with paprika and olive oil) for €12, empanadas de zamburiñas (scallop pastries) at €3 per slice, white ribeiro in a ceramic bowl at €2. Casa Manolo offers a pilgrim's menu at €12—hearty, unpretentious. The ritual: tour 3–4 bars, one dish per stop, finish with the queimada (flambéed eau-de-vie) with an incantation to the spirits, theatrical and effective.

The Parque da Alameda, just west of the centre, is Santiago's green lung—90,000 m² of century-old oaks, eucalyptus, magnolias, and viewpoints offering the postcard view of the cathedral at sunset. The statue of the “Dúas Marías” (two eccentric sisters from the era of Franco's dictatorship who became local icons) attracts selfies. Flat 30-minute loop walk, or a leisurely hour with a coffee stop at the historic kiosk. Free concert on Tuesdays at 7pm in July–August.

If you are here in the second half of July, the Apostol festival is in full swing - fireworks against the cathedral façade at midnight on July 24 (“Os Fogos do Apóstolo”), a solemn procession on the 25th with incense, bagpipes and the king's presence every 7 years (Compostelan Holy Year). Outside the festival, the queimada at La Bodeguilla de San Roque is worth a visit: grape spirit flambéed with lemon, coffee and sugar, accompanied by a 2-minute ritual incantation against witches. Touristy but sincere.

places.name: Santillana Del Mar

visits.text: The Collegiate Church of Santa Juliana dates from the 12th century and stands as Cantabria's finest Romanesque monument. Its cloister preserves carved capitals depicting biblical scenes and medieval daily life.
The Altamira Museum houses the Neocave, a faithful replica of the original cavern. The polychrome bison paintings date back 14,000 years—dubbed the 'Sistine Chapel of cave art.'
Walk along Calle del Rey to Plaza Mayor. The armorial mansions of the Peredo, Tagle and Estrada families line cobbled lanes that have barely changed since the 16th century.
The Merino and Don Borja towers are among the oldest secular buildings in the village.
On Plaza de las Arenas, the Velarde Palace displays its 16th-century Renaissance facade. Underfoot, scallop shells remind visitors that Santillana is a waypoint on the Camino del Norte.
The Regina Coeli Diocesan Museum exhibits a collection of Cantabrian religious art: altarpieces, gold and silverwork, and medieval sculpture.

activities.text: Taste Cantabrian specialties: cocido montañés (a hearty stew of beans, cabbage and pork), sobaos pasiegos (buttery sponge cakes) and local cheeses.
Head down to Santa Justa beach in Ubiarco; plan to drive there from Santillana del Mar. A cave hermitage carved into the cliff overlooks a wild cove.
The artisan shops on Calle Juan Infante sell ceramics, leather goods and regional produce. Stroll beneath the arcades in the late afternoon.

places.name: Santuario De Belen

visits.text: The Santuario de Nuestra Señora de Belén rises among the holm oaks, 11 km from Cabeza del Buey. Its origins go back to the 13th century: the Templar cloister, austere and massive, sets the tone. The murals at the east end are worth the detour. It's the most visited monument in the whole area.

The walled gardens of the Santuario de Belén form an unexpected haven in this arid sierra. Orange trees, stone benches, silence. The cells of the old convent adjoin the cloister. Free entry, no ticket.

activities.text: From the Santuario de Belén, a trail heads towards the sierra del Pedregoso. Dehesa landscape, holm oaks, chances of spotting vultures. Allow an hour round trip for a first taste.

days_plan.itin_title: La Siberia and La Serena: Secret Extremadura in 6 Days

map_keywords: Santuario de Nuestra Señora de Belén Cabeza del Buey

visits.text: Welcome to Segovia. The city's silhouette is recognizable from afar: some say it resembles a ship. The Alcázar as the bow, the cathedral as the mainmast, the aqueduct as an anchor cast into the sierra. The Roman aqueduct is where you arrive: 167 arches, 28 meters high at its highest point, dry-laid granite—not a drop of mortar along the 800 meters still visible. Built around 50 CE, more likely under Domitian than Trajan. For the best photo, climb the Postigo stairs on the right: you'll find yourself level with the water channel, and it's from there that you grasp the brilliant absurdity of the undertaking.

The Alcázar, perched at the tip of the promontory, did inspire Walt Disney's castle for Snow White—he visited it in 1935. Built from the 11th century on former Roman fortifications, expanded in the 13th by the kings of Castile, ravaged by fire in 1862 and rebuilt immediately afterward in fairy-tale fashion. Inside you'll find the throne room, the chamber of the Catholic Monarchs where Isabella was proclaimed queen in 1474, and—for the truly brave—152 spiral steps up to the Tower of Juan II. The view looks down over the Sierra de Guadarrama and the convents of the Eresma valley.

The cathedral, nicknamed "the Lady of Cathedrals" for its elegance, is the last Gothic cathedral built in Spain—construction began in 1525 under Charles V after the previous one burned during the Comuneros revolt in 1520. Latin cross plan, 18 chapels, spectacular 16th-century Flemish stained glass. In the Concepción chapel, Ignacio de Ries's Tree of Life is a macabre curiosity: a giant crucifix as tree root, the damned falling to hell from the lower branches. Far from joyful.

The Church of Vera Cruz, 10 minutes downhill from the Alcázar (then plan for the climb back), is one of the city's best-kept secrets. Dodecagonal plan—twelve sides—built by the Templars in 1208 and consecrated April 13 of that year by papal decree of Innocent III. At its center, a two-story shrine where knights kept vigil over a relic of the True Cross. It's rare in Europe, and that's what makes it remarkable: Vera Cruz has barely changed since the 13th century. Further on, the Parral monastery is under permanent restoration but accessible.

On Plaza Mayor, facing the cathedral, don't miss Casa de los Picos—“House of Spikes”—a Renaissance façade bristling with 617 diamond-cut granite points, designed by the Marquises of Quintanar in the late 15th century. Calle Juan Bravo brings together Segovia's finest façades: Renaissance sgraffito with geometric motifs, aristocratic palaces, Casa de la Tierra, Torreón de Lozoya. Five minutes on foot between all these sights. Everything in Segovia fits within two kilometers.

activities.text: Roast suckling pig—cochinillo asado—is Segovia's gastronomic institution. The benchmark: Mesón de Cándido, steps from the aqueduct, serving the dish since 1786. Tradition dictates that the maître d' carves the pig with the edge of a plate to prove it's cooked to perfection—tender enough not to need a knife—then breaks the plate on the floor. Expensive (€60–70), but it's an experience. More modest but excellent alternatives: José María (Cronista Lecea) or Mesón de José María.

A sunset walk along Paseo del Salón or higher up, around the sanctuary of the Fuencisla, Segovia's patron saint. The view of the Alcázar ablaze in the low sunlight is the image you'll remember. In winter, the old town's façades are illuminated and the aqueduct becomes even more dramatic. Locals take their evening stroll here: Segovians are so accustomed to their city that they forget about it even as they love it.

places.name: Segura De La Sierra

visits.text: Final stop: Segura de la Sierra, ranked among Spain's Most Beautiful Villages, perched at 1,230 metres altitude in the park's northeast corner. The village of Muslim origin (conquered in 781 under the name Saqura) has preserved its steep alleyways, vaulted passages, and end-of-the-world atmosphere. The castle, built by the Almohads then transformed by the Order of Santiago in the 13th century, dominates the village from its rocky outcrop. Its 18-metre keep offers a 360° panorama over the sierras, pine forests, and olive groves. The Arab baths, discovered beneath the village, are among the best preserved in the province.

Segura is also the birthplace of the poet Jorge Manrique (15th century), author of the Coplas por la muerte de su padre - one of the most famous poems in Spanish literature. His father, Don Rodrigo Manrique, was commander of Segura for the Order of Santiago. The poet's birthplace, in the upper part of the village, is not open to visitors, but its façade can be seen from the street. Wander the lanes looking out for details: carved coats of arms, the imperial fountain of Charles III, the Catena gate and the remains of the old walls.

If you have time before leaving, detour to Hornos de Segura, another spectacular hilltop village 30 minutes' drive away. Its ruined castle dominates the Tranco lake—the view from the village terraces over the lake and mountains is one of the park's most photographed. The Cosmolarium, installed in the castle tower, is a small astronomical observatory and planetarium that takes advantage of the Sierra de Segura's excellent night sky quality.

activities.text: Segura de la Sierra produces a Sierra de Segura PDO olive oil, considered one of Spain's finest. The mountain terroir (700-1,200 m altitude) and the Picual variety produce an intense oil with notes of fresh grass and green tomato. Village cooperatives offer tastings. Leave with a bottle—it's the best souvenir you can bring back from the province of Jaén.

days_plan.itin_title: Madrid to Cazorla: La Mancha, the Sierras of Jaén, and the Forgotten Renaissance

visits.text: The Irati Forest spans 17,000 hectares of beech and fir between the Aezkoa and Salazar valleys. It's the second-largest beech forest in Europe after the Black Forest.
The Casas de Irati Visitor Center provides maps and information. Marked trails depart from this point: Cubo Waterfall, Urbeltza River, Zabaleta Forest.
Follow the Urbeltza River trail as it winds beneath the beeches. Clear water flows over a pebble bed between the roots.
The Irabia Reservoir mirrors the wooded peaks. A trail circles the artificial lake through pristine surroundings.
Ochagavía, about 11 km from the stage point, a 16-minute drive, is one of Navarre's most beautiful villages. Its Pyrenean houses with steep roofs line cobbled streets.
The stone bridge marks the entrance to the village. Admire its arches.

activities.text: Hike the Errekaidorra trail: a 10-kilometer loop through fir and beech forest with clearings offering superb views.
Watch for black woodpeckers, red deer, and roe deer inhabiting the forest. Early morning offers the best chances of spotting wildlife.
Picnic at one of the designated areas along the Irati or Urbeltza rivers. The murmur of water accompanies your meal.
In autumn, the beeches turn from green to red, yellow, and orange. The chromatic spectacle draws photographers and hikers.

days_plan.itin_title: Navarre Road Trip: Castles, Irati Forest & the Camino

places.name: Sequeros

visits.text: Sequeros, once the administrative capital of Sierra de Francia, sits at 870 meters altitude with three-story houses and wrought-iron balconies that tell the story of a prosperous 19th-century local bourgeoisie. Declared a site of historic interest in 2004, the village counts fewer than 250 inhabitants, yet its center remains remarkably preserved. Don't miss Plaza de Eloy Bullón—this is what's left of a former aljama, the medieval Jewish quarter, with lanes so narrow the rooftops nearly touch. The labyrinthine layout reflects centuries of coexistence among Christian, Jewish, and Muslim communities.

The Church of Virgen del Robledo stands as Sequeros's most symbolic monument. Its baroque altarpiece and mudéjar coffered ceiling at the main altar deserve your attention. In its crypt lie the remains of Simón Vela—the French pilgrim Simon Roland who, according to legend, received an apparition of the Virgin in 1434 directing him to a statue hidden for centuries atop Peña de Francia. When he died in 1438, he was buried here in Sequeros, not on the mountain.

Push up to the summit of Peña de Francia at 1,727 meters—count on 20 minutes' drive from Sequeros. The sanctuary of Notre-Dame-du-Rocher-de-France, run by Dominicans since the 15th century, offers 360-degree views spanning the plains of Salamanca, Portugal, and Extremadura. Cervantes mentioned it in Don Quixote, and the Black Virgin is venerated as far away as Latin America and the Philippines. The road is passable from April to November—avoid other months when the summit can remain snowbound.

activities.text: Walk to the Cruz viewpoint to contemplate the Béjar-Candelario range—the village's finest lookout. The Barrero trail leading there edges past the old circular bullring, now converted to public space. Have a glass of mountain wine in one of the bars on Church Square, beneath the granite arcades.

Come evening, explore the Robledo trail departing from the village—a marked 2-3 km path crossing oak forests and reaching the hermitage of Robledo where rest the bones of Juana, 'la Moza Santa,' Sequeros's local prophetess whose legend is intimately bound to the discovery of the Virgin of Peña de Francia.

days_plan.itin_title: Sierra de Francia Medieval Villages Route

map_keywords: Sanctuaire Peña de Francia El Cabaco

visits.text: Salt crunches underfoot along the pink and turquoise basins of Ses Salines Natural Park. Protected since 2001 across 2,838 ha on land and over 13,000 ha at sea, this area harbors flamingos and UNESCO-listed posidonia meadows. Paid parking, arrive before 10 AM in summer.

Packed in August, deserted in May: Platja de Ses Salines unfurls 1,200 m of white sand facing Formentera. Chiringuitos Sa Trinxa and Jockey Club animate the northern stretch, while the southern tip remains wild and naturist. Arrive early or accept the shoulder-to-shoulder towel mosaic.

activities.text: Walk to Torre de Ses Portes, a 16th-century watchtower at the end of the beach. The 20-min trail offers panoramic views across the strait separating Ibiza from Formentera. Perfect photo spot in late afternoon.
If the wind shifts east, leave Ses Salines and head west: southwest-facing beaches stay sheltered. That's the scooter advantage—you can switch coasts in 20 minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: Ibiza & Formentera by Scooter: Calas & Beaches in 7 Days

places.name: Setenil De Las Bodegas

visits.text: Setenil resembles nothing else: houses and bars built under enormous tuff ledges that literally form their roofs. The calle Cuevas del Sol (south side, sunny) and calle Cuevas de la Sombra (north side) are the two streets to see - two rows of façades either side of the same ravine, with rock as a common ceiling.

Setenil's Nasrid castle, at the summit of the cerro, offers the overview of the carved architecture. What you see from above finally makes sense of what you've just walked through below: the ravine, the overhanging ledges, the rock roofs. The climb takes ten minutes from the main street.

A roof of rock above a terrace: Calle Cuevas del Sol captures the essence of Setenil. The houses are built against natural overhangs rather than inside fully excavated caves, a detail that changes how you understand the village. Arrive before the crowds and keep passageways clear, even when taking a photograph.

Calle Cuevas de la Sombra takes the impression of a covered street even further. The rock extends over the walkway, very close to the river, explaining the contrast with its brighter neighbor. Walk over from Cuevas del Sol and leave your car outside this tightly confined area.

activities.text: The popular etymology of Setenil - septem nihil, seven times nothing in Latin - refers to the unsuccessful Christian assaults before the final capitulation to the Catholic Monarchs in 1484. The name's origin is however disputed by some historians. A terrace café on calle Cuevas del Sol to grasp the setup: behind your cup, several tons of rock overhang the tables.
