visits.text: Bright pink in summer, lilac in winter: the lagoon changes with the salt concentration and the light. Its color is produced by halobacteria and the algae Dunaliella salina. At 350 grams of salt per liter, its concentration equals that of the Dead Sea. Flamingos regularly feed here. Swimming is prohibited - but the greenway allows you to follow the lagoon at sunset.

activities.text: The salt flats have produced salt since Roman times at this site—remains of a probable Roman factory were found in underwater excavations. Today Europe's largest salt producer, the complex extracts significant quantities annually, much of it sent to salt Northern European roads in winter. A tourist train departs from Paseo de la Libertad for a guided tour of the salt flats. Available in high season.

days_plan.itin_title: Costa Blanca & Alicante Hinterland: 12 days

visits.text: Tortosa preserves the most visible trace of seven centuries of Muslim rule in Catalonia: the Castell de la Suda, an Arab fortress founded in the 10th century under Caliph Abd al-Rahman III (interior well dated 944), perched 60 meters above the Ebro, converted into a parador in 1972. The interior courtyard combines an Almohad cistern and a repurposed Visigothic chapel. Views looking down over the Ebro's meanders, the cathedral 100 meters below, and, on clear days, the delta 30 km away. The exterior can be visited freely; to enter the courtyard, have a coffee at the parador bar (€5). Clever and legal.

Tortosa's Cathedral of Santa Maria, begun in 1347 on the foundations of the great mosque, is Gothic in the tradition of Catalan cathedrals (Barcelona, Girona)—a wide single nave, a polygonal apse with an ambulatory. Its peculiarity: six centuries of construction, and still no proper west facade. The 15th-century alabaster altarpiece and treasury (manuscripts, goldwork) are worth the €5 admission. A shaded cloister, ideal for taking a breather between 1pm and 4pm when the city melts in the 38°C heat in July.

The Reials Col·legis, Catalonia's most important Renaissance complex, were founded as an institution by Charles V in 1544 to educate the sons of Moors converted to Christianity. Construction of the Col·legi de Sant Jaume i Sant Maties—the main building—began in 1564; its design is now attributed to Francisco de Montehermoso. A Renaissance courtyard unique in Catalonia, a sculpted frieze of royal couples of the Crown of Aragon from Ramon Berenguer IV to Philip III. The evangelization experiment ended with the expulsion of the Moriscos in 1610; the buildings became a seminary and continued to function as a college. Today, a museum and Renaissance Interpretation Center. Admission €3, allow 1 hour.

The Jardins del Príncep, created in 1992, display 26 sculptures by Tortosan Santiago de Santiago (1925–2024)—monumental bronzes on the themes of couples and dance. Original, sometimes surprising, never dull. Plenty of benches, ideal in the evening.

activities.text: Tortosa is home to one of Spain's last events commemorating its history: the Battle of the Ebro (July–November 1938), the longest and deadliest battle of the Civil War—30,000 deaths in 115 days. The Centre d'Interprétació de la Batalla de l'Ebre (COMEBE) offers 4 memorial sites in the region, including 115 Dies in Corbera d'Ebre, reached by car from Tortosa—a ruined village preserved as it was after the 1938 bombing. A moving visit, with a French audio guide for €5. A sensitive subject treated with seriousness. Allow 2 hours for the round trip including the drive.

For lunch, suquet d'anguila—delta eel stew—is the Tortosan specialty. Restaurants Mas de Pau and La Galera serve a traditional version for €18, accompanied by aioli and potatoes. Baix Ebre olive oil (PDO Terra Alta) is used everywhere—fruity, peppery, among Spain's finest. Also try coques de recapte, thin savory tarts with peppers and anchovies. Weekend reservations recommended.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Catalonia in 10 Days: Tarragona, Priorat & the Ebro Delta
Catalonia - Complete 24-Day Grand Tour

places.name: Tossa De Mar

visits.text: The Vila Vella of Tossa de Mar is the only intact medieval fortified town on the entire Catalan coast, listed as a historic monument in 1931. Its walls were built from 1186 to defend against Barbary pirates - Ramon de Berga, the abbot who governed the town, ordered their construction after centuries of raids. The perimeter includes three cylindrical towers and four keeps, including the Clock Tower (which housed the town's only public clock) and the Tower of Homage overlooking Codolar beach. Climb up to the lighthouse - built in 1917 on the site of the old castle - for the best coastal view.

Platja Gran stretches for 400 meters below the medieval walls. Its waters are clear and sheltered. For more tranquility, walk 15 minutes to Cala Codolar, a small rocky cove tucked beneath the walls of Vila Vella and ideal for snorkeling.

The Tossa Municipal Museum, founded in 1935 in the former governor's residence, is Spain's first contemporary art museum. It holds a painting by Marc Chagall - who stayed in Tossa and dubbed it “blue paradise” - and Roman mosaics from the 1st-century BC villa dels Ametllers found on the hillside.

activities.text: Sea kayaking along the cliffs and coves between Tossa and Sant Feliu de Guíxols: the coast is carved with caves and small beaches accessible only by water. Local operators offer 2 to 4-hour guided outings. Allow 2 hours to paddle to Cala Giverola.

Snorkeling at Es Codolar cove or Cala Pola: the transparent waters of the Costa Brava allow you to see the bottom several meters deep. Posidonia (seagrass meadows) and sea urchins are the most common species. Bring your mask if you have one.

Have dinner on the seafront with suquet de peix, a local fish stew simmered with potatoes and saffron - the house speciality in almost every waterfront restaurant. White wine from the region (Alella or Empordà) is an ideal accompaniment to seafood.

days_plan.itin_title: Barcelona and Costa Brava Road Trip: Coves and Villages

map_keywords: Platja Gran Beach Tossa de Mar

visits.text: Take the road east through the Alpujarras, passing through Pitres and Pórtugos. At Pórtugos, stop at the Fuente Agria - a spring rich in iron that stains the waterfall and surrounding rocks rust-orange. Locals attribute healing properties to it. It's a lovely 20-minute stop in a surprisingly verdant setting for Andalusia.

Trevélez is a mountain village at an altitude of 1,476 meters, on the slopes of Mulhacén. The village is divided into three districts (barrios) - bajo, medio and alto - linked by steep lanes. Barrio Bajo attracts the most visitors; Alto feels the most authentic. The smell of ham is everywhere: Trevélez is famous throughout Spain for its jamón serrano, naturally cured for 14 to 24 months in drying rooms above 1,200 meters, without preservatives. The “Jamón de Trevélez” PGI traces its history to 1862, when Queen Isabella II granted the village the right to stamp its hams with the royal seal after they had won a national competition.

Continue towards Válor, about 36 km from Trevélez and a 45-minute drive away. This quiet village has a dramatic history: Fernando de Córdoba y Válor was born here. He took the Arabic name Abén Humeya, claiming descent from the Umayyad caliphs of Córdoba. On Christmas night in 1568, he led the last great Morisco revolt against Philip II. Within weeks, 25,000 armed men joined him and the uprising spread across the region. Don John of Austria intervened with 20,000 soldiers to crush the revolt in 1571. More than 80,000 Moriscos were then deported across the peninsula. Every September, Válor reenacts this episode during its Moors and Christians festival.

activities.text: Visit a ham-drying facility in Trevélez - several producers open their doors to visitors. You'll see hundreds of legs suspended from the ceiling, smell the dry Sierra Nevada air doing the curing work, and taste slices cut right in front of you. The secret of this ham is the altitude: the cold, dry air of the Sierra Nevada, combined with the Mediterranean breeze, creates natural curing conditions that no cold storage facility can replicate.

If you're a hiker, Trevélez is the starting point for climbing Mulhacén (3,479 m), the highest peak of the Iberian Peninsula. The round trip via the Siete Lagunas trail takes 8 to 10 hours and requires good physical condition. For a gentler option, the trail along the río Trevélez through the chestnut groves is family-friendly.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret Granada: Alpujarras, Guadix and the Sierras
Al-Andalus: From the Mezquita to the Alpujarras in 10 days

visits.text: The equestrian statue of Francisco Pizarro (1929) dominates Plaza Mayor. Charles Rumsey's bronze depicts the conqueror of Peru, born in Trujillo in 1478.
The Castillo de Trujillo (9th century) crowns the hilltop. This Moorish fortress offers panoramic views across the plains for up to 30 kilometers in every direction.
The Iglesia de Santa María la Mayor blends Romanesque, Gothic, and Renaissance styles. Fernando Gallego's plateresque altarpiece is remarkable.
The Palacio del Marqués de la Conquista belonged to Hernando Pizarro. Its carved corner balcony displays busts of the Pizarro family and their Inca wives.
Step inside the Casa-Museo de Pizarro. This 15th-century house tells the conquistador's story through period documents and artifacts.
The Iglesia de San Martín (14th-16th century) combines Gothic and Renaissance. Two towers flank a single nave with an octagonal presbytery.
The Palacio de Orellana-Pizarro features a Renaissance portal and a Plateresque courtyard. It belonged to Francisco de Orellana, the first European to travel down the Amazon.

activities.text: Climb to the castle for sunset. Golden light sets the tile roofs ablaze and the Renaissance palaces of Plaza Mayor glow below.
The local market sells Ibores cheese (goat cheese aged with pimentón), Iberian cured meats, and honey from the nearby sierras.
Take a seat on a terrace on Plaza Mayor in the evening. Migas extremeñas, moraga, and ibérico tapas accompany the local wine.
In late April and early May, the Plaza Mayor becomes a huge market. More than 100,000 visitors sample cheeses from Spain.

days_plan.itin_title: Extremadura Road Trip: Cáceres, Mérida & Trujillo

visits.text: If Baeza is the ecclesiastical and university town, Úbeda is the noble and palatial one—the other half of the UNESCO inscription. It all begins at Plaza Vázquez de Molina, considered one of Spain's most beautiful Renaissance squares. Francisco de los Cobos y Molina, Secretary of State to Charles V, and his nephew Juan Vázquez de Molina, who succeeded him under Philip II, had an ensemble of palaces and chapels built here that rival anything in Tuscany. The architect Andrés de Vandelvira, a native of the region, designed most of the buildings—his influence would later be found in Latin American cathedrals.

The Sacra Capilla del Salvador, commissioned by Francisco de los Cobos as a private funerary chapel, is Vandelvira's masterpiece in Úbeda. Completed in 1559, its Plateresque façade displays extravagant sculptural richness—mythological scenes, grotesques, atlantes, the entire vocabulary of the Italian Renaissance translated into Andalusian stone. Inside, Vandelvira's sacristy is a jewel of proportion, with its caryatids and atlantes framing the windows. Berruguete's monumental altarpiece was partially destroyed during the Civil War, but what remains is impressive.

Opposite the chapel, the Palacio del Deán Ortega (16th century), now a Parador hotel, deserves a visit even if you're not staying there—go in to see the two-level arcaded Renaissance courtyard and the gallery with views over the olive groves. At the other end of the square, the Palacio de las Cadenas (Palace of the Chains), former palace of Juan Vázquez de Molina, now serves as the town hall. Its façade is a model of Spanish purist Renaissance.

Head down into the old quarter to discover the Sinagoga del Agua, found by chance during renovation work in 2007. This underground site includes a prayer hall, a ritual bath (mikveh), a women's gallery and a well. The guided tour is fascinating and sheds light on the life of Úbeda's Jewish community before the expulsion of 1492.

activities.text: The barrio alfarero (potters' quarter) of San Millán, in the lower part of town, keeps alive a ceramic tradition dating back to Moorish times. The workshops produce emerald-green pieces on a white background - the typical Úbeda style. Push open a workshop door to watch the craftsmen at work, and leave with a dish or a jar as a souvenir. Here, traditional pottery is still a living trade, not a tourist attraction.

days_plan.itin_title: Madrid to Cazorla: La Mancha, the Sierras of Jaén, and the Forgotten Renaissance
Jaén Province Tour: Renaissance and Olive Trees
Al-Andalus: From the Mezquita to the Alpujarras in 10 days

visits.text: The sanctuary-fortress of Santa María de Ujué dominates the village from the hilltop at 815 meters elevation. Built between the 11th and 14th centuries, it blends Romanesque and Gothic styles.
Two crenellated towers and the rampart walk encircle the church. This medieval fortification was one of the principal strongholds of the kings of Navarre from the 10th century onward.

Inside, the sculpture of the Virgin of Ujué from 1190 stands as one of the finest examples of Romanesque carving in Navarre. King Charles II the Bad had his heart deposited in a niche near this statue.
Walk the Gothic rampart path with its covered galleries. The 14th-century wooden balustrade offers views across the Ribera plain and the Pyrenees.
The medieval village ranks among Spain's most beautiful. Its 300 inhabitants live in stone houses with vaulted passageways along steep climbing lanes.

activities.text: Follow a circular trail from the village to observe the landscapes of middle Navarre, where vineyards meet grain fields.
Sample the migas de pastor, a traditional dish of bread, tomatoes, garlic, ham, and mushrooms. On the third Sunday of September, the entire village celebrates Migas Day.
Ascend to the Ujué viewpoint at twilight. The sky ignites above the Bardenas Reales desert visible to the south.
After dark, the absence of light pollution transforms Ujué into a natural observatory. Gaze upward at the Milky Way.

days_plan.itin_title: Navarre Road Trip: Castles, Irati Forest & the Camino

visits.text: To finish in style: the Bodega Redonda of Utiel, dating from 1891, today houses the Museo del Vino de la DOP Utiel-Requena, C/ Sevilla 12. It's a former cooperative cellar with dome, converted into a museum on the history of the vine in the region since Iberian Antiquity. Free entry. Buy a few bottles of Bobal on the way out—you'll hardly find it outside Spain.

activities.text: If time permits, descend into Utiel's underground bodegas—the town has hundreds of medieval cellars under its streets, the most important underground wine heritage in the Valencian Community according to the local tourist office. Several are accessible via the Ruta del Vino Utiel-Requena (rutavino.com). Ideal to close this circuit between windmills, sierra, and vines.

days_plan.itin_title: Castilla-La Mancha: Windmills and Sierra in 11 days

visits.text: Locals named it Ciudad Encantada—the Enchanted City—because the limestone formations resemble animals, ships, faces. Declared a Natural Site of National Interest in 1929, it has been taking shape for 90 million years: back then, this plateau at over 1,400 metres altitude lay at the bottom of the Tethys Sea. The circuit runs about 3 km, well marked and easy; allow 1h30. Buy your ticket at the taquilla on site—no online sales.

Declared a Natural Site of National Interest in 1929, the Ciudad Encantada contains named formations: El Tormo (a mushroom rock), Los Barcos (three giant ships), and La Tortuga. Look for the formation La Lucha del Elefante y el Cocodrilo. Choose the guided tour if you come at the weekend—the explanatory workshops are worth the extra hour.

activities.text: Take the 3-km circular trail on your own—turquoise markers outbound, pink for the return. Altitude: 1,450 m, so even in June it can be cool. Bring a layer, water, and a snack. Entry is paid; check seasonal hours before you leave, as the Ciudad Encantada sometimes closes early off-season.

days_plan.itin_title: Castilla-La Mancha: Windmills and Sierra in 11 days

visits.text: The Museo del Vino de Valdepeñas occupies the former Leocadio Morales winery dating from 1901: a Manchego courtyard with a well, a hall of giant tinajas, and an underground cellar. The visitor route explains the history of the Valdepeñas DO. The professional tasting room is open to visitors.

Valdepeñas means “valley of stones” and takes its name from the Sierra Morena foothills that begin here. Plaza de España, the town center, is lively and lined with tapas bars. The Museo Gregorio Prieto, dedicated to the local painter who was a friend of Lorca and the Generation of '27, rounds out the cultural visit.

Visit a traditional bodega to see the clay tinajas: some hold over 1,000 liters of wine. The Valdepeñas DO is one of Spain's oldest. Vineyards around town are dominated by tempranillo, locally known as cencibel.

activities.text: From Valdepeñas, head to the Cerro de las Cabezas, an Iberian oppidum excavated since the 1990s. The streets and dry-stone walls are clearly visible. Free guided tours on weekends.

days_plan.itin_title: Campo de Calatrava and Valle de Alcudia in 5 Days

visits.text: Drive east to enter Lower Aragón. First stop at Alcañiz (1h40 from Daroca), the second city of Teruel province. Climb to the Calatrava castle, a fortress of the military Order of Calatrava that has dominated the town since the 12th century - it now houses a Parador. The Gothic Lonja (market hall) from the 15th century, one of Aragón's finest, stands out with its three pointed arches opening onto the Plaza de España. The collegiate church of Santa María la Mayor and the medieval underground passages beneath the square complete the visit.

Continue 30 minutes east to reach Valderrobres, capital of the Matarraña comarca, nicknamed “Aragonese Tuscany.” The arrival is spectacular: the medieval stone bridge spans the Río Matarraña and leads straight to the San Roque gate, one of seven gates in the old wall. At the village summit, the archbishop's castle-palace (14th-15th centuries) connects to the church of Santa María la Mayor, one of Aragón's finest examples of Levantine Gothic. Its sculpted facade and rose window are remarkably delicate.

If time allows, carry on to Calaceite, the other gem of the Matarraña, about twenty minutes' drive north of Valderrobres. Listed as a Historic Site, this stone village with steep lanes and wrought-iron seigneurial houses has kept its Mediterranean character intact. The Plaza de España, the Renaissance town hall (1609) and the church of la Asunción form a harmonious ensemble. The Catalan influence - the border is only a few kilometers away - can be felt in the architecture and the cuisine.

activities.text: In the evening, have dinner in Valderrobres. The cuisine of the Matarraña is Mediterranean country cooking: PDO Bajo Aragón olive oil, roast lamb, black truffle in season, goat's cheeses and Calanda peaches. Pair your meal with a wine from the DO Bajo Aragón - powerful reds made from Garnacha.

days_plan.itin_title: Aragonese Pyrenees and Lower Aragón: From Ordesa to Teruel

places.name: Valencia

visits.text: The City of Arts and Sciences impresses by its sheer scale—the complex designed by Calatrava and Bofill stretches two kilometers along the old Turia riverbed. The Hemisfèric and Museu de les Ciències merit the entrance fee; the Oceanogràfic, Europe's largest aquarium according to its official site, deserves an entire half-day.

The Lonja de la Seda dates from 1482 and was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996. This Gothic trading hall—built when Valencia was one of the Mediterranean's busiest commercial centers—gives a tangible idea of the city's mercantile power at that time. Quick visit, under 45 minutes.

Valencia's central market is perhaps Spain's most beautiful covered market—an Art Deco nave of iron and ceramic inaugurated in 1928 that still houses over 900 stalls today. Come between 9am and 11am to see it in action. After 1pm, half the stalls close.

The railway station's architecture astonishes: closer to a Belle Époque palace than a utilitarian station, the Estació del Nord was inaugurated in 1917 with Valencian ceramic frescoes on every wall. It still functions—travelers await their trains surrounded by orange-tree mosaics.

activities.text: Explore the Barrio del Carmen in the evening, when galleries and tapas bars open their doors. This medieval quarter between the city's two old walls concentrates street art, vermouth taverns, and lively terraces. No reservation needed before 9pm; after that, it's packed.

The blue smoke and scent of toasted rice escaping from the large paëlleras signal the good addresses. The true paella valenciana contains no seafood—beans, chicken, rabbit, rosemary. Avoid restaurants that offer it all hours: a proper paella is prepared to order and takes 30 minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Valencia Road Trip: 10 Days of Villages
Northern Valencia Road Trip: 10 Days of Villages

map_keywords: City of Arts and Sciences Valencia

visits.text: On the surface, Vall d'Uixó has nothing remarkable. Beneath its feet, that's another story: the San José caves shelter the longest navigable underground river in Europe, according to official site data. The main gallery extends over 700 meters explored by boat.

activities.text: The boat glides under calcite vaults where stalactites brush within centimeters of your face. The underground river remains at a constant 18°C year-round—bring a light jacket even in August. Book online in high season, morning slots fill quickly.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Valencia Road Trip: 10 Days of Villages

places.name: Vall De Boi

visits.text: Before anything else, call in at the Centre del Romànic in Erill la Vall to make sense of what you are about to see. A small museum – 30 minutes is enough – that sets the valley's nine churches in context: Lombard masters who came from northern Italy in the 12th century, the true fresco technique, the Erill school of sculpture, and the rediscovery by Puig i Cadafalch in 1907 during an expedition by the Institute of Catalan Studies. The combined ticket gives access to several churches in the valley – economical if you plan to see three or four.

The high point of the trip: Sant Climent de Taüll. Consecrated on 10 December 1123 by the bishop of Roda, it is the best-preserved Romanesque building in the valley. A basilican plan with a nave and two aisles, three apses and above all that square six-storey bell tower, with the blind arcading and saw-tooth friezes typical of Lombard work. Inside, the original apse was decorated with a masterly fresco of Christ Pantocrator, removed using the strappo technique in 1919 and now kept at the MNAC in Barcelona. On site, a projection-mapping display recreates the original frescoes on the walls: technically spectacular, and more moving than you would expect.

200 metres away in the upper part of the village, Santa Maria de Taüll – consecrated the day after Sant Climent, on 11 December 1123, by the same bishop. More modest, more rustic, but the atmosphere is unique: surrounded by its cemetery, encircled by medieval houses. The nave holds a reproduction of the original apsidal paintings, including the characteristic Lombard orant. Its character differs from Sant Climent's: Santa Maria has remained the village's living centre, still used for worship.

Sant Joan de Boí, in the village of Boí 3 km away, preserves more of the architecture from the valley's first building phase than the others – the 11th century. A nave and two aisles, three apses, medieval paving. The original paintings – known as the “Bestiary paintings” – are at the MNAC, but the church has a raw, almost prehistoric presence you will not find elsewhere. For lovers of Romanesque architecture, it is the most archaic of the nine.

Santa Eulàlia d'Erill la Vall, right next to the Centre del Romànic, possesses one of the most elegant bell towers in the whole valley – six storeys, square plan, like Sant Climent and Sant Joan. This is where the Erill workshop worked, the school of sculpture that carved the famous Descent from the Cross whose originals are at the MNAC and the Episcopal Museum of Vic. On site, a polychrome wooden copy reconstructs the group: Christ, Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea, the Virgin, Saint John, two thieves. Moving.

To enter the western zone of Aigüestortes National Park, leave your car at the Palanca de la Molina car park (free) and take the “Otter Path” – a 1-hour walk to the Planell d'Aigüestortes through the Sant Nicolau valley. The river winds in gentle meanders between meadows and forests of century-old black pines. On the route, stop at the hermitage of Sant Nicolau, a modest Lombard Romanesque building with a single nave. If you prefer to save your legs, official taxis run from Boí to the plain – the only authorised transport.

Sant Feliu de Barruera, in the valley's administrative centre, is one of the nine UNESCO-listed churches. Dating from the 11th–12th centuries, it has kept its rural appearance almost intact. It's the most modest of the valley's great Romanesque churches – small, low, with a single nave – but it's also the most representative of ordinary rural architecture of the period. It housed medieval frescoes now removed and preserved at the diocesan museum of Lleida.

The Ermita de Sant Quirc de Durro, standing on its own on a ridge above the village, is the ninth and last of the valley's UNESCO listings. Smaller than the others, barely more than a chapel, it has a charm all its own: isolated, wind-battered, reached by a 20-minute path from Durro. Panoramic view over the whole valley basin and the Maladeta massif in the distance. The patronal feast on 16 June still brings the villagers out for open-air mass.

activities.text: If you arrive early and still have time in the late afternoon, go up to Durro (1,386 m). The church of La Nativitat has a bell tower, and the village centre has retained a rugged medieval atmosphere. Away from the main road, few tourists make their way up here. Allow 30 minutes for the visit; above all, there is the view over the entire valley basin.

In the evening, dinner at the Caldes de Boí baths or at an inn in Barruera, the valley's administrative centre. The classics of Catalan Pyrenean cooking: olla aranesa (a stew), trinxat (potato and cabbage mashed together with bacon pieces), duck confit with hazelnuts, homemade tarts. The Caldes baths sit at an altitude of 1,500 m – 37 springs, temperatures from 4 to 56°C, in use since Roman times. Therapeutic bathing is possible during the day.

Hiking in Aigüestortes: from the Planell, several options depending on your fitness. The accessible trail (wooden boardwalks) loops around the plain in 1 hour without difficulty, ideal for families. More demanding options: climb to Estany Llong (3-hour round trip, 200 m elevation gain) or to Portarró pass to cross to the other side of the park. The park has more than 200 glacial lakes – the highest concentration in the entire Pyrenean range. Highest peak: Pic de Comaloforno, 3,030 m.

A thermal alternative: spend the afternoon at the Termes de Caldes de Boí. A good antidote to sore muscles after hiking. At an altitude of 1,500 m, the water emerges at 56 °C from the hottest springs. The Romans already came here.

map_keywords: Centre del Romànic Vall de Boí

visits.text: Valladolid, the final stop. 300,000 inhabitants, capital of Castile and León, but a city often underestimated. Yet it was Spain's capital under Philip II and Philip III (1601–1606), the place where Cervantes published the first edition of Don Quixote in 1605, the city where Christopher Columbus died in 1506, and the site of the Catholic Monarchs' marriage in 1469. Plaza Mayor (1561), rebuilt after the fire of that same year, is one of Spain's oldest enclosed main squares and served as a model for Madrid and Salamanca. Red façades, white arcades, a lively square.

The National Museum of Sculpture, in the Colegio de San Gregorio, is probably the finest museum in Castile and León—and one of northern Spain's least known. The college's Isabelline Gothic façade (1488–1496), carved like stone lace, is a work of art in itself. The collection: the world's most complete collection of Spanish polychrome sculpture from the 15th to the 18th century. Berruguete, Juan de Juni, Gregorio Fernández—the three giants of Castilian Spanish baroque. The raw realism of Christ on the cross, hyperrealistic expressions, preserved polychrome decoration. Allow 2 hours.

The Cervantes House Museum, on Calle Rastro. The house where the writer lived from 1604 to 1606 with his family—his wife, sisters, and daughter born outside marriage. Here he corrected the proofs of the first edition of Don Quixote, published in January 1605. A small two-story house typical of 17th-century Valladolid, refurnished in period style by the Hispanic Society of America (Archer Huntington, American patron). Free on Sundays, modest but evocative. Steps from Plaza Mayor.

The Church of San Pablo, on Plaza San Pablo, has a Plateresque façade resembling an altarpiece, dating from 1486–1492 and considered one of Spain's most extraordinary—four levels of sculpture, biblical scenes, coats of arms. The work of Simón de Colonia. Philip II was baptized here in 1527 (his father Charles V was in Valladolid). Right beside it, the Royal Palace (16th century), where the court temporarily settled between 1601 and 1606. Inside the church, an altarpiece by Pedro de Mena.

activities.text: Valladolid Cathedral tells a story of incompletion. Designed in the 1580s by Juan de Herrera—the architect of El Escorial—to be Spain's largest cathedral. But the court moved to Madrid in 1606, and construction was never completed. Today, a quarter of the original design is visible: an austere Renaissance façade, a neoclassical interior, a single tower (its twin collapsed in 1841). The adjoining diocesan museum displays pieces from the 13th–18th centuries. More a historical curiosity than an aesthetic one, but worth a visit to discover it is less finished than expected.

A walk in Campo Grande park—115,000 m², Valladolid's Central Park. Free-roaming peacocks strolling along the paths (since 1877), the Swan Fountain, formal French gardens, a bandstand. Ideal for a final stroll before leaving the city. Beside it, Plaza Zorrilla and the monument to José Zorrilla—author of Don Juan Tenorio (1844), a play whose performance has become an annual All Saints' Day tradition throughout Spain. Born in Valladolid in 1817.

days_plan.itin_title: Duero Castile: From Valladolid to Cuenca via Ribera and Alcarria
Castile and León and Galicia: 21 days from Roman aqueducts to the Atlantic
Castile and León - 14-Day Grand Tour
Ribera del Duero in 7 days: The Plateau That Rivals Rioja

visits.text: Valldemossa Charterhouse was built in 1309 as a royal residence for the asthmatic son of Jaume II. Converted to a monastery in 1399, it hosted Chopin and George Sand during the winter of 1838–1839.
You can visit Chopin and Sand's cells and see the authentic Pleyel piano. The walls preserve memories of the winter that inspired the Preludes and “A Winter in Majorca”.
The monastic pharmacy dates to 1722. Considered one of Europe's best-preserved, it displays jars, alembics, and medicinal plants cultivated by the monks.
The church's turquoise-green bell tower is visible from afar. Its azulejo tiles depict Saint Catalina Tomàs, Majorca's patron saint, born in Valldemossa in 1531.
Cobbled lanes climb between stone houses with potted geraniums. Every facade displays a different azulejo illustrating the life of the beatified woman.
The Charterhouse gardens cascade in terraces. Orange, lemon, and almond trees offer panoramic views over the verdant valley.

activities.text: Serra de Tramuntana trails wind between century-old olive trees. The hike toward Deià crosses karst landscapes and dry-stone terraces.
Several olive oil estates offer tastings and tours. Majorcan olive oil has held protected designation status since 2002.
Coca de patata is dipped in thick chocolate. This local potato-based pastry can be enjoyed in cafés on Cartuja Square.
The Chopin Festival is held every summer. Piano concerts ring out in the Charterhouse in August.

days_plan.itin_title: Majorca Road Trip: Serra de Tramuntana and Coves

places.name: Vejer De La Frontera

visits.text: Vejer de la Frontera, designated a Historic-Artistic Site in 1976, reveals itself as you climb its cobbled lanes to the castle dating from the 10th–11th centuries. Pass through its only gate, a horseshoe arch: two patios and ramparts offer views down into the Barbate valley and out to the distant sea.

Medieval ramparts snake 2 kilometers around the old town. Four gates survive: Arco de la Segur, Arco de Sancho IV, Arco de la Villa, and Puerta Cerrada. The latter, facing the Jewish quarter, was walled up for centuries to protect the town from North African pirates.

Plaza de España, the heart of the village, is dominated by a fountain adorned with multicolored Sevillian tiles. The church of Divino Salvador, erected in the 16th century on the site of the former mosque, has retained the original minaret, converted into a bell tower.

Head to Mirador de la Cobijada to discover the statue of this enigmatic figure: a woman wrapped in a black cloak revealing only one eye. This clothing tradition of Castilian origin, dating to the 16th century, has become Vejer's symbol. The view extends to Barbate's beaches and, on clear days, to Africa.

Vejer's seven windmills, built in the 1960s, stand on the windy ridge above the village. They've become the town's iconic image, offering panoramic views of the coast, El Palmar beach, and the hills of La Janda.

Lose yourself in the old Jewish quarter, the judería, where vaulted passages and whitewashed houses crowd so closely together that they touch. The 18th-century Casa del Mayorazgo boasts a patio overflowing with 450 flowerpots.

Approaching through the narrow streets gives the Castillo de Vejer de la Frontera more context. Its elevated position explains the layout of the fortified town, and its gateway still reflects its Islamic heritage. Leave your car outside the walls and walk uphill through the narrow streets to the horseshoe-arched gateway.

A passage bears the name of its former neighbors: the Arco de las Monjas stands beside Vejer’s convent. The arch frames a view of the white houses, without requiring a lengthy visit. Find the viewpoint from the street and keep the passage clear when other walkers arrive.

The fountain’s colors enliven the white surroundings of Vejer’s Plaza de España. This square brings together facades and outdoor seating at the lower end of the old town, offering a change of atmosphere after the narrow streets around the castle. Settle into the shade for a short break before continuing toward Bolonia.

activities.text: The Barbate and Zahara de los Atunes region keeps alive the practice of bluefin tuna fishing using almadraba, a millennia-old technique inherited from the Phoenicians. From May to June, Vejer restaurants serve tuna in every form: encebollado, tartare, tataki, and grilled belly.

Head down to El Palmar beach, which belongs to the municipality of Vejer, approximately 13 km from Vejer de la Frontera, a 20-minute drive. This strip of wild sand battered by Atlantic waves attracts surfers and lovers of spectacular sunsets.
Sample local cuisine in a restaurant in the town center: Vejer-style chicken pie, couscous with tuna and pumpkin, or retinta, beef from local cattle raised free-range in the surrounding countryside.

visits.text: Market documented since the 9th century. Tuesday and Saturday morning, Vic's Plaça Major—78 × 47 m, vast medieval esplanade bordered by arcades on three sides—transforms into a living producers' market, not a tourist market. Residents and market gardeners truly meet. Neo-Gothic, baroque, modernist façades: three centuries of architecture blended seamlessly. The center, in packed earth, is unique in Catalonia. Time your visit for a Tuesday or Saturday, it changes everything.

Sert painted Vic cathedral twice. First version done between 1926 and 1930, deliberately burned in July 1936 at the start of the Civil War. Second version redone between 1940 and 1945—2,000 m² of murals in black, gold and red, overwhelming, theatrical, expressionist. The artist's last major work, completed just before his death. Sant Pere cathedral blends four eras: Romanesque crypt and bell tower (11th century, under Bishop Oliba), Gothic cloister, 18th-century neoclassical nave. Never renovated to look pretty. Touristy, but genuine.

Twenty thousand pieces. That's what the Episcopal Museum of Vic houses, one of the most important collections of Romanesque and Gothic art in Europe. The 'Davallament d'Erill la Vall' (12th century), polychrome wood carved group depicting the Descent from the Cross, is perhaps the best-preserved Romanesque wood ensemble in the world. Magnificent modern building attached to the cathedral, impeccable chronological route. If you only do one museum in Catalonia to understand Romanesque art, this is it.

Unexpected historical curiosity: the Roman Temple (2nd century) was rediscovered in 1882, hidden inside a medieval castle. The lords of Montcada had simply transformed the temple into a keep in the Romanesque era, without demolishing. It's one of the rare Roman temples preserved in Catalonia. Small, sober, moving.

activities.text: Perfect souvenir: 'llonganissa de Vic', dry sausage with protected designation of origin, first written mentions dating to 1456. Several historic butchers sell it: Casa Riera Ordeix (since 1852), Salgot, Jaume Tió. The sausage travels well. At El Petricó, a local institution, they serve it with pa amb tomàquet (bread rubbed with tomato), as it should be.

If you're here in September, Mercat de Música Viva is an international festival that transforms the city into a giant stage: concerts in monuments, theaters, bars, squares. Four days, festival atmosphere, book accommodation well in advance. If you're here in December, the Mercat Medieval recreates a life-size medieval market with craftsmen, jugglers, troubadours. A fine way to end the journey.

days_plan.itin_title: Catalonia - Complete 24-Day Grand Tour

places.name: Vielha

visits.text: Welcome to the Val d'Aran, the one valley in Catalonia that faces the Atlantic – the Garonne rises here, at the Pla de Beret. Vielha (974 m), the capital, has 6,000 inhabitants, 40% of the valley's population. People speak Aranese here, a variety of Gascon Occitan and an official language alongside Catalan and Spanish. The old centre, with its stone houses and steep slate roofs, feels far more French Pyrenean than Catalan. A walk along the Nere, the tributary that cuts through town, is a must.

On the main square stands the church of Sant Miquèu, the jewel of Aranese Romanesque, built in the 13th and 14th centuries as the style shifted towards Gothic. Carved facade with angels and biblical scenes, tympanum with Saint Michael slaying the devil. The octagonal bell tower of 1506 was added on the orders of Ferdinand the Catholic to serve as a defence against French raids. But the piece that changes everything is inside: the Christ of Mijaran, a 12th-century polychrome sculpture of which only the bust survives, attributed to the Erill la Vall workshop, the very one that carved the Descents from the Cross in the Vall de Boí.

The Musèu dera Val d'Aran occupies the Tor deth Generau Martinhon, a late Gothic house of the 17th century. Three floors given over to the valley's history, ethnography and language, an unusual case in Europe for a territory of 10,000 inhabitants. Rooms on transhumance, on the centuries of isolation before the 1948 tunnel, on the civil war (Aran was the last territory Franco reconquered), and on winter smuggling over the Toro pass. The original Christ of Salardú is not here but in Salardú itself, which we will visit tomorrow.

In the south-west of the valley, 17 km from Vielha, Bossòst is home to Era Mair de Diu dera Purificacion, one of the finest Romanesque churches in the Val d'Aran, 12th century. A basilican plan with a nave and two aisles, barrel vaults, and a fragment of wall painting of the Epiphany in the central apse, dated to the late 13th century. Bossòst is also the last village before the French border, which explains an atmosphere slightly unlike the rest of the valley: busier, and more commercial too (petrol and alcohol cheaper than in France).

Take the C-28 towards Baqueira as far as Arties, 7 km from Vielha. The church of Santa Maria d'Arties, a listed national monument, is one of the five main stops on the Aranese Romanesque Route. Built in the 12th and 13th centuries, halfway between Romanesque and Gothic. Inside, the Gothic altarpiece attributed to the Master of Arties shows scenes from the life of the Virgin, and above all there is a wall painting of the Last Judgement: heaven and hell side by side, with a devil devouring a miser who is still spitting out his gold coins. Nobody in a 13th-century congregation was left in any doubt.

Salardú, 5 km further up (1,267 m), is home to Sant Andreu, a fine example of late Romanesque architecture (end of the 13th century), with Gothic vaults and 17th-century wall paintings. The centrepiece is the Crist de Salardú, a 12th-century polychrome wooden sculpture that also came out of the Erill la Vall workshop, a stylistic sibling of the Christ of Mijaran in Vielha and the works of the Vall de Boí. It is one of the rare cases where the original Christ has stayed in situ, in the very place it was carved for. Moving for that reason.

Another 4 km up an even steeper route: Bagergue (1,419 m), the highest inhabited village in the Val d'Aran, ranked among Spain's most beautiful villages. Around a hundred inhabitants, stairways, lanes full of flowers from April to October, cats everywhere. The church of Sant Feliu (12th–13th centuries), at the village entrance, has the unusual feature of an altar resting on a Roman funerary stele – itself carved in low relief and turned over to serve as a base. An almost unique case of visible reuse.

activities.text: The Fabrica dera Lan, a wool mill that ran from the 19th century until 1960, has been turned into a working museum. You follow the whole process: from the shorn sheep to the dyed skeins, by way of carding, spinning and weaving. Water from the Nere once drove the machinery. The old wooden carding frames are still in place, and the demonstrations in season are well done. Oddly, very few people come, even though there is nothing else like it in the valley.

Aranese dinner at the Taberna Urtau, right in the centre. Tapas and traditional dishes: olha aranesa (the stew that defines the valley's cooking – beef, hen, bacon, vegetables, simmered for three hours), game pâtés, mountain-stream trout cooked on a griddle, local cheeses including Tarter de Bagergue, made at 1,419 m. For dessert, ask for a crepa aranesa (a kind of thick pancake with honey) or prunes in armagnac. Family atmosphere, fair prices for the quality.

Saut deth Pish, in the Varradòs valley, is the best-known waterfall in the Val d'Aran: a 20 m drop, reached via a car park followed by a 5-minute walk. Spectacular in spring with the snowmelt, a little thin in August. You can combine it with the Uelhs deth Joeu (“devil's eyes” in Aranese) at Es Bòrdes: springs where the underground Joeu river resurfaces deep in the forest, with an easy trail running past a succession of waterfalls. Photography enthusiasts will spend hours there.

To end the trip in style: the Banhs de Tredòs, thermal baths at an altitude of 1,720 m, the highest in Europe. Sulphurous water at 39°C, open-air pools in natural surroundings, views of the snow-covered peaks. 8 km from Salardú, with a forest track for the last few kilometres. Around 25 euros a session. Picture it: the back of your neck in hot water, white summits all around, not a sound. It is exactly what you hope for at the end of a week in the Pyrenees.

visits.text: Vigo, Galicia's largest city (300,000 inhabitants), isn't the most beautiful at first glance—industrial port, tower blocks, traffic. But the Casco Vello (old quarter) sloping down to the port, with its cobbled lanes and oyster bars, retains a rough charm. The rúa Pescadería, known as “calle de las Ostras”, is where women (“ostreiras”) have sold oysters directly from the fish auction since 1860—€12 a dozen, opened in front of you, no fuss. Allow 1 hour for the quarter and tasting.

The Castelo do Castro, on the hill of the same name at 147 m, dominates the entire bay of Vigo. 17th-century fortress built on the remains of a Celtic castro (Iron Age fortified village). Ramparts, moats, ruins of Civil War bunkers. The surrounding park offers the most complete panoramic view of the ría: bridges, islands, mussel farms in parallel lines. Free access, free parking. Perfect at sunset. Allow 1 hour.

The Museo do Mar de Galicia, 3 km from the centre in a former cannery in Alcabre, tells the story of 2,000 years of Galician maritime history—whaling from the 13th to the 19th century (Vigo was a major whaling port), the evolution of sardine canneries, Galician immigration to the Americas (over a million departures between 1850 and 1960). Basement aquarium with species from the ría. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes, €3. Perfect for rainy days.

activities.text: Vigo's key attraction is the Illas Cíes—an archipelago of three islands 14 km offshore, designated national park since 2002. Rodas beach (1.5 km of white sand, turquoise water) voted the world's most beautiful beach by the Guardian in 2007. Access only by boat (Mar de Ons, departure from Estación Marítima de Vigo, €19 return, 45 minutes). Quota of 1,800 visitors per day in summer—authorisation mandatory, request 5-7 days ahead at autorizacionsillasatlanticas.xunta.gal. Marked trails on the island, western lighthouse with Atlantic views. Full day.

If Cíes is fully booked or it is out of season, a food tour of Berbés (the old port, under the metal bridge) remains the best evening in Vigo. Tabernas Otilio (rúa Carral) for zorza (paprika-marinated pork) at €8, Bar Eligio for oysters at €1.50 each and red ribeiro served in a bowl. Allow €20–25 per person across 4–5 bars. Avoid the tourist chains on rúa Velázquez Moreno. The parallel rúa Real is more authentic.

visits.text: MACVAC occupies the Palau del Batlle, a 15th-century Valencian Gothic palace. Since 1972, it has exhibited over 700 works of contemporary art—including pieces by Miró—donated by the artists themselves.
The Roca Grossa dominates the village. This monumental pink limestone boulder supports several traditional houses and defines Vilafamés' visual identity.
Climb up to the castle perched at the summit. Conquered by James I in 1233, it blends Roman, Muslim, and Christian remains. The circular tower and cistern are its most striking features.
The lanes of Arab origin wind between ochre facades. The El Cuartijo quarter, enclosed by walls, preserves its medieval layout intact.
The Church of the Assumption dates from the late 16th century. Its baroque style is enhanced by frescoes by the Guilló family and a remarkable main altarpiece.
The Abric del Castell shelters UNESCO-listed schematic rock paintings. These panels with religious motifs bear witness to prehistoric Levantine art.

activities.text: The village's arts cafés attract painters and sculptors. Take a seat on a terrace to watch the flow of visitors between galleries and workshops.
Every lane makes a photogenic setting. Pink stone houses, pots of geraniums, and views over the countryside come together like ready-made pictures.
Vilafamés produces wines from Castellón. Several village wineries offer tastings of wines made from Mediterranean grape varieties grown on the surrounding hillsides.
The Fuente de las Picas is a cascading fountain surrounded by century-old olive trees. The spot combines cool air with a panorama over the old town.

places.name: Vilafranca Del Penedes

visits.text: VINSEUM, housed in the medieval palace of the Kings of the Crown of Aragon, is one of the world's oldest active wine museums—inaugurated as the Museum of Wine in 1943, Spain's first. The visit descends from the third floor through six themed spaces down to the tavern, concluding with a tasting included in the ticket. Don't miss: Àngel Escudé's collection of 100,000 wine labels from around the world, part of a total holding of 150,000 references—unique in Europe. Allow 90 minutes.

The Basilica of Santa Maria de Vilafranca, pure 14th-century Catalan Gothic, lacks VINSEUM's appeal but rewards a 20-minute detour. Vaults soar to 30 meters, partially preserved original stained glass. The bell tower climb (€3) reaches a viewpoint overlooking the Penedès sea of vineyards—on clear days you can spot Montserrat 40 km north. Typically empty on weekdays.

Head to Sant Sadurní d'Anoia, world capital of cava 12 km away. Over 60 producers coexist in this town of 12,000, their kilometers of underground galleries sheltering millions of bottles aging on racks. Codorníu, founded in 1551, is Spain's oldest family business, and here Josep Raventós crafted the first Spanish cava in 1872, from macabeu, xarel·lo, and parellada grapes. The buildings designed by Puig i Cadafalch, Gaudí's contemporary, have been a national historic monument since 1976.

Bodegas Torres in Pacs del Penedès is Spain's largest winery and has remained family-owned since 1870—five generations. Guided tour with tasting: €25, electric train to traverse the cellars (really), three wines with commentary at the end. Renowned for reds, but this is also where Sangre de Toro was created in 1954, one of the world's first wine brands. Booking essential.

activities.text: Tour and tasting at Codorníu, 90 minutes, €24. A little electric train takes you into underground cellars 30 meters deep—85% humidity, constant 14°C temperature, perfect for secondary fermentation. The network extends 30 km, equivalent to the distance from Vilafranca to Barcelona. The visit ends with two flutes of cava and the opportunity to buy bottles at producer prices, roughly 30% cheaper than retail.
Dinner at Cal Ton, an award-winning local institution, with a single market dish for €32 and an optional Penedès wine pairing. Booking is recommended.

places.name: Villafranca Del Bierzo

visits.text: Villafranca del Bierzo owes its name to the French pilgrims who settled there in the 11th century at the invitation of King Alfonso VI—“villa francorum” became Villafranca. The Cluniac monks whom the king brought from Occitania founded Santa María de Cluniaco there and introduced vine growing to the valley. The Romanesque church of Santiago, built between the 12th and 13th centuries, has a Puerta del Perdón: pilgrims who were physically unable to go any further obtain the same indulgences here as in Compostela. Pope Callixtus III had granted this extraordinary privilege, acknowledging that the climb toward the Cebreiro pass was the most daunting stretch of the Camino.

The castle of the Marquises of Villafranca, a 16th-century building with massive towers on either side, dominates the town from above. Part is still inhabited—you can't visit inside, but the view from its surroundings over the confluence of the Burbia and Valcarce rivers is magnificent. In 1822, Villafranca briefly became capital of Bierzo province—a status that lasted only a decade.

Calle del Agua is the town's historic spine: an arcaded street lined with Renaissance and Baroque palaces, a 15th-century Mudéjar manor, and several convents. It's now an open-air heraldry museum—the coats of arms carved on the façades tell the story of five centuries of noble families from El Bierzo. The old town has been designated a Property of Cultural Interest.

activities.text: Wine tasting in the Bierzo - the protected designation of origin produces reds made from mencía, a grape variety known for its red-fruit notes and volcanic minerality. The vineyards cling to the slate-covered slopes of the valley. Several producers offer tastings at their estates around Villafranca.

Dinner around Plaza Mayor to try botillo del Bierzo—a local butcher describes it as “smoked pork ribs and backbone, stuffed into the stomach”. Served boiled with vegetables, it's the region's emblematic dish, recognized with protected geographical indication status.

visits.text: Trapped between Alicante and Benidorm, La Vila Joiosa chose to be itself. Those red, orange, and yellow façades overlooking the Amadorio River? Fishermen painted them with leftover boat paint so they could spot their homes from offshore. The 15th-century Gothic church-fortress of the Assumption and the 16th-century ramparts complete a tour of the old quarter in 45 minutes.

activities.text: Valor chocolate: a family factory founded in Villajoyosa in the 19th century, now in its fifth generation. The Valor chocolate museum offers free tours but with very limited spots—online booking essential. Fans of fish auctions can also attend the port's sale, Monday through Friday at 5 PM.

places.name: Villanueva De Los Infantes

visits.text: Quevedo died here in 1645, in a cell at the convent of Santo Domingo. His remains were discovered in 2007 in the crypt of the Iglesia de San Andrés on the Plaza Mayor. To see them, stand on the glass floor panel in the chapel: the light switches on automatically. Historic-Artistic Site since 1974.

The neoclassical Plaza Mayor of Villanueva de los Infantes ranks among the most harmonious in Castilla-La Mancha. The arcaded town hall, the classicist façade of San Andrés (1612), and the houses bearing coats of arms form an intact Golden Age setting. Complutense University has identified this village as the “Lugar de La Mancha” from Don Quixote.
Continue to the Casa del Arco to see its neoclassical portico.

activities.text: Villanueva is the capital of the Campo de Montiel, Don Quixote's comarca. The town has more noble coats of arms per capita than almost any other in Spain. Wander the lanes to spot them.

days_plan.itin_title: Campo de Calatrava and Valle de Alcudia in 5 Days

map_keywords: Villanueva de los Infantes Ciudad Real

visits.text: Begin at the Church of Santiago, in the heart of Villena's historic center, then cross Plaza de Santiago and Plaza Mayor. Observe the church's portal, tower and Gothic structure before continuing through the streets of the old quarter to the town hall. This compact walk at the foot of the Castillo de la Atalaya offers an introduction to Villena's heritage without leaving the center.

The castle proudly dominates this little-known town, which is good news for those who arrive on the spur of the moment. The Castillo de la Atalaya, of 12th-century Almohad origin, retains a four-story keep with ribbed vaults. It was declared a Historic-Artistic Monument in 1931. A guided tour is recommended to understand its full history.

days_plan.itin_title: Costa Blanca & Alicante Hinterland: 12 days

places.name: Viso Del Marques

visits.text: An Italian Renaissance palace in the heart of La Mancha: the Palacio del Marqués de Santa Cruz conceals behind its austere façade 8,000 m² of Mannerist frescoes painted by Italian artists between 1564 and 1588. When Philip II saw it, he hired the same Italians for the Escorial balustrades. National Monument since 1931.

Álvaro de Bazán, first Marquis of Santa Cruz and admiral of the Spanish Navy, had this palace built between the court in Madrid and the ports from which he operated. He fought at Lepanto in 1571. The chapel houses his funerary statues and those of his wife María de Figueroa. The palace also houses the Archivo Histórico de la Marina.
The courtyard frescoes span naval battles, mythological scenes, and city views. Pompeian red dominates. The guided tour, led by a local guide, offers the best way to decode the iconographic program.

activities.text: The palace served as a location for the film El Capitán Alatriste with Viggo Mortensen. After your visit, allow for a return trip from Viso del Marqués to the Ermita-Santuario de las Virtudes to see the Baroque frescoes in its camarín.

days_plan.itin_title: Campo de Calatrava and Valle de Alcudia in 5 Days

map_keywords: Palacio del Marqués de Santa Cruz Viso del Marqués

visits.text: Santa María Cathedral has been undergoing restoration in public view for more than fifteen years. The “Open for Restoration” tour takes visitors along walkways through the scaffolding, up to the top of the tower, and down into the medieval crypt.
The Casco Medieval forms an almond shape on the hill. Narrow lanes, houses with overhanging upper stories, and Gothic palaces. Cuchillería Street is lined with pintxos bars.

The Plaza de la Virgen Blanca opens onto the monument to the Battle of Vitoria. White wrought-iron balconies, café terraces, and a statue of Celedon, who descends from the bell tower during the festivities.
The Anillo Verde encircles the city over 33 kilometers. Six parks linked by bike paths: the Salburua wetlands, the Armentia forests, and botanical gardens. 42 m² of green space per resident.
Want to visit the Artium Museum? A collection of contemporary Basque and Spanish art in a glass and concrete building. Oteiza, Chillida, Tàpies, and Barceló feature in the permanent collection.

activities.text: Rent a bike to explore the Anillo Verde. The full circuit takes 2 hours, with stops at birdwatching observatories and a picnic break in Zabalgana Park.
Try the creative vegetarian pintxos on Cuchillería Street. Wild mushrooms, pimientos de Padrón, artichoke confit, and smoked sheep’s milk cheese. Vitoria’s culinary scene is innovating.

Visit a traditional cider house outside the city; allow for a round-trip drive from Vitoria-Gasteiz. An age-old barrel, tastings straight from the tap, and a typical menu: cod omelet, bone-in rib steak, and cheese with quince jelly.

days_plan.itin_title: Spanish Basque Country Tour: Bilbao and San Sebastián

visits.text: Xàtiva is the town most travellers miss between Valencia and the Costa Blanca. That's a mistake: its double castle—one Iberian, the other Arab-medieval—commands the plain from a 120-meter ridge and can be visited in two hours. The lower town preserves several intact Gothic palaces.

The portrait of Philip V hangs upside down in the municipal museum—symbolic revenge for the city's burning in 1707 ordered by that same king. This small detail of iconographic defiance sums up the city's pride better than any explanatory panel.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Valencia Road Trip: 10 Days of Villages

places.name: Yaiza

visits.text: Timanfaya National Park is Lanzarote's volcanic heart—and one of Europe's most surreal landscapes. Between September 1, 1730 and April 16, 1736, dozens of volcanoes erupted successively for six years, burying 167 km² of the island, destroying 420 houses, and forcing half the population to emigrate. The 5,107-hectare park was created in 1974 to protect this intact lunar landscape. The visit begins with the Route of the Volcanoes: a 14 km bus circuit through craters, lava tunnels, and red ridges, with multilingual commentary. Arrive early—parking fills fast and the last Route of the Volcanoes entry is at 5 pm.

At Islote de Hilario, don't miss the geothermal demonstrations: staff thrust brushwood into a simple hole in the ground—it ignites within seconds. Then a bucket of water poured into a pipe erupts in a geyser of boiling steam, because the earth's crust is only two metres thick here and temperatures exceed 400°C below. At 27 metres depth, near the main crater, the thermometer reads 700°C. Since 2013, NASA astronauts have trained in this park—the basaltic soil geologically resembles Mars.

The El Diablo restaurant, designed by César Manrique above a natural volcanic vent, cooks its meat and fish with geothermal heat - at around 400 °C, on a grill set over a five-metre pit. Its architecture of volcanic stone and glass blends into the landscape so well that it is almost invisible from the road. Note that the restaurant does not take reservations.

activities.text: Dromedary ride at Echadero de Camellos, just outside the park gates. Camels were long essential to Lanzarote's agriculture, and a small museum on-site traces their history. The 20-minute ride takes you up the volcano flanks—an unexpected perspective on the sea of lava.

Detour to Los Hervideros in late afternoon: a stretch of volcanic coastline where Atlantic waves surge into caves and chimneys formed by the 1730-1736 lava flows. The effect is especially spectacular when the sea is rough. Just nearby, El Golfo's green lagoon—an emerald lake nestled in a former crater open to the sea—offers one of the island's strangest landscapes.

End the day in Yaiza, considered Lanzarote's prettiest village. Its flower-filled white houses and manicured streets contrast with the lava fields surrounding it. The Iglesia Nuestra Señora de los Remedios dates to the 17th century. It's also the best sunset viewpoint over the Montañas del Fuego—the red light on black lava is stunning.

days_plan.itin_title: Lanzarote & La Palma: Volcanoes and the Art of César Manrique

map_keywords: Parc national Timanfaya Montañas del Fuego
Iglesia Nuestra Señora de los Remedios Yaiza

visits.text: Castillo de Yeste, planted on Cerro del Águila, dates back to the 11th century under Islamic rule and was reconquered by Castile in 1242, then passed to the Order of Santiago. Its Gothic parade ground today houses a Medieval Interpretation Centre 'Tierra de Frontera' with seven visitable halls: Order of Santiago, watchtowers, Muslim life, armoury. Entry is modest; the audio guide is worth the detour.

Head down to the Iglesia de la Asuncion, the first Gothic-style fortress-church in the entire comarca, dating from the 16th century, featuring a Renaissance facade with Corinthian columns and statues of Saint Peter and Saint Paul. Worth seeing if it's open—hours vary. The village also retains some noble houses and an intact frontier-town atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Castilla-La Mancha: Windmills and Sierra in 11 days

places.name: Zafra

visits.text: Zafra is nicknamed "little Seville" for its white streets, flower-filled patios, and Andalusian atmosphere—but it's stayed far quieter than its big neighbor. Start with the Alcázar de los Duques de Feria, a 15th-century fortress flanked by nine crenellated towers, now converted to a Parador. Hernán Cortés stayed here before sailing off to conquer Mexico. Even if you're not spending the night, step inside to see the arcaded interior courtyard and coffered ceilings—Parador staff are used to curious visitors.

Zafra has two adjoining squares forming the town's heart. Plaza Grande, vast and airy, is lined with porticoes sheltering cafés and terraces. Plaza Chica, more intimate, was the medieval market site—the stone columns bordering it still bear the marks of standard measures carved by merchants to verify weights and lengths. The covered passage connecting the two squares is a charming detail.

The Colegiata de la Candelaria, from the 15th century, is Zafra's main church. Its main altarpiece is impressive and its position on Plaza Grande makes it a natural landmark. Just next door, the Convento de Santa Clara (15th century) shelters remarkable altarpieces and wrought-iron grilles.

Enter Zafra through the Puerta de Jerez, one of Extremadura's finest town gates. From there, wander the historic center's streets, declared a Bien de Interés Cultural—the whitewashed palaces, wrought-iron balconies, and patios glimpsed through half-open doors justify the town's nickname. In the evening, the atmosphere on Plaza Grande's terraces is delightful.

Spend the day in Olivenza, about 75 km from Zafra, a one-hour drive. It is a Portuguese town on Spanish soil. Founded by the Knights Templar in the thirteenth century, it remained Portuguese for five centuries (1297–1801) before Spain annexed it during the brief War of the Oranges. Portugal has never recognized the annexation—Lisbon still officially claims Olivenza. As a result, Portuguese-style black-and-white paving, Manueline architecture, and azulejos stand alongside signs in Spanish. Since 2010, street names have appeared in both languages.

The Iglesia de Santa María Magdalena is Olivenza's masterpiece and the finest example of Manueline architecture outside Portugal—after Lisbon's Jerónimos Monastery. Commissioned by King Manuel I in 1510 and completed in 1560, it has three naves resting on eight twisted granite columns typical of Manueline style. The walls are covered with 18th-century blue-and-white azulejos, and six baroque altarpieces complete the ensemble. In 2012, Spanish internet users voted it “Spain's most beautiful corner”—a delicious paradox for an utterly Portuguese monument.

Olivenza's castle, built by the Templars then reinforced under Portuguese kings, has a keep tower 37 meters high—the tallest on the entire Spanish-Portuguese border. Erected in 1488 on flat terrain, it had to compensate through height what the land didn't provide in natural defense. It's accessed by a ramp (no stairs)—so it's accessible to all. From the top, the panorama sweeps across the plain to the Guadiana and Portugal. The castle also houses the Museo Etnográfico González Santana, one of Extremadura's richest ethnographic museums.

Stop by the Santa Casa de la Misericordia, founded in 1501 by King Manuel I himself. The chapel's interior walls are covered with 18th-century Portuguese azulejos depicting Old and New Testament scenes—a remarkable collection. The town hall on Plaza de la Constitución preserves a Manueline doorway that's the town symbol.

activities.text: From Zafra, operators offer visits to nearby bodegas, particularly around Almendralejo, at the heart of Tierra de Barros, Extremadura's main wine-growing area. Allow for a drive from Zafra to visit the wineries. Almendralejo is the region's “wine capital.” Extremaduran wines, long overlooked, have improved considerably—try reds made from tempranillo and garnacha, and whites made from pardina and cayetana.

If you prefer to stay in town, stroll around Zafra's Plaza Grande, with its arcades and café terraces. The Feria Internacional Ganadera (livestock fair) in September and October is one of the main events in southern Extremadura—if you're there at that time, don't miss it.

Olivenza is a gastronomic border post: you'll eat migas extremeñas alongside bacalhau Portuguese-style, and convent pastries blend traditions from both countries. Lunch in the historic center and taste both cuisines—it's the only place in Spain where that's possible in the same village.

visits.text: In late December 1481, Nasrid warriors scaled Zahara's walls by night and retook control - an act that triggered the final war for Granada. In 1483, Rodrigo Ponce de León recaptured it for the Catholic Monarchs. The Nasrid castle's Torre del Homenaje still overlooks the turquoise reservoir. Steep but short climb: 20 minutes from the village.

Climb up to the church of Santa María de la Mesa to see the village from within - its white roofs crowded above the reservoir water, with the sierra as backdrop. Only takes a few minutes, it's a waypoint between the main street and the castle path.

Climb to the Castillo de Zahara de la Sierra to see how the village fits into the surrounding terrain. The keep and the remains of the fortifications overlook the houses and the Zahara-El Gastor reservoir; the climb gives the panorama context. Wear shoes with good traction and skip the climb if heat or wind makes access difficult.

The stop matters more than the drive at Puerto de las Palomas. This pass connects Zahara de la Sierra to Grazalema along a mountain road, with views of the reservoir and surrounding terrain. Stop only in designated areas and adjust the crossing to the weather conditions.

activities.text: The turquoise of the reservoir appears between white houses at every street corner - it's this contrast that gives Zahara its reputation. A swim in the reservoir lake is possible from the banks accessible on foot from the village. In April-May, the water stays cold but the setting is incomparable.

days_plan.itin_title: White Villages: Arcos, Grazalema, Ronda - 6 Days

visits.text: Walk along the 5 km of sand facing Africa and stop at the Castillo de las Almadrabas, a ruined watchtower that reminds you Zahara lived exclusively from tuna fishing before tourism. The village is small, with no monuments to speak of—its beauty lies in the wide, unspoiled beach, the white houses, and the off-season silence. In high season, the population jumps from 2,000 to 20,000.

The Iglesia de Nuestra Señora del Carmen, built between the 16th and 17th centuries, is Zahara's patroness. Small and unpretentious, it sums up this village's relationship with the sea: understated and direct. The few local craft shops are clustered along Calle Marqués de Montemar opposite—vacuum-packed mojama (salt-cured dried tuna) to take home.

activities.text: A simple fishing village, but tuna is treated like a religion here. The almadraba—a maze of nets fixed to the seabed to trap tuna migrating toward the Mediterranean—has been practiced on these coasts for over 3,000 years, a Phoenician technique kept alive by the Arabs. The season runs from April to June. El Campero in Barbate (20 minutes) is the regional benchmark for gourmet tuna dishes. In Zahara itself, beachfront chiringuitos offer the simpler, equally authentic version.

places.name: Zalamea De La Serena

visits.text: The Dístylo of Zalamea, erected in AD 102 in honour of Trajan, stands on the Plaza de la Constitución. 23.23 m high, two columns, the only preserved example in Europe. The other survivors are in Syria. Free and visible from the street, impossible to miss.

The ochre walls of Cancho Roano emerge from a moat that holds water year-round. This Tartessian palace-sanctuary, occupied from the 6th to the 4th century BC, is the best-preserved on the Iberian Peninsula. The bull-hide-shaped altar, reproduced at the nearby interpretation centre, evokes a cult of Astarte. 6 km north of the village.

The Casa de Pedro Crespo, named after a character in Calderón de la Barca's The Mayor of Zalamea, is a middle-class house in the centre. The link between the play and this village is disputed by historians, but the people of Zalamea hold fast to it. Take a quick look as you pass.

Nebrija stayed here, at the Palacio de Don Juan de Zúñiga, Extremadura's first literary court in the 15th century. It was among this circle that he worked on his Castilian grammar. The Renaissance façade survives; the rest is private. Zalamea was then a cultural hub, surprising given its current size.

activities.text: Reach Cancho Roano by the road to Quintana de la Serena. The on-site interpretation centre presents a model, Phoenician objects (caballito pasarriendas, necklaces), and detailed panels. The large 2,000 m² shelter has protected the site since 1988. Check opening hours before you leave.
If you climb up to the Castillo de Arribalavilla, above the village, the view stretches across all of La Serena. Modest ruins but a superb setting. Free access, steep 15-minute climb.

places.name: Zamora

visits.text: On the road from Salamanca, a recommended stop at Toro—a 30 km detour via the N-122. Toro PDO vineyards and the 12th-century Romanesque-Byzantine Collegiate Church of Santa María la Mayor, with its golden octagonal façade. If time is tight, go straight to Zamora. Otherwise, a quick tasting at Bodegas Liberalia or Estancia Piedra is enough to understand why Toro wines have been gaining prominence for 20 years: tannic tinta de toro, plenty of structure, perfect with Castilian meats.

Zamora is nicknamed “the pearl of the Duero” and “the city of Romanesque art”. With 24 Romanesque churches from the 12th–13th centuries, it has the world's greatest urban concentration of Romanesque architecture. The cathedral, founded by Alfonso VII and consecrated in 1175 after 25 years of construction, is a unique blend of Romanesque, Byzantine, and Herrerian styles. Its lantern tower—the cimborio—is its signature feature: a 16-sided dome covered with stone scales like a Japanese mushroom, inspired by Constantinople's Hagia Sophia via the Crusaders. Don't miss the Bishop's Door, one of Spain's finest Romanesque portals.

The cathedral museum preserves one of the world's most important collections of Flemish tapestries—12 pieces from the 15th and 16th centuries, workshops of Arras, Tournai, and Brussels. The Trojan War series (1480), 4 by 7 meters each, recounts the fate of Hector and Achilles with a thousand figures embroidered in gold thread. Acquired by Zamoran bishops at mind-boggling prices, they survived the Napoleonic Wars and the Civil War. It's the textile equivalent of the Sistine Chapel—and nobody queues here.

Five minutes on foot, the 11th-century castle, restored, today houses a public park—free entry, panoramic view over the Duero and stone bridge. Further on, the Church of San Pedro y San Ildefonso (12th century) guards the tomb of Saint Ildefonsus, Archbishop of Toledo in the 7th century, whose relics were transferred here in the 12th to protect them from the Moors. La Magdalena, on Calle Damas, has an exceptionally ornate Romanesque portal—one of Spain's finest, finely worked with floral motifs and figures.

The stone bridge—Puente de Piedra—is Zamora's symbol. Built in the 12th century on the remains of a Roman bridge, 16 arches, 320 meters long. It was the obligatory Duero crossing for 800 years. From here you get the best view of the old town's silhouette at dusk. Locals do their evening jog here and stop to watch lights come on one by one on the façades. Walk along the banks (Senda del Duero) to the Aceñas de Olivares, ancient 12th-century water mills.

activities.text: If you are here during Holy Week, Zamora holds one of Spain's most impressive celebrations, declared a Festival of International Tourist Interest. Seventeen brotherhoods and 50,000 nazarenos parade in pointed hoods through silent streets lit only by their candles. The Cristo de las Injurias, a 16th-century sculpture, is carried in procession in absolute silence at 11:30 p.m. on Holy Wednesday—even coughing is forbidden.

The Ethnographic Museum of Castile and León, 5 minutes from the center, is one of northern Spain's most surprising museums. Four thematic floors—space, time, forms, body—tracing Castilian rural ways of life before industrialization. Tools, costumes, objects used in transhumance, toys; modern museum displays that are anything but dusty. Allow 1.5 hours. A museum you leave feeling you've learned something, which isn't so common in the provinces.

places.name: Zaragoza

visits.text: The Basilica del Pilar, Spain's largest baroque sanctuary, stretches 130 meters along the Ebro riverbank. Its eleven domes and four towers dominate the Plaza del Pilar. Inside, two cupolas bear frescoes by the young Goya, a native of the region: the Adoration of the Name of God and Regina Martyrum.

Take the elevator to the top of the Pilar tower, 62 meters high: the panorama sweeps across Zaragoza's rooftops, the ribbon of the Ebro, and distant mountain ranges. Below, the Holy Chapel houses the jasper column where the Virgin is said to have appeared to the apostle James in the year 40 AD.

La Seo del Salvador, Zaragoza's oldest cathedral, layers seven centuries of architecture on the site of the ancient Roman forum and later mosque. Its exterior Mudéjar wall, a UNESCO World Heritage site, is a tapestry of brick and glazed ceramics in geometric patterns. Inside, the Gothic polychrome alabaster altarpiece ranks among Europe's finest.

The La Seo Tapestry Museum preserves one of the world's finest collections of Flemish tapestries, woven between the 15th and 17th centuries. Their biblical and mythological scenes remain remarkably well preserved.

The Aljafería Palace, built in the 11th century as the "Palace of Joy" by King Al-Muqtadir, is the northernmost Islamic palace in Europe. Its polylobed arches, the Patio de Santa Isabel with its orange trees, and the Golden Hall form—together with the Alhambra and Córdoba's Mosque—the triad of Hispano-Muslim architecture.

Cross the Puente de Piedra, a 15th-century stone bridge spanning the Ebro. From the far bank, the Basilica del Pilar reflected in the river makes Zaragoza's most iconic picture, especially striking at dusk.

activities.text: Dive into El Tubo, the labyrinth of narrow downtown alleys dedicated to tapas. Each bar has its specialty: borage in béchamel, Aragonese migas, ternasco from Aragon. The ritual: one glass of wine and one tapa at each bar, then move on.
The Fountain of Hispanidad, on Plaza del Pilar, depicts Latin America as an upside-down map. In the evening the square comes alive and the floodlit basilica is mirrored in the fountain's basin.

Every October 12th, the Fiesta del Pilar turns Zaragoza into a week of processions, giant floral offerings to the Virgin, concerts, and fireworks. Off-season, the landscaped banks of the Ebro invite you to stroll among bridges and gardens.

places.name: Baelo Claudia

visits.text: At Baelo Claudia, the Roman city faces the Atlantic, with no modern urban backdrop around it. The forum, theater, and fish-salting facilities reveal different functions; garum connects the remains directly to fishing. Start early, bring water, and check which areas are accessible before your visit.

activities.text: Walk along Playa de Bolonia to extend your visit without feeling compelled to climb its dune. The shifting sand and pine forest reveal an evolving landscape right beside the Roman remains. Follow the marked access routes from the beach and turn back if a route is closed, without cutting through the pine forest.

places.name: Priego De Cordoba

visits.text: The sound of water announces the Fuente del Rey before its sculptures come into view. Its 139 jets surround the pools, with an abundance of faces and decorative details: it is better to study a few figures than try to count everything. Use this brief stop as a break and check for any access restrictions.

The Barrio de la Villa draws Priego de Córdoba into narrow streets lined with white buildings and cobbled passageways. The Balcón del Adarve then opens up views of the surrounding terrain, offering a breathing space at the edge of the neighborhood. Explore on foot after parking outside the neighborhood, and keep residential entrances clear during your stops.
